Sports.title: Sainz proposes intriguing DRS solution for F1 2030
Sports.content:
With F1 close to signing off on the overarching tenets of its 2030 return to V8 power units, some of its leading drivers have fleshed out ideas of how to make those into a compelling product.

F1 is set to move to all-new turbo V8 engines in 2030, with a smaller electric unit of up to 200kW and sustainable fuel. That should make engines simpler, cheaper and lighter, and therefore reduce the reliance on energy from the battery compared to today's oft-criticised formula.

By signing off the V8 move at the next FIA World Motor Sport Council gathering in Shanghai on 12 December, F1 and the FIA are giving themselves time to properly flesh out the chassis and aerodynamic regulations that should work in unison with the V8 power units to produce a better on-track show.

Last weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix has given the series some food for thought about what it really wants from its next rules cycle. At the Las Vegas street circuit, F1 delivered an absorbing spectacle featuring a record 35 lead changes, aided by a combination of the powerful slipstreaming effect and the boost mode from the power unit, which led to so-called yo-yo racing as the lead car often ended up a sitting duck on the straight.

While there was debate on whether that's the kind of show F1 wants to see more of, or whether Vegas was too artificial for its own good, it further highlighted the importance of developing a combination of power unit parameters and aerodynamic overtaking aids that can be fine-tuned on a race-to-race basis to deliver a solid spectacle without making overtaking too trivial either.

It prompted Williams driver and Grand Prix Drivers' Association director Carlos Sainz to come up with an intriguing idea on how to tune a DRS-like overtaking system for 2030, suggesting a straightline boost that aids chasing drivers coming right out of the corners. That would offset the loss of cornering speed from following a car in its dirty air.

"I think for 2030 I have an idea of where I would like it to be," Sainz explained. "I think the delta on speed should come more at the beginning of the straight when you are trying to get the slipstream rather than at the end of the straight when the overtaking and the delta speed is too high. It would also leave more overtaking down to driver skill rather than simply sailing past the car in front.

Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"The power on the overtake mode, push to pass, DRS, whatever you want to call it, should happen exiting the corner, so that you have an extra power boost, let's say, to catch up what you are losing in the corner [due to dirty air] but the boost shouldn't then help you to finish the overtake. I think the boost should help you manage to get back into the very close slipstream and then use the draft and the rest of the braking point to make your own move."

Rather than a straightline boost that kicks in when cars are already approaching terminal velocity, it would also avoid creating a dangerous top speed deficit, which Sainz said is actually discouraging drivers from defending their position.

"The weird overtaking that happened also a bit with DRS is when you get delta top speeds of 30 km/h and you arrive so quick that even when you are in front you are too scared to defend and cut him off, because the delta speed is so high," Sainz added. "So that is my idea of how I would like it to be and go racing with. Similar to a DRS and overtake mode that when you get into a certain distance you get that advantage, because you earn it through speed and through having to suffer the dirty air and manage to get yourself into a certain opportunity to get that advantage."

The current thinking is for the KERS unit of F1's next power units to make 100kW of electric energy available in standard mode, with an additional 100kW of boost mode accessed in a way that has yet to be fully defined and a total harvest of 200kW.

The next generation of engines will no longer require active aerodynamics, but the FIA hasn't ruled out pairing that push-to-pash system with a return of the DRS overtaking device on the rear wing.

While Las Vegas showed how crucial the role of slipstreaming can be with this year's Straight Mode, four-time world champion Max Verstappen is wondering if cars can be made draggy enough so that DRS is no longer necessary.

"You can still come up with a formula where maybe a car is just super draggy in a straight line, so you don't need to rely so much on DRS," Verstappen suggested. "A push-to-pass system for me is fine, but it needs to be a much easier engine. Every time I do a show run, for example in an RB7 or whatever, it's just so nice to drive because the throttle responds, everything is just easy, it drives off nice, the car is not shaking about, it has no lag, stuff like that. It's just a lot nicer to drive than what we have currently.

"I know it needs to be some kind of hybrid element, probably turbocharger, because otherwise you are not even allowed to drive at some tracks anymore because it's too loud. That is fine, as long as it's not overruling the natural driving element, which of course at the moment is happening."

Sports.title: Honda can't find an issue after Fernando Alonso's intriguing "broken engine" radio message
Sports.content:
On his final lap of the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix, Fernando Alonso called it a day. The two-time world champion locked up at the end of the long straight before telling the team over the radio: “Box, box, broken engine.”

In the media pen afterwards, the Spaniard reiterated that something was wrong with the power unit in his Aston Martin: “The engine was down from the beginning of the race, I think. We saw already in qualifying that the engine was down and I think it was down the whole race as well.

“So I was losing a lot of time on the straights, not only to the rest of the field but also to Lance. I think in the last two laps the engine completely gave up.”

In the days that followed, engine supplier Honda examined all the data, but remarkably, chief engineer Shintaro Orihara revealed in Qatar that no problem had been identified.

“After the weekend, we have checked all the data that we have now and also in the maintenance we have checked the engine physically. At this moment, we haven't found any issue on the engine from the data and also from the maintenance check, but again, we will check on Friday to see how the engine works at this track,” Orihara told media including Autosport on Thursday.

The latter is not only to see how the power unit performs at the Lusail International Circuit – a completely different type of track – but also to obtain more feedback from Alonso himself to determine whether this particular unit is still fit for use or whether an engine change is needed.

“Yes, we carefully analysed his comments and we also respected his comments,” Orihara continued. “That's why we checked all the data and why we checked the engine condition. From the data, at this moment, we haven't seen any issue, but as I mentioned, we will check again on Friday to get some feedback from Fernando.”

Shintaro Orihara, Trackside General Manager and Chief Engineer of Honda Racing Corporation Photo by: James Sutton / Formula 1 / Formula Motorsport Ltd via Getty Images

Orihara added that it was difficult for the drivers to feel exactly what was happening in Las Vegas, precisely because the circuit was extremely power-sensitive and energy-poor.

“In Las Vegas, it was difficult to analyse how engine performance affected car speed, because there was a lot of torque effect and also different energy management across the two cars. Our metrics say that the power itself is okay, but we should probably check carefully at this track again.”

Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack underlined the complexity of the situation and explained that the poor feeling Alonso experienced – which led him to believe there was a power unit problem – could also be related to MGU-K deployment and difficulties in that area.

“I think we need to be careful because the MGU-K part is so much higher. And that means that as soon as you have a small variation in MGU-K [deployment], it could be felt like a problem with the internal combustion engine. And you have different MGU-K power in different places. So very often, it's much more difficult for drivers to judge than it used to be in the past, and I think some of it is coming from there.”

Although some of the confusion may indeed stem from uncertainty surrounding MGU-K deployment, Orihara acknowledged that another part of it could simply come from sheer frustration. Both Alonso and Lance Stroll stressed that they were losing two seconds per lap purely due to a lack of power, meaning that, according to Orihara, Alonso's retirement could also be related to that frustration.

“Please ask Fernando. From the data viewpoint, we haven't seen any issue, but probably this year our engine performance is not enough to give satisfaction or confidence to the driver and then probably they feel some, how to say, feeling that the engine performance is not great.”

Stroll once again expressed that frustration during media day in Qatar, stating that under these circumstances the Aston Martin drivers cannot even put up a fight, particularly at a circuit such as Las Vegas.

“We know the areas we're going to work on with the car, and what we have to improve on the chassis side, but going to races like Vegas and missing like two seconds with just the engine, there's really not much we can do. We just need a lot more power, and hopefully we get that next year.”

Stroll is optimistic that Aston Martin will make progress on the chassis side for 2027, but immediately pointed out that such progress will be worth little unless the power unit improves considerably.

“Everyone at Silverstone is pushing flat out to hit our targets. And then, like I said, the engine, it doesn't matter how good of a chassis you have, if you're missing two seconds of power on the long straights. I mean, then it's going to be almost impossible to compete. That's where we are, so we really hope we get a lot more power next year.”

Sports.title: F1 drivers go through quizzical exercise in stewarding debate
Sports.content:
Few matters of day-to-day business in a Formula 1 weekend divide opinion as deeply as stewarding decisions, particularly their consistency. A vocal minority of drivers tend to dominate this debate while others pointedly avoid getting involved.

The FIA leaned into this in its annual summit with the drivers, deploying the online quiz platform Kahoot! to solicit a broad spectrum of opinion. It's understood this took the form of multiple-choice questions about various incidents from throughout the year and the penalties applied to them.

While some readers may decry ‘gamification' in this way as trivialising an important subject, the fresh approach to the meeting attracted some drivers, including Lewis Hamilton, who usually don't attend on the grounds that they feel little of use eventuates from it. Enabling the drivers to play on their phones boosted engagement from a demographic with a notoriously short attention span – especially since many were tired and still jet-lagged from Las Vegas.

It also had a ‘flattening' effect in that everybody could make themselves heard, whereas in a traditional meeting format some drivers would sit quietly and fulminate while the more vocal ones monopolised the floor.

"I didn't go last year but I'm going to go tonight," said Lewis Hamilton ahead of the meeting.

"Ultimately, just because I want to help them, help the racing be better – and the ruling system I'm sure we can improve."

Hamilton attended Qatar meeting, having turned his back on it last year Photo by: Getty Images

Historically, this annual forum has been important in that it shapes the continuously evolving ‘driving standards guidelines' which the FIA usually updates, along with the associated penalty tariffs, over the winter. This is the drivers' opportunity to discuss what has and hasn't worked in the current guidelines.

Although consistency of stewards' decisions is a perennial topic, and one which the FIA hopes to address by appointing a permanent panel of professional stewards, the recent run of triple-headers has put several incidents in the spotlight. The draconian nature of some sanctions have been called into question, along with the process of handing a position back if it has been gained by going off the track.

Hamilton has been involved in two of those recent cases. Firstly in Mexico, where his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc gained the lead by short-cutting Turn 5 while attacking Hamilton on the opening lap, then took the time penalty rather than handing the position back. That penalty, usually 10s, was mitigated down to 5s because the stewards deemed that Hamilton also overcommitted to the corner and ran wide.

In that instance alone there are a lot of questions to unpack. Are the guidelines governing when a driver is entitled to ‘racing room' fit for purpose? Under what circumstances should a driver give the position back? How can the system be improved to prevent drivers minimising the downside of a penalty by consolidating track position before taking it?

The most recent incident came last weekend in Las Vegas, when Leclerc launched an opportunistic move up the inside at Turn 7 and rode partly over the kerb, tapping Hamilton into a spin. For this he was penalised 10s as well as being given a furious dressing-down by team principal Frederic Vasseur.

This affair highlighted what remains a grey area in the driving guidelines despite several refinements since the topic first came up in the 2024 season. While the guidelines attempt to establish a threshold around the relative positions of the cars for when a driver is entitled to ‘racing room', there is a caveat concerning whether the attacking driver is in control of their car or not. Relative position can be objectively measured but the question of control is open to interpretation, and therefore subjective.

When drivers are operating at the limit, this facet takes on a high degree of significance.

Russell was penalised for leaving the track and gaining an advantage on the opening lap of the US GP Photo by: Getty Images

Speaking ahead of the meeting, Alex Albon laid out his thoughts on the recent crop of incidents.

"I'm jet-lagged, I don't really want it to happen tonight," he said.

"It's just a general understanding of what we're racing with. I feel like there's a few incidents that stand out to me: George [Russell] in Austin [for leaving the track and gaining an advantage on the opening lap], Oscar [Piastri] in Mexico against Lindblad.

"I'd even honestly say the Charles incident itself in Mexico, the five seconds – which I think a lot of drivers would say it should be a fundamental position change that's instructed by the FIA. And then for me there's still question marks around… I looked at the Charles and Lewis crash [in Las Vegas]. Maybe I'm the only one in that I thought, I don't think there was anything wrong with what Charles did.

"And I think the rules are still a bit, it's one of those weird ones, where if you release the brake more and then make contact, is that better? A lot of those really grey areas for me, where I'm like, I don't like this. Certain positions, it's so dominating over, the further you can get in front of a car before contact or whatever, determines you're more in control."

The 'anonymised' format naturally discouraged ‘groupthink', so there was broader consensus in some instances than others. Interestingly, the timing of the meeting – on Thursday evening in Qatar – meant it split the usual round of media engagements. Two drivers, Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli, spoke after the gathering, and one was more loquacious than the other.

"It's just a general discussion that we have with the stewards, we don't need to go into detail here about it," said Verstappen.

"They will make their minds up about what we said about certain incidents and then we'll see what we can change maybe for next year potentially.

"I think we all agree that compared to maybe two years ago this is better. I think we can also all say that in some scenarios I think we can still change maybe certain penalties a little bit. I think that's always going to be like that, work in progress and things maybe need to change a little bit, but that's something that we'll keep on discussing with them."

Hardly a melodious endorsement of the new meeting format, but this has to be viewed in the context of stewards' consistency having been a topic of ongoing debate for much of Verstappen's long F1 experience. Equally, many of the tweaks to the driving standards guidelines have been applied as a result of him having been seen to have expertly ‘gamed' the system, such as in the 2024 championship run-in.

On-track incidents between Verstappen and Norris late in 2024, such as here in the US GP, triggered changes in guidelines of when a driver is entitled to 'racing room' Photo by: Getty Images

Antonelli took a somewhat less jaundiced view of the meeting's outcome.

"It was good for, especially the stewards, to see how we see certain scenarios and to give them our point of view," he said.

"And also the good thing is that most of us in the room were all aligned on the episodes we saw – it was good for the stewards to see. And as well to talk about guidelines, which they don't really need to change.

"It's just seeing, understanding our point of view, and understanding that in some scenarios it would just need to be [declared] a racing incident and no penalty. Some scenarios are so borderline that it's so hard to establish who is at fault, and instead of giving a penalty it should just be a racing incident."

It's understood the meeting also involved inviting the drivers to set their phones aside briefly and discuss other contentious topics, including the where and when of handing back a position which has been gained by running off-track. The preference is for drivers to be instructed to hand the position back straight away in these circumstances, rather than sticking it out and potentially using clear air to bolster track position and mitigate – or even negate – the impact of any penalty.

But even this isn't necessarily straightforward. In Mexico, for instance, Verstappen overtook Hamilton as the two Ferraris had their dispute, so Leclerc couldn't yield to his team-mate without handing Verstappen the lead. And in any case, race control had already made it clear ahead of the event that drivers gaining position by short-cutting the track at Turns 1-3 and 4-5 had to move over straight away, which Leclerc did not.

Thus we can anticipate more contentious outcomes next year. And what, then, will the FIA do to enliven the Qatar drivers' summit? Host a game of Spin The Bottle?

Sports.title: How Rosberg beat Hamilton – and his demons – to clinch F1 world title
Sports.content:
“My superpower was preparation.”

This may not make for a fascinating storyline but perfectly encapsulates how Nico Rosberg surpassed Lewis Hamilton on his way the 2016 Formula 1 world title.

You won’t often hear drivers downplay their natural ability, but 10 years on from his triumph with Mercedes, Rosberg was very open about it in the latest Beyond The Grid podcast. He couldn’t match Hamilton’s talent – “Lewis is the GOAT,” he candidly admitted – so he had to dig deep in every other field to come out on top.

“It’s just extracting 110% of my potential,” Rosberg explained. “That’s what it’s about. And that means every single area that there is – and there are many: there’s food, there’s sleep, there’s working with the engineers, there’s car development, there’s media, there’s fitness, there’s body weight.”

So the German’s work with a psychologist was crucial, as what he describes as a “demon” kept creeping in. “In preparation for 2016, two hours of mental training every two days,” he detailed. “It was harder than the physical training.

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

“It’s loads of things: meditation, repetition, visualisation, techniques to remain present when you feel emotions of fear coming, when you’re terrified to mess up and have the world laughing at you because you’re leading the race and you mess up the starts.”

This helped Rosberg not only out on track but also when addressing the media, as he attempted to assuage the immense pressure on his shoulders.

“It’s a whole game you have to play, because the media is so powerful,” he pointed out. “It’s such a key part of sporting performance, because you guys get to us, because we have to stand in front of you every single race weekend, throughout the whole weekend, and we cannot say ‘no comment’. I have to engage. When you [journalists] tell me, ‘Are you the new Rubens Barrichello?’, the always-number-two? Boom! That hurts.

“You guys repeat things, and you start to believe them at some point. So it’s a game you really need to master. So with my psychologist, very important for me in my championship year was also, never, ever, ever use the word ‘championship’, in any media conversation. Because you [as a journalist] would always say, ‘You’re the favourite for the championship, right, Nico?’ – [so] just deviate.”

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes, Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

There were reasons to believe Rosberg was ideally positioned for a more sustained title bid. After claiming the runner-up spot in 2014 and 2015 and also being outscored by Hamilton in 2013, his campaign began in ideal fashion with four consecutive victories – marking seven straight wins from the end of the previous season – despite Toto Wolff swapping the engineers’ and mechanics’ squads around, which had been a shock to the German.

“Every race matters,” Rosberg said of his strong end to the 2015 campaign. “And it was my chance, because of course he was now I-don’t-know-how-many-times world champion – and you just lose an inkling of motivation then. It’s normal, because the races don’t count for anything anymore. And he was up against me, who was as motivated as ever in my life because it was just, ‘I don’t want to lose anymore’ – it sucks.

“And so I won the last three, and it naturally just puts a dent in the confidence. It’s the way it is in sport. And you carry that into the long winter. Now he knows, yes, he’s champion, but I won the last three really driving amazingly.”

Read Also:

Hamilton did fight back after Rosberg’s perfect score of 100 points in the opening four grands prix, clinching six wins in seven races from Monaco to Hockenheim. Going into the Malaysian GP, the Briton was just eight points down on his team-mate, but his engine failed as he led the race by 23 seconds – with Rosberg fourth, more than a minute adrift, after being spun around by Sebastian Vettel at the start.

Rosberg inherited third, meaning Hamilton’s retirement induced a 28-point swing: instead of leading the standings by five points, the reigning champion now was 23 points behind.

This was ideal for Rosberg, but started mentally crumbling under the weight of pressure as the title favourite – though he did win the following race in Suzuka. Meanwhile a terrible start dropped Hamilton to eighth on lap one, and he could only recover to third amid robust defence from runner-up Max Verstappen.

“Japan already, I don’t even know how I still managed to drive so well, because if I think about my qualifying lap, I am terrified,” said Rosberg, who snatched pole position away from his team-mate by 0.013s. “I am like shaking, my hands are shaking in the race car – and I’m still able to put her on pole, which I don’t even know how that’s possible.

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

“Because I’m the big favourite now, my dream is within reach! It’s mine! I just need to bring it home every time, that’s enough. I’m just, like, ‘Don’t mess it up’. It’s scary. Am I ever going to get another opportunity? I don’t know, I’ve got the greatest of all time in the car next to me. You never know.”

The Japanese result meant Rosberg now was 33 points up on Hamilton, so he could afford to finish second in every of the four remaining races – but this did not make him feel any lighter.

“Just terrified, absolutely terrified, because this is my chance,” he said of his mindset going into the title decider. “And all the last races before – it’s not that easy to be second, because you have Max with the Red Bull, [Daniel] Ricciardo, the Ferraris, they’re close. Especially when you’ve got the demon in your head, then it really is not easy to be second.

“Max was all over me all the time. In Mexico, bumping into me in Turn 1, knocking me off the track, lunging me later in the middle of the race. This guy was the highest-risk driver at the time, because he’s the young, crazy Max, you know.

“Brazil, he’s all over me again in the wet, which was treacherous conditions. It was massive survival mode out there to not spin and crash like most others were, and then Max is hammering it round the outside of me, Turn 3, without even seeing that he’s there, so I jump in my car when I suddenly see him. It was not a walk in the park.”

Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes, Nico Rosberg, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Adam Pretty / Getty Images

Rosberg was supposed to be joined by family and friends at the Abu Dhabi finale, but as his anxiety skyrocketed, he explained he initially asked them to stay away as he wanted the weekend to be “business as usual”, though it hardly was.

“Last race weekend, I was just terrified, completely terrified – from the beginning to the end, it’s just so bad,” he said. “And the whole world looking at you – you walk in, you see the eyes, like everybody trying to see, ‘How nervous is he?’. It’s just unbelievable.”

The stress took a toll on the Mercedes driver, who was struggling to sleep any more than two hours a night, despite help from a sleep doctor and meditation techniques.

“Terrible,” he commented. “The heart racing, all night long, adrenaline pumping. And when you do two hours, it’s a spiral, because you think, ‘I’ve got to drive with two hours of sleep’ – so it just gets worse and worse, the demon just goes nuts and you sleep even less.”

And when Rosberg was awake, eating was not any easier. “I couldn’t even eat properly anymore, I was so scared,” he confessed.

“The only thing that would go down is my childhood memory food, which was Frosties. I hadn’t eaten Frosties in 20 years, because it’s not really healthy, it’s not very good. It’s the only thing that my brain would tell me, ‘Yes, this will go down’. I tried pasta, wouldn’t go down – it literally would not go in. So that’s what I was living on, Frosties, which is not really good either, because that’s not a very solid food to let you perform for a whole weekend.”

As a consequence, Rosberg wasn’t exactly in the ideal shape to compete, as his free practice out-laps showed: “Nauseous, in the car, because I’m living on Frosties. Nauseous! Can you believe that?. I’ve never had nausea in a race car in my life. And then the demon tells you, ‘You can’t drive a race car if you’re nauseous’. It went away, fortunately – I don’t know how.

“It’s just my preparation and my natural talent that carried me through the weekend, somehow. Even mentally not being there at all, I was still able to do decent, and really well. This is incredible. To this day, I don’t know how it’s possible.”

Hamilton outpaced Rosberg in all three practice sessions and took pole by 0.303s over his team-mate. The order was unchanged at the start, and the Briton kept the pack bunched up in the hope that his rival might drop out of the podium positions – which was necessary for Hamilton to have a shot at the title.

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Lars Baron / LAT Images via Getty Images

Both drivers pitted very early, on laps seven and eight. Rosberg’s stop, however, was longer than planned as his mechanics avoided an unsafe release, and he emerged right behind Verstappen, who was yet to pit after spinning on lap one. It took 12 laps for him to find a way past the Red Bull.

“Horrible. Horrible,” Rosberg commented. “Understandably, [Hamilton] has to do something, so he tries something and it was working.

“He put me behind Max Verstappen with that strategy. I should never have been behind Max Verstappen, and suddenly I’m behind Max Verstappen – the worst guy to be behind. It was Mad Max at the time, it was a 50/50 chance of a crash, if you ever tried to pass him or whatever.

“Probably the most extreme moment in my whole career is when [race engineer] Tony Ross comes on the radio and says, ‘Nico, your championship is at risk. You need to now pass Max Verstappen in the next two laps.’ What? You don’t pass Max Verstappen, like it’s not something you do.

“I’m forever thankful to Max, because he played it fairly, left the space.

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

“I came out of that and my foot starts shaking so much from fear and adrenaline that I am uncontrollable on the throttle pedal. I’ll never have that in my life again, I’ll never experience that, I’ve never had it before. The whole foot is jumping, because of Max. So now I cannot push the throttle properly anymore. My demon starts off again, ‘Okay, it’s done, you cannot drive anymore because you cannot control the throttle pedal anymore’.

“I get lucky, because the next is a long straight. I push my whole leg down into the cockpit from my buttocks onwards, so that allowed me at least to get the full throttle. And then, for some reason, somehow the foot again found a little bit of control, so then my brain said, ‘Okay, yes, it’s coming, this should be okay’. So I was able to drive again. It’s nuts, it’s completely nuts.

“And all the mental training I did helped zero in that moment. Zero. All my techniques, zero point zero. It was just red mist. But I’m sure the preparation did, because I probably would have been that 1% more out of control if I hadn’t prepared myself the way that I had.”

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes, Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

Rosberg swiftly caught Hamilton, who desperately intensified his backing-up tactics in the final laps – to no avail, with the German leading Vettel and Verstappen under the chequered flag to clinch his maiden world title.

“The first [feeling] is relief,” he said. “Relief that it’s over and it’s done, and you did it. And then it just goes ecstatic, it just goes nuts, the feeling. It’s the most extreme feeling, apart from the birth of your child and getting married, maybe. A little bit comparable, but different. Anyway, it’s the most extreme, ridiculous feeling.”

Five days later, Rosberg announced his retirement from Formula 1.

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images Nico Rosberg, Mercedes Photo by: Peter J Fox / Getty Images

Sports.title: Vowles explains why Williams exceeded F1’s cost cap by £627,000 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Williams has become the second Formula 1 team to over-spend under the cost cap introduced five years ago.

The team has accepted it spent £627,000 more than it was allowed to during 2025, exceeding the cost cap by 0.48%. The FIA announced the team has been fined – but did not declare how much it was fined by – and given a 1.5% reduction in the amount of aerodynamic testing time it is permitted next year.

In comparison, Red Bull exceeded the budget cap by £1.86 million – 1.6% – in 2021. They were fined £6,059,092 and given a 10% reduction in their CFD allocation.

Vowles said Williams breached the gap because it incurred costs he expected would not count towards the cap while restructuring its business.

“The background to it is that the company structure of Williams was largely unchanged from 1977 and wasn’t really fit for purpose in a modern world,” he said. “We went into it with every intention of being open and transparent with the FIA, which is what we held all the way throughout, but believed those costs, because it’s company restructuring, not to be a cost cap expense.

“It was the company restructuring that put us over, and as you saw, put us over by £600,000 in that circumstance. The FIA themselves have noted we haven’t had any financial benefit from it, no sporting benefit as a result of it. And you can see that the penalty is pretty much adjusted to be in line with that as well at the same time.

“But it was our interpretation that those costs are out of cap. The FIA’s interpretation of it is that they are in cap. And obviously, we went with the FIA’s interpretation after much discussion.”

The change which led to the overspend was a one-off adjustment, said Vowles. “You don’t restructure your company every year,” he said. “Ideally, you do it one-off.”

Williams has been in discussions with the FIA about the breach for around a month. “They approached us and let us know that there was a potential overspend,” he said.

“I have to say the FIA have been very good throughout. I think they have a terribly difficult job of adjudicating this, not just us, up and down the grid as a result of it.

“And yes, as I said, we went into it really with every belief that what we were doing was compliant with the cost cap. We put our hands up and go, fine, it’s an overspend. We’ll accept it.”

Vowles has criticised F1’s cost cap in recent months, arguing it makes it difficult for midfield teams to make the investment needed to improve their systems and catch the front runners. He said Williams’s overspend was “nothing to do with what I’ve been talking about.”

“That was very much that I think the sport would benefit from a closing up as a result of things. What you can see, though, is we are right on the knife edge.

“I’m just trying to do basic things like restructure a company, which, up and down the grid, by the way, this structure is pretty much the norm. The difference is I’m trying to do it in a cost cap now as a result of it.

“So, I think it reinforces the message that we’re on the back foot here a little bit, and this is hurting.”

Sports.title: F1’s ‘NASCAR-style’ racing at Las Vegas won’t disappear in 2027, say teams | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The extreme ‘yo-yo racing’ seen in Las Vegas will remain a feature at some tracks despite next year’s rules changes, team principals believe.

Multiple factors combined to produce over 350 exchanges of position during last weekend’s race: the low energy harvesting limit applied at Las Vegas, Overtake Mode, the power of the slipstream and the low track temperatures.

New rules for next year will slightly decrease the power of F1 cars’ electrical systems compared to their internal combustion engines. However team principals suspect tracks like Las Vegas, where drivers have limited opportunities to generate electrical energy, will still see frequent swaps of position.

“Vegas is more complicated than just energy,” said Williams team principal James Vowles. “What was really happening there is the tyres definitely were below their temperature window and we could push absolutely flat-out. In fact, you gained a benefit by being in the tow of someone else, and your surface temperatures just came up a little bit more.

“There’s a second effect, which is these regulations, once you have a build-up of cars, almost like NASCAR, you’ve actually got quite a powerful tow effect once you’re the fourth, sixth, seventh car in that whole sequence. So I wouldn’t focus too much on the energy starvation.

“I think actually there are other factors that came in there together at the same time. I don’t think next year’s regulations – this is now personal opinion, looking at sims – are going to kill what happened if we can recreate those circumstances.”

After the race Lando Norris pointed out drivers often swapped positions because of differences in their power deployment patterns. “Some overtakes weren’t overtakes,” the McLaren driver pointed out.

Vowles said the Las Vegas Grand Prix was “great racing.”

“I know there’s controversy around it. I thought it was absolutely fantastic. I was listening in to what Max [Verstappen] and the team were talking about, and they were thinking ahead to how do we do a chess play in the last lap, same as what Carlos [Sainz] was doing at the same time. That, for me, is extraordinary.

Several drivers pointed out they deliberately slowed down before reaching the detection point for Overtake Mode at times in order to ensure they passed through it after the car ahead of them and gained the subsequent power boost. However Vowles claimed they were “pushing to the absolute limit.”

“It really was qualifying laps and [they were] still able to think about how we’re going to fight each other on the last dying metres of a track,” he said.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said the fact teams will be able to generate more power from their internal combustion engines next year won’t alter the nature of the racing at tracks like Las Vegas.

“Technically, we don’t think the 5% increase in fuel flow will change the nature of what is giving the nice battles in the race,” he said. “So we think you will still have those nice gaming possibilities with energy management.

“But we will hopefully and pretty much surely move a little bit closer to flat-out qualifying or to flat-out racing. Then in 2028, there is another step in the same direction, same thing.

“I don’t think it will remove the increased battles that we have been seeing this year, which most of us enjoy. But it will again move the balance towards flat-out racing.”

Sports.title: “Not worth thinking about” being able to beat Mercedes even with new floor – Norris | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lando Norris says Mercedes are too quick for McLaren to be able to compete with them in this weekend’s Qatar Grand Prix.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli lapped four tenths of a second faster than Norris in second practice. However Antonelli set his quickest time on the medium compound tyres and had to abandon his later lap on the softs.

Norris says McLaren are in good shape compared to the rest of the competition but Mercedes are comfortably ahead of the field.

“It depends how you want to look at it,” he said. “I don’t think we’re too bad relative to most, but to Mercedes, I don’t think we’ve been further off.

“They just seem in a different category compared to us today. Quicker in every single corner by a mile.

“I would say the battle’s for [third] and we seem in relatively decent position. We seem similar in pace to Red Bull and similar-ish to Ferrari. So I would say there’s things we need to improve and things that can certainly be better but I guess you always look to the top. So when you look at ourselves compared to the Mercedes we need to improve a lot everywhere.”

McLaren did not run their latest floor specification in practice due to concerns over potentially damaging it on Losail’s punishing kerbs. But Norris doubts they will be significantly closer to Mercedes when they fit the new floor again tomorrow.

“I don’t know how much that will help around here relative to Vegas and other things but I’ll see tonight and see how much we can gain from that,” he said.

“It’s not going to be the gap that we need. I would say we’re around six or seven tenths – probably seven tenths off the Mercedes a lap. So it’s not even worth thinking about them.

“I think relative to the rest, we seem like in a good place. The fact that we can have the new floor on tomorrow will add a little bit, but a little bit is always better than nothing, so we seem in a relatively decent place.”

Sports.title: Antonelli leads another Mercedes one-two despite red flag interruptions | Formula 1
Sports.content:
For the second practice session in a row, Andrea Kimi Antonelli topped the times despite setting his best lap on the mediums compound tyres.

He and several of his rivals had to abandon their flying laps on soft rubber due to a pair of red flags.

Antonelli exchanged quickest times with team mate George Russell early in the session on the medium tyre compound. He set his quickest time on 1’23.077 on his seventh lap.

The Red Bull drivers were unable to improve their times when they switched to the soft rubber. The McLaren pair did lap quicker but were unable to beat the two Mercedes drivers.

Russell began his first run on the soft rubber strongly, setting the quickest times through the first two seconds. As he approached the final corner he looked set to take the fastest time, but he had to back off as race control threw a red flag.

The session was interrupted to allow marshals to clear away gravel and a piece of debris left when Charles Leclerc had a dramatic spin at turn seven. That forced the Ferrari driver to pit for floor repairs.

Soon after the session restart, Antonelli took to the track on a set of soft tyres. But in a repeat of what happened to his team mate, the red flags flew as he neared the end of his lap.

This time Pierre Gasly was responsible. The Alpine driver dropped his left-hand wheels into the gravel at the exit of turn 14 and lost control, spinning into a gravel trap from which he never emerged.

That put paid to Antonelli’s hopes of improving his lap time, but nor was any other driver able to do better. He therefore ended the session on top, followed by his team mate and the two McLarens.

Max Verstappen, fifth fastest, was unimpressed to be overtaken by Lewis Hamilton as he began one lap. “You saw that under braking?” he asked his team. “My God.” Verstappen had overtaken Hamilton approaching the finishing line moments earlier. The stewards chose not to investigate the incident.

Hamilton ended the session eighth-fastest behind his team mate. However the Ferrari driver suffered a power unit problem shortly before the chequered flag appeared.

The two Racing Bull drivers made it five consecutive pairs of team mates in the top 10, Liam Lawson ahead of Arvid Lindblad.

Despite his spin, Gasly set the 12th fastest time behind Gabriel Bortoleto. Franco Colapinto took 15th after a near-missed with Carlos Sainz Jnr at turn one.

Sports.title: Social Media: Alonso pays tribute to retiring Moto GP champion Marquez | Brief
Sports.content:
Fernando Alonso paid tribute to Moto GP champion Marc Marques, who has announced he will retire from the series at the end of this weekend.

Marquez, 33, won the world championship for this eighth time in his career this year. This weekend’s race in Valencia will be his final appearance.

“One of the things I’ve enjoyed most about watching you race is that I never knew what you were going to do,” said Alonso in a post on social media. “Even when it seemed like the race was already decided, I’d still keep watching to see what you’d do!

“It’s going to be hard to get used to Sundays without that. I’m so lucky to have seen you race, Marc. Thanks for everything, and enjoy this next chapter! Thanks a million!”

Sports.title: Court of Appeal rejects Audi’s call for Tsunoda penalty in Italian Grand Prix | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The International Court of Appeal has rejected Audi’s attempt to have a penalty applied to Yuki Tsunoda in the Italian Grand Prix.

Audi argued the Racing Bulls driver should have received a stop-and-go penalty for causing an aborted start.

The ICA upheld the stewards’ decision not to penalise Tsunoda.

Audi brought the case after Gabriel Bortoleto finished 11th behind Tsunoda in the Italian Grand Prix. The original start of the race was abandoned and an extra formation lap ordered by the race director and the stewards noted Tsunoda had not lined up in his grid box correctly.

However the stewards ruled Tsunoda’s position in his grid box was not the cause of the extra formation lap, meaning he should not receive a penalty. Audi contested the decision and Bortoleto said they had a “straightforward” case against the Racing Bulls driver.

The FIA is yet to issue the full reasoning for the ICA’s decision to uphold the stewards’ original decision.

Tsunoda made the second of his three appearances for Racing Bulls at the Italian Grand Prix. His 10th place finish was the only point he scored during his stint substituting for Liam Lawson.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

This is the second decision by the ICA concerned a grand prix this year. In September the ICA overturned a decision by the stewards of the Monaco Grand Prix and re-applied two penalties to Pierre Gasly, dropping him from third place to seventh.

FIA statement on ICA’s decision

The following hearing of the International Court of Appeal took place on 25 November 2026 in Paris: Hearing A Case ICA-2016-14: Appeal lodged by Audi Revolut F1 Team against Decision No. 69 of the Stewards of the 2026 Italian Grand Prix, dated 6 September 2026, counting towards the 2026 FIA Formula One World Championship. On 6 September 2026, at the end of the formation lap during the race restart following a red flag, the Race Director ordered an additional formation lap. Following the race, the Stewards investigated a potential breach of Article B5.9.4 of the 2026 FIA Formula 1 Sporting Regulations by Mr Yuki Tsunoda (Driver of Car No. 22), which requires any driver who caused an extra formation lap to start from the end of the pit lane. Failure to do so, a Stop-and-Go penalty should be imposed on the Driver. In Decision No. 69, the Stewards decided to take no further action against Mr Yuki Tsunoda. On 9 September 2026, Audi Revolut F1 Team lodged an appeal against that decision, arguing that Mr Yuki Tsunoda had caused the extra formation lap and should therefore have received the prescribed Stop-and-Go penalty.

Decision of the International Court of Appeal The Court, after having heard the parties and examined their submissions, decided to: – declare the appeal admissible; – dismiss the appeal on the merits; – uphold the Decision No. 69 of the Stewards of the 2026 Italian Grand Prix, dated 6 September 2026, counting towards the 2026 FIA Formula One World Championship; – and order the competent Sporting Authority to draw, as appropriate, the consequences of this ruling. The International Court of Appeal was presided over by Mr Laurent Anselmi (Monaco), and included, Mr Mark Kletter (Austria), Mr Philip Moser (United Kingdom) and Mr Laurent Nuss (France). The full decision will be available at a later date.

Sports.title: Spotlight: Some F1 broadcasters choose not to attend Qatar Grand Prix | Brief
Sports.content:
After months of discussion over whether Formula 1’s final two rounds in the Middle East would go ahead, first practice for the Qatar Grand Prix took place today.

But not all of F1’s broadcasters chose to attend. France’s Canal+ does not have correspondents at the Losail International Circuit.

Sky’s German coverage team are also not attending the race. “We have decided not to send an editorial team on-site,” the broadcaster told Sport1. “Commentary will be provided from Unterföhring, and pre-race coverage will begin 60 minutes before the start of the race.”

Sports.title: Antonelli quickest by half a second on medium tyre compound in first practice | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli was emphatically quickest in the opening practice session for the Qatar Grand Prix.

The new world championship set his best lap time of 1’23.217 on the medium tyre compound. No one was able to beat that time, even on the softer rubber.

Teams found the tyre performance dropped off more quickly than expected around the Losail International Circuit. Lewis Hamilton’s race engineer Carlos Santi told him tyre degradation was “much higher than expected on all compounds” at the end of the session.

George Russell made it a one-two for Mercedes, though his best time on the soft rubber was over half a second off his team mate’s best.

Isack Hadjar was next for Red Bull, though both he and team mate Max Verstappen were stunned by the lack of front grip they had as the session progressed.

“Is the front wing still there?” Hadjar asked at the end of the session, while Verstappen at one point said he needed “10 clicks more” on his front wing angle.

The two McLaren drivers split the Red Bull pair. They opted not to use their new-specification floor for the first day of running, which appeared to be a wise move as several drivers ran wide and kicked up sparks on Losail’s punishing kerbs.

Charles Leclerc, seventh fastest, ran wide onto the kerbs at least twice during the session. Hamilton, who came eighth, also went off at one point.

Arvid Lindblad and Pierre Gasly completed the top 10. The latter had one of the more spectacular impacts with the kerbs, sparks flying from his Alpine’s tail.

Only one team ran a junior driver in the session. Jak Crawford took over Fernando Alonso’s Aston Martin, making his sixth appearance in a practice session this year.

The stewards will investigate Red Bull after the session after ruling a member of the team personnel was “in an unsafe position in the pit lane” while attending to Hadjar’s car.

Sports.title: Teofimo Lopez Needs WBA Belt for 400% Ryan Garcia Payday
Sports.content:
Teofimo Lopez has no interest in fighting Jack Catterall right now, and his manager Keith Connolly basically admitted the WBA welterweight belt is only useful for getting more cash out of WBC champion Ryan Garcia. Connolly traded comments with Catterall on X and let it slip that Lopez makes “roughly 400% more” in a unification fight with Garcia on February 6 than if he is without the belt. Teofimo needs that belt because without it, he is negotiating in a position of weakness with Ryan.

That tells you everything you need to know about what is really going on here, and why the WBA strap has not been vacated. Lopez (23-2, 13 KOs) is coming off a razor-thin 12-round majority decision over Rolando ‘Rolly’ Romero in August after getting completely dominated 12-0 by Shakur Stevenson earlier this year in January. He has no business asking Ryan Garcia (26-2, 21 KOs) for a 50-50 purse split even with that WBA strap around his waist, because Garcia brings all the ticket sales and PPV buys to the table. He is the money man in the welterweight division. If Garcia gives Lopez parity just to get the fight signed, he is making a big mistake when Lopez has nowhere else to go for real money.

Catterall (33-2, 14 KOs) called out Lopez’s whole game on X. “Lopez coming off a 12 zip loss and got rewarded with a title shot that belonged to me. The mandatory is due and all this going to court shit to avoid it is absolutely pathetic. If you want to fight Ryan go ahead but it shouldn’t be and won’t be for the @WBABoxing title !!!”

Connolly then posted a reply to Catterall with the money excuse. “Jack you’re a great fighter and a great person but we are looking to do a fight where Teo makes roughly 400% more it’s a unification and legacy wise a bigger fight so to act like we are afraid to fight you is disingenuous. We fought Loma & Shakur”

Eddie Hearn says Catterall is finished waiting around and will not take step-aside money before next week’s purse bid. “I get the other team, they want to do a unification, but guess what? Tough.” Hearn added, “Jack don’t want to do that. Jack’s been messed around for too long.” His message to the WBA made it clear what he wants: “Give the man either the championship or the fight.”

Hearn added that he expects Lopez to vacate the belt rather than risk getting outboxed by Catterall. They have Conah Walker lined up as a possible replacement if he beats Alexis Rocha on December 5. Hearn sees it this way: Lopez either fights his mandatory or walks into the Garcia negotiations empty-handed.

Sports.title: Eddie Hearn Campaigning to Move Joe Cordina vs. Mauricio Lara to Main Card
Sports.content:
Eddie Hearn is campaigning hard to move Joe Cordina vs. Mauricio Lara onto the Netflix main card for Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua on December 11 in Cardiff, upset and confused about why organizers left what he considers a major fight off the broadcast. In reality, a ten-round non-title lightweight bout between two rebuilding fighters belongs right where it’s currently placed on the prelim portion of the card.

On Friday, Hearn told Matchroom Boxing that he was “completely baffled” to see Cordina (19-1, 9 KOs) and Lara (31-3-2, 24 KOs) placed on the YouTube and TikTok prelims before the four-fight heavyweight main broadcast at Principality Stadium. Hearn even congratulated himself for pressuring Sela and Turki Alalshikh to add the bout, predicting “Netflix will have no choice but to elevate Joe Cordina to the main card.”

When looking at the less than stellar opposition Cordina and Lara have been fighting since they were beaten, you can give the organizers of the event credit for getting the placement right. Their fight isn’t big enough to be a value add to what is already a weak main card.

Two Rebuilding Fighters With Nothing on the Line

From a quality standpoint, Hearn should be grateful Cordina made the show at all rather than demanding he be placed on the main card. The 34-year-old Welshman lost his IBF 130-pound belt in May 2024 when Anthony Cacace stopped him in eight rounds in Riyadh, and his two wins since moving up to lightweight came against Jaret Gonzalez Quiroz and Gabriel Flores Jr. We’re not talking about murderers’ row type fighters. Based on those two wins over lower-level opposition, this feels like Cordina is placed right where he belongs.

Netflix Wants Heavyweights for American Viewers

Hearn criticized Sela advisors Dana White and Nick Khan for not being in tune with British boxing, saying fans in Wales will go mad for Cordina over main-card heavyweights like Da’Mazion Vanhouter against Michael Essomba and Moses Jolly against Igor Adiel Macedo.

The Netflix card is built for an American audience tuning in at 8 p.m. ET. With the way the main card has been put together, the organizers are betting that four heavyweight fights will draw more interest than Cordina and Lara trying to rebuild their careers.

Sports.title: Eddie Hearn Stalling Ben Whittaker Mandatory Shot Against Dmitry Bivol
Sports.content:
Eddie Hearn is dressing up another protective detour as major news, claiming a “big domestic fight” for Ben Whittaker is “pretty much signed” for early 2027. Hearn didn’t name the opponent, though it is safe to say it won’t be a rematch with Conor Wallace after Whittaker (13-0-1, 9 KOs) barely survived him in their IBF final eliminator last October in Birmingham.

Whittaker already holds the mandatory spot for the Dmitry Bivol vs. Callum Smith winner. Hearn admitted in a Matchroom interview that “coming off the back of the last fight, I think he needs one more fight.” That tells you Whittaker had major problems against Wallace, came close to losing, and Matchroom knows he would get battered by Bivol or Smith.

Matchroom Branding Over Real Contenders

A genuine domestic test would mean matching the 29-year-old Whittaker against Joshua Buatsi or Willy Hutchinson. Instead, Matchroom is protecting him like a young prospect by looking toward worn-out UK names like Craig Richards, Dan Azeez, or Lyndon Arthur, guys who sell tickets without risking Whittaker’s payday against Bivol.

If Hearn believes one soft outing prepares Whittaker for Bivol, he is kidding himself. Facing a non-pressing domestic opponent actually hurts Whittaker by letting him get away with showboating and lazy movement, building bad habits that Bivol will punish.

The Canelo Waiting Game on Bivol

What we are likely seeing is a stalling strategy to age out the 35-year-old Bivol, who is already dealing with injuries from a long career. After Whittaker wins this domestic bout, Hearn can easily claim he needs another tune-up, stringing things out the same way Canelo Alvarez waited until Gennady Golovkin turned 35 and lost a step.

Putting Whittaker in with Bivol in 2027 would ruin years of careful building. Judging by how Whittaker looked against Wallace, he is not cut out for the top of the 175-pound division, and turning him into a protected ticket-seller like Conor Benn is a bad look for the sport.

Sports.title: Andy Cruz Wins IBF Title as One Judge Backs Artur Subkhankulov
Sports.content:
Andy Cruz beat Artur Subkhankulov by a competitive 12 round split decision to win the vacant IBF lightweight title Friday in Ufa, Russia. The split was difficult to explain. Subkhankulov had one round at best, even with a knockdown in the eighth, and somehow convinced a judge that he’d done enough to win the fight.

What was strange was how often Subkhankulov threw rabbit punches and got away with it without being penalized until late in the fight. It was like clockwork: he hit Cruz in the back of the head whenever they clinched, and there were a lot of those. The clinching was mostly initiated by Cruz, who had no real inside game to speak of. Still, the referee should have taken points off Subkhankulov much earlier for the fouling.

Two judges scored it 116-110 for Cruz, while the third had it 114-112 for Subkhankulov. Even the two cards for Cruz made the fight look closer than it was. The 2020 Olympic gold medalist scored knockdowns in rounds two and eight and spent most of the 12 rounds catching the hometown fighter with jabs and straight right hands as he came forward.

Cruz turned what could have been an easy fight for him into a difficult one by failing to let his hands go consistently against the weaker-punching Subkhankulov. It was as if Cruz lacked an overdrive gear to press with nonstop punches. He’d shown repeatedly that the Russian fighter was vulnerable to his right hand, yet he was selective in throwing it for some reason.

Both Fighters Go Down in the Eighth

Cruz had the better of the fight at a distance from early on, dropping Subkhankulov in the second round. His jab kept the southpaw from getting set, and when Subkhankulov tried to close the distance, Cruz had the timing to catch him with the right hand. Subkhankulov kept pressing with swelling around an eye, but he was taking the cleaner punches on the way in and rarely did enough once he got there.

The eighth was the one round in which Subkhankulov gave Cruz real trouble. Cruz hurt him with a right hand and put him down early in the round. Subkhankulov got up and dropped Cruz late in the same round, forcing him to take a count for the first time as a professional. Subkhankulov also had a point deducted during the fight for repeated punches behind the head.

The knockdown gave Subkhankulov his best opening of the night, but he couldn’t build on it. Cruz recovered and went back to landing straight rights, and Subkhankulov’s pressure lost some of its bite in the closing rounds. With two knockdowns banked and the cleaner work on either side of the eighth, Cruz was clearly in command down the stretch. The 114-112 card for Subkhankulov was completely baffling because he didn’t win the fight based on the action. Even in a couple of rounds, he appeared to win late in the fight, eating jabs and hard right hands.

Cruz Takes the Belt on His Second Try

Cruz (8-1, 4 KOs) had wanted a stoppage after losing a close majority decision to Raymond Muratalla in his first title attempt in January. Muratalla subsequently moved up and vacated the IBF belt, giving Cruz another shot at it against Subkhankulov (12-1, 6 KOs) in the IBA Pro 22 main event at the Wrestling Palace.

The two had met as amateurs in 2019, when Cruz also won a split decision. Seven years later, Subkhankulov gave him a scare in front of his home crowd, then spent the closing rounds trying to get past the same jab and right hand that had troubled him all night. Cruz left Ufa with his first professional world title. The eighth showed what Subkhankulov could do when he got close enough to land, but the rest of the fight showed how rarely Cruz let him do it.

All in all, it was not an impressive performance by Cruz, given how tentative he was against a fighter that wasn’t a devastating puncher. Cruz showed the same flaws in this fight that led to his loss to Raymond Muratalla: he didn’t attack aggressively and focused too much on single right hands. He spent too much time on his defense, and not enough on attacking Subkhankulov.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury Medical Clearance Keeps $100M Anthony Joshua Cash Out on Track
Sports.content:
It’s interesting how quickly Tyson Fury’s medical diagnosis changes when huge cash is involved in a fight. Fury (36-2-1, 25 KOs) has been cleared by the British Boxing Board of Control to face Anthony Joshua (30-4, 27 KOs) on December 11.

All it took for the British Boxing Board of Control was three sentences from board secretary Robert Smith and Fury’s wife, Paris Fury, retracting her comments about Tyson Fury being diagnosed with schizophrenia.

“Fury cleared last night. All up to date medicals cleared. Promoter told this morning,” Smith said to Sky Sports.

Earlier in the week, video on Netflix showed Paris saying that Fury had been told by doctors that he had mild schizophrenia after his victory over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015. Fury even said to the Guardian a week ago that he “went to a leading specialist and was diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar.”

Things changed quickly after BBBofC General Secretary Robert Smith revealed that the board was looking into the comments. On Thursday, Paris said that Fury had never been diagnosed with schizophrenia. Netflix edited footage of the earlier comments from Paris before Friday’s release, and now Robert Smith has confirmed that Fury has passed his pre-fight medicals and is clear to face Joshua on December 11.

Nobody should be surprised that this got ironed out overnight without the fight being canceled after Paris’s revelation about Fury. Losing this fight would have likely led to a stampede of fans wanting their money back from ticket sales.

If the BBBofC pulled Fury’s license, the entire December 11 card would have fallen apart, wiping out the huge rumored $100 million paydays that 38-year-old Fury and 37-year-old Joshua are getting for this.

The undercard lacks any marquee-level fights that could be moved into the main event to save the ticket sales. And there’s zero chance fans would subscribe in large numbers to watch the event without Fury facing Joshua in the main event. The co-feature bout is Deontay Wilder vs. Martin Bakole, a fight widely criticized as lackluster.

Even if Joshua had stayed on the card, it would be impossible to find a big enough name to create interest without someone like Moses Itauma or Daniel Dubois stepping in at the last minute. That would be highly unlikely.

Fury and Joshua are both at a career stage where they’re fighting on fumes with little left of the talent they once had. Neither of them can be thrown into the general population with the younger top heavyweights without being plundered and left in pieces.

They’ve both been in protective situations lately, matched against the weakest possible opponents to ensure they don’t get beaten again before they meet for their cash-out fight. It’s kind of pathetic, but this is what it’s come to for these two aging fighters in their retirement run. Get the money on their way out of the sport.

The board cleared the paperwork, Netflix edited their video, and the gravy train stays on the tracks for December 11.

Sports.title: UK Boxing Pundits Worry Saudi Gravy Train Is Stopping
Sports.content:
All-expenses-paid trips to Riyadh are becoming scarce, and some in the British boxing media worry the Saudi gold rush is running dry.

Ade Oladipo and Gareth A. Davies are remembering when they had it good during the brief two-year span from 2023 to 2025, when UK commentators got used to the red-carpet treatment of traveling to Saudi Arabia for big events.

“It felt like we were out there every week. Like we were in the sky on the way to Riyadh every single week for these big cards that you never thought were going to stop,” Oladipo said on talkSPORT Boxing.

Those big events have largely disappeared, leaving Ade and Gareth wondering if Turki Alalshikh will close up shop for UK fighters after Tyson Fury (36-2-1, 25 KOs) fights Anthony Joshua (30-4, 27 KOs) on December 11. You kind of knew it would end sooner or later, with wealthy, underperforming fighters doing the minimum to win and events that failed to attract PPV buys.

Oladipo harped about it being six or seven months since he was flown out to Riyadh, saying he was not even sent over for Canelo Alvarez’s fight against Christian Mbilli on October 31. That was an expensive event for fans, who had to pay $79.99 in the U.S. and £24.99 in the UK.

Not Built for U.S. Fans

Gareth questioned whether the British media are now “at the close of a particular era” when the Fury vs. Joshua event concludes in Cardiff. For Riyadh Season, that would be them finishing with a bang, but only because they are giving UK fans the fight they wanted, not because it is a matchup that non-Brits want to see.

If this is it for Turki and Riyadh Season, it is not a great deal for Americans, watching two heavyweights 10 years past their prime fight it out for the vacant WBA Super belt.

Riyadh Season Did Not Leave Boxing

Turki has not stopped spending money on the sport entirely. Instead, he is putting money into Zuffa events, which are less costly than massive cards like Canelo Alvarez vs. Terence Crawford and Fury vs. Joshua.

The difference is that Zuffa cards involve less well-known fighters who put on surprisingly more entertaining fights than the well-paid superstars. What those fights have shown is that Zuffa does not have to pay huge money to get good action.

For the last three years, British promoters leaned on Saudi budgets to bail out domestic matchups that could not sell on UK pay-per-view alone. If Saudi money disappears for average British cards in 2027, UK promoters will have to pay fighters based on what they actually bring in for ticket and PPV sales. It is going to be a shock for British promoters to go back to the old ways of putting events together.

Sports.title: Dmitry Bivol Puts Canelo Alvarez Rematch Odds At Five Percent
Sports.content:
Dmitry Bivol doubts that Canelo Alvarez will fight him again, rating it as just a 5% chance. Both Canelo and his trainer, Eddy Reynoso, said last month they want to fight Bivol or Terence Crawford next, following Canelo’s win over Christian Mbilli on October 31. Interestingly, Bivol says his team has never received any offer from Canelo for a rematch.

Bivol (25-1, 12 KOs) is defending his IBF, WBA, and WBO light heavyweight titles next month against Callum Smith (31-2, 22 KOs) in Ekaterinburg, Russia, at the UMMC Arena.

“To be honest, I’m feeling like on 5% it could happen,” Bivol told The Stomping Ground. “Yeah. Just kind of past that.”

Canelo lost a 12-round unanimous decision to Bivol in May 2022 in Las Vegas. Despite the close scorecards, the fight was one-sided. Bivol dominated Canelo with combinations and in-and-out movement.

“Well, look, I would like an immediate rematch with Crawford. Hopefully, Crawford can return to boxing, which I think he already said he might come back, and I would like the rematch with him. And if that is not possible, someday also have a rematch with Bivol,” said Eddy Reynoso to Fight Hub TV Español.

Saudi Funding And U.S. Box Office Reality

The lack of movement on a rematch with Bivol may not be entirely Canelo’s fault. For the fight to happen, the Saudis would need to finance it. Canelo is signed with Turki Alalshikh and Riyadh Season and is being paid well, reportedly in the hundreds of millions, with his per-fight purses being large.

Unless Riyadh is willing to fund rematches with Bivol and Crawford, those fights have little chance of happening because of the purse requirements. Those two would want large purses as well, perhaps as much as Canelo.

The problem is, Bivol isn’t a big name in the U.S., so the PPV buys wouldn’t likely cover the guaranteed purses for him and Canelo. The interest from casual fans isn’t enough to make the rematch worth funding. Moreover, Bivol’s inactivity has hurt the measure of popularity that he’d gotten from his wins over Canelo and Artur Beterbiev.

It makes sense for Riyadh Season to not pursue rematches between Canelo and Bivol or Crawford. If Canelo loses again to one or both, his value to the Saudis declines. Also, what fans may be overlooking is how boring those fights were.

Bivol just boxed Canelo from the outside and rarely stood in front of him to go toe-to-toe, as fans like to see from their fighters. If the Saudis want to see pure action, they can get more return by targeting fighters with more entertaining styles for Canelo.

Bivol admitted that Canelo has a lot of options for other fights to keep him busy in this late stage of his career. Canelo doesn’t need him.

The Saudi spending changes have also been seen affecting Bivol’s trilogy fight with Artur Beterbiev, which still hasn’t taken place after they fought for the second time in 2025, due to Riyadh Season no longer choosing to finance it. With both fighters reportedly getting $10 million each for their first two fights that were funded by the Saudis, fighting for less than that without their involvement doesn’t work. It’s too risky a fight for Bivol and Beterbiev to take without receiving outside financing.

Why Bivol Rejects The Easy Rematch Talk

“Never. Never. Second fight is never easier against anybody. Maybe it even harder,” Bivol said when asked if a rematch with Canelo, now 36, would be easy, believing the adjustments the Mexican star would make would present a problem.

If the Canelo vs. Bivol rematch is going to happen, the Saudi financiers will need to come up with the money to fund it. Ideally, it would be great if Bivol agreed to take a smaller purse just so he could make the rematch happen, but that doesn’t sound realistic. If anything, he’d want a massive purse that doesn’t balance out with the low number of PPV buys the match would likely bring in.

Sports.title: Agit Kabayel Brushes Off Pressure Ahead Of Nelson Hysa Defense
Sports.content:
Agit Kabayel says he feels no pressure going into Saturday night’s title defense of his WBC heavyweight belt against fringe contender Nelson Hysa at the Merkur Spiel-Arena in Düsseldorf, Germany. This is the type of fight where Kabayel can win and receive absolutely no credit. It’s considered a pure 100% mismatch.

Kabayel (27-0, 19 KOs) will be making his first defense of his WBC belt against the 42-year-old Hysa. It’s not the ideal type of fight for Kabayel, but the top contenders were all busy, leaving him with limited options. He’s in the ‘who needs him’ club, where he’s too risky for big-money stars like Anthony Joshua, Tyson Fury, or Oleksandr Usyk to face. That leaves Kabayel stuck, fighting no-names like Hysa, and not getting much press because of that.

Since Hysa (25-0, 23 KOs) is also with Queensberry, it was a no-brainer match-up to be made. It’s an in-house fight, and a large crowd of nearly 50,000 is expected.

“I was the underdog over and over again, and then right now I’m the favorite, and there is no pressure,” Kabayel said at Thursday’s DAZN Boxing press conference via a stage translator. “I am Agit Kabayel. I want to be better in every fight and I want to show that to the people, and there’s no pressure for me.”

Spencer Brown Calls Out The Resume Gap

Hysa made a big deal during the buildup for this fight, boasting about having done well in sparring with Kabayel in the past, and criticizing him about his delay in signing.

“About that I call him rabbit, it was before that he and his team accept the fight,” said Hysa. “He’s not a rabbit. He’s a good guy. He’s a good boxer.”

Hysa had to say something to get fans into the fight, because this match-up had been largely ignored by people for obvious reasons. Hysa is not a household name, has never beaten anyone recognizable, and is not exactly young at 42. In situations like this, there’s desperation to come up with trash talk that gets the attention of fans.

“He can talk so much bullst, you know, this is no problem,” said Kabayel. “I give him, you know, he’s the better trash talker than me, but in the ring you must fight. After that, he say, ‘You are afraid from me.’ So bro, I never scared from one guy in the heavyweight division.”

Well, Hysa looked powerful in his last fight, knocking out previously unbeaten Thomas Narmo (14-1, 14 KOs), but he was facing a guy with a resume filled with second-tier opposition. Hysa beat him, but he was just as unknown as his previous 24 opponents.

“Let’s have a look at the levels of the different fighters that you’ve faced and he’s faced,” Brown told Hysa on the dais. “Let’s not get into it because they’re completely different levels. Anybody they’ve thrown in front of him, he has taken them out. These are world-class one, two, three boys.”

Returning Heavyweight Boxing To Düsseldorf

Saturday’s heavyweight championship event in Düsseldorf, Germany, will be the first one at the venue since Tyson Fury defeated 39-year-old Wladimir Klitschko in 2015. That fight wasn’t the most entertaining to watch, as there was very little action between the two large heavyweights. Kabayel vs. Hysa should provide more sparks while it lasts in their fight live on DAZN.

“The fight 11 years ago when Wladimir Klitschko lost to Tyson Fury, it was bad for Germany, but Tyson Fury kind of inspired me, and now I got the same manager, and this was kind of the starting point,” said Kabayel.

Kabayel will surely take the fight to Hysa immediately, targeting his body, looking to wear him down and score a stoppage to please the large German crowd.

Ghana News.title: Mahama sings Peter Tosh’s ‘African’ in Barbados Parliament
Ghana News.content:
President John Dramani Mahama brought a touch of reggae and Pan-African history to the Parliament of Barbados when he broke into lines from Jamaican reggae icon Peter Tosh’s 1977 song, African, during an address highlighting the ancestral ties between Ghana and the Caribbean nation.

The president used the musical interlude to reinforce his message that geographical boundaries and nationalities could not erase the common heritage of Africans and people of African descent.

Addressing a joint sitting of the Barbadian Parliament on Friday, November 27, 2026, during his state visit, President Mahama drew on Tosh’s celebrated song to make the case for a stronger sense of identity and solidarity among people of African descent.

Quoting from the song, he reminded his audience of its central message: that African identity transcends nationality and geographical origin.

“We are all Africans,” he declared, adding that genuine brotherhood required the courage to continue seeking justice for their ancestors.

The moment provided a cultural highlight to an address that traced the historical connections between Ghana and Barbados to the transatlantic slave trade and the forced displacement of millions of Africans.

President Mahama said the Atlantic Ocean, which had historically separated Africans from their ancestral homes, should now serve as a bridge for renewed relationships, cooperation and shared prosperity.

He pointed to cultural similarities between the two countries, including language, food, music, communal savings traditions and respect for elders, as evidence of their enduring connections.

He cited the similarities between Ghanaian staples such as kenkey and banku and Barbados' cou-cou, as well as the presence of the Akan-derived susu savings tradition in Caribbean society.

The President also paid tribute to Africans who endured enslavement and whose labour contributed to the wealth of Europe and North America.

He argued that the historical injustice remained an unfinished matter, particularly because enslaved Africans received no compensation when slavery was abolished, while slave owners were compensated by imperial governments.

On reparatory justice, he said the pursuit was not intended to promote retribution but to secure historical recognition, accountability, reconciliation and the restoration of human dignity.

He referenced the adoption of a United Nations General Assembly resolution on the trafficking and enslavement of Africans, describing it as an important step in the continuing campaign for reparatory justice.

The President also called for greater practical cooperation between Ghana and Barbados, including stronger trade relations, direct air links, educational exchanges and closer economic integration between Africa and the Caribbean.

He said Ghana was committed to making the African Diaspora's designation as the African Union's Sixth Region operational when the country assumes the AU chairmanship in 2027.

Mr Mahama's address was delivered as Barbados marked 60 years of independence and five years as a republic. He congratulated the country on the milestones and praised its development and governance record.

He was the second Ghanaian President to address the Barbadian Parliament, an occasion he described as a reflection of the longstanding friendship between the two countries.
