MSF says Israeli attack on Gaza clinic a ‘direct hit’ and calls for those responsible to be held accountable.

Share Israeli strike on Doctors Without Borders clinic in Gaza kills two staff on social media

Two staff members of Doctors Without Borders, the humanitarian relief agency known by its French initials MSF, have been killed in an Israeli strike on one of its clinics in Gaza City.

“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” MSF said on X on Friday.

It called the attack a “direct hit” and said the deaths bring the number of its staff killed in Gaza to 17.

The agency’s premises were “clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military”, the group said.

It called for those responsible to be held accountable.

In a statement following the strike, the Israeli military claimed, without providing evidence, that the two workers were members of Hamas.

World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the attack “outrageous and unacceptable”.

“Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked,” he wrote on X.

The Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor condemned the “attack on a clearly marked MSF clinic” and accused Israel of “systematic targeting of humanitarian personnel and facilities”.

A pattern of attacks

Israeli forces have killed more than 1,700 health workers in Gaza, including 15 MSF staff as of January.

In January, MSF said Israel had blocked its supplies and denied entry to all its international staff since the start of the year.

Israeli officials have alleged, without proof, that aid groups are linked to Hamas, while aid organisations say such accusations have helped normalise attacks on humanitarian workers.



Earlier this week, an Israeli strike in Gaza killed Adel al-Helou, who had worked for 35 years for UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees.

Al-Helou was supplying water to residents of the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza. Three other people were wounded in the attack, UNRWA and medics said.

The strike came despite a ceasefire that took effect in October 2025, which Israel has repeatedly violated.

World.title: Parts of US clean up after Thanksgiving storm lashes East Coast
World.content:
Power is being slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers following a round of heavy wind, rain and snow.

Share Parts of US clean up after Thanksgiving storm lashes East Coast on social media

Heavy rain and flooding have begun to ease along the US East Coast as power is being slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers following a round of holiday storms.

The storms disrupted travel and downed trees and power lines, leading to water rescues in multiple states, from New York to Virginia.

In New York City, preparations were under way for the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade on Saturday after an unprecedented postponement because of rain and high winds.

The parade, an annual spectacle usually held on Thanksgiving Day, sees brightly coloured balloons travel through the heart of Manhattan. The festivities also kick off the holiday shopping season for the US.

The same balloons and floats, and most of the original celebrities, are still set to take part, organisers said.

Elsewhere, wet snow fell as far south as the Tennessee Valley and freezing rain moved across northern New England. Cold rain was reported in parts of the Midwest, including the Ohio Valley and the lower Great Lakes.

While conditions are expected to improve across the entire eastern US, the National Weather Service warned that “this huge system will take some time to weaken”.

The low-pressure system that brought the storm to the East Coast, the service added, would continue to slowly exit to the northeast, “bringing lingering showers and isolated freezing precipitation through Saturday”.

Coastal flood warnings were also issued in several states from New Jersey to Virginia.

Power restored, travel disruptions ease

The number of power outages, which peaked on Thursday at more than 900,000, fell to 264,000 by Friday evening as crews worked to restore electricity, according to poweroutage.us.



Pennsylvania had the most, followed by Missouri.

Some flight disruptions also lingered on Friday, with about 1,600 delays and more than 500 cancellations, according to the tracking service FlightAware.

In the southern US, part of Tennessee was under a winter storm warning for up to 2.5cm (one inch) of snow on Friday, after rain turned into light snow on Thanksgiving.

In the Midwest, conditions were calmer than they were the previous day, when as much as 38cm (15 inches) of snow fell in eastern Missouri.

The weather service said heavy snow was still expected in parts of Montana and Wyoming, however.

Along the Pacific coast, waves driven by high tides caused flooding and continued to affect train services. Record tides along the California coast prompted evacuations from Humboldt County in the far north to Ventura County near Los Angeles.

World.title: Bulgarians demand action by French after Marseille match violence
World.content:
NewsFeed Bulgarians demand action by French after Marseille match violence

Bulgarians protested outside the French embassy in Sofia after violence at a Europa League match between Marseille and Levski Sofia fans left six hospitalised on Thursday. French authorities are investigating amid reports of Nazi salutes by Bulgarian fans.

World.title: Hunted beyond borders: Allegations of Tanzanian repression in Kenya
World.content:
The case of a missing activist raises fears for the safety of Tanzanian dissidents.

Share Hunted beyond borders: Allegations of Tanzanian repression in Kenya on social media

Nairobi, Kenya – On October 25, 2026, Tanzanian opposition activist Twaha Salim Mwaipaya was travelling in a taxi to visit friends in Kamulu, in Kenya’s Machakos County, when three vehicles intercepted it.

According to the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR), unidentified individuals forcibly removed him from the taxi and took him away. His whereabouts remain unknown.

Amnesty International reported that the vehicles included a Toyota Land Cruiser Hardtop. The organisation called on Kenyan authorities to establish Mwaipaya’s whereabouts, guarantee his safety and investigate the circumstances of his disappearance.

The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT) subsequently described the incident as an enforced disappearance and called for an independent investigation, including into possible cross-border involvement.

The identities of those responsible have not been established, and it remains unclear who ordered the abduction.

Mwaipaya, a former youth organiser of Tanzania’s opposition party Chadema, had fled to Kenya in 2025, citing threats to his safety.

On November 3, Kenya’s inspector general of police, Douglas Kanja, appeared before the High Court to explain the activist’s whereabouts. He denied that Kenyan police had arrested or detained Mwaipaya.

“We do not have him in our custody,” Kanja told the court, adding that investigations were ongoing. He acknowledged that Mwaipaya’s relatives had reported him missing at a police station in the Ruai area.



Kanja also said he had consulted other security agencies but had received no information confirming that Mwaipaya had been transferred to Tanzania.

The case returned to the High Court on November 23. Judge Alexander Muteti summoned Mohamed Amin, head of the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI), to provide an update on the investigation into Mwaipaya’s disappearance.

The judge said Amin’s appearance was necessary because the inspector general had placed the investigation within the DCI’s mandate. The court declined to summon Deputy Inspector General of Police Eliud Lagat, ruling that his testimony would not add significant value to the proceedings. Amin was ordered to appear on a date to be determined by the court.

Tanzania’s high commissioner to Kenya, Bernard Kibesse, told news outlet The Citizen on October 26 that the embassy was following up on the disappearance but had not received an official report.

Mwaipaya’s disappearance recalls the January 2025 abduction of Tanzanian activist and government critic Maria Sarungi Tsehai in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi. Unidentified men forced her into a vehicle before releasing her several hours later following public pressure and intervention by human rights defenders, according to reports at the time by Amnesty International Kenya and other organisations.

Sarungi believes her abductors intended to take her across the border into Tanzania.

“In 60-90 minutes, they would have reached the border and crossed with me, and I would have disappeared for good like hundreds of Tanzanians who have disappeared in such manner in Tanzania under Samia Suluhu,” she told Al Jazeera.

She said some of the men appeared to be Kenyan, while another appeared Tanzanian based on his Kiswahili. She alleged that a Tanzanian national directed the operation. The identities of her abductors and who organised the operation have not been independently established.

The incidents have renewed concerns about the safety of Tanzanian dissidents in Kenya and allegations of transnational repression.

In May 2026, President Samia Suluhu Hassan made remarks about dealing with antigovernment protesters that drew criticism.

Speaking alongside Kenyan President William Ruto at State House in Dar es Salaam on May 4, Hassan said protesters should be flogged with canes if they crossed into either country, The Standard reported.

The leaders were attending a joint press briefing following the signing of eight bilateral agreements.

“I have told President William Ruto we must stand firm against those who lack discipline. We should not choose between Tanzanians or Kenyans. If they come to me, I flog them with canes; if they come to you, you flog them with canes, so that they behave,” Hassan said, according to The Standard’s May 5 report.



Former Kenyan Chief Justice David Maraga condemned the comments, describing them as abhorrent. No evidence has emerged linking the remarks to either abduction.

History of repression

Political repression in Tanzania predates Hassan’s presidency. Under her predecessor, John Magufuli, human rights organisations documented restrictions on political freedoms, intimidation of opposition figures and attacks on government critics.

In September 2017, opposition leader Tundu Lissu survived an assassination attempt in Dodoma, the capital of Tanzania, during which he was shot 16 times by unidentified men. He received treatment in Nairobi before continuing his recovery in Belgium. The attack remains unresolved.

Hassan initially raised hopes of political reform after taking office in 2021, easing restrictions on political rallies and allowing some politicians who had fled the country to return.

However, human rights organisations subsequently documented renewed restrictions on opposition activity, arbitrary arrests and intimidation of critics. The African Union’s 2025 election observation mission also noted that the political opening following her accession had been short-lived.

Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason. On November 6, 2026, a Tanzanian court acquitted him of treason but convicted him of incitement, sentencing him to four years in prison.

The Reuters news agency reported that the charges arose from remarks prosecutors said urged supporters to disrupt the election. Lissu denied wrongdoing.

The treatment of critics has also affected activists from neighbouring countries.

In May 2025, Kenyan activist Boniface Mwangi and Ugandan human rights defender Agather Atuhaire travelled to Dar-es-Salaam to observe Lissu’s treason proceedings. They were arrested on May 19 and subsequently deported.

Both later described being held incommunicado and subjected to abuse. Amnesty International reported allegations of torture and ill-treatment, including sexual violence, while United Nations human rights experts issued a communication to the Tanzanian government detailing allegations of enforced disappearance, torture and other abuses. These were allegations documented by the organisations and UN experts, not judicial findings.

The aftermath of the 2025 elections

Tanzania’s political crisis intensified following the October 29, 2025 general election, which was marked by restrictions on opposition participation and deadly post-election violence.

The African Union Election Observation Mission concluded that the elections did not comply with AU democratic principles and international standards. It cited restrictions on political competition, shortcomings in the electoral framework and an internet shutdown that disrupted observation.

The disputed vote triggered protests, arrests and a security crackdown. Human Rights Watch reported that police and people in civilian clothing killed hundreds of protesters and bystanders.

A year later, the organisation said authorities had yet to make arrests for human rights violations committed before and during the election.



A presidential Commission of Inquiry reported that 518 people died from unnatural causes during the unrest. Its chairman, retired Chief Justice Mohamed Chande Othman, said the figure might not be conclusive.

The commission also recorded allegations that security officers shot people in their homes and shops. Human Rights Watch criticised the inquiry for failing to meaningfully scrutinise the conduct of security forces.

The figures remain contested. Chadema and other sources have reported higher death tolls, although these estimates have not been independently established.

A CNN investigation published on November 20, 2025, analysed geolocated videos, audio evidence and witness accounts showing police and armed men shooting at protesters, including some who appeared unarmed.

It also documented evidence supporting witness accounts of overflowing morgues and possible mass graves. The Tanzanian government disputed aspects of the reporting.

Kenya’s responsibility

Mwaipaya’s disappearance raises questions about Kenya’s responsibility to protect foreign nationals within its territory, particularly those fleeing political persecution.

Kenya has long provided refuge to activists and opposition figures escaping repression elsewhere in the region. However, the cases of Mwaipaya and Sarungi have raised concerns about whether that protection can be guaranteed when critics of neighbouring governments are allegedly targeted on Kenyan soil.

The Kenyan authorities must establish Mwaipaya’s whereabouts, investigate the circumstances of his disappearance and identify those responsible. Tanzania, meanwhile, must address allegations that its critics are being pursued beyond its borders.

For Tanzanian human rights lawyer Tito Magoti, the disappearances are part of a wider human rights crisis facing the country.

“Tanzanians are not free. Abduction is one side of the coin. There are plenty of other atrocities committed against Tanzanians and they run hand in hand with the abductions. It starts there. You abduct, you torture, you extrajudicially kill, persecute through judicial forums, sexual assault and more, so the state of political freedom is in limbo,” he said.

World.title: Taiwan votes in local elections to choose mayors, other leaders
World.content:
Key mayoral race in Taipei, a stronghold of the opposition Kuomintang, tests the governing Democratic Progressive Party.

Share Taiwan votes in local elections to choose mayors, other leaders on social media

Taiwan is choosing mayors, council members and other local leaders across its 22 cities and counties in an election that has been unusually competitive in some of the island’s biggest cities.

Polls opened at 8am (00:00 GMT) on Saturday and will close at 4pm (08:00 GMT), with results expected early in the evening.

Voters are casting ballots at schools, temples and community centres.

About 11,000 positions are at stake in the “nine-in-one” elections, named for the nine categories of local government posts being contested.

Taipei mayoral race

A key contest is for the mayor of the capital, Taipei, a traditional stronghold of the opposition Kuomintang (KMT).

Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT, who won by a double-digit margin in the last election and is seen as a possible future presidential candidate, faces a strong challenge from Puma Shen of the governing Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).

Shen is an academic-turned-lawmaker and an expert on China’s information warfare. China has denounced him, and Chinese police say he is wanted for “separatism”. He entered the race as the underdog, but has drawn huge crowds at his rallies.

Shen’s victory in the KMT’s heartland could be seen as “quite shameful” in Beijing, said Austin Wang, a political scientist at the University of Nevada.



Chiang told supporters the race was “very close”.

Shen cancelled a final rally over traffic concerns and held an online event instead, which drew more than 500,000 viewers on YouTube. President William Lai Ching-te of the DPP also urged voters at a rally in neighbouring New Taipei City to back the party’s candidates there.

Other notable races are in New Taipei City, Taiwan’s most populous city, and Kaohsiung, in the south. New Taipei City’s incumbent mayor is from the KMT, while Kaohsiung’s mayoral office is held by the DPP.

China’s pressure

The vote will not directly change Taiwan’s China policy, and campaigns have focused on local issues such as transport, childcare and the environment.

Beijing, which claims Taiwan as its own territory, has repeatedly weighed in, and the vote is being closely watched there.

Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense counted some 33 sorties from China’s People’s Liberation Army warplanes between Friday and Saturday flying toward Taiwan, including bombers and fighter jets.

Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council has warned that Beijing is trying to influence the outcome through “cognitive warfare” and “transnational repression”.

China’s Defence Ministry said this week that “reunification” is an unstoppable trend.

In the last local elections four years ago, the KMT won 14 cities and counties, the DPP five and other parties or independents three. The KMT traditionally favours closer ties with Beijing, while the DPP rejects China’s sovereignty claims.

Analysts say local results are an unreliable guide to the outcome of the next presidential election, due in early 2028. Lai is expected to seek a second term.

The KMT could begin debating its presidential ticket soon after the vote. The likely candidates include outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen and parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu.

KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun, who met Chinese President Xi Jinping in April, is also seen as a possible challenger, though she could face pressure to step down if the party does badly.

World.title: Israel kills two MSF staff in targeted strike on Gaza clinic
World.content:
NewsFeed Israel kills two MSF staff in targeted strike on Gaza clinic

An Israeli strike on a clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders (MSF) in Gaza has killed two watchmen, bringing its staff death toll to 17. MSF called it a ‘direct hit’, saying its logos were visible and Israel knew the location. Israel said the two were Hamas fighters.

World.title: Thousands of Puerto Ricans join ‘Day of National Outrage’ protest
World.content:
Anger and frustration erupt over record-high electricity rates, surging cost of living and deteriorating basic services.

Thousands of Puerto Ricans have protested in the capital, San Juan, as anger and frustration erupted over record-high electricity rates, the surging cost of living, deteriorating basic services and other issues.

Retirees, university students, bus drivers and others joined Friday’s protest organised by some 30 groups ranging from unions to religious organisations. The crowds gathered in front of a mall for what organisers dubbed the “Day of National Outrage”.

Hundreds of demonstrators arrived by bus in San Juan from dozens of cities and towns across the island.

Asked what problems Puerto Rico had, 74-year-old Radames Garcia Badillo said: “Where to start? The outrage is absolute.”

He said that power and water services are unreliable and that his neighbourhood goes dark at least once a week for several hours. He also decried a sharp increase in the cost of living.

“We’re buying less because things are extremely expensive,” he said. “For us retirees, it is essential to make every dollar stretch.”

The protest, one of the largest in the US territory since Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez took office in January 2025, grew throughout the day as demonstrators took over one of the island’s main highways, forcing its closure.

Organisers estimated that some 8,000 people took part, according to local media.

Many in the crowd waved or wore the Puerto Rican flag. Some chose the flag from before the island became a US commonwealth in 1952, often a sign of cultural pride and sometimes of resistance.

Soaring electricity bills

“Things have never been good in Puerto Rico, but they keep getting worse,” said Veronica Ishtar, a visual arts student.



This week alone, she said the power in her neighbourhood went out 12 times.

In addition, monthly electricity bills for some residential customers recently rose about 18 percent, with the new rate per kilowatt-hour far surpassing the average for residential customers on the US mainland, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Some protesters blamed Luma Energy, a private company that oversees the transmission and distribution of power on the island.

Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court approved a move to cancel the government’s contract with Luma on Wednesday, but many now worry about what comes next.

Puerto Rico’s Association of Industries said the cancellation could discourage private investment and jeopardise existing projects as crews continue to repair a grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017.

The leaders of several groups that organised the protest pledged to keep pushing for change.

“We must begin to channel the rage,” said Hernaliz Vazquez, executive director of Sierra Club Puerto Rico. “We must begin to organise the indignation felt by people who do not know what to do.”

World.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
World.content:
While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, SÃ¡nchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.

The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.

SÃ¡nchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.

FeijÃ³o sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.

Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, AragÃ³n, and Castilla y LeÃ³n.

FeijÃ³o has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.

"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.

One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by SÃ¡nchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".

World.title: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
World.content:
Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.

Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer MahiroÄlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.

MahiroÄlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.

In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.

Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator KÃ¼rÅad OÄuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.

MahiroÄlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.

"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.

The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip ErdoÄan and his administration.

The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.

ErdoÄan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.

However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.

Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.

ErdoÄan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem ImamoÄlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws, which he and his party have fiercely denied.

Hundreds of ImamoÄlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.

World.title: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash
World.content:
Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.

Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.

Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.

The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.

In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".

It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".

The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.

No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.

Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".

In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.

Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine, according to the United Nations.

World.title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
World.content:
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.

Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.

The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."

He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims

Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.

At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.

"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."

The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.

Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.

Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

World.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

World.title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
World.content:
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.

Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (Â£267,000) in just a few hours.

Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

World.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
World.content:
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.

"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."

The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.

In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.

Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.

There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.

But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.

"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.

"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."

Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.

Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.

In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

World.title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
World.content:
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.

The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.

The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."

The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".

Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

World.title: Super Falcons camp bubbles as Nnadozie, Oshoala, Alozie arrive for Algeria friendlies
World.content:
Eight more players have joined the Super Falcons camp ahead of their international friendly matches against Algeria, bringing the total to 18.

Goalkeeper Chiamaka Nnadozie, forward Asisat Oshoala and defender Michelle Alozie are among the latest arrivals as preparations gather momentum for the two matches scheduled for 30 November and 4 December.

The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) earlier announced a 24-player squad for the double-header, part of the team’s preparations for the third round of the African qualifying series for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games.

The latest arrivals also include Glory Ogbonna, Suliat Abideen, Comfort Erhabor, Nicole Payne and Jennifer Echegini.

According to the camp update, 10 players had arrived before the latest group, including Christiana Uzoma, Glory Edet, Valentina Uroko, Joy Igbokwe, Fatimoh Solaty, Blessing Nkor, Shukurat Oladipo, Regina Otu, Folashade Ijamilusi and Olamide Adugbe.

Four more players are expected to join the camp ahead of the team’s first training session scheduled for Saturday.

The Super Falcons are expected to use the two matches against Algeria to assess their readiness for the Olympic qualifying campaign, with Nigeria facing Morocco in the third round between 23 February and 6 March 2027.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nigeria booked their place in the third round after defeating Comoros 7-0 on aggregate in October. The tie against Morocco will determine which team advances to the next stage of the qualifying competition.

The first friendly against Algeria will be played at the 5 July 1962 Stadium in Algiers on 30 November, while the second is scheduled for the Hocine Aït Ahmed Stadium in Tizi-Ouzou on 4 December.

Interim head coach Augustine Eguavoen named 24 players for the friendlies, with captain Rasheedat Ajibade missing as she continues her recovery from surgery following an injury sustained during the Olympic qualifiers against Comoros.

The squad includes players drawn from clubs in Nigeria and abroad, with Nnadozie, Oshoala, Alozie and Echegini among the prominent international players expected to strengthen the team ahead of the Algeria tests.

Algeria have also named a 25-player squad for the two encounters. The North Africans are preparing for their own Olympic qualifying campaign and advanced to the third round after defeating the Central African Republic 15-0 on aggregate.

They are scheduled to face Burkina Faso in the next round.

The Super Falcons’ double-header is expected to provide the coaching crew an opportunity to evaluate players, build cohesion and fine-tune the team before the crucial Olympic qualifying tie against Morocco in February.

World.title: Group sensitises PWDs on voting, warns against vote buying
World.content:
TAF Africa has sensitised persons with disabilities (PWDs) in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) on their participation in the forthcoming elections, urging them to resist vote buying and demanding greater political commitment to disability inclusion.

The exercise, held in Abuja, was part of the organisation’s nationwide campaign to educate persons with disabilities about the electoral process, their voting rights and provisions made by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to support their participation.

According to the INEC, 232,658 persons with disabilities (PWDs) were registered voters, representing approximately 0.23 per cent of Nigeria’s 103,428,715 registered voters for the 2027 general elections.

The electoral commission has also listed plans to increase PWD participation in the elections, including adopting disability-inclusive election security protocols, training security personnel on disability rights, improving coordination among election security agencies, and establishing accessible channels for reporting incidents involving voters with disabilities.

The Programme Manager at TAF Africa, Andrew Adaji, said the organisation was rounding off the exercise in the FCT after taking it to several communities across the country.

Mr Adaji said other members of the organisation’s team were also conducting sensitisation exercises in Karu and Gwagwalada.

“We are moving around several communities in the FCT. We have been to Kuje and Nyanya. We are currently here in Karu Mararaba,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the organisation had identified communities of persons with disabilities and was educating them on what to expect during the forthcoming elections.

According to him, participation by persons with disabilities increased during previous elections, particularly off-cycle elections, following sensitisation efforts and measures introduced by INEC.

He cited the provision of assistive devices, including Braille ballot papers, ballot guides, and magnifying glasses, as measures that have helped improve participation.

Sign language in elections

Mr Adaji said although TAF Africa supported INEC with sign language interpreters during elections in Osun, Ekiti and Anambra states, the organisation would not be able to do so for the 2027 elections because of the wider geographical scope.

He said TAF Africa was discussing with INEC and the Sign Language Interpreters Association of Nigeria to encourage the commission to engage sign language interpreters as ad hoc staff at polling units where voters with hearing impairments are present.

“Where they have three ad hoc staff, one of them can be a sign language interpreter so that when they communicate, that person can interpret,” he said.

Mr Adaji said the provision of interpreters had increased participation among voters with hearing impairments in the three states, although each state had only 25 interpreters.

He expressed hope that the proposed arrangement with INEC would make more interpreters available during the forthcoming elections.

PWDs urge politicians to prioritise inclusion

Also speaking at the sensitisation event, Secretary to the Emir of Persons with Disabilities in the FCT, Muhammad Danjani, described the sensitisation exercise as timely, saying it would help educate persons with disabilities about electoral processes and government programmes designed for them.

Mr Danjani said the exercise was particularly important to communities with polling units, as it would help residents understand their rights and make informed decisions during elections.

He warned that politicians often exploit the economic hardship facing vulnerable communities to induce voters with money during election periods.

He urged persons with disabilities not to sell their votes but to elect candidates who would protect their interests and ensure their inclusion in governance.

“We don’t elect parties; we elect people. Somebody good, that’s where we go,” he said.

Mr Danjani said political parties seeking the support of persons with disabilities should explain what they intended to do for the community if elected into government.

He called for more accessible public infrastructure, including markets, hospitals and banks, noting that while some schools and vocational training centres had ramps, many public facilities remained inaccessible.

“We want that in the market, in the hospital and in the banks. Let us be cared for,” he said.

He added that persons with disabilities needed leaders who would recognise their needs and speak up for those unable to speak for themselves.

“Anytime a physically challenged person is being cared for, that is the time when Nigeria will be great,” he said.

World.title: PANDEF opposes 20% cut from local content fund for new research agency
World.content:
The Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF) has urged members of the National Assembly to reconsider the proposed funding arrangement in a bill seeking to establish the National Council on Research, Science, Technology and Innovation.

Godknows Igali, the national chairman of PANDEF, the apex socio-political organisation in Nigeria’s South-South geopolitical zone, made the call at a press briefing in Abuja on Friday.

The bill, an executive proposal sponsored by Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele, was read on the floor of the Senate on 13 October, passed second reading on 22 October, and scaled third reading on 19 November. It is currently at the second reading stage in the House of Representatives. If the House passes it, it’ll be transmitted to President Bola Tinubu for assent.

The proposed council is intended to provide sustainable funding for research, development and innovation activities in Nigeria, as well as offer strategic direction, policy oversight and general supervision of the sector.

However, Section 19(a) of the bill proposes that 20 per cent of the Nigerian Content Development Fund (NCDF) be deducted as a primary source of funding for the proposed research council.

The Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB), established in 2010, is mandated to promote the development, acquisition and application of indigenous capacity in Nigeria’s oil and gas industry. It also supports research, industrialisation and economic diversification.

Mr Igali, however, opposed the proposed funding arrangement, arguing that the NCDMB extends support beyond the oil and gas industry to other sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing and transportation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the board’s interventions had contributed significantly to job creation and industrial development, particularly in communities across the Niger Delta grappling with the environmental consequences of oil and gas exploration.

Mr Igali warned that diverting 20 per cent of the fund to the proposed research council could undermine the board’s existing commitments and weaken its capacity to sustain ongoing investments.

“Consequently, diverting 20 per cent of the Fund to another institution at this stage would undermine its existing commitments, weaken its capacity to sustain ongoing investments and potentially slow down the momentum of local content development,” he said.

He maintained that reducing the fund’s resources by 20 per cent would constrain the board’s ability to expand its programmes and fulfil its development responsibilities.

“Reducing the Fund’s resources by 20% would inevitably constrain the Board’s ability to deepen these interventions, expand its programmes and fulfil its development responsibilities. PANDEF therefore considers any attempt to weaken this important institution a matter of serious regional and national concern,” he said.

Mr Igali urged the National Assembly to review the funding provisions before passing it and transmitting it to President Tinubu for assent.

The PANDEF chairman maintained that the proposed research council should have a dedicated and sustainable funding framework that would enable it to discharge its responsibilities without undermining the mandates and financial capacities of existing statutory institutions.

He recommended that, if necessary, the proposed funding provision should be referred back to the executive for a more thorough review and the development of an appropriate, sustainable and independent funding mechanism.

NCDMB and its contributions to local content development

The NCDMB was established in April 2010 following the enactment of the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development (NOGICD) Act, 2010, signed by former President Goodluck Jonathan.

The board was established amid concerns about foreign companies’ dominance in Nigeria’s oil and gas industry, particularly in providing technical services, equipment, engineering, fabrication, and other specialised activities. Despite being a major oil-producing country, Nigeria relied heavily on foreign expertise, equipment and service providers, resulting in significant capital flight and limited opportunities for indigenous companies and workers.

The NOGICD Act was therefore designed to increase the participation of Nigerian companies and professionals in the oil and gas industry, promote the use of locally manufactured goods and services, develop indigenous technical capacity and retain a greater proportion of the industry’s expenditure within the country.

Under the Act, the NCDMB monitors and enforces compliance with local content requirements, reviews and approves Nigerian Content Plans submitted by oil companies and contractors, and develops indigenous capacity through training, research, infrastructure a, nd financial interventions.

To support these objectives, Section 104 of the NOGICD Act established the Nigerian Content Development Fund (NCDF), which is financed through a mandatory one per cent deduction from the value of every contract awarded in the upstream sector of the oil and gas industry.

The fund is managed by the NCDMB and is dedicated to financing projects, programmes and activities aimed at increasing Nigerian content in the oil and gas industry.

One of the board’s major financing initiatives is the Nigerian Content Intervention Fund (NCI Fund), launched in 2017 in partnership with the Bank of Industry (BOI), initially with $200 million.

The intervention fund provides affordable financing to indigenous oil and gas companies, manufacturers, contractors, and service providers to help them acquire equipment, finance contracts, expand their businesses, and improve their capacity to compete with foreign companies.

Its financing windows include manufacturing loans, asset acquisition, contract financing, loan refinancing and financing for community-based contractors.

The fund was subsequently expanded to $350 million in 2020 to accommodate additional financing needs, including special intervention windows for women-owned businesses in the oil and gas industry and working capital and capacity-building support for indigenous companies.

World.title: 2027 Polls: Obi, Makinde, Dino join Dunamis Church at all-night prayer
World.content:
The Presidential Candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, and his Allied Peoples Movement (APM) counterpart, Governor Seyi Makinde of Oyo State, attended the all-night service of the Dunamis International Gospel Centre (DIGC) headquarters in Abuja on Friday.

Also attending were African Democratic Congress (ADC) chieftain Dino Melaye and an unnamed aide to Delta State Governor Sheriff Oborevwori.

The service, held in the church’s kingsize Glory Dome, was a celebration of the 30th anniversary of Dunamis, which began on Monday.

Dunamis was founded in November 1996 by Paul Enenche and his wife, Becky, both medical doctors turned pastors.

Although the church held its first service on 10 November 1996, it usually marks the anniversary with a week-long conference in November, called Kingdom Power and Glory World Conference (KPGWC).

This year’s edition, themed “Opened Heaven,” drew delegates from 82 nations, including Nigeria.

During the all-night service, at about 1 a.m. on Saturday, Mr Enenche invited Messrs Obi, Makinde, and Melaye to the altar for a special prayer session for Nigeria and the peaceful conduct of the 2027 general election.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

They were joined by Mr Oborevwori’s aide, who represented the All Progressives Congress (APC), and a member of the church, who belongs to the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

The Delta governor is a member of the APC.

The five representatives were then asked by Mr Enenche to hold their hands together, after which he led the congregation in a four-point prayer session.

The prayer points anchored on Job 42:10 were that:

-God’s perfect will for our nation, Nigeria, be done;

-God prevail upon the electoral umpire (INEC) to do the right thing during the elections;

-All its systems, gadgets, and equipment, namely, including BVAS, IREV, and the internet, work perfectly during the elections; and

-God give Nigeria a clean election, without bloodshed, crisis or struggle afterwards.

Before the prayer session, the church’s South-South coordinator, David Majiyebo, had announced the presence of Messrs Melaye, Makinde, Obi and a former government minister in that order. The announcement was greeted by a thunderous ovation from the congregants.

After the session, which lasted less than 15 minutes, Mr Enenche reminded the politicians that life does not end on earth and that they will stand before God at the end of their lives to give account of what they did with power entrusted to them.

He also said that every genuine church has members of all political persuasions in its congregation.

Thereafter, he asked the five politicians to shake hands and embrace one another to show there is no bitterness. They did not give any speeches.

Mr Enenche rounded off the session by turning to the congregants and asking them if holding the joint prayer session was good for Nigeria. They chorused in the affirmative.

World.title: Gov Lawal pledges more projects as APC campaign storms Shinkafi LGA
World.content:
Zamfara State Governor Dauda Lawal has pledged to deliver more projects in Shinkafi Local Government Area. The governor made the promise on Friday during the APC Zamfara North campaign flag-off rally, held at the Eid ground in Shinkafi.

The rally brought together key party stakeholders, including the Director General of the Tinubu/Shettima Presidential Campaign Council and former governor Abdul’aziz Yari; former governor Mahmuda Aliyu Shinkafi; Zamfara State APC Chairman Kabiru Moyi; and other party leaders.

Tens of thousands of supporters welcomed the entourage at the city gate, chanting slogans in support of the party.

In his speech, Governor Lawal thanked the people of Shinkafi for their solidarity and warm reception.

He noted that the referral hospital project being undertaken by his administration would mark a turning point for healthcare in Zamfara and across the North West.

He said, “I am delighted by the reception we received today in Shinkafi. It is encouraging and shows that the people are pleased with the work we are doing.

“We have achieved a lot in education, healthcare, infrastructure and the economy, among other areas.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“My administration has rehabilitated six primary healthcare centres, including those in Badarawa, Birnin Yero, Galadi, Jangeru and Kurya.

“The referral hospital project in Shinkafi is a legacy project that is very important to my government.

“Over the past three and a half years, my administration has completed 22 of 31 projects. The remaining nine are ongoing and more than 80 per cent complete.

“I am here once again to seek your votes. Vote for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, vote for me, and vote for the APC from top to bottom in the upcoming 2027 general election.”

World.title: Four PREMIUM TIMES journalists emerge finalists for 2026 Wole Soyinka Investigative Reporting Award
World.content:
Four journalists from PREMIUM TIMES have emerged as finalists for the 2026 Wole Soyinka Award for Investigative Reporting, alongside nine others from media organisations across Nigeria.

The four PREMIUM TIMES journalists are Folashade Ogunrinde, Oladeinde Olawoyin, Qosim Suleiman and Ekemini Simon.

The Wole Soyinka Centre for Investigative Journalism (WSCIJ), in a statement signed by its Executive Director, Motunrayo Alaka, on Friday, said the 13 journalists were selected from 238 entries submitted for the 21st edition of the award.

Other finalists are Dayo Oyewo of The Punch, Omolabake Fasogbon of ThisDay, Juliet Buna of Crest 91.1FM, Gift Ufuoma of BBC News, Chukwuemeka Emenike of New Telegraph, Atsahyel Aaron of Trust TV, Olayide Soaga of The Guardian, Francis Esenwa of News Central, and Patience Yerima of Production House.

According to the statement, the finalists were selected by the 2026 WSAIR Judges’ Board, chaired by Dayo Aiyetan, Executive Director of the International Centre for Investigative Reporting.

The statement did not provide details of the stories submitted by the finalists and the categories they were shortlisted for.

Lifetime achievement awards

The 2026 edition will also honour veteran journalists Ray Ekpu and Taiwo Obe with the Lifetime Award for Journalistic Excellence.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The WSCIJ said Mr Ekpu was being recognised for his pioneering contributions to investigative journalism in Nigeria, particularly his role in co-founding Newswatch magazine and his editorial leadership across major media organisations.

Mr Obe will receive the award for his contributions to editorial excellence, professional journalism practice and the development of successive generations of journalists.

Also, Yemi Adamolekun, founder of Enough is Enough (EiE), will receive the Human Rights Defender Award.

The centre said Ms Adamolekun was being recognised for her work in strengthening democratic accountability, promoting active citizenship and civic participation, and championing citizens’ rights and responsibilities in Nigeria.

“The Lifetime Award for Journalistic Excellence recognises individuals whose professional contributions have significantly shaped journalism and its practice over time,” the statement said.

Award ceremony

The finalists and honorary recipients will be honoured at a ceremony on 9 December at the NECA Event Centre, Alausa, Ikeja, Lagos.

The ceremony, scheduled for 6 p.m. to 8 p.m., will be part of the 2026 Amplify In-Depth Media Conference and Awards (AIMCA), which will hold from 8 to 10 December at the same venue. The red carpet begins at 5 p.m.

ALSO READ: PREMIUM TIMES journalists win at 35th DAME Awards

The conference, themed ‘Truth. Power. Rights. Journalism at the Heart of Democracy,’ will bring together journalists, media leaders, policymakers, development partners and other stakeholders to discuss journalism, accountability and democracy.

About the award

Established in 2005, the Wole Soyinka Award for Investigative Reporting recognises outstanding journalism across print, radio, television, photography, online media and editorial cartoons.

Over the years, the award has introduced specialised categories covering areas such as local government, climate change, Report Women and sports.

“In recognition of the connection between investigative journalism, anti-corruption efforts and human rights, the WSAIR presentation ceremony has been held annually on 9 December, International Anti-Corruption Day, on the eve of International Human Rights Day, since 2009. This tradition underscores the important role of investigative journalism in exposing corruption, defending rights and advancing democratic accountability,” the statement added.

World.title: Presidency hails Rarara’s new Tinubu campaign song, says APC has ‘support’ across north
World.content:
The Presidency has applauded a new campaign song by popular Hausa political singer, Dauda Kahutu, popularly known as Rarara, in support of President Bola Tinubu, describing it as another musical endorsement of the president from Northern Nigeria ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Bayo Onanuga, Special Adviser to the President on Information and Strategy, described the song as “another banger from Northern Nigeria for President Tinubu” in a post on his verified X @aonanuga1956 account on Friday.

Mr Onanuga also expressed confidence in the All Progressives Congress (APC)’s growing campaign activities, dismissing earlier suggestions that the ruling party would struggle to mobilise support in Northern Nigeria.

“Remember the pre-electioneering propaganda that said the APC couldn’t campaign up north, erect billboards, or wear APC or Asiwaju symbols. The APC’s intense campaign has put them all to shame, not only in the North but nationwide,” he wrote.

He further predicted that Mr Tinubu will win the January 16, 2027 presidential election by a “very comfortable margin”.

The presidential spokesperson also shared a video posted by an X user, [@Ayofe], showing a female supporter enthusiastically singing along to the new track while driving in her car.

The video offered a glimpse into how campaign music is being circulated and embraced by supporters through social media platforms as political activities gather momentum ahead of the elections.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Rarara’s growing influence in political campaigns

Rarara has become one of the most recognisable voices in Northern Nigeria’s political music scene, particularly through his campaign songs for the APC and its prominent political figures.

The Kano-based musician rose to national prominence through his politically themed Hausa songs, which played significant roles in mobilising support for former President Muhammadu Buhari during the 2015 and 2019 elections.

His musical influence has continued under the Tinubu administration, with several songs dedicated to the president, including the popular Omo Ologo, a Yoruba expression meaning a glorious or fortunate child.

His political music has, however, not been without controversy, particularly when his lyrics target opposition politicians and other public figures.

Mixed reactions trail new song

Onanuga’s post had attracted about 186,000 views and 420 comments as of the time of reporting, with supporters and critics expressing contrasting opinions about Rarara’s latest release and the APC’s campaign.

While Àdùnní TMO (@adunni_tmo) praised the enthusiasm of Northern supporters of Mr Tinubu, saying their passion for the president was unmatched across the country, other users were less impressed.

Jamilu Bin Salih (@jamilubinsalih) argued that Rarara’s songs no longer enjoyed the popularity they once commanded in the North, predicting that the APC would face electoral difficulties in 2027.

Another commenter, Muofunanya Chizoba (@CMuofunanya), used the opportunity to remind Nigerians of campaign promises Mr Tinubu reportedly made to people in the North-east during an APC campaign rally in Jos in November 2022.

The reactions reflect differing perceptions of Rarara’s influence, the APC’s popularity in Northern Nigeria and the performance of the Tinubu administration ahead of the 2027 elections.

Election ahead

The presidential and National Assembly elections are scheduled for 16 January, 2027, according to the revised timetable of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

The APC’s campaign strategy has increasingly incorporated music and entertainment as tools for communicating political messages, building campaign identity and sustaining enthusiasm among supporters.

Rarara’s latest song adds to the growing collection of musical releases supporting Mr Tinubu as the 2027 presidential contest approaches.

World.title: Court reserves judgement in N3.1bn fraud case against Suswam
World.content:
The Federal High Court in Abuja has reserved judgement in the alleged N3.1 billion money laundering case involving former Benue State Governor Gabriel Suswam and a former Commissioner for Finance in the state, Omodachi Okolobia.

The trial judge, Peter Lifu, announced on Friday that the date for judgement would be communicated to the parties after their lawyers adopted their final written addresses.

Mr Suswam and Mr Okolobia, through their respective lawyers, urged the court to acquit them, while the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) asked the judge to find that the prosecution had proved its case against them.

Mr Suswam’s lawyer, Chinelo Ogbozor, told the court that the defence filed its final written address in December 2025. She added that the defence submitted a reply on points of law in April after receiving the commission’s final address.

Adopting the submissions, Ms Ogbozor urged the court to discharge and acquit Mr Suswam on counts one to seven of the 11-count amended charge, which contain allegations against the former governor.

The counts centre on the alleged misappropriation of N3.1 billion, said to have come from the sale of shares owned by the Benue State Government through the Benue Investment and Property Company Limited.

Mr Okolobia’s lawyer, Paul Erokoro, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), also asked the court to acquit his client. He said the defence filed its final written address in January and later submitted a reply on points of law in June, following receipt of the prosecution’s address.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I adopt these two processes as our final address in urging your lordship to discharge and acquit the second defendant of all the counts in the amended charge,” Mr Erokoro told the court.

He argued that the prosecution had failed to prove the allegations against Mr Okolobia in counts eight to 11, which concern the former commissioner alone.

The commission’s lawyer, Rotimi Jacobs, SAN, urged the judge to uphold the prosecution’s case. He adopted the commission’s final written address, filed in March.

Mr Jacobs described the case as “a straightforward case” and outlined the prosecution’s allegations that the defendants diverted funds belonging to Benue State.

The 11-year corruption trial

Mr Suswam is a lawyer and politician who represented Katsina-Ala/Ukum/Logo Federal Constituency of Benue State in the House of Representatives between 1999 and 2007. He was elected governor in 2007 and served two terms until 2015. He later represented Benue North-East Senatorial District in the Senate from 2019 to 2023.

The allegations in the case relate to transactions carried out during his second term as governor. The EFCC accused him and his then Commissioner for Finance, Mr Okolobia, of diverting N3.1 billion from proceeds of the sale of shares owned by the state government.

The shares were held through the Benue Investment and Property Company Limited (BIPC). According to the prosecution, part of the proceeds from their sale through Elixir Securities Limited and Elixir Investment Partners Limited was diverted between August and October 2014.

Abubakar Umar, a bureau de change operator who operated Fanffash Resources Limited, testified that he converted the money into $15.8 million and delivered the dollars to Mr Suswam. His account of where he delivered the money changed during the trial.

The commission also accused Mr Okolobia of conducting transactions totalling N578 million in four tranches between December 2014 and January 2015, in breach of the cash transaction limit under the money laundering law. Both defendants denied the allegations.

The commission first arraigned the duo before the Federal High Court in November 2015. They pleaded not guilty to the charges, which were later amended to 11 counts. The case passed through three judges before it was reassigned to Mr Lifu in 2023. The defendants were re-arraigned before him in March 2024 and again pleaded not guilty.

During the trial, Junaidu Sa’id, an EFCC investigator, testified about the investigation and the alleged transfer of the money. Brigid Shiedu, then managing director of BIPC, gave evidence about the sale of the shares and the governor’s authorisation.

Mr Umar, the fourth prosecution witness, described how he converted the money into dollars. In January 2018, he told the court that his earlier evidence about delivering the money to Mr Suswam’s Maitama residence was wrong. He also alleged that people close to the former governor had pressured him to change his account.

The prosecution called nine witnesses and tendered documentary evidence before closing its case. One of the witnesses, Adewale Agunbiade, a compliance officer with Guaranty Trust Bank, testified about Mr Suswam’s naira and dollar accounts.

He told the court that more than $200,000 entered the dollar account in installments between August 2014 and July 2015, while Mr Suswam personally paid $175,000 in cash.

During cross-examination, however, Mr Agunbiade said the inflows were not unusual and that he had not noticed any breach of banking regulations. Appea Sunday, an EFCC investigator, also testified for the prosecution.

The defendants then asked the court to dismiss the charges without requiring them to present a defence, arguing that the prosecution had failed to establish a case against them. Their lawyers, Ms Ogbozor and Mr Erokoro, said the evidence was insufficient to sustain the charges, but the prosecution opposed the application, insisting that the evidence linked the defendants to the alleged offences.

In July 2025, Mr Lifu dismissed the application and directed the defendants to present their defence. He held that the prosecution had presented enough evidence to require them to respond to the allegations.

Mr Suswam subsequently testified as the sole defence witness, while Mr Okolobia did not testify or call any witness. They concluded their defence in November 2025, after which the judge directed the parties to file and exchange their final written addresses.

Although he gave the prosecution 14 days to file its address and allowed the defendants 14 days to respond after receiving it, the adoption took almost a year.

Series of adjournments over final addresses

The court initially fixed a day in January this year for the adoption of the addresses, but the proceedings were postponed several times. The matter was later moved to May and then to July before another adjournment to September.

At the July proceedings, the judge adjourned the case after the prosecution informed the court that Mr Suswam and his lawyer, Mr Erokoro, were indisposed.

The matter suffered another delay in October when Mr Suswam’s lead lawyer, Joseph Daudu, was absent. The prosecution told the court that Mr Daudu had written to say he would be travelling to Denmark for the International Bar Association’s annual conference.

The prosecution described that request as a deliberate attempt to frustrate the trial but agreed to the adjournment to avoid any question of denying the defence a fair hearing, while the judge subsequently adjourned the case to November.

The lawyers have now adopted their arguments, while Mr Lifu said the date would be communicated to the parties.

World.title: Messi’s defending champions Miami knocked out of MLS Cup playoffs
World.content:
Santiago Rodriguez of Columbus Crew is challenged by Lionel Messi of Inter Miami CF during the 2026 MLS Cup playoff match between Columbus Crew and Inter Miami CF at ScottsMiracle-Gro Field on November 27, 2026 in Columbus, Ohio. Photo: Jason Mowry/Getty Images/AFP.

Columbus Crew, with an injury-time goal from Santiago Rodriguez, beat Lionel Messi’s Inter Miami 1-0 to knock the defending champions out of the first round of the MLS Cup playoffs on Friday.

Rodriguez’s goal in the second minute of stoppage time gave Columbus a 2-0 triumph in the best-of-three first-round series, after their stunning 3-0 victory in game one in Florida.

The defeat was a season-ending disappointment for the star-studded Miami side that features Messi, Luis Suarez, Casemiro and Rodrigo De Paul, which also came up short in the CONCACAF Champions Cup and the Leagues Cup.

For Argentine superstar Messi, MLS’s top scorer in the regular season and the favorite to win an unprecedented third straight Most Valuable Player award, it was a second first-round exit in the three MLS Cup playoffs he has contested.

Miami, facing a must-win game after dropping the opener at home to seventh-seeded Columbus, had chances to score on a cold, rainy night in Ohio.

German Berterame had a golden opportunity six minutes from full time, but his header from point-blank range went over the crossbar.

The match appeared headed for a penalty shootout with injury time ticking away. But Inter’s defense allowed Rodriguez to bring down a cross in the box from Moroccan Anass Zaroury and blast it past Canadian goalkeeper Dayne St. Clair.

Miami’s early exit extends the champion’s curse in MLS. No team has retained the title since the Los Angeles Galaxy in 2012.
