World.title: Giving back is success secret mother taught me — Dangote
World.content:
Dangote’s daughters

*…why I’m teaching my daughters too

Following his delivery of the Keynote address themed “The Geography of Opportunity: Why the World Needs What Africa Has,” recently at the 25th anniversary conference of Women in Management, Business, and Public Service, WIMBIZ; special guest and

President/Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Ltd, Aliko Dangote, GCON sat down to a historic fireside chat with Rolake Akinkugbe Filani.

The chat, anchored by the CEO, EnergyInc Advisors while also fielding questions from an audience of about 2000 women, was according to him, with the largest exclusive assembly of women he has ever addressed. Excerpts:-

When your IPO closed some weeks ago, we heard that you had received a hundred and twenty applications and every single one of the 54 African countries had also applied. In your mind, Africans investing in the continent, is that one example of the geography of opportunity?

Yes. What we have done with this IPO is trying to do something where, when there’s an offer in Kenya Nigerians will participate. When we did the private placement the whole idea was for us to sell 2.5 billion dollars. 1 billion was for private placement, 1.5 billion was for IPO.

When we rolled out the private placement we got 3.7 billion, so we took only 2.5. What we want to do is spread this prosperity.

Did this particular IPO change your view on how you mobilise capital from the African continent ?

It has changed dramatically. Things are really changing very fast. Even abroad, people have a change of mind about Africa.

We’ve gotten amazing demand. We’re talking about millions participating. Saudi Aramco worldwide was about 5million. We didn’t reach 10 million because of time constraints.

A lot of people didn’t know how to access but the sheer trust of public enterprise that we have today in Africa, that’s why people are starting to remove their money from under their mattress to come and invest.

Incredible achievement. You came from a long line of women who were in commerce, your mother, your great aunt and even your step grandmother. We want to hear if there are principles you learned by watching, by trends, by conversations, from the women in your family.

From my mum it’s learning how to give back. she was always talking about giving back and she in the 80s would make sure that everyday we were feeding the poor, about 12000 people, three square meals and then we gave about 35,000 loaves of bread everyday.

But right now, because there are so many in need I don’t want to announce it here, but we are looking at the possibilities of going to most of the vulnerable people to see if we can we do XYZ. We’re targeting feeding about 100m people every year.

My children are ready to give. As a Muslim I am allowed to allocate one third of my wealth to charity and can actually donate to you. You don’t want when something happens to you then there will be arguments, so we actually put it in writing and got all of them to sign that in the event of my debut, one third is for the Foundation. All the good we are doing now will continue.

You had a lot of naysayers when you were building the refinery and every woman here has a smaller version of that whether it be delayed contract, change in FX etc and women are used to being underestimated especially when the voices become loud and progress is invisible. During those times, what was really going through your mind?

I must admit that when we were building the refinery we didn’t know what we were doing. If we knew we wouldn’t have gone near there at all. I always say that my greatest enemy, if I want to pray bad for him, I will pray that he will go and start building a refinery.

Right now, that is history because we not only have one in Nigeria we have one in Namibia and possibly an additional one because we have a vision and that vision is x billion per annum but the x billion per annum which was 50 billion now has moved to 60 billion.

First of all you must be trustworthy because money follows trust before profit. That your name that you have, protect it as much as you can. There will still be some few people who will try some stuff but then just be very careful, don’t let anybody frighten you. Let me give you a simple example, we have never ever gone abroad to try and raise funds but in June we went out to the market to say, we don’t have a rating and we are not going to do any guarantees.

We went to what we call No Deal Road Show and at the end of it there was demand of 1.3 billion. We took 750 million. They came back to us, JP Morgan, bank of America, Merrill Lynch. We are making good money now, we went and raised another 750 in July.

In August we thought, why don’t we do something that has not been done for a very long time in sub Saharan Africa, which is for a company to raise 10 years’ money. The 5 years’ money we raised, we had no rating, no collateral but you won’t believe we raised money. Our interest rate was below Federal Government rate. 10 years’ money, the demand was almost 1.5 billion but we took 750m. The sky is the limit. A lot of you should try. Don’t be scared.

You say don’t be scared but it’s interesting that in order to succeed in business you have to be a bit delusional. For the women here looking for business opportunities whether local or international, how do you determine which opportunity to hold on to and which to hold back on?

Whether you are a man or woman, don’t go into a business you don’t understand.

You must understand that business both in and out and don’t let your own management come and be telling you. Today if you tell me, go into banking, I am not going to go into banking.

You take a lot of money from the bank …

It’s easy when I am borrowing the money, I have to read every single dot to make sure I do the right thing. There are some things, maybe if you look at numbers, maybe building a port, you can never ever go wrong. Port will make money. The capacity of demand is there. In 24 years by the Grace of God , we are going to be at 150 million and most of us don’t know, the population growth of Nigeria is 8.7 million babies every year.

We must use every available land, we haven’t even used 10% of our arable land. People should please stop taking their money abroad no matter what. Why you see that Asia has done very well is because majority keep their money in their country at home and that money is useful to their economy. That’s why we want to bring something new. We want to start having our AGM in a stadium, not in a hall. It has to be a stadium because we have millions of shareholders. We don’t have the Asian culture of savings

One in 5 people today is African. By 2050 it will be 1 in 4. Yet Africa contributes less than 3 cents of every dollar global output. When you see those stats is it a warning about what we need to do?

Unfortunately we don’t plan. We need to plan ahead. Now, Let’s look at the price of food, does Europe have the land to grow their food? They don’t.

Everyone in the next 24 years will turn to Africa because we have 60 percent of the world’s arable land, more than 37 percent of the minerals resources, critical minerals. The difficulty and the difference is that these people have seen us keeping our money abroad, we’re not investing here so they believe there’s a danger they don’t know. We Africans must derisk the real and also perceived risk. That is the only way other people would come and invest here.

The median age in Africa is 19, in Europe it’s 40.

Today if we don’t change, these GenZ s, if they get tired of us they will come and drive us away and they believe we have wasted so much time and we are not doing the right things. We have what it takes to turn around our fortunes.

I can’t understand how someone that has a British passport can travel more freely in Africa than Africans. We are sort of scared of our own acceleration. Today we have 240 million Nigerians, but the president of Sao Tome when he gets to UN, has the same vote as president Tinubu. Life is not about fairness. You have to make sure that you grab your own. We must give that leadership whether people like us or they don’t. When things are good, people will come.

What about the female entrepreneur just starting out and doesn’t have the balance sheet to be her own one woman system. Is that sort of model even sustainable for Africa?

Of course it’s sustainable. You are just looking at what has happened in the last 20 years. You should also go back to ask where I started from. I started with just buying 4 trucks and I was very happy, in fact that was the only business I did at that time because even the 500 thousand my grandfather gave me as a loan, payable when able, I returned it after 3 months. We used to call him Baba. I said, Baba, I don’t need this money. He said, why? I said I have enough.

At that time people would come and deposit their money for cement. People used to queue up for 6 months to collect cement. We used to have queue for petrol since 1972. The budget of Nigeria in 1975, you know how much it was? N30bn naira, 46 billion dollars back then.

Make sure you focus on addressing exports or manufacturing. I am not saying that you shouldn’t trade but trade does not have the future and benefits. All these problems that you see today will be sorted. The future is brighter than where we are now.

World.title: What Pete Edochie wanted to be remembered for
World.content:
Pete Edochie

By Benjamin Njoku

When Vanguard encountered Pete Edochie, the Lion of Africa in his den on two different occasions, it was never just an interview.It was an audience with a king.

Ebubedike sat on his throne, spoke in proverbs, laughed loudly, sipped from a glass of fresh palm wine and dropped revelations that have now become timeless.

Those conversations carried the full weight of Pete Edochie and what he represented on the big screen and in real life.

The first encounter was in a hotel room in Owerri, in 2015, where he displayed rare qualities that set him apart from his contemporaries: his sense of humour, his values as a father and an actor, as well as his impeccable command of the English language.

The second encounter was at his Trans Ekulu, Enugu residence in 2022. During the encounter, Ebubedike was in his element. His imposing duplex dotted with images of his artistic journey, laurels and his image as the godfather of the Nigerian movie industry set the tone for the timeless conversation.

When you were eventually ushered into his living room, you were bound to appreciate why Chinua Achebe preferred to call him ‘Ebubedike’ after the iconic role he played as Okonkwo in the NTA adaptation of the classic novel, ‘Things Fall Apart.’

The Lion of Africa roared as he sat on his throne, “You are welcome to my home, feel comfortable.”

Indeed, Pete Edochie was inseparable from his movie characters. In real life, he was a man of honour and class. When you were with him, you would not be tired of laughing. Intermittently, he would smile to encourage his guests while sharing his story passionately with them.

As we recount those encounters spanning our august visit to him in Enugu in 2022, his repeated battles with rumours of his death, his reflections on Nollywood, family and mortality, now read like a final testament after his death on Wednesday, due to prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

His love for

classical music

Beyond acting, Pete Edochie was an ardent lover of classical music and once presented a programme called ‘Music from the Masters’ while working as a broadcaster with Eastern Nigeria Broadcasting Corporation, ENBC and the Anambra State Broadcasting Service.

Recalling how he developed the passion for classical music, the movie legend revealed that his wife influenced his interest in classical music.

“My wife influenced me. She was very fond of classical music. When I met her she looked me in the face and said: ‘there’s something you don’t know about yourself, you are deeper than you think. You are very emotional, I see you with your friends expressing yourselves at a social gathering. But deep down, you are a very serious person’.

“One day, she joined me in the preview room, where we played some classical music. At one point, when we were playing some aspects of Mozart’s songs, I got drawn into it, forcing me to go back to play it again. Before I knew what was happening, it stuck,” he told Vanguard.

Edochie, however, boasted of having in his archives all the works of Mozart and George Campbell who wrote songs such as “Messiah”, “Saul”, “Solomon” among others. He confessed to placing orders for classical music from abroad, and even urged his friends travelling abroad to buy classical music for him as a gift, instead of shoes, ties and wrist watches.

How he wanted to

be remembered

There are many things to remember Pete Edochie for. His deep baritone voice. His age-long beard. His intimidating look. His danc steps and his father-figure role in Nollywood.

But beyond all of these, Ebubedike wanted to be remembered for something far simpler, and far deeper. He wanted to be remembered as a man who brought happiness and joy to many homes in Africa and beyond with his craft.

Speaking with Vanguard as he celebrated his 76th birthday in 2023, Edochie opened up on his legacy, honour and fulfilment:

“If people feel that my contributions toward the growth of the Nigerian movie industry have affected their lives in one way or the other, it means that posterity would award me good marks. Our industry is very challenging. While you are playing different characters in movies, you are still expected to live up to your billing as a man of honour.

“People enjoy me going by their reactions to what I do. It gives me a lot of satisfaction that people think this man knows what he’s doing. If I am remembered as one who injected some life into his audiences in Nigeria and beyond, I feel accomplished,” he said.

It was a simple but profound desire from a man whose career spanned more than five decades.

For Edochie, acting was not just entertainment. It was a ministry. It was a service. It was a calling to heal homes with laughter, with wisdom, and with stories that mirrored real life.

In his own words, all he ever wanted was to bring joy into people’s homes. And by all accounts, that is precisely what he did for more than 50 years, before bowing out of the stage.

Landing role of Okonkwo in the NTA adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s ‘Things Fall Apart’

Pete Edochie did not start his journey as an actor. He started as a broadcaster in 1967 before gaining widespread recognition through his portrayal of Okonkwo in the television adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s celebrated novel, “Things Fall Apart” in the 80s.

Recalling how he landed that iconic role in our 2022 interview with him, Edochie said his former colleague, the late G. C. Ugwu, recommended him for the role of Okonkwo.

“He was the Zonal Director of NTA in Benin in those days. Engr Ugwu had always watched me in the broadcasting house, and the moment they decided to produce the play, the first person that came to his mind, who would play the role of Okonkwo was me”, he said.

He disclosed that he had never read “Things Fall Apart” before the adaptation and his first encounter with the story was through the script.

According to him, he auditioned at the University of Nigeria’s Enugu campus. In his account, the production team offered him the role after hearing him read. The performance drew attention beyond Nigeria, and the BBC team travelled to the country to interview him about it.

That one role changed African television forever. It made him a household name. It made Okonkwo very popular. And it made Pete Edochie the standard by which every other African actor would be judged.

Narrating the story, Edochie agreed that there was always a reflection of the Okonkwo character in most of his roles in movies. “That’s what many people said. When I started in ‘Things Fall Apart’, I was 38 years old. People still call me, “Ebubedike.” Before Chinua Achebe died, he was calling me Ebubedike. He never called me Pete, and we were very close.

“Each time people visited him in America then, he would ask after me. Achebe created the character and he felt I interpreted the role excellently. He named me after Okonkwo- Ebube Dike. So, many people still see me and refer to me as an Ebubedike.”

He said when the script was handed over to him, he felt it was an opportunity to read the novel since he didn’t have the privilege to do so while he was in school.

“I was delighted to read the novel. Before then, I had not read it, I knew nothing about it,” Edochie stated.

Ebubedike was not the only actor who auditioned for the iconic role of Okonkwo, but his talent stood him out in the crowd. According to him, “there were other actors who came for the audition held at the main auditorium of the University of Nigeria, Enugu campus. The moment I walked into the auditorium, the white woman who was invited to handle the costume and other things sighted me and screamed, ‘if this man could act, that’s the man we want for the role’.

“She never met me before. I walked in and was given the script. Other people were also given the script to read, and when I read mine, they shook hands with me and said, we are good to go. They said there was no point continuing with the audition. That was how I landed the role.”

Before featuring in the drama series, Edochie said he had starred in other smaller productions like William Shakespeare’s, ‘Every Man’, ‘Realm of Violence’, ‘Resurrection’ and others. But ‘Things Fall Apart’, was the production that gave him prominence.

Carrying my beard

for 26 years

Edochie’s beard was part of his identity. He revealed how he had carried the beard for 23 years as of 2023, and he would rather go to the grave with it.

“I could trim it, I wouldn’t shave my beard. I will carry it till the end of my time. I have a lot of hair on my head, and there is so much power in the hair. You read about the Bible story of Samson and Delilah. Our Lord Jesus Christ never shaved off his hair. There’s so much power in the hair,” he said, noting that his beard gave him character.

“I have always played a big man in my movies. If I am not a leader of a cult, I am an Igwe or a native doctor. There must be something inspiring about you. Something that frightens people, terrifies them and intimidates them when they know that you are coming. But when you clean-shave, you lose that”, he added.

Until his exit last Wednesday, Ebubedike never shaved his hair, making good his vow.

As a family man

Many people had described Edochie as a disciplinarian, a dedicated Christian and a good husband. He wasn’t far from those descriptions. His love for his family was incomparable. In the course of encouraging his children to stand out in life, Ebubedike bought cars for them as soon as they graduated from the university. The gesture, he explained, was to inspire them.

“That was intended to be a source of inspiration for them. And they had it at the back of their minds. As they were graduating, I was buying cars for them and I don’t regret it,” he added.

Edochie also spoke briefly about his marriage and his background.

“My wife and I were contemporaries in broadcasting. I liked her and she liked me too. With time, it developed into a very strong affection that we thought if we didn’t give a definition to our relationship before the end of the war, there would be a strong possibility that tongues would wag and I would be accused of exploiting this young girl and disappearing at the end of the day.

“I hail from a very strict paternal religious background. I am not that kind of person who would be ‘in and out’ of a woman. So, we got married and that’s it.”

Death rumours

For years, Pete Edochie was repeatedly declared dead on social media. In February 2026, his family dismissed another viral death rumour, with his eldest son, Leo Edochie, describing the reports as false and malicious.

Speaking to Vanguard on the rumour, Edochie himself laughed off the hoaxes. “I’m alive and will die when my maker calls me home,” he said, adding that hoaxes had “killed” him about seven times since 2012.

Ahead of his birthday on March 7, 2026, he pointed to family history as a source of confidence: “On the 7th of March, I will be 79. My father died at 96, so we have longevity in my family.” But he didn’t live up to his father’s age.

Each time the rumour of death came, he kept going with strength to continue working. He kept shooting. He kept granting interviews. He kept showing up at movie locations.

Edochie’s daughter in-law, May Edochie in her tribute after his death wrote: “For so many years, every year, someone somewhere made a false announcement of your death but you kept going with strength to continue working. This time, the news was true”.

On his health challenges

Although his family announced that he died after a prolonged battle with prostate cancer, the screen patriarch never named the illness publicly, speaking instead about the physical toll of ageing while continuing his schedule in Ghana and Nigeria.

Eight months after his February interview, he acknowledged on camera that his mobility had declined. Visiting Ghanaian actor Emmanuel Armah at his home in Accra on Thursday, October 1, 2026, Edochie prayed with him, offered financial support, and spoke about his own symptoms.

“Sitting down here, I am not very well myself. Walking is a problem for me now, but I still have hope that I will recover,” Edochie said on October 1.

Despite difficulty walking, Edochie continued his Accra tour for the Pete Edochie Legacy Project on Tuesday, October 6, 2026.

It was the Lion refusing to lie down. Even in pain, he was still giving. Still encouraging. Still fathering a generation.

On Olu Jacobs:

‘Our mates are gone’

Edochie died ten weeks after his fellow Nollywood pioneer, Olu Jacobs died at 84 on September 16.

In a recording from early May 2024, Edochie traced their bond to growing up in the northern part of the country, where Edochie schooled in Zaria and Kaduna and Jacobs spent his early childhood in Kano.

Recalling their final meeting when they walked out of separate film locations onto the same road, Edochie quoted Jacobs’s words verbatim: “Olu looked at me. He had tears in his eyes. He said, ‘Our mates are gone.’ And immediately he said this, the tears came to my eyes. We just held each other like this,” Edochie said, adding that he prayed: “May the good Lord keep us so that we can represent those who are not.”

He also dismissed a longstanding rumour that he had once asked Igbo film producers not to cast Jacobs, an Ogun State native, as an Igbo traditional ruler, or Igwe. “I have never disagreed with Olu for one day. No,” he said.

Vanguard had dubbed the pair the twin godfathers of Nollywood. Now, both are gone within a period of time, leaving the Nigerian movie industry mourning.

Tributes pour in

Edochie’s demise has sent shockwaves through the film industry, with fans and members of the entertainment fraternity mourning the loss on their various social media platforms.

Minister of Art, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy, Barr. Hannatu Musa Musawa, led the tributes session, describing him as an iroko, a national treasure, and one of the finest custodians of Nigeria’s culture, language and storytelling tradition.

Musawa said,”I received with great shock and deep sadness the news of the passing of Chief Pete Edochie. This is a painful loss, not only for his family and the creative industry, but for the entire nation. An iroko has fallen.

“Edochie was an outstanding actor who will not be easily replaced. He was more than an actor. He was a broadcaster, a cultural ambassador, a teacher and a father figure to generations of artists. His unforgettable interpretation of Okonkwo in ‘Things Fall Apart’ remains one of the greatest performances in African storytelling, a role that brought Chinua Achebe’s iconic character to life for the world.

“He was a lover of tradition and culture, and the epitome of an African man. From his commanding roles as a traditional ruler, father and elder, he gave voice to our proverbs, our wisdom, our dignity and our identity. He carried Nigeria with pride on screens across Africa and the world.”

Musawa noted that Edochie’s death comes at a particularly poignant moment, as the nation gathers in Enugu for NAFEST Enugu 2026.

“That he departed in Enugu, in the heart of the land he loved and served, while Nigeria celebrates its culture, is a solemn reminder of his enduring connection to our heritage. His legacy will continue to live in our films, our language, our theatre and in the countless young creatives he inspired.”

National President of the Actors Guild of Nigeria, AGN, Alhaji Abubakar Yakubu, described the late actor as “a father figure in the industry” who left his footprints in the sands of time.

According to him, “the country has lost a cultural treasure, and the film industry has lost one of its most distinguished figures and enduring champions of artistic excellence. Pete Edochie was more than a gifted actor.

“His passing is an immeasurable loss to Nollywood, Nigeria’s creative industry and the wider African entertainment community. He was an institution whose extraordinary talent, commanding presence, professionalism and storytelling skills helped shape Nigerian cinema and bring it international recognition. Pete Edochie was a man of the people, a detribalised Nigerian who spoke different languages. He lived a noble life, a dedicated Christian and a disciplinarian. He died when the industry needed him most. But as a thorough-bred actor, he left when the ovation was loudest,” Yakubu said.

Executive Director/CEO of the National Film and Video Censors Board, NFVCB, Dr Shaibu Husseini, said a giant has taken his final bow, but his legacy remains immortal.

“Today, Nollywood and the entire African film landscape have lost an iroko — a towering pillar whose commanding presence, diction, unmatched proverbs and wise sayings, and whose distinguished career in broadcasting defined an era.

“From his unforgettable portrayal of Okonkwo in the NTA adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s ‘Things Fall Apart’ to decades of unequalled performance in Nollywood movies, Edochie elevated Nigerian storytelling on the global stage and championed the cultural values the NFVCB strives to preserve,” Husseini said.

Dr Ali Nuhu, Managing Director/Chief Executive of the Nigerian Film Corporation, NFC, described Pete Edochie as an institution, a custodian of African culture, a moral voice, and a towering figure. “His commanding presence, rich proverbs and uncommon mastery of the craft gave Nigeria and Africa dignity on the global screen.

“From his unforgettable portrayal of Okonkwo in the television series adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s ‘Things Fall Apart’ to his countless roles as a king, father, elder and custodian of culture and tradition in several Nigerian movies, he represented an era of excellence, discipline and professionalism. His departure is a monumental loss, not only to his family and the Nollywood community, but to Nigeria, Africa and the global community of arts and culture”.

Edochie became famous after the iconic role he played as Okonkwo in the NTA adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s best-selling novel, Things Fall Apart in the 80s.The role not only earned him accolades, but also launched his long, celebrated career in Nigerian cinema.

Known for his deep voice, commanding delivery and rich use of proverbs, Edochie became synonymous with roles as kings, community leaders and family patriarchs.

His film credits include “Igodo”, “Rituals” and “Lionheart”(2018), directed by Genevieve Nnaji.

He was honoured with the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON) in 2003, the Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards Industry Merit Award and several lifetime achievement honours.

World.title: Uduere Killings in Delta: Six trucks of policemen, yet  bullets still found targets
World.content:
File image of Governor Sheriff Oborevwori of Delta State with some officers of the Armed Forces during his visit to Ughelli community, where he ordered arrest of perpetrators of the killings during the NDC campaign.

By Egufe Yafugborhi

The sound of gunfire shattered the campaign atmosphere at Uduere, Ughelli North Local Government Area of Delta State, November 23.

People who had gathered for a political rally suddenly scrambled for safety. Women ran, campaigners scattered and, in the ensuing chaos, bullets found human targets.

By the time the shooting stopped, families had lost loved ones, several people critically wounded and communities plunged into mourning.

Among the disturbing details was that six truckloads of policemen had reportedly been deployed to provide security. Former Deputy Senate President, Senator Ovie Omo-Agege, put their number at close to 50. Yet, according to accounts from both political camps, the violence escalated despite the robust security presence.

The tragedy has since generated competing accusations between the All Progressives Congress, APC, and the National Democratic Congress, NDC.

Beneath the political blame game are grieving families, wounded survivors and ordinary citizens asking why a political gathering should become a death trap.

A Trail Of Troubled Political Gatherings

Uduere was not an isolated incident in the build-up to Delta 2027 elections.

September 18, a one-million-man march organised by the NDC in the Warri-Effurun axis was disrupted by violence, leaving persons wounded. An AK-47 allegedly recovered from a suspect identified as Collins became a subject of controversy between the party and police.

The NDC alleged the suspect was released the following day, a claim that formed part of its subsequent complaints about police handling of the incident.

October 3, the party held a 10,000-man march against hunger in Ughelli. The following day, the Ughelli North Local Government Council, chaired by Chief Jaro Egbo, issued a notice, sealed the business premises and impounded truck belonging to Tobore Alex Agbah, who led the march.

Agbah would later become one of the victims of the Uduere violence.

November 7, another NDC one-million-man march in Asaba ended in violence, with one fatality recorded.

The recurrence of disturbances has fuelled allegations that NDC gatherings are being targeted by political opponents allegedly linked to the ruling APC.

Delta State Commissioner for Information, Charles Aniagwu, however, rejected the suggestion of a pattern.

“It’s not a pattern, because when you talk about a pattern, it means that it’s continuously and then you are linking it to be able to join one to the other,” he said.

He argued: “The NDC is not being attacked, there are a number of local governments where we have not had any disturbances. The APC in Delta is holding sway, the underdogs in this case are the members of the NDC who are few.”

But NDC governorship candidate, Chris Iyovwaye, disagreed, recalling the September incident.

“Another thug of APC was caught with an AK-47 and was handed over to the police. To our surprise, he was let off the hook the very next day,” he alleged.

On the Asaba attack, he said: “Every time we are exercising our democratic rights, they’re always there to stop us.”

Regarding Uduere, Iyovwaye said the party had secured police approval and was promised six truckloads of policemen.

“Yet the consequence of that is that four of our men are dead and 15 seriously injured, some of them still in ICU,” he said.

Two Camps, Competing Accusations

The Uduere violence has produced sharply conflicting accounts from Egbo and Omo-Agege. Egbo, who hails from the community, accused Omo-Agege and his entourage of instigating the violence. He claimed two of his associates, Prince Oharisi and a man identified simply as Oche, were shot dead as Omo-Agege was concluding his campaign activities.

Egbo alleged that Omo-Agege arrived after APC members had secured the town hall for a ceremony. “He came there and started abusing everybody, according to what I was told, saying I was his PA, I was his boy, and all of that,” he said.

He further alleged: “On his way out, he ordered one of his boys, Efemena Umukoro, Akhima, one of the NDC key mobilisers who lost his life in the melee, to open fire on our people.”

Egbo also said the community’s President-General, Cosmos Ejovwoke, was attacked and killed.

“I found out that they clubbed and shot the President-General of the community,” he said.

He demanded investigation by the Inspector-General of Police, declaring: “You come to my community to kill my President-General, killing my people, and you don’t even feel any remorse? We must do something about it. If we continue like this, then our democracy is in danger.”

Omo-Agege, however, accused Egbo and his alleged political backers of orchestrating the attack. He listed four members of his campaign organisation as dead, including former Federal Character Commissioner, Moses Anaughe, while about 15 others sustained critical injuries.

He questioned why the violence occurred despite the deployment of policemen.

“We went to the campaign with full expectations, that with six trucks of policemen deployed to that venue to protect us in that event, we expected protection for everybody in that venue,” he said.

“It never occurred to us that they (police) were merely coming to watch me principally executed.”

He added: “There is no way you have close to 50 policemen in a venue and a minute after commencement of the attack, all of them ran away and left only you there.”

Survivors’ Accounts Of Blood And Bullets

One of the most harrowing accounts came from Chief Evans Ivwurie, Chairman of Omo-Agege’s campaign organisation, who was shot during the violence.

Ivwurie alleged that the atmosphere became tense as the rival political gatherings proceeded, adding he personally complained to police officers about gunfire from the opposing gathering.

“The Policemen told me they (APC supporters) were not shooting guns, that they were shooting knockouts (fireworks). I said but you can see them brandishing pump actions openly, shooting it,” he recounted.

He alleged that violence erupted while Omo-Agege was addressing the campaign.

“These APC thugs led by Egbo, the LG Chairman, started throwing stones at the direction of Omo-Agege and our people gathered there. They ended throwing the stones and all of a sudden they started shooting.”

As people fled, he said, he tried to establish whether Omo-Agege was safe, alleging a man identified as Gueke, chairman of Ughelli Motor Parks, shot him in the head.

“Immediately he saw me at a close range, he just shot at me, on my head. The bullet was so heavy, I fell flat to the ground without any energy,” he said.

He further alleged that the gunman shot Anaughe twice in the chest.

Another victim, Agbah, who had earlier been affected by the council’s action following his October rally, was shot in the neck.

During a visit by Peter Obi, the NDC presidential figure, Agbah, who was receiving treatment, disclosed that five bullets remained lodged in his body.

“I’ve five bullets in me. I’m happy to see you Sir. The target was to kill me. There are five bullets in me now,” he told Obi.

Mothers And Communities Mourn

The killings have provoked emotional reactions beyond the two political camps.

Peter Obi, who visited the families of slain Anaughe and Efemena Umukoro, popularly known as Akima, alongside Omo-Agege and Iyovwaye, condemned the killings.

“This is totally unexpected during these campaigns period, that people would die because they have a different view or belong to a different party from the ruling party,” he said.

“We cannot kill people, harm people because we want to be political leaders.”

President-General of the Urhobo Progress Union, Ese Gam, expressed concern that political rivalry was tearing the Urhobo nation apart.

“Now we’re not contending with others. It’s now Urhobo against Urhobo,” he said.

“If we continue to kill ourselves like this in the name of fighting for power, who are we going to lead at the end of the day?”

Unanswered Security Questions

The reported failure of security personnel to prevent the violence has become a major issue in the aftermath.

Lawyer and activist, Austin Nyekigbe, who passed through Uduere before and after the incident, called on the IGP to order an independent investigation into the killings and the conduct of officers deployed.

Human rights lawyer, Inibehe Effiong, condemned the killing of Umukoro, describing him as a courageous rights activist.

“The brutal assassination of Comrade Efemena alias Comrade Akima is senseless and despicable,” he said.

“The fact that this dastardly killing happened in the presence of dozens of police officers is a shameful indictment of the Nigeria Police Force.”

Niger Delta Peace Coalition Coordinator, Zik Gbemre, also demanded an investigation, insisting that politicians, alleged attackers and uniformed personnel must all be held accountable where culpability is established.

Meanwhile, activist Austin Aghomi criticised Governor Oborevwori for continuing his campaign activities shortly after the killings.

Apparrently laying the blame on NDC and suggesting justification for the NDC killings, the governor during his campaign tour of Oghara and Koko, had said: “You can’t go for campaign and carry gun. If you carry a gun, it means you have an intention to do something. “You cannot come to my community and kill my president-general, and the community will let you go? No! You can’t do that. It’s not done anywhere.”

Aghomi faulted the governor’s response, arguing that the police had a duty to prevent violence at the gathering.

For the families who have to bury loved ones, political accusations cannot restore lost lives. For survivors as Ivwurie and Agbah, the battle to recover continues.

The questions remain: Who tried to stop a party from campaigning? Who fired the fatal shots? Why did the police reportedly fail to stop the violence despite their deployment? And will an independent investigation establish responsibility?

As Delta approaches 2027, citizens should not have to risk their lives to exercise their democratic rights.

Six truckloads of policemen were reportedly deployed to Uduere. Yet the bullets still found their targets.

The dead cannot speak, but their families and the survivors are demanding answers.

World.title: How Tinubu fought Obasanjo to reclaim Lagos coastline – Fashola
World.content:
By Juliet Umeh

As the 2027 general elections draw closer, political defections, shifting alliances and questions about leadership are beginning to shape the debate over who should govern Nigeria for another four years.

But for former Lagos State Governor, Mr Babatunde Fashola, one important test for anyone seeking to lead the country is the ability to build relationships, work with others and remain committed to a political team, even in difficult times.

Fashola believes President Bola Tinubu has demonstrated these qualities, arguing that his ability to retain political associates and bring former opponents into his camp makes him better placed to manage Nigeria’s diversity.

In a pointed challenge to opposition leaders, the former governor asked voters to examine what happened to the people who worked with other presidential contenders and why many of them were no longer in their political camps.

Speaking during an interview on Arise Television, Fashola said political relationships should serve as a reference point for assessing the leadership capacity of those seeking the presidency.

“Where are all the people who worked with them today? That’s a job reference question. For those who want to vote, where are all the people who worked with these people? Why is it only President Tinubu that has all those who worked with him when he was governor still with him? And they were with him for 16 years or so, out of office, when he wasn’t a president,” he said.

According to him, the ability to work with people is essential for anyone entrusted with managing a country as diverse as Nigeria.

“If you are going to get entrusted with managing Nigeria’s diverse family, you must be able to work in a team. And you don’t just get up and jump away when there’s a crisis in the fold,” he said.

Fashola noted that Tinubu remained in the All Progressives Congress, APC, despite internal disagreements, while some political leaders had abandoned parties that helped build their political careers.

He also pointed to Tinubu’s ability to bring former opponents into his political fold, describing it as evidence of his capacity to build relationships across political divides.

“Not just those who worked with him before, those who opposed him are now working with him. That’s how he has built a coalition of 30 state governors from one state, from Lagos. And that is profound, whether you like him or not,” he said.

Why I refused to join another party

Fashola’s argument about political loyalty also reflects his own experience as Lagos governor, when he said he resisted pressure to abandon his political platform in exchange for certain benefits from the Federal Government.

He recalled that during a meeting with a former President, an unnamed governor suggested that Lagos would only regain access to Lagos House, Marina, if he joined the ruling party at the time.

Fashola said he rejected the condition, insisting that political conviction should not be traded for government privileges.

“I said, look, Mr President, if that is the condition, keep the house. And as long as I am alive, I won’t join your party. If unfortunately I die, and they bring my body into your party, I’ll wake up,” he recalled.

He said his administration also faced disagreements with the Federal Government over issues including approval for the proposed Lekki Port and access to funds belonging to Lagos State.

How Tinubu fought Obasanjo over Lagos coastline

Fashola also defended Tinubu’s claim that he played a major role in efforts to protect the Lagos coastline from the Atlantic Ocean, particularly around Victoria Island.

He recalled that the Federal Government had spent about N4 billion pumping sand to protect the coastline, but erosion continued to threaten properties and infrastructure.

According to him, Tinubu repeatedly wrote to former President Olusegun Obasanjo seeking approval for a lasting solution, but the requests were initially rejected.

Fashola, who served as Tinubu’s Chief of Staff at the time, said he personally drafted several of the letters.

“I drafted those letters on his instructions to President Obasanjo every time. President Obasanjo would reply, no. The last one, I think it was something like, almost like, look, get out of my life, I will find a copy of the letter. I still have it in my records,” he said.

He said about seven letters were written, with Tinubu insisting that the administration should continue pressing for approval.

“Nobody should take the credit away from him. I was his Chief of Staff,” Fashola said, maintaining that Tinubu deserved recognition for the initiative.

Certificate controversy, foreign trips

On the controversy surrounding Tinubu’s academic records, Fashola described the debate as a distraction from pressing national issues, arguing that attention should instead be focused on the cost of living, fuel prices, employment, education and security.

“How does this (controversy on certificate) reduce the cost of living crisis? No, how does that reduce the cost of fuel? How does it reduce their travel time? How does it pay their children’s school fees, which NELFUND does? How does it create jobs?” he asked.

He also defended the President’s foreign trips, while acknowledging that Nigerians had the right to demand explanations about public spending.

“Nigerians are entitled to ask questions about their president’s utilisation of the time and resources,” he said.

However, he challenged opposition parties to go beyond criticising the administration and present practical alternatives to its policies. He argued that international engagements could support investment, infrastructure development and service delivery.

Funsho Williams: Fashola seeks better investigations

Away from the 2027 political debate, Fashola reflected on the unresolved murder of former Lagos governorship aspirant, Funsho Williams, who was killed at his Ikoyi residence in July 2006.

Following the discharge and acquittal of the six men charged over the case in 2014, Fashola expressed sympathy with the Williams family, describing the late politician as a peaceful man and an outstanding public servant.

“Funsho Williams was a man of peace, a fine gentleman, an outstanding public servant. No one deserved to be treated the way he was cruelly murdered,” he said.

He said the case demonstrated the need for more effective police investigations and the use of forensic tools, including DNA analysis and fingerprint evidence, to identify suspects and secure convictions.

Fashola also called for the prosecution of sponsors of electoral violence, arguing that holding prominent offenders accountable could discourage others. He, however, opposed the ‘rig and die’ slogan for election riggers, insisting that punishment must follow the law and respect due process.

Electricity providers owe Nigerians explanation

On Nigeria’s persistent electricity challenges, the former Minister of Power said electricity providers must explain their service failures to consumers.

He recalled that more than 11 million Nigerians were connected to electricity during his four years as Minister of Power, adding that his administration pursued incremental improvements towards stable and uninterrupted supply.

Fashola also welcomed the decentralisation of the power sector, saying greater participation by state governments could attract investment and introduce new solutions.

No plans to return to politics

After years in public service, Fashola said he was rebuilding his legal practice and had no immediate plans to return to elective politics.

Asked whether he would consider another political contest, he suggested that his time in public office had run its course.

“I’ve run as hard as I can. So it’s time to stop running. It was a very humbling privilege to have served my country. I don’t take that for granted,” he said.

World.title: Ndigbo ‘ve bright future despite current challenges – Bianca Ojukwu
World.content:
Bianca Ojukwu

By Steve Oko, Regional Editor, South-East

Nigeria’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Bianca Ojukwu, has enthused that the future of Ndigbo is great despite their current challenges.

She, however, lamented the disunity among Igbo political leaders, particularly governors in the South-East, accusing them of allowing political rivalries and personal interests to undermine the collective progress of the region.

The Minister urged Ndigbo to build bridges across existing divisions and embrace unity, mutual respect and collective purpose.

Mrs Ojukwu also lamented the abandonment of her late husband, the Biafran leader, Chukwuemeka Odumegwu-Ojukwu, by some political leaders who benefited from his political influence and support, accusing them of turning their backs on his legacy after attaining power.

Bianca spoke at the 15th anniversary memorial of Ojukwu held at the Ojukwu Memorial Library, Owerri, Imo State, where she called for a renewed commitment to Igbo unity, peace and development.

She lamented that Igbo governors had failed to demonstrate sufficient unity in addressing issues affecting the people, noting that political antagonism and mutual suspicion were weakening the region’s ability to speak with one voice.

“We cannot continue to celebrate Igbo greatness while tolerating the disunity that undermines it,” she declared.

The minister said Ndigbo could not demand recognition and solidarity from other ethnic groups while failing to extend the same values to one another, stressing that unity must go beyond speeches, cultural celebrations and symbolic gestures.

She urged political leaders in the South-East to put aside their differences and work together for the common good, insisting that the region’s future could not be built on rivalry, personal ambition and political bitterness.

Bianca expressed disappointment with some political elites who, despite benefiting from the political legacy and influence of her late husband, had abandoned him and his ideals

She recalled that some politicians Ojukwu supported and campaigned for to attain political power would, upon succeeding, make removing his portrait from their offices a priority and replacing it with their own.

“I know people my husband gave flag and campaigned for to gain political power, the first thing they want to do is to remove his portrait and replace it with their own,” she lamented.

She said Ojukwu’s legacy should not be reduced to his military exploits, titles, speeches and political struggles, but should be reflected in his convictions, humanity and commitment to justice, dignity and the welfare of the people.

Describing her late husband as a soldier, statesman, intellectual and patriarch, Bianca said his life was driven by a deep conviction that people deserved to live in dignity and without fear.

Reflecting on the painful history of the Igbo, including the 1966 pogroms, displacement and civil war, she said Ojukwu’s memorial should inspire a commitment to ensuring that such tragedies never happen again.

She called on traditional rulers to provide moral leadership, political leaders to rise above personal interests, and businessmen and women to invest in the homeland, while urging young people to channel their energies into innovation, enterprise and productive ventures.

The minister also cautioned Igbo youths in the diaspora against the pursuit of illicit wealth, warning that criminal activities had brought disgrace to the people and landed some young people in detention rather than helping them build meaningful futures.

She urged them to become worthy ambassadors of Igbo culture and contribute to creating a homeland where businesses could thrive, investors could operate confidently and families could celebrate festivities without fear.

Bianca lamented the insecurity and economic difficulties in parts of the South-East, saying the region could not attract investment or encourage its people in the diaspora to return home if communities remained unsafe, businesses shut down and streets deserted.

“Our land must once again become a place where our children are excited to return,” she said, stressing the need to restore confidence in the region’s business and investment climate

She said Ojukwu’s ideals would only endure when they were translated into practical actions by those who inherited his legacy, noting that annual memorials alone could not adequately preserve the values of a great leader.

The minister also criticised the neglect of prominent Igbo leaders and their legacies, citing the prolonged delay in completing the Zik Mausoleum.

She regretted that it took former President Muhammadu Buhari to build a mausoleum for Nnamdi Azikiwe, 22 years after his death, accusing successive administrations in Anambra of failing to give the project the attention it deserved.

Bianca said some leaders lived as though they were immortal but eventually faded into obscurity, unlike those whose courage, sacrifices and contributions continued to inspire generations.

She thanked individuals and groups who had sustained Ojukwu’s memory through the annual memorial and particularly commended the founder of the Movement for the Actualisation of the Sovereign State of Biafra, MASSOB-BIM, Chief Ralph Uwazurike, for instituting the event.

Uwazurike demands Nnamdi Kanu’s release

Meanwhile, Uwazurike renewed his call for the release of detained Biafra agitator, Mazi Nnamdi Kanu, insisting that he had committed no offence deserving of his continued detention.

The MASSOB founder compared Kanu’s situation with that of Yoruba agitator, Sunday Igboho, who he said had been released, arguing that the difference in their circumstances was political.

“Where is Sunday Igboho? Kanu didn’t commit any offence that is bigger or more sinister than that of Igboho. The only difference is that Sunday Igboho has a brother that is presently the President of Nigeria,” Uwazurike said.

He added that Kanu would have been released if Peter Obi were Nigeria’s President.

Uwazurike, who advocated non-violent agitation for Biafra, cautioned youths against resorting to violence, saying many had misunderstood the principles of self-determination and allowed social media narratives to distort the struggle.

He urged the younger generation to embrace peaceful advocacy, insisting that violence was incompatible with the pursuit of self-determination.

“I urge the new generation of indigenous people to abide by the principles of non-violence,” he said, citing Mahatma Gandhi as his inspiration.

Uwazurike said he had no regrets over the sacrifices he made in the course of the Biafra struggle, including persecution and the destruction of his residence, insisting he was prepared to make even greater sacrifices if the quest could be achieved through peaceful means.

“I want to even sacrifice more if Biafra could be actualised through non-violence,” he said, warning that violence would only undermine the struggle.

He lamented the absence of a unifying Igbo leader since Ojukwu’s death, expressing hope that another leader with the capacity to rally the people around a common cause would emerge.

Uwazurike said Ojukwu remained a rallying point for many Igbo people despite his death, adding that the memorial was also an opportunity to promote unity and preserve his ideals.

He dismissed the absence of political elites at the event, saying the memorial was primarily about the people and not politicians, whom he accused of being divided by personal interests.

He urged Ndigbo to preserve unity, which he described as one of Ojukwu’s enduring legacies.

The event featured cultural displays, masquerades, a march-past by delegations from states in the old Eastern Region, lectures and goodwill messages.

World.title: ‘Fuji Vibrations’ returns with timeless celebration of Fuji music
World.content:
By Prisca Sam-Duru

Lovers of Fuji music are in for a treat as Fuji Vibrations, an annual celebration returns to Lagos. The event is scheduled for Thursday, December 3, 2026, at Muri Okunola Park, Victoria Island, Lagos.

Now in its sixth year, the live music platform continues its mission to preserve, promote and reimagine Fuji music, bringing together legendary performers, emerging talents and audiences from across generations.

The 2026 edition, themed “Timeless”, celebrates a genre that has consistently evolved without losing its identity. From its origins in the Yoruba-speaking communities of southwestern Nigeria to its unmistakable influence on contemporary Afrobeats, Fuji has remained an enduring part of Nigeria’s expression.

This year’s line-up features an exciting mix of emerging and established Fuji artistes. Representing the emerging generation are Musa Talent, Bukola OmoDaddy and Sanjay Rasheed Abefe. They will share the stage with established names including Atawewe, SK Sensation, Taye Currency, Shefiu Alao, King Saheed Osupa, Obesere and K1 De Ultimate.

Since its debut in 2020, FUJI: A Opera has facilitated the introduction of the genre to new audiences through exhibitions, live performances and brand collaborations, including its international showcase at The Africa Centre in London. Its flagship concert, Fuji Vibrations, has become a fixture on Lagos’ December entertainment calendar, bringing together thousands of music lovers and some of the genre’s most celebrated performers.

Speaking ahead of this year’s edition, Bobo Omotayo, Founder of FUJI: A Opera, said: “One of the most remarkable things about Fuji is how it continues to find new audiences without losing the people who have loved it for decades. The music our parents listened to is still very much part of the soundtrack of our lives today. You hear its influence everywhere, particularly in contemporary Nigerian music. That’s what “Timeless” means to us. It’s a celebration of a genre that has never stopped evolving, and the extraordinary musicians who have kept it alive.”

Beyond the performances, Fuji Vibrations has become known for its vibrant celebration of Nigerian fashion and culture, particularly its annual signature aso-ebi, which has grown into a much-anticipated tradition among attendees. This year’s official colour is purple, with guests encouraged to interpret the colour through their own personal styles.

The 2026 edition is supported by Supakomando, ZURI, Regal Dry Gin, whose partnerships reflect a shared commitment to celebrating Nigerian music, creativity and heritage.

The event is also supported by the Lagos State Government, LASPARK, Events By Claud, AWCA, Dave Acoustics Production, Cantagali and DALA, whose contributions help bring the annual celebration to life.

FUJI: A Opera also continues its longstanding collaboration with the Fuji Musicians Association of Nigeria (FUMAN), an important partner in its efforts to honour the genre’s pioneers while creating opportunities for a new generation of performers.

World.title: INEC tests BVAS, result portal today
World.content:
File image.

By Omeiza Ajayi

The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, will today run a nationwide mock accreditation and result transmission exercise in all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), about seven weeks before the 2027 general election.

INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, disclosed this at the INEC and Office of the National Security Adviser, ONSA) Strategic Election Security Conference in Abuja on Thursday.

He said the exercise would put the Commission’s new equipment and result systems under live conditions. “While this exercise allows INEC to stress-test our upgraded BVAS devices and verify our stricter INEC Result Viewing Portal, IReV, v,lidation safeguards—which automatically block arithmetic inconsistencies and over-voting, it also serves as an essential live dry run for our security architecture,” he said.

The presidential and National Assembly elections hold on 16 January 2027 across 177,299 polling units, with governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections to follow on 6 February 2027.

Amupitan said the Commission had procured new accreditation machines and set a lower voter threshold for the actual election in January.

“INEC will deploy over 1.41 million ad hoc personnel alongside 57,000 newly procured Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) devices, calibrated at a reduced threshold of 850 voters per machine,” he said.

He told the gathering that the rehearsal was as much a test of coordination with security agencies as of technology. “Strategy without rehearsal is merely aspiration,” he said.

The INEC chairman called on the Commission’s Resident Electoral Commissioners and the Commissioners of Police in the states to take part fully.

“I urge all Resident Electoral Commissioners and Commissioners of Police to treat November 28 as a full-scale operational rehearsal: test your communication lines, evaluate rapid-response times around mock polling centres, and identify any logistical or security blind spots while there is still ample time to resolve them,” he said.

INEC had earlier published the list of polling units selected for the nationwide mock accreditation exercise, naming 17,656 locations across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory FCT.

The commission said the exercise is a “Mock Accreditation and Result Upload Exercise” using the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, BVAS.

The list gives the state, local government area, ward, polling unit and delimitation code of each selected location. It runs alphabetically from Abia State to Zamfara State, with the FCT last.

Abia has 368 entries, while Adamawa follows with 452. In the FCT, 124 polling units were selected across the six area councils. Abaji, Bwari, Gwagwalada, Kuje and Kwali have 20 each, while the Municipal Area Council has 24.

The exercise will simulate the Presidential election, with polling units opening by 8:30 a.m. and accreditation running from 8:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m.

INEC said the value of the exercise lies in the faults it finds. “Its value lies in finding faults while there is still time to fix them, so a fault recorded on Saturday is the exercise doing its job,” it said.
