World.title: 2027: INEC Tests BVAS, IReV in Mock Election, Vows No Repeat of 2023 Glitch
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

• Deploys 57,000 new BVAS, upgrades IReV

• New eEC8A result sheet to block upload errors, overvoting

· Declares AI-generated names, photos won’t pass accreditation

• 17,676 polling units selected for nationwide exercise

• Promises tighter security, safeguards against result manipulation

Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja and Felix Omoh-Asun in Benin City

The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) is conducting a nationwide mock accreditation and electronic result transmission exercise across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) today as part of efforts to prevent a recurrence of the glitches that marred electronic result transmission during the 2023 general election.

This is as the electoral umpire assured Nigerians that names and photographs allegedly generated through Artificial Intelligence (AI) cannot be used to vote in the 2027 general election.

The exercise is designed to test the commission’s upgraded Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) devices and the strengthened INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV), alongside its new electronic polling unit result sheet, Form eEC8A, which has built-in validation rules to prevent upload errors and detect arithmetic inconsistencies.

INEC said the exercise would also enable Resident Electoral Commissioners (RECs) and Commissioners of Police test communication channels, assess emergency response times around polling units and identify logistical and security gaps ahead of the 2027 elections.

The Chief Press Secretary to the INEC Chairman, Adedayo Oketola, told THISDAY that the Commission, under the leadership of Prof. Joash Amupitan, SAN, had introduced measures to address potential IReV failures, BVAS breakdowns, result manipulation at collation centres and attacks on election personnel.

He said the Vommission had strengthened the IReV against cyber disruptions and overhauled its result management process to improve the reliability of electronic transmission.

Oketola said: “Ahead of 2027, INEC has done a lot to safeguard the IReV against cyber disruptions, and improved the result management workflow. The Commission has also deployed an electronic polling unit result sheet (Form eEC8A) with built-in validation rules that prevent upload errors, alongside rigorous technical stress-testing—beginning with tomorrow’s nationwide mock exercise on 28th November 2026—to identify and resolve bottlenecks well before January 16, 2027.

“Under Prof. Joash Amupitan, a repeat of the 2023 glitch will not happen.”

He explained that the new Form eEC8A had built-in validation rules designed to prevent errors before results were uploaded to the IReV.

To prevent human interference and arithmetic discrepancies at collation centres, Oketola said INEC had introduced multiple layers of technical and procedural safeguards.

“The upgraded Form eEC8A and IReV ingestion system automatically run real-time consistency checks before a result can be uploaded—blocking entries where total votes cast exceed the number of BVAS-accredited voters or where party scores do not tally with total valid votes,” he said.

He added that under the Electoral Act 2026 and INEC guidelines, collation officers were required to cross-check physical Form EC8A sheets against BVAS accreditation records and electronically transmitted IReV images in the presence of party agents, accredited observers and security personnel before entering figures into ward, local government and state collation sheets.

According to him, the nationwide mock exercise would subject the upgraded system to further stress-testing ahead of the January 16, 2027 presidential and National Assembly elections.

Oketola said INEC had procured 57,000 new BVAS devices, replaced the batteries of existing ones and built climate-controlled storage facilities in states to prevent heat-related battery damage.

He added that the Commission had reduced the deployment threshold from 1,250 to 850 registered voters per device, allowing multiple machines to be deployed in high-density polling units.

“In areas with no network, BVAS will store the encrypted result and transmit automatically to IReV once the Presiding Officer reaches network coverage on the way to the Ward collation centre. The physical Form EC8A will still move under security escort,” Oketola said.

On the selection of 17,676 polling units for the mock exercise, he explained that the number was designed to ensure nationwide geographical coverage rather than merely achieve a numerical target.

He said: “The 17,676 polling units selected for nationwide mock exercise represent two designated polling units across all 8,809 Registration Areas (Wards) in all 36 states and the FCT—roughly 10 per cent of Nigeria’s 176,846 polling units.

“Sampling every single ward in the country ensures that the exercise tests urban centres, rural communities, riverine terrain, and varied telecommunications footprints simultaneously, rather than focusing only on easily accessible cities.”

Oketola said INEC had already tested the upgraded systems during recent off-cycle governorship elections in Anambra, Ekiti and Osun states, the FCT Area Council elections and 16 legislative bye-elections.

He said the mock exercise would give the Commission, political parties, observers and citizens the opportunity to assess device speed, IReV uploads and field support response times, with seven weeks remaining to address any operational gaps.

On the safety of election personnel, Oketola said INEC considered the protection of ad hoc staff a priority and was working with security agencies to ensure that anyone who intimidated or attacked election workers was arrested and prosecuted.

He said recruitment was ongoing through the INEC Portal for the Engagement of Election Staff (INECPRES), adding that the application deadline had been extended to December 2, 2026, to ensure adequate nationwide coverage.

According to him, the personnel, drawn mainly from members of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC), civil servants and university academics, would undergo structured training on the updated BVAS and electronic result transmission procedures.

He added that INEC was working with the Nigeria Police Force and other security agencies under the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES) to restrict access to collation centres to accredited officials, authorised party agents, observers and the media, in order to prevent unauthorised interference and intimidation of collation officers.

AI-generated Voter Records Cannot pass BVAS aaccreditation

In a related development, INEC assured Nigerians that names and photographs allegedly generated through AI cannot be used to vote in the 2027 general election.

Edo State Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC), Obo Effanga, gave the assurance yesterday, in Benin City while responding to concerns over irregular voter registration and allegations of AI-generated entries in the voter register.

Effanga explained that voting would be strictly restricted to eligible human voters whose identities can be successfully verified through the commission’s accreditation system.

“AI-generated voters cannot vote because you have to be a human being. It is only a human being whose face matches the photograph on the INEC register that will be allowed to vote,” he said.

He added that AI-generated photographs could not successfully pass the accreditation process involving the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS).

According to him, any voter who fails to undergo the mandatory fingerprint and facial recognition verification will not be allowed to cast a ballot.

“Anybody who is not verified through fingerprint and facial recognition cannot vote. There is no way around it,” he emphasised.

The REC described the mock exercise as critical to ensuring the effectiveness of the electoral process, urging political parties, civil society organisations, individuals and the media to participate and observe the exercise.

On the ongoing voter register clean-up, the REC said the names removed from the register would be made public on December 15, when the national commission releases the list of prospective voters.

He disclosed that more than three million names had been removed from the register, bringing the total number of registered voters to approximately 100 million.

Also speaking, INEC National Commissioner representing the South-South geopolitical zone, Rhoda Gumus, assured Nigerians that the commission would investigate those responsible for the alleged submission of AI-generated voter details and make the findings public.

She said the Commission was determined to establish the circumstances surrounding the development, adding that no stone would be left unturned.

“I want to assure you that, as a commission, we are working day and night. We are doing everything possible to ensure that the 2027 election goes smoothly,” she said.

Gumus reiterated that the mock accreditation exercise was part of the commission’s efforts to assess its level of preparedness and identify possible challenges ahead of the general election.

“This exercise is simply a test to assess how the process will work during the election. I also want to assure the public that we are doing our part,” she said.

She urged members of the public to turn out and observe the exercise, stressing that credible elections required the collective commitment of all stakeholders.

Gumus cautioned against dismissing the exercise because it was only a mock accreditation, noting that the cooperation of security agencies and other relevant stakeholders was essential to its success.

She also urged INEC officials to remain proactive and professional in the discharge of their duties.

World.title: Fashola: APC Won’t Let Peter Obi Repeat 2023 Lagos Upset
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

*Says party’s scientific polls failed to identify state as battleground

*Rejects death penalty for election riggers, seeks stiffer jail terms

*Says 11m Nigerians gained electricity under his watch

*Blames bureaucracy for stranded power equipment

Demola Ojo

Former Governor of Lagos State, Babatunde Fashola, has admitted that the All Progressives Congress (APC) was “blindsided” by Peter Obi’s victory in Lagos State in the 2023 presidential election, insisting that the party would not allow a repeat of the upset.

Obi, then the Labour Party presidential candidate, defeated Bola Tinubu in Lagos, the state where Tinubu had served as governor and built much of his political base. Official results showed Obi securing 582,454 votes against Tinubu’s 572,606, a margin of 9,848 votes.



Speaking in an exclusive interview with ARISE News, Fashola expressed confidence that the APC had learnt from the result.

“We were blindsided. It won’t happen again,” he said.

Asked what he meant by being blindsided, Fashola said the party’s polling ahead of the 2023 election had not suggested that Lagos was seriously in play.



“Lagos didn’t look like a battleground at the time, not from the numbers,” he said.

When asked whether that meant the APC had taken Lagos for granted, Fashola rejected the interpretation.

“No, no. I don’t use words that I don’t use,” he responded.



“We do very scientific surveys, and Lagos didn’t look like a battleground in that sense. So that’s why I say I was blindsided, on reflection.”

Fashola said the APC nevertheless recovered quickly from the presidential result, pointing to subsequent electoral outcomes in the state as evidence that the setback did not represent a permanent political realignment.

“In spite of that setback at the presidential election, we turned it around very quickly,” he said.

He also pushed back against suggestions that Obi’s victory demonstrated an irreversible weakening of the APC’s hold on Lagos.

“What has happened has happened,” Fashola said, arguing that the political focus should now be on the competing records and policy offers of the parties.



The former governor said the APC should campaign on issues and its record rather than rely on rhetoric, while condemning political violence and hate speech.

“You are entitled to very vigorously and vociferously campaign for your party, as I am doing now, and showing what our record is, without damaging anybody’s name, anybody’s reputation, and without hate speech,” he said.

He described democracy as a “non-contact sport” rooted in competing ideas, with parties making their case to voters on policies and performance rather than intimidation.

Tinubu’s political relationships

Fashola urged Nigerians to examine the political relationships surrounding President Tinubu and his rivals, arguing that Tinubu’s ability to retain longtime associates and win over former opponents offered voters a “job reference” for judging presidential candidates.

He said Nigerians should look beyond campaign promises and examine what had happened to people who previously worked closely with those seeking the presidency.

“Where are all the people? That’s a job reference question,” Fashola said.

“Why is it only President Tinubu has all the people who worked with him still with him?”

Fashola argued that many of Tinubu’s political associates remained with him through the years he was out of government before eventually becoming president.



He said the durability of those relationships demonstrated an ability to work with others, which he described as particularly important for anyone seeking to govern a country as diverse as Nigeria.

“It shows an ability to work with others,” Fashola said.

“If you are going to get entrusted with managing Nigeria’s diversity, you must be able to work with people.”

Fashola contrasted Tinubu’s political trajectory with that of his presidential rivals, arguing that some had left the parties that brought them to national prominence and parted ways with former political associates.



“There was crisis in the APC. He didn’t leave the party,” Fashola said.

“The others have left the party that brought them to prominence. They’ve left people who worked closely with them.”

He said voters should examine candidates’ histories of managing relationships when deciding whom to entrust with political power.

Fashola also argued that Tinubu had gone beyond retaining longtime allies by bringing former political opponents into his expanding coalition.

“All of the people who opposed Tinubu, when he used to be called the last man standing, all of them are now working with him,” he said.

“Not just those who worked with him before. Those who opposed him are now working with him.”



Fashola linked the political expansion to the APC’s growing control of state governments, describing it as evidence of Tinubu’s capacity to build coalitions beyond the political base he developed in Lagos.

“That’s how he has built a coalition of 30 state governments from one state, from Lagos,” he said.

“And that is profound, whether you like him or not.”

He maintained that the ability to retain allies, accommodate former opponents and build coalitions should form part of the electorate’s assessment of those seeking Nigeria’s highest office.

“That is a big reference for the job he’s seeking,” he said.

INEC, electoral integrity

Fashola cautioned against placing responsibility for Nigeria’s electoral problems solely on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), arguing that politicians, electoral officials and citizens must also take responsibility for the integrity of elections.

He said Nigerians needed to “look in the mirror” when assessing the credibility of the electoral process.

“What kind of democracy do they want?” he asked.



“The outcome is as good as participants want to make it.”

Fashola said citizens should follow electoral rules, avoid attempts to manipulate registration and voting processes, monitor voting and counting at polling units and retain records of results announced at their polling stations.

He was also asked whether an INEC chairman appointed by an incumbent president seeking re-election could be genuinely independent.

Fashola responded: “Which INEC chairman has not been appointed by the president?”

He argued that during a presidential election, the INEC chairman principally serves as returning officer, receiving results that have travelled through the electoral system from polling units through other levels of collation.

“In the presidential election, he’s the returning officer,” Fashola said.



“He sits in that conference hall, or wherever he designates, and waits for the results to come from the states.”

Fashola said Nigerians should pay greater attention to what happens at polling units and throughout the collation process rather than assume that the national chairman alone determines the outcome.

“If there has been any failure of the process, it has taken place in the remote 176,840 polling units where you and I have operated,” he said.

He said the scale of conducting elections simultaneously across Nigeria made perfection difficult, noting that thousands of electoral personnel were required to perform similar tasks across different locations and terrain.

“It’s never a perfect undertaking,” Fashola said.



“176,000 people can’t behave the same way in 176,000 different locations.”

He also pointed to the role of other officials in the electoral chain, including returning officers and academics appointed to supervise aspects of collation, saying some had performed their responsibilities properly while others had “dropped the ball.”

Fashola maintained that improving elections required responsibility at every level rather than concentrating all scrutiny on the person occupying the office of INEC chairman.



He urged voters to participate actively in protecting their votes by remaining engaged through the counting process.

“Stay and watch where ballot votes are counted,” he said.

Tinubu deserves credit for Eko Atlantic

The former Lagos State governor backed Tinubu’s claim that he “tamed the Atlantic” in Lagos, revealing that, as Tinubu’s Chief of Staff, he personally drafted repeated letters to then President Olusegun Obasanjo seeking federal action against the encroaching ocean.

Fashola said Tinubu deserved credit for initiating the intervention that ultimately developed into the Eko Atlantic project, insisting that the idea predated his own tenure as governor.

“Let me set the record straight,” Fashola said.

“When the President says he tamed the Atlantic, he tamed it. Nobody should take the credit.”

Fashola, who served as Tinubu’s Chief of Staff before succeeding him as Lagos governor in 2007, said he was directly involved in correspondence with the Obasanjo administration as Lagos sought federal intervention.



“I was the Chief of Staff. I drafted those letters on his instructions to President Obasanjo,” he said.

According to Fashola, the requests were repeatedly rejected, but Tinubu continued to push the issue.

“There were several letters to Obasanjo. Obasanjo would reply, ‘No.’ He would say, ‘Write another one.’ I would draft it,” Fashola recalled.

He said he still had copies of the correspondence in his personal records.

Fashola said Tinubu’s persistence eventually led Lagos to pursue a different solution, with the state partnering with South Energyx Nigeria Limited on what became the Eko Atlantic development.

He recalled that the project attracted considerable scepticism at its inception, including questions about the company involved and the feasibility of reclaiming land from the Atlantic Ocean.

But Fashola argued that the development visible today vindicated the decision.

“All the waterfront properties arethere. Banks are back. Restaurants are back. Hotels are back. There’s a road. A big shopping mall has opened there,” he said.



“That is what infrastructure does — a new town.”

Fashola said when he became governor, his responsibility was not to claim ownership of the project but to protect and continue a vision he had already helped implement as Tinubu’s Chief of Staff.

“The idea was his,” he said. “And it’s not being hyperbolic. And it’s not being bombastic. I was in the room. And I still have those letters.”

He said the area had previously been an eroding beachfront, with the Atlantic threatening adjoining parts of Victoria Island and flooding roads around Ahmadu Bello Way and the Federal Palace Hotel axis.



Fashola argued that the transformation demonstrated how major infrastructure projects could create economic activity beyond their immediate physical purpose, pointing to residential developments, hotels, restaurants, construction activity and other businesses operating in the area.

“I believed in it. I continued it. The result is there,” he said.

Rejects death penalty for election riggers

Fashola rejected calls for election riggers to be killed, warning that Nigeria must move away from extreme political rhetoric as the country approaches the 2027 elections.

The Senior Advocate of Nigeria and former Minister of Power, Works and Housing said electoral offences must be punished firmly within the law rather than through threats of extrajudicial killing.

Reacting to the “rig and die” slogan attributed to former Deputy Senate President Ovie Omo-Agege and comparisons with former President Muhammadu Buhari’s controversial comments about ballot-box snatchers ahead of the 2019 elections, Fashola rejected capital punishment for electoral offenders.



Asked directly whether election riggers should face the death penalty, he replied: “Absolutely not. I mean, come on.

“I think we must move away from what I think are extreme narratives and rhetoric,” he said.

“The punishment under the Electoral Act is not death. And even if it were death, which I will not support, there’s a process before you take human life; a charge, a trial, an opportunity to defend yourself.”



Fashola said Nigerians should be unequivocal in condemning electoral manipulation without turning elections into a licence for violence.

“The penalty for rigging is not death. But don’t rig. Go and campaign for your party,” he said.

The former governor argued that political parties should concentrate on mobilising voters in areas where they were strong and reducing their losing margins elsewhere rather than attempting to manipulate electoral outcomes.

“There are places where each party is popular. There are places where parties will never win, no matter what they do there. That is the reality across the world,” he said.



Pressed on whether existing punishment for electoral offences was sufficient to deter offenders, Fashola said serious attacks on democracy could justify tougher custodial punishment, but maintained that the death penalty would be excessive.

He said some grave offences should not simply attract fines that allow offenders to effectively monetise their way out of punishment.

“I think maybe there might be stiffer sentences without option of fine, maybe a defined custodial sentence that is deterrent in nature,” Fashola said.

“I always hold the view that some very serious, really impactful conduct should not be allowed to be monetised, and undermining of democracy is seriously impactful.”



But on capital punishment, he remained categorical.

“I don’t think it goes that far.”

Fashola also called for greater public education on elections and democratic conduct, arguing that Nigeria had repeatedly amended its electoral laws without devoting comparable attention to educating citizens about the principles underpinning elections.

He proposed sustained nationwide enlightenment on electoral conduct and ethics, including education beginning from primary school and delivered in Nigeria’s major languages.

According to him, reducing desperation around elections required citizens and politicians to understand that democracy was a contest in which parties could win in one cycle and lose in another.

Funsho Williams’ Murder

Fashola recalled how the murder of Lagos governorship aspirant Funsho Williams confronted him with the possibility that entering politics could cost him his life, saying he nevertheless believed public service was “worth dying for.”

He reflected on Williams’ killing at his Ikoyi home and the failure to secure a conviction two decades later.

Asked how the murder affected him personally as he subsequently entered the Lagos governorship race, Fashola said it brought the risks of political participation sharply into focus.

“It showed me that, for me, it was like, look, listen, if you’re doing this election thing, this is it. These are the odds. You can lose your life in the process,” he said.



“So that’s the way it affected me.”

Fashola said the killing did not deter him from seeking office.

“As I told friends of mine, for me, speaking for myself at the time, it was worth dying for, to serve the country,” he said.

The former governor said the experience strengthened his determination to tackle violence and establish law and order if elected.

“My resolve was to then, from there, enthrone law and order, remove violence from our country,” Fashola said.

He pointed to his administration’s use of the Lagos State Ministry of Justice to prosecute offenders and its support for the police through reforms to the Rapid Response Squad, the establishment of the Lagos State Security Trust Fund and investment in equipment and other resources for law enforcement.

Fashola also recalled providing life insurance protection for security personnel whose work exposed them to violent crime, saying such protection should remain part of the support offered to officers undertaking dangerous assignments.

Turning to the continued absence of a conviction for Williams’ murder, Fashola said the case illustrated the importance of effective criminal investigation and evidence gathering.

“The justice system involves a process of investigation,” he said.

He argued that Nigeria needed stronger systems for identifying people and gathering forensic evidence, including DNA material, fingerprints, blood and other biological evidence capable of connecting suspects to crimes.

Fashola also lamented the destruction of a DNA facility during a protest, saying attacks on such infrastructure ultimately weakened law enforcement and the administration of justice.

He said unresolved murders underscored the need for highly skilled investigators capable of revisiting difficult cases and following evidence even years after a crime.

11m Nigerians Gained Electricity

Speaking further, Fashola said more than 11 million Nigerians gained access to electricity during his four years overseeing the power sector, describing it as a record he remained proud of.

“At that time, we connected, I think, 11 million-plus people to electricity supply for the first time in the history of this country,” the former Lagos State governor said.

“That is a record I’m proud of. Eleven million people extra have access to electricity.”

He acknowledged, however, that expanding access was different from guaranteeing reliable supply, saying the next challenge was ensuring that electricity became increasingly stable.

“I promised them incremental energy. And I said we will get to stable power before we go to uninterrupted power,” he said.

Fashola said Nigeria’s electricity problem could not be understood without considering the restructuring and privatisation of the sector before he became minister.

Generation and distribution were transferred to private operators in 2013, while the Federal Government retained responsibility for transmission.

According to Fashola, that fundamentally changed the government’s role in electricity delivery, with the federal power ministry’s workforce falling dramatically from the era when the state directly controlled generation and distribution.

He argued that electricity service providers must therefore be held accountable for the power they deliver to consumers rather than placing responsibility exclusively on the Federal Government.

Blames Bureaucracy for Stranded Power Equipment

Fashola blamed government bureaucracy and procurement constraints, rather than corruption, for more than 1,000 containers of electricity equipment stranded at Nigerian ports.

Speaking in the interview, he recalled initially struggling to understand how equipment intended for Nigeria’s electricity infrastructure could remain trapped at the country’s ports.

“Is it an alien port? It’s our port. Go and get the thing out of there,” Fashola recalled thinking when he first encountered the problem.

But he said a closer examination revealed a complicated chain of contractual and financial problems involving government procurement, changing prices and outstanding obligations to shipping and warehousing companies.

“When you contract with the government, most of this equipment had to be ordered,” he said.

“In the process of ordering, prices changed. There were no budgetary provisions. So, the contractor then looked at it and said, ‘If you don’t review my contract, my profit is gone.’”

Fashola said shipping and warehousing charges accumulated while the equipment remained uncleared, compounding the difficulty of getting the containers released and deployed.

He said his administration eventually recovered 910 containers, cancelled most of the affected contracts and recalled engineers with experience from the former National Electric Power Authority and the Transmission Company of Nigeria to help deploy the equipment.

“We cancelled most of the contracts. We called back the engineers from the old NEPA and TCN. They were the ones who were installing those equipment,” he said.

Fashola said the recovered equipment was subsequently deployed to electricity infrastructure projects in different parts of the country.

The former minister said the experience exposed deeper problems with Nigeria’s public procurement system, which he argued was too slow for the country’s infrastructure requirements.

“I was one of the very vocal voices while I served about the difficulty of our procurement law,” Fashola said, arguing that the system was inconsistent with the pace at which Nigeria needed to develop.

He said restrictions on advance payments could leave contractors exposed to substantial price changes between the award of a contract and the eventual manufacture and importation of equipment.

“If, for example, those contractors had been paid up to 70 per cent, they would have imported the equipment, brought it in before prices changed,” he said.

“But they give them 15 per cent, and while production is going on, the price suddenly changes.”

Fashola said such problems illustrated why delays in public projects should not automatically be attributed to graft.

“It’s less of corruption than the bureaucracy of public service,” he said.

He called for reforms to procurement processes to ensure that rules designed to protect public funds did not become obstacles to delivering critical infrastructure.

Advocates Electricity Decentralisation

Fashola, who left the power portfolio in 2019, said he no longer possessed the detailed operational information he had while running the ministry and would not attempt to speak authoritatively about its day-to-day performance several years later.

“I can’t speak about that ministry anymore,” he said. “I don’t have the detail I used to have.”

On what could accelerate improvements, Fashola identified the decentralisation of electricity regulation and supply as a significant opportunity, particularly for state governments.

“Well, I think that decentralisation has already happened,” he said.

He argued that removing restrictions that previously limited state participation had created a more favourable environment for governors to develop electricity solutions tailored to their states.

Recalling his tenure as Lagos State governor, Fashola said his administration had attempted to provide electricity to streets, communities, schools and other public institutions despite the legal constraints that existed at the time.

“If, when I was governor, I had this enabling environment, I don’t know what I would have done,” he said.

“We were powering streets, we were powering communities, we were powering schools, and we were powering many communal institutions at that time, in spite of the restrictions that we had.”

Fashola said the present legal framework consequently gave governors considerably more room to intervene in electricity provision.

“This is a more enabling environment for governors to play an even bigger role,” he said, adding that Lagos was already moving ahead in that direction.

APC Delivered Infrastructure, PDP Spent on Subsidy

Fashola also drew a contrast between the records of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the APC, arguing that the PDP spent scarce national resources sustaining fuel subsidies while the APC delivered major infrastructure projects and reforms.

Speaking in the interview, he said the subsidy system operated under previous administrations consumed foreign exchange that could have been deployed to expand Nigeria’s productive and industrial capacity.

“That administration ran a subsidy scheme that was impoverishing people in a way that they probably didn’t come to terms with,” Fashola said.

“Because all our foreign exchange income was spent not on developing the economy, not on expanding its productive or industrial needs, but on paying for fuel.”

Fashola, who served as Minister of Power, Works and Housing under former President Muhammadu Buhari, said the consequences included rising debt and government revenues being consumed by subsidy payments rather than investment in other sectors.

He contrasted that record with what he described as the APC’s delivery of major infrastructure projects that had remained unresolved for years.

“Big infrastructural ticket items, rail, major roads, the Second Niger Bridge that was a topical issue in every election cycle — all of these problems were solved under an APC government,” he said.

“A new port for this country was built under an APC government.”

Fashola said improvements to infrastructure serving Nigeria’s ports had directly affected traders, importers, exporters and industrialists whose businesses depended on the movement of goods.

He also cited the revival and expansion of rail transportation as evidence that the APC had tackled infrastructure bottlenecks with wider economic consequences.

“Rail transport in Nigeria, solved by an APC government, and that is helping businesses, that is helping people, that is helping the movement of goods and services that are needed,” he said.

Fashola said the distinction extended beyond physical infrastructure to major legislation, pointing to the Petroleum Industry Act, which was enacted under the Buhari administration after years of unsuccessful attempts to reform the petroleum sector.

He argued that the legislation had helped restore confidence in the industry and establish a framework for greater investment.

Fashola also rejected arguments that the current cost-of-living crisis could be attributed solely to APC policies, pointing to the economic disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent global shocks.

But he acknowledged that Nigerians were experiencing hardship, while maintaining that government policy should be judged by whether it addressed the structural problems facing the economy.

For Fashola, the comparison between the PDP and APC ultimately came down to what each party had done with the opportunity to govern.

“In terms of differential ideology, performance over a relatively shorter period, we have solved some of the biggest problems in Nigeria’s household,” he said.

World.title: Tinubu Pledges to Overcome Security Challenges, Seeks Public Support
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Laleye Dipo in Minna

President Bola Tinubu yesterday reiterated the federal government’s determination to overcome the security challenges facing parts of the country, saying no responsible government would be happy to see its citizens suffer.

President Tinubu made the remarks in a message to the 9th International Maulud Day celebration organised by the Jam’iyyatu Ansariddeen Attijaniyya Islamic Organisation at the Trade Fair Complex in Minna, Niger State.



Represented by the Director-General of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Organisation, Senator Abdul Aziz Yari, President Tinubu appealed to Nigerians to exercise patience, remain calm and support efforts towards restoring peace and stability in the country.



He called on Nigerians to embrace peace and work for national unity, adding that mutual understanding was essential for sustainable national growth and development.

The President urged Muslims to uphold the teachings of Islam and the exemplary lifestyle of Prophet Muhammad (SAW), particularly his virtues of peace, righteousness, compassion and tolerance.



Niger State Governor, Alhaji Mohammed Umaru Bago, in his remarks, commended the organisers for sustaining the annual religious gathering, reaffirming the importance of allowing the teachings of the Holy Qur’an and the exemplary conduct of Prophet Muhammad (SAW) to guide the lives of Muslims.

Governor Bago urged Muslims to practise the values of Islam, particularly peace, honesty, tolerance, compassion and respect for one another in their daily lives.



The governor called on Nigerians to continue praying for President Tinubu, the peace of the nation and the success of ongoing efforts towards national growth and development.

The Grand Khalifa and President of Jam’iyyatu Ansariddeen Attijaniyya Islamic Organisation, Sheikh Muhammad Mahi Ibrahim Niass, reminded Muslims of their responsibility to remain steadfast in the worship of Almighty Allah and abide by His commandments.

World.title: CBN Hits $1bn Monthly Diaspora Remittance Target, Eyes $1.5billion
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

*Plans interbank repo, overnight swap markets for Q1 2027

*Unveils comprehensive regulatory rulebook for financial institutions

Nume Ekeghe

The Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), Olayemi Cardoso, yesterday announced that Nigeria has achieved its long-standing target of attracting $1 billion in monthly diaspora remittances, setting a new goal of raising the inflows to $1.5 billion by June 2027.

Equally, the Body of Bank Chief Executive Officers in Nigeria assured customers of seamless banking services during the forthcoming festive season, pledging that digital transactions would remain uninterrupted despite the anticipated increase in payment activities.

Cardoso spoke at the 61st Annual Bankers’ Dinner of the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN) in Lagos, where he outlined the next phase of the apex bank’s financial sector reforms, including plans to deepen money markets, strengthen regulatory oversight and expand credit to the private sector.



The remittance milestone represents a significant development in the CBN’s efforts to channel more diaspora funds through formal financial institutions, particularly as Nigeria seeks to strengthen foreign exchange liquidity and reduce pressure on the naira.

Beyond remittances, the CBN Governor announced plans to introduce interbank repo and overnight indexed swap markets in the first quarter of 2027, while setting a target for the banking industry to at least double the private sector credit-to-GDP ratio by 2030.

He said: “When I stood before you last year, I spoke of our ambition to increase monthly remittances to $1 billion. I am pleased to report that this milestone has been achieved.



“We are now working towards increasing monthly remittances to $1.5 billion by the end of the first half of 2027.”

The planned introduction of the interbank repo and overnight indexed swap markets, which will be undertaken in collaboration with market participants, is expected to deepen liquidity management and strengthen financial institutions’ capacity to manage financing and interest rate risks.



It is also expected to gradually reduce dependence on the apex bank for functions that can be effectively handled by market participants.

“To further deepen liquidity and improve market efficiency, we will work with market participants to launch the interbank repo and overnight indexed swap markets in the first quarter of 2027,” Cardoso said.

He added that the development of these instruments would give market participants greater capacity to manage liquidity and longer-term financing risks.



“As these capabilities develop, our markets should become better equipped to manage liquidity and longer-term financing risks, with less reliance on the Central Bank for functions that can be performed effectively by market participants,” he said.

The planned introduction of the markets comes as the CBN continues to strengthen the infrastructure supporting monetary policy transmission and price discovery.



Earlier this year, the apex bank introduced the Nigeria Overnight Financing Rate (NOFR) as a pricing benchmark, which Cardoso said should see wider adoption by banks, including in loan pricing.

He said the benchmark would provide a more transparent reference point for financial transactions and support the development of more sophisticated lending, financing and risk-management products.

The governor also disclosed plans to introduce a comprehensive regulatory rulebook in 2027 to provide financial institutions with greater clarity on regulatory requirements and supervisory expectations.

According to him, the proposed framework was part of efforts to ensure that reforms undertaken over the past three years become embedded in the operations of the financial system rather than remain dependent on individual policy decisions.

“In the coming year, we will take a further step towards this objective with the introduction of a comprehensive and accessible regulatory rulebook, bringing greater clarity to regulatory requirements and supervisory standards.

“This will promote consistency, strengthen accountability and give financial institutions greater certainty in their dealings with the Central Bank,” Cardoso said.

He explained that institutionalising the reforms would require the CBN to strengthen the frameworks guiding monetary policy, improve transparency and accountability in its regulatory processes, and ensure that decisions are based on clear rules, sound analysis and consistent application.

For financial institutions, he said, the priority would be to strengthen market practices, institutional capabilities, risk management and governance.

“Deeper and more liquid markets, stronger risk management, effective governance and greater reliance on transparent market mechanisms will all be important to this endeavour,” he said.

On lending, Cardoso said the target to double private sector credit-to-GDP by 2030 was necessary to deepen financial intermediation, particularly as the cost of borrowing remains high and access to credit continues to constrain businesses despite the successful conclusion of the banking sector recapitalisation exercise.

“There is considerable scope to deepen financial intermediation in Nigeria. As inflation moderates and the broader lending environment improves, our ambition should be to at least double the private sector credit-to-GDP ratio by 2030, consistent with sound lending practices and financial stability,” he said.

Achieving the target, he noted, would require more than stronger bank balance sheets. It would also depend on increased domestic institutional investment, deeper capital markets and financial institutions with the capacity to finance businesses at different stages of growth.

The CBN governor acknowledged that affordable credit remained a challenge, even after banks raised approximately N4.65 trillion in fresh capital under the recapitalisation programme.

The exercise, introduced in March 2024, was concluded earlier this year, with 33 banks meeting the revised minimum capital requirements.

For Cardoso, the successful completion of the exercise was only the first step. The bigger test, he said, would be whether the additional capital could be translated into financing for productive businesses and investment across the economy.

“The next challenge is to put that strength to work,” he said.

He acknowledged concerns over why businesses continued to struggle with expensive and difficult-to-access financing despite the stronger capital positions of banks.

“Many may reasonably ask: if our banks are now stronger and better capitalised, why does credit remain so costly and difficult to access for many productive enterprises?

“Strong balance sheets are necessary, but the capacity of banks to lend affordably also depends on the environment in which they operate. The monetary policy stance required to contain inflation, elevated credit risks across several sectors, and weaknesses in the infrastructure for credit assessment, collateral and enforcement all influence the cost and availability of financing,” he said.

Cardoso also highlighted the gap between access to financial services and the ability of Nigerians to obtain credit, saying the next phase of financial inclusion must focus on how effectively the financial system serves households and businesses.

According to the 2026 Access to Financial Services Survey, approximately 79 per cent of Nigerian adults now use formal or informal financial services, while 64 per cent use digital financial services.

However, while 53 per cent of adults save formally, only 10 per cent borrow through formal financial channels.

For the CBN governor, the figures point to a financial inclusion challenge that goes beyond opening accounts and enabling digital transactions.

“We have made considerable progress in bringing Nigerians into the financial system. The next frontier is to make financial access more useful in people’s daily lives,” he said.

He illustrated this with the example of a market trader in Kano who receives about 200 transfers daily and saves consistently, arguing that her transaction history should help her secure financing to expand her business.

“For a market trader in Kano who receives 200 transfers a day, saves consistently and has built a viable business, financial inclusion should mean more than access to digital payments. A stronger, better-capitalised banking system should enable her to use that financial track record to access credit for expansion,” he said.

He also highlighted the CBN’s Payments System Vision 2028, which targets 95 per cent financial inclusion by 2028, alongside wider acceptance of QR and contactless payments, reduced reliance on cash outside the banking system and a significant reduction in payment fraud.

On the foreign exchange market, Cardoso said the naira had strengthened by approximately six per cent over the past year, while daily FX market turnover had at times exceeded $1 billion.

He also disclosed that daily turnover in the fixed-income market averaged N1.5 trillion, supported by a credible and tradable benchmark yield curve extending to 10 years.

However, he cautioned against interpreting a market-driven exchange rate as one that should remain stable at a particular level, noting that currency movements in either direction were a normal feature of such a system.

“As recent movements in the foreign exchange market remind us, a well-functioning market does not mean that prices remain static. Volatility is an inherent feature of global financial markets, and a market-determined exchange rate must be allowed to move in both directions in response to macroeconomic fundamentals and global developments,” he said.

He said emerging market currencies had experienced volatility amid changes in the United States interest rate environment and global risk sentiment, adding that Nigeria was now better positioned to withstand external pressures because of its stronger reserves and improved macroeconomic fundamentals.

Meanwhile, the Body of Bank Chief Executive Officers in Nigeria has assured customers of seamless banking services during the forthcoming festive season, pledging that digital transactions would remain uninterrupted despite the anticipated increase in payment activities.

The Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of United Bank for Africa (UBA) and Chairman of the Body of Bank CEOs in Nigeria, Oliver Alawuba, gave the assurance, saying banks were putting measures in place to ensure customers had access to cash and could carry out digital transactions without disruptions.

Speaking on behalf of bank chief executives, Alawuba said the industry was committed to ensuring a hitch-free banking experience throughout the festive period.

“We ensure you have all the cash you need. I will ensure that all your payments through our digital systems are seamless,” he said.

Earlier, the President and Chairman of Council of the CIBN, Dele Alabi, commended Cardoso for his leadership and reform initiatives, saying they were strengthening the resilience of the banking sector.

Alabi said Cardoso’s tenure had recorded significant milestones in foreign exchange market reforms, investor confidence and the successful implementation of the banking sector recapitalisation exercise.

He said: “Since assuming office, Mr. Governor has provided purposeful leadership through bold and disciplined reform, anchored on transparency, market efficiency, macroeconomic stability, and institutional credibility. His stewardship has witnessed far-reaching milestones in the foreign exchange market, decisive measures to strengthen investor confidence, and the successful implementation of the banking sector recapitalisation exercise, laying a solid foundation for stronger, more resilient and globally competitive financial institutions.

“Equally remarkable are the renewed emphasis on sound corporate governance, enhanced regulatory oversight, modernisation of payment systems, and improved consumer protection. Together, these initiatives reflect a resolute commitment to restoring confidence, deepening financial system resilience and positioning the banking industry as a formidable catalyst for investment, innovation and sustainable national development.”

World.title: 2027: Akpabio Urges Akwa Ibom Politicians to Sustain Peace, Unity
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

President of the Senate, Godswill Akpabio, has urged political leaders and residents of Akwa Ibom State to sustain the prevailing atmosphere of peace and unity ahead of the 2027 general elections, expressing confidence that the All Progressives Congress (APC) would record an overwhelming victory.

Akpabio, who spoke at the funeral service of Deaconess Esther Moses Enoidem, mother of Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), Emmanuel Enoidem, in Utu Ikot Eboro, Etim Ekpo Local Government Area of the state, yesterday, commended Governor Umo Eno for bringing prominent political figures in the state together under the APC.

He urged the people to work collectively to preserve the peace, stressing the importance of unity as political activities gradually intensify ahead of the next general election.

Akpabio expressed optimism that the ruling party would win overwhelmingly in the state, attributing the growing political cohesion to the governor’s efforts.

Enoidem, served as a commissioner during Akpabio’s tenure as governor of Akwa Ibom State. He was also a former National Legal Adviser of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) before recently joining the APC.

In his tribute, the Senate President expressed sadness over the death of Deaconess Enoidem, who died at the age of 92, describing her passing as a painful loss to her family.

He acknowledged the strong bond between the deceased and her son, noting that mothers play vital roles in shaping family values, character and the lives of their children.

While acknowledging the pain of losing a mother, Akpabio urged the bereaved family to draw comfort from her long life and the opportunity she had to witness her son’s achievements.

He also praised the late matriarch’s commitment to Christian values, describing her life as one marked by faith, love and service.

Reflecting on the importance of motherhood and family in nation-building, Akpabio said the family remained fundamental to moral development, social stability and national cohesion.

He noted that Nigeria’s challenges, including insecurity, economic hardship, social dislocation and declining societal values, made it imperative for citizens to embrace compassion, integrity, discipline, tolerance and collective responsibility.

According to him, while legislation, public policies and institutional reforms are essential to national development, the character of a nation ultimately depends on the values its citizens uphold.

He stressed that building a peaceful and prosperous Nigeria required collective commitment to ethical conduct, respect for human dignity, national unity and responsibility towards future generations.

The Senate President urged Enoidem and his siblings to uphold the values their mother represented, saying the best tribute to the deceased would be to sustain the principles she lived by.

World.title: Johannesburg Stock Exchange Courts Dangote Refinery for Listing in Expansion Push
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Sunday Ehigiator with agency report

The Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), Africa’s biggest stock exchange is working with Dangote Group to pave the way for a potential secondary listing of its giant oil refinery in South Africa, an outcome the bourse’s chief said would be the ideal next step after its landmark Nigerian initial public offering.

JSE Ltd. worked “very closely” with the company owned by the continent’s richest man, Aliko Dangote, as well as the Nigerian Stock Exchange ahead of the IPO of what will be Africa’s largest company with a primary local listing, CEO Valdene Reddy said in an interview on Bloomberg Television.

“The optimum would be to get to a secondary listing,” Reddy said. “There would still be some regulatory alignment that we would need to do” given Nigerian listing rules don’t match South Africa’s, “but this is a high-priority item for us to get right.”

A Johannesburg listing would give Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE access to Africa’s deepest capital pool and some of its largest institutional investors.

The company would also need to meet JSE listing rules that include a minimum 10 percent free float. Dangote Petroleum is selling just 3.3 percent of its enlarged share capital in the IPO, rising to about 4.25 per cent if it fully exercises a 30 perent overallotment option.

The IPO — Africa’s biggest to date — attracted the equivalent of about $4.3 billion of applications, almost three times the base amount it sought to raise.

South African funds are also subject to prudential limits on foreign investments; an inward listing in Johannesburg could open Dangote to the country’s large investor base without those institutions having to use part of their offshore allocations.

“There’s much more that they need to do to diversify their shareholder base, to get deeper institutional investors behind them, to get diverse investors from across the globe,” Reddy said. “The South African institutional investor is one they are acutely aware of that they would like to attract.”

The refinery is offering depositary receipts in Botswana and Kenya, but that’s “not quite the same as having another listing,” Reddy said, adding that working with Dangote will remain a high priority.

The JSE is on a “massive drive” to add new listings and the “pipeline looks

strong,” Reddy said.

“We’re not going to be India or Saudi or Hong Kong with 10 to 15 fresh IPOs,” she said, adding that South Africa still needs more catalysts to galvanize its economy. “But what we are seeing is a mix of fresh IPOs, secondary listings, additional capital raises, converting some of the interesting continental plays in listings.”

She said the bourse expects an IPO in the first quarter, without disclosing the name of the South African company.

World.title: Oando Signs N203.8bn Rights Issue Agreements to Strengthen Financial Position
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Oando Plc has signed agreements for its proposed N203.8 billion rights issue at N50 per share, advancing its broader recapitalisation programme aimed at strengthening its operations and financial position.

The Group Chief Executive of Oando Plc announced the development in a post on X, explaining that the proceeds would be channelled towards developing the company’s oil and gas assets, boosting the working capital of its trading business and reducing its debt burden.

“Today, we signed the agreements for our rights issue of approximately ₦203.8bn at ₦50 per share, an important step in our broader recapitalisation programme,” he said.

He explained that the funds would help advance the company’s oil and gas projects, improve liquidity in its trading business and lower its indebtedness.

“The proceeds will support the development of our oil and gas assets, strengthen the working capital of our trading business and reduce indebtedness, enabling stronger cash flows, reinvestment in growth and sustainable returns to shareholders,” he stated.

The chief executive said the company opted for a rights issue to allow existing shareholders to participate first in its next phase of expansion.

“We chose a rights issue deliberately, to give existing shareholders the first opportunity to participate in this next phase of Oando’s growth. Ultimately, our performance must justify the confidence placed in us,” he said.

He thanked shareholders for their continued support and confidence, noting that the company’s founders were also investors who had experienced the successes and challenges of its business journey.

“To our fellow shareholders, thank you for your steadfast belief in Oando. As founders and shareholders ourselves, we have shared in the achievements and challenges of this journey, and we remain committed to building an enterprise that delivers the returns our collective investment deserves,” he added.

The executive also recognised the contributions of the company’s Board, regulators, issuing houses, professional advisers and the wider transaction team in reaching the milestone.

Looking ahead, he said the company would focus on stepping up drilling activities, expanding its businesses, improving its financial position and delivering greater value to investors.

“The task before us is clear: drill more wells, grow our businesses, strengthen our financial position and deliver greater value to shareholders,” he said.

World.title: Uduere Killings: Omo-Agege Denies Police Invitation, Police Arrest Egbo
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

.CSO decries rising political violence ahead of 2027 elections

Sylvester Idowu in Warri and Linus Aleke in Abuja

The former Deputy President of the Senate, Senator Ovie Omo-Agege, has denied snubbing an invitation by the Delta State Police Command over last Monday’s deadly attack at Uduere community, insisting that neither he nor his office has received any formal invitation from the police.

This came as the Chairman of Ughelli North Local Government Area of Delta State, Olorogun Jaro Egbo, was reportedly arrested by the police in connection with the violence, while civil society organisation, Global Rights, raised concerns over growing political violence and attacks on political actors ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Egbo was among several persons invited by the police for questioning over the killings that occurred during a political campaign organised by the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Uduere.

The council chairman was directed in an invitation letter to appear at the Delta State Police Headquarters, Asaba, by 2pm on Thursday, to assist investigators with their inquiries.

However, sources disclosed yesterday that, rather than merely honouring the invitation, Egbo was arrested by security operatives and subsequently flown to Abuja.

The circumstances surrounding his reported arrest and transfer to Abuja remained unclear, as the police had yet to provide an official explanation.

While one account said he was arrested before honouring the invitation, another source told THISDAY that he honoured the invitation at Asaba, where he was picked up and flown to Abuja by a special squad.

A visit to the council secretariat yesterday showed that workers had fled the premises for fear of a reprisal attack.

The Delta State Police Public Relations Officer, SP Edafe Bright, could not be reached for confirmation at the time of filing this report.

Meanwhile, Omo-Agege, the NDC candidate for Delta Central Senatorial District, described reports that he had refused to honour a police invitation as false, arguing that he could not have declined an invitation that had not been formally communicated to him.

According to a statement issued yesterday and signed by his Media Adviser, Sunny Areh, the former deputy senate president said he first learnt of the purported police invitation through the Command’s announcement in the media.

“It isn’t true. You can’t turn down an invitation you never received,” Omo-Agege declared.

According to him, no letter had been delivered to him or his office, nor had any police officer personally served him with an invitation.

Omo-Agege also challenged the credibility of reports suggesting that he refused to honour the police invitation, describing the allegation as being based on information from a single unnamed source.

“The Senator hasn’t told the police, or anyone else, that he won’t appear,” the statement said.

Revisiting the bloody incident at Uduere, Omo-Agege maintained that he was himself a victim of the attack, which he characterised as an assassination attempt.

He alleged that senior members of his campaign team were killed during the incident, while others sustained serious injuries and remained hospitalised.

The former senator insisted that he was interested in seeing the circumstances surrounding the violence fully investigated and those responsible brought to justice.

“He wants this case resolved, and he wants justice for the dead and the wounded,” the statement said.

Omo-Agege, however, declared his readiness to honour any lawful invitation from the police, provided it was formally communicated through his office to enable both parties to agree on a convenient date.

He also faulted the decision to announce the purported invitation publicly before it was formally served on him, describing the approach as inconsistent with due process.

“A summons announced in the press before it reaches the person named is not due process, and he won’t be tried in the media,” he added.

The development comes amid heightened political tension in Delta State following the deadly violence at Uduere, which has generated controversy and calls for a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the attack.

In a related development, the Country Director of Global Rights, Brenda Nwosa, expressed deep concern over growing reports of political violence, attacks on political actors and their supporters, and the increasingly hostile atmosphere surrounding political activities ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Nwosa said the reported attack on the campaign entourage of Omo-Agege in Uduere, Ughelli North Local Government Area of Delta State, was particularly disturbing.

Citing recent reports, she said gunmen opened fire during a campaign tour, leaving four people dead and several others critically injured, while the senatorial candidate reportedly escaped unharmed.

“We strongly condemn this attack and extend our deepest condolences to the families of those killed, while wishing the injured a full recovery. No political ambition, disagreement or rivalry can justify the taking of innocent lives. The right to campaign, organise, associate and participate in the political process must be protected, irrespective of party affiliation or political persuasion.

“Nigeria cannot afford a political environment in which seeking public office or supporting a candidate becomes a risk to one’s life. We are equally concerned by the reported incident involving President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s convoy after Juma’at prayers at the Shehu Shagari Central Mosque in Abuja on 13 November.

“While reports of the President’s personal exposure to physical assault remain disputed, the police confirmed that his departing convoy was attacked with stones and other objects, damaging vehicles and injuring security personnel. We condemn any act of violence or destruction of property, just as we recognise the right of citizens to express dissatisfaction with the government and public leadership through peaceful and lawful means.

“These incidents, alongside other reported attacks and disruptions of political gatherings across the country, must not be treated as isolated disturbances or dismissed as ordinary political rivalry. They point to the urgent need for political actors, party supporters, security agencies and citizens to reject violence, intimidation, inflammatory rhetoric and political intolerance,” the statement said.

Nwosa said anger must never become a justification for assault, arson, assassination attempts or the destruction of lives and property.

She urged political leaders not to mistake public restraint for public satisfaction, stressing that citizens have the right to demand accountability, question leadership and express their displeasure without intimidation or being silenced.

Nwosa maintained that neither violence nor the suppression of peaceful dissent had a place in a functioning democracy.

According to her, “The ballot must remain the most powerful instrument through which Nigerians determine their leadership and hold elected officials accountable. Political disagreements must be resolved through democratic participation, peaceful civic engagement, lawful protests and the electoral process, not through threats, violence and intimidation.

“Equally, political leaders must earn public support through credible leadership, responsible conduct and policies that reflect the realities of ordinary Nigerians.

“Global Rights calls on the Nigeria Police Force and other relevant security agencies to conduct prompt, thorough, impartial and transparent investigations into the Ughelli North attack and other reported incidents of political violence. Authorities must identify and prosecute those responsible in accordance with the law, regardless of their political affiliations or positions. Security agencies must also take preventive measures to protect political gatherings, candidates, campaign teams, supporters and ordinary citizens as political activities intensify.

“Political leadership carries a responsibility to promote tolerance, restraint and respect for democratic processes, particularly in an increasingly charged political environment.

“As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general elections, the Incident Centre for Election Atrocities (ICEA) will continue to monitor and document incidents that threaten the safety, integrity and credibility of the electoral process. We are watching, documenting and counting. Every life lost, every person injured, every attack and every attempt to intimidate citizens out of political participation matters,” the group said.

The Country Director said the incidents must not disappear into a cycle of political rhetoric and impunity, adding that those responsible must be held accountable.

World.title: Julius Malema wins court battle against Helen Zille
World.content:
EFF leader Julius Malema has secured an interim court interdict against the DA’s Helen Zille, who previously refused to retract her allegations against him. Images: X

EFF leader Julius Malema has secured an interim interdict against the DA’s Helen Zille over allegations she made about his involvement in Johannesburg’s affairs during Herman Mashaba’s previous tenure as mayor.

The Gauteng High Court in Johannesburg ruled in favour of Malema and the EFF on Friday, 27 November.

The ruling came on the same day that Zille lost the Johannesburg mayoral race to Mashaba.



COURT BARS ZILLE FROM REPEATING MALEMA ALLEGATIONS

The dispute stems from an eNCA interview on Sunday, 8 November, during which Zille accused Malema of influencing municipal decisions while Mashaba served as Johannesburg mayor.

Judge Marcus Senyatsi barred Zille from repeating four specific allegations against the EFF leader.

These relate to Malema’s alleged control of City Power, interference in municipal fleet tenders, influence over Shadrack Sibiya’s appointment as head of Johannesburg’s anti-corruption unit and use of the EFF’s political support to secure these decisions.



The court found that Zille had not presented sufficient evidence to substantiate the specific allegations at this stage of the proceedings.

ZILLE REFUSED TO APOLOGISE

Malema’s lawyers recently sent Zille a letter of demand on 9 November, calling on her to retract her statements and publicly apologise.

Zille responded with a single word on social media: “No.”



She maintained that her allegations were true and indicated that she was prepared to defend them in court.

Malema denied the allegations and, together with the EFF, launched an urgent court application.

MALEMA GIVEN 15 COURT DAYS

The court gave Malema and the EFF 15 court days to institute defamation proceedings.



Should they fail to meet the deadline, the interim interdict will lapse.

The court also ordered Zille to pay the legal costs of the application, including those of two counsel where applicable.

However, Friday’s ruling does not prevent Zille from criticising Malema, the EFF or Johannesburg’s coalition arrangements.



The trial court will ultimately determine whether Zille’s allegations were defamatory and whether she can substantiate them.

World.title: Mashaba wins Joburg mayoral vote, Zille vows to fight on
World.content:
ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba has reclaimed the Johannesburg mayoral chain after defeating the DA’s Helen Zille. Image: X

ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba has reclaimed the Johannesburg mayoral chain, prompting a swift response from defeated DA candidate Helen Zille.

Zille took to Facebook on Friday, 27 November, to take aim at ActionSA and its coalition partners, vowing that the DA would continue fighting for Johannesburg residents.

“For the DA, it was just the end of the beginning. For ActionSA and their coalition of chaos, this is the beginning of the end,” Zille wrote.



“We will fight for you!”

MASHABA DEFEATS ZILLE IN JOBURG MAYORAL VOTE

Mashaba secured 170 votes against Zille’s 97 during Friday’s Johannesburg council sitting, returning to the position he vacated seven years ago.

His election followed days of coalition negotiations after no party secured an outright majority in the 4 November local government elections.



Mashaba secured the backing of the ANC, EFF and uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party.

Despite emerging as the biggest party in Johannesburg with 91 council seats, the DA failed to garner enough support to govern the metro.

I have been just elected as the Executive Mayor of Joburg! 🇿🇦



Now, it’s time to roll up our sleeves and hit the ground running. The hard work of delivering for the residents of Johannesburg begins immediately!#OperationFixJoburg https://t.co/IasaSuH8SF pic.twitter.com/crflbFA4cN  November 27, 2026

ZILLE REFUSED TO STEP ASIDE

Hours before councillors elected Mashaba, Zille defended her refusal to withdraw from the mayoral race.

ActionSA had previously proposed that both Mashaba and Zille abandon their mayoral ambitions, allowing the DA to nominate another candidate.

However, Zille described the proposal as undemocratic, arguing that Mashaba had no right to dictate who the DA nominated.



“Then Herman Mashaba may as well be the leader of the DA,” she said.

ACTIONSA SECURES TWO GAUTENG METROS

Earlier this week, ActionSA’s Nasiphi Moya defeated the DA’s Cilliers Brink to retain her position as Tshwane mayor.

ActionSA now holds two of Gauteng’s three mayoral positions.



Mashaba’s return comes exactly seven years after his resignation as Johannesburg mayor took effect on 27 November 2019.

He previously served as mayor under the DA banner before founding ActionSA in 2020.

World.title: Bitter SWEET: Geely E5 Apex Plus driven
World.content:
Warning, this Geely E5 Apex Plus drive fully is a purely subjective piece. It will likely not resemble anything a customer of this excellent EV will actually experience. However, it is what we experienced during our test. And so, it is what we must convey.

Firstly, woah, what a brilliant vehicle. Congrats, Geely. We’ve driven more or less every new-energy entrant from China in the last two years. And the E5 Apex Plus is definitely out of the top drawer. We’d probably put it in the same rarefied category as the Haval H6 PHEV and BYD Dolphin Surf, which we rate very highly.

GEELY E5 APEX PLUS DRIVE

However, coming to this conclusion was no easy feat due to a number of logistical challenges, shall we say. The vehicle arrived with no charging card. Now, to the fleet manager’s credit, she did warn me beforehand. For those who don’t know – most EVs do have a dedicated card. It’s just easier for the manufacturer to pair a card with their vehicle than have every journalist setup multiple accounts for any possible charging scenario.



Also, when you buy one of these wonderful Geely E5’s, you’ll most likely get the home charger fitted. So, like we said, this scenario won’t even occur for an actual owner. Nevertheless, here we are, charged (pun intended) with reviewing this car, but without many of the physical tools to do so …

TETHERED-CABLE CHARGERS

What a truly wonder space to occupy. Centre screen is massive and responsive. Wireless phone charger works well. And the seats are wonderfully comfortable. Image: Ray Leathern

We took delivery of the EV in the city with roughly a quarter charge, a range of 140 km. It’s about a 40 km drive down South where we’re based. And the public charging infrastructure is sorely lacking beyond the city. Wanting to top up the battery right away, we headed for the Constantia Emporium, where the Rubicon Charging app reliably told us a charger was available. Some shopping while the Geely E5 tops up? Lovely …

Except, of course, this particular charger doesn’t have a tethered cable. We rummage beneath the cavernous boot to find only a charger with a three-prong wall socket. Not good. Between here and home there are no more chargers. One possible option is to double back to Canal Walk where we know there’s a DC fast charger with a tethered cable.



TIME-MILEAGE MANAGEMENT

However, just to get there will use up perhaps half of the already limited range, and it is late afternoon. Then there’s the thought of what if it’s offline or occupied when we get there? Now we don’t have enough range to get home and we’re stuck in rush-hour traffic, driving even less efficiently. We cut our losses and head home instead. At least we’ve got the wall-socket connection …

Of course, it’s not advisable to charge a full EV like the Geely E5 through a wall socket. But this is beginning to feel like an emergency scenario. A 68 kWh lithium iron phosphate battery does not like that sort of treatment. It’s the equivalent of a trickle charge. We know this because we used to charge an e-Golf – one of the few brought in by Volkswagen a few years back – through a wall socket at our old office. A full 9 am-to-5 pm charge wouldn’t come close refilling the battery.

TRIP THE SYSTEM

With nowhere to go, we had plenty of time to poke about. Under the bonnet is the 160 kW electric motor that drives the front wheels exclusively. Image: Ray Leathern

True to form – with range down to 100 km – we get the Geely E5 connected to a wall socket at home. The computer says a full charge will take 14 hours. Oh well, could be an interesting exercise to see how this goes. About one hour in, the house power trips. The cable is burning hot when we go to disconnect it. In that time, that battery has gained about 5 km range.



Wait for everything to cool and try the wall socket again. Another hour goes by and, boom, house power goes down again. We decide to abandon this plan of attack and save a potential visit from the fire department. And would you like to know the craziest part? Just two hours quadrupled our daily energy consumption. Four times what we spend on any given day to run an entire house won’t so even get us back over OuKaapsWeg.

AND SO IT GOES

Later in the week, we try a slow charger down at the Sun Valley mall. It has a tethered cable but in our experience it rarely works. As it proved yet again. The issue is there’s no QR code/command screen, you must swipe a physical card. Of course, we have the Rubicon app with the charge wallet topped up, but the charger simply won’t initiate.

Despite this, in between our attempts to recharge, we were boundlessly impressed by the Geely E5 Apex Plus. The steering is light and quick but still feels sporty and connected. Its performance is perfectly adequate, all in sumptuous comfort and silence. Interior tech and connectivity are some of the best in class. You have the option of auto-cooled seats, which work brilliantly well, along with numerous seat massage functions.



THE VERDICT

A 68 kWh battery requires proper juice for an efficient recharge, don’t mess about with the wall socket. Image: Ray Leathern

Finally, days later, with the range down to 60 km, we bit the bullet and set course for Canal Walk. No matter if it took all day, we would plug in there. Well, that was the plan until we encountered roadworks on OuKaapseWeg. Normally free flowing mid-morning, we must’ve sat stationary for nearly 30 minutes in a stop and go, range silently draining away. We abandoned this plan, too, and chalked the whole thing down to bad EV juju.

In conclusion, even in our limited time behind the wheel, the Geely E5 impressed immensely. If you’ve driven any of the competition, you’ll be able to tell right away this is one of the good ones. However, we’d love another crack it at. Either starting with a full charge, a charge card or, at the very least, a suitable range of cables included.
