His need was genuine. But the price he paid was far greater than the temporary relief he received.” Boakai’s message is that Liberians will see real benefits from the deal. Cummings’ warning is that satisfying today’s hunger could cost the country something far more valuable.

Both speak for future generations, to opposite ends. Boakai called the signing “a historic day for Liberia as we lay the foundations for tomorrow.” Cummings warned that “in our urgency to solve today’s problems, we must not mortgage tomorrow’s possibilities.” To the President, the deal is a gift to future generations. To Cummings, it is a bill they may be left to pay.

They disagree on whether this is debt. The government insists the deal adds no borrowing. The President’s legal adviser, Keita, said “So we are not going to be adding to the government’s debt, and that is a big deal for all of us.” Cummings rejects the premise: “There is no such thing as free infrastructure. Someone ultimately pays.” His concern is precisely that pledging future revenue lets the government take on a debt-like obligation “outside traditional public debt transparency mechanisms.” The two sides are not arguing about the same numbers. They are arguing about whether committing future income counts as borrowing.

Both claim value for money. Boakai said “We wanted to make sure we got the best for our money and for the future.” Cummings’ closing line uses nearly the same words: infrastructure “at the right price, under the right conditions.” The difference is proof. The government points to safeguards it says are already written into the deal: audit rights and an owner’s engineer to monitor every stage and flag inferior materials or overcharging, and Keita added that “The company even agreed to be fined if they ever overcharge us.” Cummings wants independent valuation, independent certification and full publication of the documents. Both men are addressing the same risk, overcharging. The question is whether the government’s in-house safeguards are enough, or whether the checks must come from outside.

What the President left out. Published accounts of Wednesday’s speech do not mention competitive bidding, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission, the role of the Legislature, or who will build the projects. Those gaps are exactly where Cummings focused on Thursday.

The Cummings Argument

Cummings went out of his way to say he is not against the deal itself. “We are not opposed to infrastructure development. We are not opposed to investment,” he said. “What we oppose is lack of transparency.”

He listed ten concerns. They include:

• possible breach of the Public Procurement and Concessions Act;

• no competitive bidding;

• no independent valuation or engineering assessment;

• possible overpricing;

• automatic deductions from future government revenue;

• conflict-of-interest risks.

He then set out ten conditions he says must be met before the deal proceeds. Among them: publication of all transaction documents, legislative hearings, an independent debt sustainability analysis, and independent certification of project costs and completed works.

Where the Criticism Lands

On several points, the public record supports him.

No competitive bidding. Reporting on the deal shows that MAPA İnşaat ve Ticaret A.Ş. is identified as the engineering and construction contractor. The Turkish Contractors Association identifies Mehmet Günal as MAPA’s chairman and Murathan Günal as deputy chairman, linking the family to both sides of the deal. In practical terms, the company financing the projects and the company building them appear to share the same family owners. The Liberian Observer found no description of a competitive tender for selecting MAPA, and noted that the government has not publicly released its independent financial due diligence or any comparative assessment of contractors. The paper was careful to add that common ownership is not, by itself, evidence of improper conduct, but it matters when judging how the contracts are priced and supervised.

That is also why the government’s owner’s engineer matters, and why Cummings is right to ask who appoints that engineer and who that engineer answers to. Cummings lists “governance and conflict-of-interest concerns” but never names MAPA or the Günal family. That was the most concrete point available to him, and he left it out.

The Legislature was not at the table. Senator Abe Darius Dillon has said the National Legislature had no role in negotiating or signing the deal. That supports Cummings’ call for legislative review and public hearings before ratification.

The final cost is unclear. Cummings warns that the real bill could be higher than US$5.7 billion. The published project list gives him some support. Alongside the power and road works, the government has announced a further US$1 billion for road networks across all regions, and it is not clear whether that is part of the US$5.7 billion or on top of it. Keita also defended the cost by saying the Via dam is designed to expand to at least 1,000 megawatts. If that expansion is part of the plan, its cost, and who pays for it, has not been disclosed.

Where It Falls Short

Cummings’ case is stronger on principle than on evidence.

His most serious charge is that royalties, income taxes, dividends and other government revenues from Liberia’s natural resources could be “redirected toward repayment — for decades.” But he supports this only with “indications.” He does not cite a clause, a figure or a document.

The government’s position is narrower. It says it will use extra revenue that higher gold prices make possible, while the company will also keep making its regular payments into the Consolidated Account. Who is right depends on how much that “extra” revenue is, how it is calculated, and what happens if gold prices fall. Neither the President on Wednesday nor Cummings on Thursday put those numbers before the public.

The scale is worth noting. LEITI’s FY2023 reconciliation report lists government revenues attributed to Bea Mountain at approximately $33.47 million for that fiscal year. Gold prices have risen sharply since then. Even so, paying off a US$5.7 billion program from one mine’s revenue would require gold earnings far above anything Liberia has recorded. Cummings could have made that point with hard figures. Instead, he leaned on the Esau story.

Nor does he say what he would do instead. He calls on the government to consider “alternative financing models” that could be cheaper, but he names none. For a former Coca-Cola executive who is expected to seek the presidency again in 2029, that is a missed opportunity to show how he would pay for 270 megawatts of electricity without the gold.

His description of the deal as “a human rights issue” may also strike some readers as overreach. His stronger points are the plainer ones: procurement, valuation and disclosure.

The Politics

Cummings insists this “is not a government-versus-opposition issue.” Even so, his remarks position him as the opposition’s guardian of the public purse, a role he has built since 2017.

That leaves two competing messages. The President promises the welder and the barber electricity and roads within five years. Cummings warns that the meal may cost the birthright. With much of the country still without reliable electricity, the President’s message may be the easier one for voters to accept.

What Comes Next

The deal now goes to the Legislature for ratification. That is where the two speeches will be tested against each other.

Dillon has said he wants the agreement scrutinized before any vote but has not said which way he leans. The questions lawmakers can fairly ask are the ones neither the President nor his critic fully answered:

• How much new revenue does the deal assume, and at what gold price?

• What happens to the repayment schedule if gold prices fall?

• Was MAPA’s pricing independently checked, and against what benchmark?

• Who appoints the owner’s engineer, and who does that engineer report to?

• Did the PPCC review the procurement?

• Is the US$1 billion road program inside or outside the US$5.7 billion?

On Wednesday, the President said the deal would lay “the foundations for tomorrow.” On Thursday, Cummings said history will judge the agreement not by “the speeches delivered on signing day,” but by what remains in 20, 30 and 40 years. Both men are appealing to the same future, and only the Legislature’s scrutiny of the deal will show which of them is right about it.

World.title: LRA Dashboard: Domestic Revenue Tops Us$1.2 Billion As Two Mining Giants Carry The Load
World.content:
ArcelorMittal, Bea Mountain pay more than a third of Liberia's domestic revenue as LRA beats FY2026 targets with five weeks left

MONROVIA – Liberia’s tax collector is on the verge of closing the books on its best year ever, but a closer look at who is paying shows how much of that success rests on a few companies.

By Rodney D Sieh

As of Thursday afternoon, the LRA’s live revenue dashboard showed a “balance to be collected” of US$13,177,571.81 against the government’s consolidated FY2026 target of US$1,301,728,411.15. The fiscal year runs to December 31.



A banner across the dashboard declared: “Congratulations, Domestic Tax! FY2026 target achieved!”

Taxes above target

According to the dashboard:

• Domestic tax collections stood at US$902.26 million against a target of US$895.79 million, about US$6.5 million over.



• Customs collected US$307.69 million against a budget of US$280.93 million, about US$26.8 million over.

• Combined domestic revenue reached US$1.21 billion against a target of US$1.18 billion, a surplus of about US$33.2 million.

That puts Liberia past the US$1 billion mark the LRA set for itself last year. In 2025, the LRA collected about US$818 million, exceeding the approved target of US$804.6 million by US$13.4 million, which it called the highest outturn in the country’s history. If the dashboard figures hold, FY2026 domestic revenue is up nearly 48 percent on that record.

Because domestic revenue is already over target, the remaining US$13 million gap sits in the US$120 million budgeted from external resources such as donor grants. The dashboard’s totals imply that about US$73.6 million of that has come in so far, leaving a shortfall of about US$46 million. The tax surplus covers most of it, but not all.

Two companies, a third of the revenue

LRA data on its top revenue contributors show how concentrated the base is.

ArcelorMittal Liberia leads with US$289.4 million, more than double the next payer. That figure likely includes a one-off payment. Under the iron ore company’s third Mineral Development Agreement, a US$200 million signature bonus was payable to the Government of Liberia within 30 days of the effective date, and the Senate passed the agreement on January 30, 2026. Without that bonus, ArcelorMittal’s ordinary contribution would be about US$89 million.

Bea Mountain Mining Corporation is second at US$134.1 million. That is a steep rise for the gold miner. LEITI’s FY2023 reconciliation report listed government revenues attributed to Bea Mountain at approximately $33.47 million for that fiscal year. Record gold prices are driving the jump.

Together, the two mining companies paid about US$423.5 million, roughly 35 percent of all domestic revenue collected this year.

The top ten together paid about US$608.3 million, just over half of all domestic revenue.

Two of the top ten are government bodies. The Civil Service Agency, in third place, appears largely because it remits income tax withheld from civil servants’ salaries. In effect, that is the government paying itself through its own payroll. The Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority is ninth.

Three of the top ten are fuel importers: Aminata & Sons, Conex Petroleum and West Oil. Orange Liberia is the only telecom company in the top ten. Its rival, Lonestar Cell MTN, is not on the list.

November snapshot

A separate LRA table shows the top contributors for what appears to be November alone. A European Union grant of US$17.8 million led the list. ArcelorMittal followed with US$13.5 million and Bea Mountain with US$9.3 million. Lonestar Cell MTN appears there at US$1.26 million, behind Orange at US$1.89 million.

Why it matters

The figures have a direct bearing on this week’s biggest economic story. On Wednesday, President Joseph Nyuma Boakai signed a US$5.7 billion infrastructure deal under which new revenue from Bea Mountain, driven by higher gold prices, would be “ring-fenced” from 2027 to pay for power plants and roads.

The LRA data show what is at stake. Bea Mountain is now the government’s second-largest source of domestic revenue. How much of its future payments go into the infrastructure deal, rather than into the national budget, will matter more than ever.

The data also point to a broader risk. When one iron ore company and one gold miner provide over a third of domestic revenue, a fall in iron ore or gold prices, or a disruption at either mine, would hit the budget hard. And ArcelorMittal’s US$200 million bonus will not recur next year. To match FY2026, the LRA would have to make up that money from other sources in FY2027.

A caution on the numbers

The dashboard describes itself as showing “unreconciled collections.” The figures may change once the LRA reconciles its accounts at year-end, and the agency has not yet published final FY2026 figures.

World.title: Liberia: LPRA Launches Five-Year Strategic Plan, Discloses US$13.8 Million Revenue Contribution
World.content:
LPRA Director General Marilyn T. Logan speaks the launch of five-years strategic plan at EJS Ministerial Complex in Monrovia/ 26/112026

The Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority (LPRA) has launched a five-year Strategic Plan covering 2026 to 2030, with a commitment to publish its first-ever State of the Petroleum Sector Report in 2027. The plan seeks to strengthen petroleum regulation, attract investment, develop local technical expertise and improve transparency and accountability in Liberia’s oil and gas industry.

The Strategic Plan, covering 2026 to 2030, was unveiled to stakeholders Thursday at the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Ministerial Complex in Monrovia by LPRA Director General Hon. Marilyn T. Logan, who said the roadmap would position Liberia to compete more effectively for global petroleum exploration investment while ensuring that the country’s natural resources are managed in the national interest.

Speaking at the launch, Minister of State for Presidential Affairs Samuel Stevquoah commended the LPRA for developing the plan, emphasizing President Joseph Boakai’s expectation that Liberians must benefit fairly from the country’s petroleum resources.



He said the President wants to ensure that Liberians have a fair share when international oil companies begin operations in the country.

“Liberians really want to know whether they will have a fair share when oil companies begin operation in Liberia,” Stevquoah said, reflecting the President’s position.

He noted that the strategic plan comes at a time when Liberia has opportunities to attract serious investors into petroleum exploration and advance development aspirations that citizens have long awaited.Stevquoah also called for stronger coordination among institutions responsible for regulating and managing the petroleum sector, saying the President expects all stakeholders to work together, respect each other’s mandates and draw on one another’s expertise.

Guests Observe prayer at the LPRA five-year strategic plan launch in Monrovia l 26/112026

At the launch, Logan disclosed that the Authority has contributed US$13.8 million to the national budget over the past three years, following what she described as an inherited situation of tax arrears and almost no revenue contribution to government.



She said the LPRA now ranks among Liberia’s eleven highest revenue contributors and is the best-performing state-owned enterprise in terms of revenue contribution.

The Director General also highlighted progress in attracting petroleum investment, revealing that Liberia went more than a decade without signing a new Production Sharing Contract before the current leadership took office in March 2024.

“Within 18 months, we changed that story: we secured and signed eight production sharing contracts, and the Legislature has since ratified all eight,” Logan said.

She added that a reconnaissance programme is underway in the Harper Basin, while the Authority’s 2026 Direct Negotiation Licensing Round, launched last month, is expected to surpass the results achieved in 2025.

Providing an industry perspective, Bertrand Touze, TotalEnergies Vice President and Country Delegate responsible for launching the company’s exploration programme in Liberia, said the country was once again attracting attention on the international petroleum exploration scene.

He disclosed that TotalEnergies has opened a new office in Liberia and engaged skilled Liberian companies to support its exploration activities.

Touze said the company expects approximately half a dozen vessels to arrive in Liberian waters in early 2027 to support exploration activities in its offshore blocks.

He added that TotalEnergies would maintain transparency in its operations and implement health, safety and environmental measures as it pursues the possibility of discovering oil or gas in Liberia.

Logan noted that Liberia is competing for a limited share of global exploration investment as international petroleum companies become more selective about where they commit capital. Citing International Energy Agency estimates, she said global upstream investment stood at just under US$570 billion in 2025, approximately four percent below the previous year.Against this background, she stressed that Liberia’s ability to attract investment will depend not only on its geological potential but also on credible regulation, ethical conduct, competitive contract terms and timely decision-making.

Guests pose for group photo at after the launch of LPRA’s five-year strategic plan launch at EJS Ministerial Complex in Monrovia/ 26/112026

Under the new strategic plan, the LPRA has outlined six priority areas to guide its work through 2030. These include strengthening the management of petroleum rights and contracts, developing Liberian technical expertise, improving petroleum data management, protecting the environment and public safety, strengthening institutional governance and promoting transparency and local participation.

A major component of the plan is the development of local technical capacity. Logan announced that the Authority’s entire Technical Department will travel to France in January 2027 for practical training in petroleum data analysis. A second phase of training will be conducted in Monrovia, focusing on petroleum operations, safety and other technical areas. The programme will also be open to other actors in the petroleum sector.

She said the objective is to build a pool of Liberian specialists capable of independently assessing the country’s petroleum resources and effectively reviewing the technical activities of international operators, reducing reliance on external technical support.

On environmental protection and operational safety, the plan provides for joint regulatory protocols between the LPRA and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), alongside specialized training for inspectors in Health, Safety and Environment audits.

The Authority also intends to establish risk mitigation and emergency response frameworks and ensure that operators’ safety plans are reviewed before petroleum activities begin. Logan said these measures are particularly important as Liberia prepares for increased offshore exploration and possible drilling activities.

The strategic plan also places emphasis on transparency and public access to information. The LPRA intends to strengthen the management of petroleum data, establish clear access rules and regularly publish information to help Liberians understand the sector and identify realistic participation opportunities.

As part of its accountability commitments, Logan announced that the Authority will begin publishing an annual State of the Petroleum Sector Report in 2027. The strategic plan will also undergo open reviews in 2028 and 2030 to assess progress and make necessary adjustments.

She cautioned against judging the Authority solely by whether commercial oil discoveries are made, noting that geological outcomes are beyond its control.

“We are optimistic about the future, but do not judge us by whether oil is found; geology is beyond our control,” she said. “Judge us by the quality of the companies we attract and by our readiness to regulate them in the interest of Liberia.”

Meanwhile, the LPRA is expected to break ground for its new headquarters in January 2027. The facility will include a modern petroleum data processing and viewing center to strengthen the Authority’s technical and institutional capabilities.

The strategic plan will be implemented in three phases. The first, covering 2026 and 2027, will focus on establishing the Authority’s operational foundation. The second phase, from 2028 to 2029, will deepen regulatory delivery, while 2030 will focus on consolidating achievements and preparing the next strategic plan.

For his part, Representative Sam P. Jallah, Chairman of the House of Representatives Committee on Hydrocarbon, described the strategic plan as a policy framework that establishes clear targets and measurable standards for the petroleum regulator.

He said the document sends an important signal to citizens and investors that Liberia is working toward a regulatory environment built on fairness, integrity and forward-looking policies.

“When our regulatory institutions operate with clarity and integrity, investors’ confidence rises, illicit financing declines and the ultimate beneficiaries are the Liberian people,” Jallah said.

He reaffirmed the Legislature’s support for the five-year plan, pledging constructive oversight and legislative and policy support to facilitate its implementation.

Jallah said the Legislature would also hold the LPRA accountable for meeting the benchmarks and commitments outlined in the strategic plan.

Calling on government institutions, development partners, petroleum operators, civil society and the public to hold the Authority accountable, Logan said: “Measure us by what we deliver, not by what we promise.”

She said Liberia’s return to the global petroleum exploration map must be sustained through credible regulation, ethical engagement and responsible management of the country’s petroleum resources.

World.title: Liberia: Senate Probes Liberian Dollar Shortage, Rising Commodity Prices
World.content:
Despite the Liberian Dollar’s Appreciation Against the U.S. Dollar, Consumers Face Rising Prices of Basic Goods, Raising Concerns Over Holiday Spending

Monrovia – The Liberian Senate has mandated its Joint Committees on Banking and Currency and Public Accounts to investigate the reported shortage of Liberian dollar banknotes and the persistent increase in prices of basic commodities, despite the recent appreciation of the local currency against the United States dollar.

By Obediah Johnson

The decision follows growing concerns from commercial banks, business owners and market vendors over the limited availability of Liberian dollar banknotes for everyday transactions.



At the same time, consumers across the country are questioning why the appreciation of the local currency has not translated into lower prices of essential commodities, leaving ordinary Liberians struggling with the high cost of living as the Christmas season approaches.

According to the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL), the exchange rate currently stands at approximately L$163 to US$1.

The Senate’s decision followed concerns raised by River Gee County Senator Jonathan Sogbie during Thursday’s regular session at the Capitol Building on November 26.

In a communication to the Senate, a copy of which is in the possession of FrontPage Africa, Senator Sogbie expressed concern that despite legislative authorization for the Central Bank to procure and print L$79 billion, the country continues to experience a shortage of its own currency.



“I write to bring to the attention of this August Body the growing shortage of Liberian dollar banknotes in our commercial banks and markets across the country,” he stated.

“On July 16, 2026, this Senate unanimously concurred with the House of Representatives to authorize the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) to procure and print up to L$79 billion. However, Distinguished Colleagues, our people continue to experience an acute shortage of Liberian dollars.”

He further observed that the limited banknotes circulating in the economy are, in many instances, badly mutilated and difficult to use for ordinary transactions.

The senator said the situation is particularly troubling as Liberians approach the festive season, when many households depend on funds from their annual savings clubs, commonly known as Susu, to meet Christmas and other end-of-year expenses.

“How will our people access their money when Liberian dollars are hardly available in the banks and markets? If our own currency is missing from our country, where do we go to find it?” he questioned.

Prices Remain High Despite Currency Appreciation

Senator Sogbie also raised concerns about the disconnect between the declining exchange rate and the prices of goods and services on the local market.

He argued that although the exchange rate between the United States and Liberian dollars has improved, consumers are yet to experience corresponding reductions in the prices of basic commodities.

According to him, the continued high cost of essential goods is placing an additional burden on ordinary Liberians, particularly households already struggling to meet their daily needs.

He questioned why the appreciation of the local currency has not translated into more affordable prices at marketplaces and called for an explanation from the relevant monetary authorities.

Senate Wants Answers From CBL

As part of his communication, Senator Sogbie requested the Senate to invite the Governor of the Central Bank of Liberia and other relevant officials to provide explanations for the reported shortage of Liberian dollar banknotes.

He wants the CBL authorities to provide an update on the progress made toward the procurement and printing of the L$79 billion authorized by the Legislature.

The senator also wants the bank to explain the delay in making new banknotes available to the public and address the apparent disconnect between the appreciation of the local currency and the persistent high prices of commodities.

He maintained that Liberians deserve clear answers and relief, stressing that the Senate must exercise its constitutional oversight responsibilities to ensure that the concerns receive urgent attention.

Senator Warns of Possible Festive Season Chaos

Speaking in a brief interview with FrontPage Africa at his Capitol Building office in Monrovia, Senator Sogbie warned that the continued shortage of Liberian dollar banknotes could trigger tensions and instability in communities across the country if the situation is not addressed.

He expressed particular concern about the potential difficulties facing leaders of annual savings clubs, who are expected to distribute accumulated contributions to their members during the festive season.

The senator fears that delays by commercial banks in releasing deposited funds could expose savings club leaders to embarrassment, confrontations and possible attacks from frustrated members.

He said the improvement in the exchange rate has yet to produce meaningful benefits for consumers in terms of purchasing power, especially during the festive season.

“The exchange rate has no positive effect on our people in terms of purchasing power, especially when they are in the festive season. Our people are expected to share their yearly Susu this December, and with the high mutilated bills and shortage of the Liberian dollars, we don’t know how they are going to do it, and I don’t foresee that happening anytime soon,” he said.

Senator Sogbie also pointed to difficulties reportedly being experienced by importers in clearing their goods from the Freeport of Monrovia, warning that the situation could worsen if consumers are unable to access local currency to purchase essential commodities.

He argued that electronic transactions cannot entirely replace physical banknotes, particularly given the country’s continued reliance on cash for everyday commercial activities.

Calling for immediate intervention, the senator invoked a popular Liberian saying about the Christmas season.

“There is a common saying in Liberia that ‘when the Christmas will be good, you will know from the eve,’ and this eve doesn’t look good. Let’s not wait to celebrate the eve only to have a bad Christmas. Let us solve the problem (of scarcity of Liberian dollars and hike in prices of commodities) now; it is a local problem,” he warned.

He held the Central Bank and other relevant authorities responsible for addressing the shortage of local currency and the continued increase in commodity prices.

Savings Clubs Face Uncertainty

Meanwhile, concerns are mounting among leaders of annual savings clubs across the country over reported delays by commercial banks in releasing members’ deposits.

Commercial banks are reportedly limiting the disbursement of large amounts of Liberian dollars to individuals and organizations amid the scarcity of local banknotes.

The situation has raised fears among savings club organizers, many of whom depend on commercial banks to safeguard members’ contributions before distributing the funds at the end of each savings cycle.

For thousands of participants, the annual distribution provides an important source of money for purchasing food, clothing, paying school-related expenses and meeting other family obligations during the Christmas season.

Economic observers warn that if the situation persists, households and small businesses could face additional financial difficulties during one of the country’s busiest commercial periods.

With the Senate now moving to investigate the matter, attention is expected to turn to the Central Bank’s explanation of the banknote shortage, the status of the authorized L$79 billion printing exercise and the factors preventing currency appreciation from translating into lower consumer prices.

For many Liberians, the immediate concern is whether they will be able to access their savings and afford basic commodities as Christmas approaches.

World.title: Liberia: PPCC Boss Bodger Scott Johnson Honored for Procurement Reforms
World.content:
Citation credits him with new procurement law, US$120m in e-procurement contracts

MONROVIA – Bodger Scott Johnson, Executive Director and Chief Executive Officer of the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC), has been honored as a distinguished public sector reformer for his role in modernizing Liberia’s public procurement system.

A citation accompanying the recognition credits Johnson with spearheading reforms aimed at strengthening transparency, accountability and efficiency in government procurement, including the amendment of the country’s procurement law, the introduction of electronic government procurement and expanded opportunities for women-owned and Liberian businesses.

The recognition highlights three major areas of reform under his leadership: the enactment of a revised Public Procurement and Concessions Act, the expansion of the national Electronic Government Procurement (e-GP) system and institutional improvements within the Commission.



New Procurement Law

The citation identifies the review and amendment of the Public Procurement and Concessions Act as one of the most significant milestones of Johnson’s tenure.

The Act for the Amendment and Restatement of the Public Procurement and Concessions Act was approved on January 12, 2026, while the PPCC subsequently issued and published amended regulations on March 18, 2026.

Among other provisions, the revised legal framework requires government institutions to conduct procurement through an electronic system and introduces provisions on sustainable and gender-responsive procurement, as well as public-private partnerships.



The law also formally recognizes procurement as a professional discipline, establishing qualifications, certification requirements and career development pathways for procurement officers across the civil service.

The reforms are intended to strengthen the professional capacity of procurement personnel while improving compliance with established procurement standards.

US$120 Million in E-Procurement Contracts

Another major achievement highlighted in the citation is the introduction and expansion of Liberia’s Electronic Government Procurement (e-GP) system, which it describes as the most visible expression of Johnson’s reform agenda.

The system was initially piloted in six institutions: the Ministries of Finance, Health, Public Works and Education, the Liberia Revenue Authority and the PPCC.

It has since expanded in phases, providing an electronic platform for the major stages of public procurement, including procurement planning, bid submission, bid opening, evaluation, contract awards and contract management.

By digitizing these processes, the system creates an electronic audit trail that allows procurement activities to be tracked and reviewed, potentially reducing opportunities for manipulation and improving accountability.

According to the citation, more than US$120 million in government contracts has been awarded through the platform since its introduction.

Approximately 18 percent of those contracts reportedly went to women-owned businesses, reflecting efforts to expand participation in public procurement.

The citation also credits the PPCC with training more than 1,300 vendors between 2024 and 2026 in bid preparation, the use of the electronic procurement platform and procedures for filing procurement complaints.

Liberia’s e-procurement reforms have also attracted regional attention, with procurement officials from neighboring countries reportedly visiting to learn from the country’s experience. The Commission has specifically reported a study visit by a procurement delegation from Sierra Leone.

Institutional Reforms at PPCC

Beyond changes to the legal and technological framework, the citation highlights improvements to the Commission’s internal operations under Johnson’s leadership.

Before becoming Executive Director, Johnson served as Chairman of the PPCC Board of Commissioners.

Since assuming the executive position, he has overseen the renovation of the Commission’s offices, installation of dedicated e-procurement workstations and construction of a 200-seat training hall.

Other initiatives include the establishment of a procurement clinic designed to provide technical assistance to procurement officers and suppliers, alongside increased targeted and random compliance inspections of government institutions.

The compliance exercises are intended not only to identify procurement violations but also to assess institutional weaknesses and recommend corrective measures.

The citation further recognizes Johnson’s efforts to improve staff welfare, logistics and working conditions within the Commission.

Johnson holds a Master of Arts degree in Public Administration from Howard University in the United States.

Liberia’s Role in Africa’s Procurement Network

The recognition also comes as Liberia continues to engage with regional and continental efforts to strengthen public procurement governance.

Through the PPCC, Liberia participates in the African Public Procurement Network (APPN), also known by its French acronym, RACOP.

Established in 2018 in Lomé, Togo, the network brings together public procurement authorities across Africa to promote cooperation, professional development, transparency and the exchange of best practices.

The APPN provides a platform for procurement institutions to share experiences in electronic procurement, sustainable purchasing, professionalization and measures to combat corruption.

Its activities also support efforts to improve the compatibility of procurement systems across African countries, potentially making it easier for businesses to participate in procurement opportunities across the continent.

The network operates through a General Assembly, an Executive Committee, a Technical Secretariat based in Lomé and five subregional networks covering North, East, West, Central and Southern Africa.

For Liberia, participation provides opportunities for the PPCC to learn from procurement reforms implemented elsewhere while contributing its own experiences to regional discussions.

The Accountability Test

Despite the reforms highlighted in the citation, public procurement remains a critical governance issue in Liberia, where substantial portions of government expenditure pass through procurement processes.

The transition from manual to electronic procurement is widely viewed as an important step toward reducing opportunities for corruption, improving competition and strengthening public oversight.

The PPCC’s commitments under the Open Government Partnership have also identified corruption risks associated with manual procurement processes, with electronic procurement presented as one of the mechanisms for addressing those vulnerabilities.

However, the long-term success of the reforms will depend on their consistent application across government institutions, effective enforcement of procurement regulations and public access to information about government contracts.

Citizens, civil society organizations and oversight institutions will also need access to contract information to determine which companies are receiving public contracts, the value of those contracts and whether the goods, services and infrastructure being procured are delivered as agreed.

For Johnson and the PPCC, the challenge ahead will be to translate the reforms and institutional improvements highlighted in the citation into measurable improvements in public spending, competition and value for money.

World.title: Liberia: Agriculture Minister, EPA Boss Warn of Food Production Decline Under Potential El Niño
World.content:
Capitol Building – The El Niño phenomenon poses a significant threat to Liberia’s agricultural sector by disrupting traditional planting schedules and causing erratic weather patterns, including extreme droughts and heavy downpours, Agriculture Minister Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Executive Director Dr. Emmanuel Urey Yarkpawolo have warned.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

El Niño, a global climate phenomenon, is driving increasingly unstable weather patterns characterized by severe droughts, intense heat waves and sudden flooding across various African regions. In Liberia, several counties are reportedly experiencing severe dryness, threatening agricultural production, food security and crop yields.



Appearing before the House of Representatives during the 13th day sitting of the Third Quarter of the Third Session of the 55th Legislature, both officials warned that the potential phenomenon could significantly affect food production, emphasizing the need for urgent measures.

Impact of El Niño on Liberia’s Cropping System

Minister Nuetah told Plenary that El Niño could disrupt Liberia’s established cropping calendar, which determines when farmers should begin planting across different regions.

He explained that if farmers plant in March in anticipation of rainfall but the rains fail because of El Niño, their crops could be destroyed. Similarly, excessive rainfall could cause seeds to rot in the soil before germinating.



He also warned that prolonged sunshine and intense heat could prevent seeds from germinating and encourage the proliferation of insects and pests.

“The intensity of the heat could also encourage the proliferation of insects and pests. These pests will not only affect crops but could also threaten other forms of life in our communities, including livestock,” the Minister asserted.

Shortened Growing Seasons and Crop Losses

Another possible impact is a shortened growing season, which could affect rice production.

Liberia has rice varieties that mature within 90 days, while others require as long as 150 days.

Minister Nuetah explained that farmers planting varieties requiring 150 days to mature depend on sufficient rainfall throughout the growing period. However, if the rainy season becomes shorter, rice plants could fail to produce grains during the booting and flowering stages because of insufficient water.

This could result in empty rice panicles and little or no harvest.

“When this happens, food insecurity could become a serious concern in communities and counties that depend heavily on rice production. In some areas, we could also experience flooding because rainfall may exceed the expected intensity. For instance, farmers who have already planted swamp rice could experience flooding when excessive rainfall occurs, potentially submerging and destroying their crops.”

He warned that severe El Niño conditions could cause rice yields to decline by approximately 30 to 50 percent for crops planted during the affected period, threatening food security, particularly in rural communities dependent on rice farming.

Effects on Cassava, Maize, and Vegetables

The Agriculture Minister said cassava, maize and vegetables could also be affected.

He pointed out that excessive rainfall could cause planted cassava stems to rot before germinating, while insufficient rainfall and intense heat could damage vegetables and increase pest attacks.

“For example, when farmers cultivate pepper and rainfall becomes insufficient, the crops may suffer even when farmers attempt to provide additional water. Due to the intensity of the heat, pest attacks could increase, causing significant damage to the crops.”

He emphasized that El Niño could have serious implications for Liberia if appropriate measures were not taken.

Implications for Rice Imports and Food Prices

Minister Nuetah caveated that the consequences could extend beyond domestic agricultural production, particularly if major rice-producing countries were also affected.

“Liberia is a rice-consuming country, and we import more than 60 percent of the rice consumed locally. If El Niño severely affects agricultural production in Asia and other major rice-producing countries, we should expect a reduction in rice supplies and potentially higher rice prices in Liberia.”

He intoned that Liberia’s dependence on imported rice makes the country vulnerable to disruptions in international food production and supply chains.

He also warned that farmers could lose their seeds when crops fail because of unfavorable weather conditions, leaving them without planting materials for subsequent farming seasons.

Consequently, the Agriculture Minister asserted the government would need to provide replacement seeds to affected farmers.

“We could also experience further food shortages in communities and across the country if the phenomenon severely affects major food-producing countries around the world. Because Liberia depends significantly on food imports, limited international supplies could lead to increased prices.”

The Way Forward

To address the potential impact of El Niño, Minister Nuetah outlined five major intervention areas.

Pillar One: Strengthening Early Warning Systems

The first recommendation focuses on strengthening early warning systems and providing timely information to farming communities.

He proposed establishing a national task force comprising the Ministry of Agriculture, Liberia Meteorological Service, Ministry of Transport, Central Agricultural Research Institute (CARI), National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA), Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), World Food Programme (WFP) and EPA.

The task force, he said, would meet weekly to monitor developments and provide updates on the phenomenon.

He also recommended regular agro-meteorological bulletins and timely planting advisories to guide farmers on appropriate planting periods.

Although Liberia already has a cropping calendar, he noted that changing climatic conditions could disrupt established planting schedules, requiring farmers to receive updated information and guidance.

Pillar Two: Building a Resilient Seed and Crop System

The second pillar recommends developing a resilient seed and crop production system to minimize the effects of El Niño.

Minister Nuetah called for a gradual shift from long-duration crop varieties, particularly rice, to varieties that mature within approximately 90 days.

He identified NERICA 4 and NERICA 14 as suitable rice varieties for upland cultivation and recommended improving farmers’ access to varieties that mature within 90 to 100 days, including a new variety known as C2.

For cassava production, he urged the country to prioritize drought-resistant varieties to help farmers maintain expected harvests during periods of high temperatures and insufficient rainfall.

Pillar Three: Expanding Irrigation and Water-Harvesting Systems

The Minister called for increased support for smallholder farmers through expanded access to irrigation facilities, including solar-powered irrigation systems and boreholes capable of supplying water to farming communities and households.

He also recommended investing in water-harvesting technologies to ensure water availability during the dry season.

“We need to develop a strategy that will enable the government to invest in water-harvesting technologies. Such investments will help us manage water resources more effectively and support agricultural production over the coming years.”

Pillar Four: Promoting Climate-Smart Agricultural Practices

The fourth pillar focuses on training at least 100,000 farmers in improved farming techniques, including mulching, which helps conserve soil moisture.

He also recommended training farmers in intercropping, the cultivation of different crops on the same land, and conservation agriculture, particularly minimum tillage, to protect soil structure and productivity.

Pillar Five: Strengthening Pest and Livestock Disease Prevention

The fifth pillar emphasizes strengthening pest surveillance and preventing livestock diseases across the country.

“The Ministry of Agriculture and the Central Agricultural Research Institute have technicians with the capacity to conduct surveillance activities across the counties to identify areas where disease outbreaks are likely to occur,” he said.

Financial Requirements and Implementation

Minister Nuetah estimated that approximately US$25 million to US$35 million would be required to implement the proposed interventions.

He accentuated that the funding would support agricultural production across approximately 25,000 hectares of lowland areas, strengthen farmers’ technical capacity and provide education on the phenomenon and measures to minimize its effects.

EPA Warns of Increasingly Severe Conditions

For his part, EPA Executive Director Emmanuel Urey Yarkpawolo informed the body that the El Niño phenomenon was occurring more frequently, with increasingly severe impacts.

He attributed the situation partly to climate change, noting that rising ocean temperatures were contributing to unstable environmental conditions.

Dr. Yarkpawolo recalled that early this year, the EPA began tracking developments using satellite technology provided by the United States. The agency has also established a website to monitor daily wind movements and other weather-related developments.

He explained that some parts of the world were experiencing increasing dryness and heat waves, while others faced heavier rainfall, sometimes followed by prolonged drought.

Climate Conditions in Liberia

Turning to Liberia, Yarkpawolo disclosed that EPA monitoring conducted between November 1 and November 10 and 12 revealed significant dry conditions across the country.

He revealed that 14 counties were experiencing severe dryness, with Lofa County appearing to be the only exception.

According to the EPA’s findings, Sinoe County recorded the highest level of dryness at 71 percent, followed by Grand Kru at 38.5 percent, Grand Gedeh at 37.5 percent, Grand Bassa at 36.8 percent, River Cess at 36.4 percent and River Gee at 33.3 percent. Maryland was also among the affected counties.

He further disclosed that approximately 1.17 million people across the seven heavily affected counties were exposed to these conditions, based on the 2022 national census figures.

Yarkpawolo also warned that prolonged heat and dry conditions could expose agricultural areas to increased heat stress, negatively affecting crop production and farming livelihoods.

EPA’s Early Warning and Public Awareness Measures

The EPA Executive Director said the agency had established an early warning system and a dedicated website to monitor environmental developments.

He also disclosed that the agency had developed public awareness messages, including jingles in simple Liberian English, to help citizens understand the prevailing conditions and potential risks.

“Additionally, we are issuing press statements and making radio announcements to inform the public about the prevailing conditions and the possible consequences. Our responsibility at the EPA is to protect the environment and inform the public about developments affecting it. As part of that mandate, we monitor emerging environmental threats, issue early warnings, and provide information to the government and the country as a whole,” Yarkpawolo stated.

House Decision

Following presentations by Minister Nuetah, EPA Executive Director Yarkpawolo, an official from the Meteorological Department of the Ministry of Transport and NDMA Executive Director Ansu Dorley, Plenary instructed its Committees on Agriculture, Lands and Environment to investigate the matter and report with possible recommendations within two weeks.

World.title: Liberia: C190 Coalition Engages House on Ratification of ILO Convention Against Workplace Harassment
World.content:
MONROVIA – A coalition of nine trade unions, civil society organizations and government institutions has called on the Government of Liberia to ratify and implement the International Labor Organization (ILO) Convention 190 (C190), aimed at ending violence and harassment in workplaces.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

In a formal petition submitted to the House of Representatives on Thursday, November 26, the Coalition for the Ratification of ILO Convention 190 Liberia urged lawmakers to take legislative steps toward the adoption of the convention, which recognizes everyone’s right to a world of work free from violence and harassment.



The coalition said workers across Liberia, particularly women, marginalized groups and people engaged in vulnerable forms of employment, continue to experience sexual harassment, intimidation, threats, bullying, exploitation and other forms of workplace abuse.

The group noted that ILO Convention 190, adopted in 2019, together with Recommendation 206, provides an international framework for preventing and addressing violence and harassment across workplaces and work-related environments.

To demonstrate the magnitude of the problem, the coalition referenced findings from national and international reports documenting persistent gender-based violence and harassment in Liberia.

The C190 Coalition also pointed to a January 2026 legal analysis by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), which highlighted the discrimination, harassment, sexual abuse and exploitation faced by women working in the informal sector, particularly market vendors and domestic workers, who often have limited access to legal protection.



It also cited an August 2025 OHCHR compilation of United Nations information for Liberia’s Universal Periodic Review, which documented 3,204 reported cases of gender-based violence in 2023 and called for stronger measures against gender discrimination, sexual harassment and gender-based violence in workplaces.

Additionally, the coalition referenced a 2025 Afrobarometer survey indicating that 36 percent of Liberians surveyed believe women often or always experience sexual harassment in public spaces, including markets, streets and public transportation.

Citing figures from the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection reported by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the coalition said Liberia recorded 3,381 cases of gender-based violence in 2024, with women and girls accounting for approximately 85 percent of survivors.

The coalition clarified that the figures reflect the broader national gender-based violence situation and are not exclusively workplace-related incidents.

It pointed out that consultations with workers across different sectors had revealed concerns about sexual harassment, unwanted physical contact and sexual demands linked to employment.

The coalition further identified underreporting as a major challenge, explaining that many survivors remain silent because of fear of dismissal, retaliation, stigma and discrimination.

“Limited awareness of what constitutes GBVH, coupled with a lack of safe and confidential reporting channels, further discourages survivors from speaking out. As a result, many forms of harassment remain normalized or overlooked in workplaces and society.These challenges underscore the need for stronger laws and policies, safe reporting mechanisms, protection against retaliation, access to support services, and effective accountability measures,” read the petition.

Against this backdrop, the coalition argued that ratifying Convention 190 would provide Liberia an opportunity to strengthen its legal and institutional frameworks, improve worker protection and ensure accountability for acts of violence and harassment.

As part of its recommendations, the coalition called on the House of Representatives to refer its communication to the appropriate legislative committees, particularly those responsible for labor, human rights and gender equality, while transmitting it to the Executive Branch for review and appropriate action.

The Coalition also urged lawmakers to support the ratification of the convention and consider adopting a resolution expressing the Legislature’s commitment to its implementation.

The group further recommended the initiation of a national tripartite dialogue involving the Government, employers, workers’ organizations and civil society to develop a roadmap for ratification and implementation.

Other recommendations include revision and strengthening national laws and policies to address workplace violence in both formal and informal employment, establishing confidential reporting mechanisms, protecting survivors against retaliation and ensuring accountability for perpetrators.

The coalition also called for increased investment in public education, awareness campaigns and data collection to improve prevention, monitoring and responses to workplace violence and harassment.

The Coalition for the Ratification of C190 Liberia comprises the Solidarity Center, United Worker Union of Liberia, Federation of Informal Workers of Liberia, WONGOSOL, BLESSING-Liberia, Health Education and Sustainable Empowerment, Inclusive Development Initiative and the National Parent Teacher Association of Liberia.

The Ministry of Labor and the National Commission on Persons with Disabilities are listed as honorary members supporting the promotion of decent work and safe, violence-free workplaces.

Among other things, the coalition urged the Government to take concrete steps toward ratifying and implementing Convention 190, emphasizing the need to protect the rights, dignity and safety of all workers in Liberia.

Receiving the petition, the Chairperson of the House Committee on Claims and Petitions, Montserrado County Electoral District #8 Representative, Prince A. Toles, promised to transmit the document to plenary for onward discussion on the matter.

“I want to thank you for assembling here in a more peaceful manner to put forth you issue. I can promise you that having received this, I will put it on the floor of plenary and this will form part of our discussion next Tuesday,” Rep. Toles assured the petitioners.

World.title: Nalolo intensifies El Niño preparedness, eyes beef exports
World.content:
Nalolo District has intensified preparations to mitigate the anticipated effects of El Niño through stakeholder engagement, climate-smart agriculture and livestock protection measures aimed at safeguarding food security and supporting the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Nalolo District Commissioner, Namatama Mupo says the district administration is working with relevant stakeholders to strengthen community preparedness and equip farmers with knowledge and practical strategies to withstand the projected drought.

Nalolo District, Ms Mupo said the district has embarked on an extensive sensitisation campaign to encourage farmers to adopt climate-smart agricultural practices and diversify their crops in response to the anticipated dry spell.

She urged farmers to consider drought-tolerant crops such as cassava, sorghum and finger millet rather than relying heavily on maize.

“We are sensitising our farmers to embrace and plant drought resistant crops such as cassava, Sorghum and Millet, saying that the named crops are not new to western Province because previously people in the area used to grow the said indigenous crops,” she said.

Ms Mupo said farmer sensitisation will be intensified across the district to ensure communities were adequately prepared for the anticipated drought.

She added that Nalolo, which has a substantial cattle population, is implementing interventions guided by the Department of Agriculture to protect livestock and minimise the potential impact of El Niño.

Ms Mupo also commended the Presidential Irrigation Initiative (PII) being implemented in the district, saying expanding irrigation farming would strengthen food production and contribute to national food security.

She called for the provision of mechanised irrigation equipment to enable the district to expand irrigated farmland and increase maize production in support of the Grow Zambia Agenda target of producing 10 million metric tonnes of maize.

“It’s our prayer that Nalolo District can have mechanised Irrigation farming equipment so that we can increase Irrigation farms to even 100 fields to be able to produce enough maize and contribute to the grow Zambia agenda of producing 10 million metric tonnes of maize,” she said.

The District Commissioner further said Nalolo has significant potential to contribute to the country’s beef export ambitions, which aim to generate about US$1 billion annually by 2031.

Ms Mupo disclosed that some large-scale cattle farmers have already approached her office seeking guidance on how to venture into beef marketing and contribute to the national development agenda.

She maintained that the district is ready to support the beef export initiative but noted that increased access to irrigation equipment would also enable farmers to maximise agricultural production by exploiting the area’s abundant water resources.

Ms Mupo has since called to help raise public awareness about the anticipated El Niño conditions and their possible effects on communities across Western Province.

Meanwhile, Nalolo District Livestock and Fisheries Coordinator Elijah Banda said his office is conducting sensitisation programmes on the anticipated El Niño effects, with particular emphasis on livestock disease surveillance and prevention.

He said farmers are being encouraged to vaccinate their animals against anthrax and other livestock diseases that can threaten animal health and productivity during drought conditions.

“We are encouraging farmers to vaccinate their animals timely before the El Nino effects come, livestock farmers have also trained on how to prepare feed for their animals, currently in partnership with a private firm we are establishing water points for livestock,” he said.

Mr Banda added that livestock farmers are also receiving training in fodder preparation to ensure animals had access to feed during periods of limited pasture availability.

And Acting Nalolo District Agriculture Coordinator, Patience Simwanda said Nalolo is strengthening its preparedness through the training of frontline agricultural officers in climate-smart agriculture.

Ms Simwanda said the Department of Agriculture is also using weather information from the Zambia Meteorological Department to guide farmers on the projected conditions and appropriate farming practices.

“As Nalolo District Agriculture office, we have formed an information platform where our farmers are constantly updated on the weather forecast situation, the other intervention we have put in place is to set up demonstration plots where sustainable early planting demonstrations are conducted,” she said.

She said the information-sharing platform and demonstration plots are intended to help farmers make informed decisions, adopt appropriate planting schedules and minimise potential losses associated with the anticipated El Niño conditions.

World.title: BOZ maintains policy rate at 10.75 percent as inflation rises to 6.4 percent
World.content:
The Bank of Zambia has maintained the Monetary Policy Rate at 10.75 percent despite a slight increase in annual inflation to 6.4 percent in November 2026 from 6.3 percent recorded in October.

Bank of Zambia Governor, Denny Kalyalya disclosed that inflation increased to 6.3 percent in October before rising further to 6.4 percent in November.

He attributed the rise largely to adjustments in domestic fuel pump prices and the depreciation of the Kwacha.

Dr Kalyalya made the remarks during the media briefing held at the Bank of Zambia Auditorium in Lusaka.

He explained that inflation had declined during the third quarter of 2026, falling to 6.1 percent in September from 6.5 percent in June, while average inflation dropped to 6.3 percent from 6.6 percent recorded in the second quarter.

Dr Kalyalya further explained that the decline was mainly driven by adequate supply of maize grain and its products, the lagged effects of the Kwacha’s appreciation against major currencies and reduced vegetable prices due to improved seasonal supply.

He stated that the Bank has revised its inflation projection for 2026 upwards to 6.9 percent from the previous forecast of 6.7 percent, while the 2027 projection has increased to 6.7 percent from 6.0 percent.

“The Committee considered that actual and projected inflation remain within the 6-8 percent target band despite elevated upside risks and the slight increase in inflation observed since the last quarter,” Dr. Kalyalya said.

The Governor disclosed that inflation is, however, projected to ease to 6.4 percent during the first three quarters of 2028, remaining within the Bank’s target band.

Dr Kalyalya added that the inflation outlook remains exposed to upside risks, including a potentially stronger El Niño weather phenomenon, which could reduce agricultural output and constrain hydroelectric power generation, thereby increasing food and energy prices.

In addition, continued conflict in the Middle East could keep global crude oil prices elevated and further raise domestic fuel pump prices,” he said.

He further added that continued conflict in the Middle East could also keep global crude oil prices elevated and further increase domestic fuel pump prices, while tighter global financial conditions could accelerate capital outflows and put additional pressure on exchange rates.

Dr Kalyalya noted that future decisions on the Policy Rate will continue to be guided by inflation outcomes, forecasts and identified risks, including those relating to financial stability.

He said the next Monetary Policy Committee meeting is scheduled for February 8 to 9, 2027.

Dr Kalyalya disclosed that the Committee would continue monitoring domestic and international economic developments to ensure that monetary policy remains appropriate in maintaining price stability.

World.title: Media urged to tell SADC success stories
World.content:
The Southern African Development Community (SADC) has called on media practitioners across the region to amplify stories showcasing the impact of regional integration programmes on communities and economies.

Speaking at the close of the SADC Regional Media Capacity Building Workshop in Gaborone, Botswana, GIZ/SADC Project Manager Robson Chakwana stressed the need for more reporting on the bloc’s achievements.

“We have competent SADC media practitioners that are going to tell the SADC story in all SADC member states. I think SADC needs that story. I think SADC needs to be told in the form of success stories,” Mr Chakwana said.

Mr Chakwana said the workshop was organised under the Strengthening National Regional Linkages Programme, a German-supported initiative aimed at enhancing communication of regional development efforts.

Meanwhile, SADC Communications Officer Innocent Mbuundula said the regional body expects journalists to strengthen coverage of development interventions taking place across member states.

“There are so many things that are happening and so many interventions that are taking place, but also there is a lot of impact. Every day we see people who are benefiting from such programmes. These are the stories that I encourage you to go back and write about,” Mr Mbuundula said.

And participants have described the workshop as both informative and practical.

Pranav Beeharry of the Mauritius Broadcasting Corporation said the training helped participants better understand regional processes and translate complex information into stories that citizens can easily understand.

“We learned a lot the first day and a half. We learned about how SADC operates and how it functions. The workshop was more about doing something practical, and I think that was the best part of the workshop,” Mr Beeharry said.

Similarly, ‘Mamahloko Ntsapi from Lesotho’s Ministry of Information said the training had equipped journalists with skills that would improve reporting on regional integration issues.

“Personally, I will be able to use and simplify the protocols and information that we learned here in the workshop on how to write some of the stories regarding SADC,” Ms Ntsapi said.

The workshop brought together media practitioners from the 16 SADC member states and focused on strengthening reporting on regional integration projects such as the Southern African Power Pool and the Lobito Corridor.

SADC and GIZ have since reaffirmed their commitment to working with the media to promote awareness of regional integration and development across Southern Africa.

World.title: BSYIG applauds Imisepela platform
World.content:
Back to School Youth Initiative Group (BSYIG) has commended the Government for using the Imisepela platform to connect young people to employment, entrepreneurship, funding and skills development opportunities.

BSYIG Executive Director Fredrick Zulu says the registration of more than 300,000 young people, disbursement of over K18.3 million to youth-led businesses and employment of approximately 2,300 people demonstrates government’s commitment to addressing youth unemployment and promoting economic inclusion.

Mr Zulu says the employment of approximately 2,300 young people is encouraging, but more opportunities are needed given the number of young people seeking employment in Zambia.

“The employment of approximately 2,300 young people is an encouraging development and a step in the right direction. It demonstrates that digital platforms can play an important role in connecting young people to employment opportunities,” he said.

Mr Zulu said more than 20,000 applications were received under the National Internship Programme, noting that the availability of only 2,000 internship placements highlights the significant gap between the demand for employment opportunities and the opportunities currently available.

He has since called for stronger partnerships between government, the private sector, civil society organisations and educational institutions to expand internships, apprenticeships, graduate trainee programmes and permanent employment opportunities.

The Executive Director said entrepreneurship should also be promoted as a complementary pathway to employment, noting that young people should not only be prepared to seek jobs but should also be empowered to create employment for others.

“Not every young person will find formal employment, but with the right financial support, mentorship and market access, young people can establish enterprises that create employment for others,” Mr Zulu said.

Mr Zulu has called for the decentralisation of youth empowerment programmes to constituency and ward levels to ensure that young people in peri-urban and underserved communities are equally reached.

He says digital platforms, while progressive, may exclude young people who lack smartphones, reliable internet connectivity, digital skills or information on how to navigate application processes.

“There should be strong collaboration with youth-led organisations, community-based organisations, Ward Development Committees and local authorities to mobilise young people, disseminate information and support applications,” Mr. Zulu said.

He says youth financing should also be accompanied by mentorship, financial literacy, business management training and market linkages, while young people should be involved in the design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of programmes affecting their economic future.

World.title: Zambia applauded for making strides in weather  reporting
World.content:
The Cross-Border Weather Intelligence Workshop has opened in Lusaka with a call to build systems that protect livelihoods.

The workshop has brought together meteorological services, civil aviation authorities, air traffic control, security agencies and regional and global partners.

Ministry of Green Economy and Environment Permanent Secretary Douty Chibamba urged participants to use the workshop to strengthen climate resilience and improve weather services across Southern Africa and beyond.

Dr Chibamba said Zambia remains committed to advancing climate resilience and building practical systems that protect lives, livelihoods and economies.

The Permanent Secretary said this in a speech read for him by Ministry of Green Economy and Environment Human Resource Director Ranford Simumbwe.

“Hosting regional colleagues and global partners here in Lusaka reflects Zambia’s strong commitment to advancing climate resilience, strengthening scientific cooperation, and building practical systems that protect lives, livelihoods, and economies,” he said.

The PS has since challenged delegates to leave the workshop with concrete clarity on priority upper-air needs, how data quality and forecast value will be jointly evaluated, domestic regulatory steps required, and bilateral and regional actions to carry forward.

Meanwhile, The Trans-African Hydro-Meteorological Observatory (TAHMO) Chief Executive Officer Ousman DE Acnad has called for stronger regional cooperation in collecting and sharing upper-air weather observations, saying a measurement taken in one country can improve forecasts in the next.

He applauded Zambia’s Meteorological Department (ZMD) for hosting the workshop and for showing how Zambia is turning better weather observations into practical advice for farmers.

He expressed hope that at the end of the workshop, delegates would agree on which upper-air observations to evaluate first and what steps neighbouring countries can take to collect and share them.

World.title: Super League title race heats up
World.content:
The MTN Super League enters the second round with Stream A leaders Nkana host struggling Trident FC at Nkana Stadium on Saturday.

Kalampa lead Stream A with 19 points from nine games, three points clear of FC MUZA and Konkola Blades, and a win against second-from-bottom Trident would keep them in control at the summit.

But the pressure is on.

FC MUZA host Napsa Stars at Nakambala Stadium in Mazabuka on Saturday, knowing victory would keep them firmly in the title hunt.

The biggest clash of the weekend in Stream A comes on Sunday, when Power Dynamos host Konkola Blades at Arthur Davies Stadium in Kitwe.

Power, fifth on 13 points, cannot afford to slip, while Konkola, third on 16 points, know a win would pile pressure on Nkana.

Elsewhere on Sunday, Kansanshi Dynamos host bottom-placed Makeni All Stars in Solwezi in a must-win game for both sides.

In Stream B, leaders Green Eagles will be favourites when they host ninth-placed Mufulira Wanderers at Independence Stadium in Choma on Sunday.

Eagles lead with 18 points, but Zesco United are just two points behind.

Zesco face a stern test on Sunday when they host Kabwe Warriors at the Trade Fair Grounds in Ndola.

Warriors are fifth on 10 points but have a game in hand, and will be out to derail Zesco’s title charge.

Red Arrows host bottom-placed Mutondo Stars at National Heroes Stadium on Sunday, with Mutondo still searching for their first win of the season after eight games.

Arrows will see this as a chance to climb from seventh place.

Roan United kick off Week 10 on Saturday when they host Nkwazi at Kafubu Stadium in Luanshya, while Chirundu United host Green Buffaloes on Wednesday in a rescheduled fixture.

With the gap at the top closing and the battle at the bottom intensifying, Week 10 could prove decisive in shaping both streams.

World.title: Social Cash Transfer beneficiaries encouraged to embrace digital payments
World.content:
Mungwi District Commissioner Muma Musonda has called for inclusive digital payment systems that cater for the elderly and other vulnerable groups.

Mr Musonda has observed that while digital platforms play an important role in enhancing access to services, measures must be put in place to ensure that the elderly and other vulnerable groups are not left behind and are adequately protected from fraud.

Mr Musonda has emphasised that government officials from various departments have a critical role to play in promoting digital inclusion and ensuring that Social Cash Transfer (SCT) beneficiaries safely embrace digital payment systems.

Speaking during a Training of Trainers in Mungwi District, Mr Musonda urged participants to encourage Social Cash Transfer beneficiaries to embrace digital payments.

He added that there is a need to strengthen sensitisation efforts to equip beneficiaries with the knowledge and skills to safely use digital payment platforms and guard against fraudulent activities.

“We cannot grow Zambia if our people are left behind digitally,” said Mr Musonda.

He further emphasised the need to ensure that beneficiaries are adequately informed and protected from fraud as the country transitions to digital payment systems.

And Northern Province Social Welfare Officer Sebastian Pasuwa has disclosed that the introduction of digital payments had made the department’s work easier by improving the payment process and enhancing efficiency in service delivery.

Mr Pasuwa has however, said the department receives reports of suspected fraud involving some Social Cash Transfer beneficiaries.

He also acknowledged that the system has presented some challenges which require concerted efforts from stakeholders to address and ensure beneficiaries are protected from fraud and other risks.

“There are reports of suspected fraud involving some beneficiaries, and this is a concern that requires concerted efforts from all stakeholders,” Mr Pasuwa said.

Mr Pasuwa said the Training of Trainers was aimed at equipping participants with the knowledge and skills to sensitise Social Cash Transfer beneficiaries on the benefits of digital payments, their safe use and measures to prevent fraud.

World.title: MTN opens Connect Store in Namwala to boost digital connectivity
World.content:
Namwala District Commissioner, Ephraim Shandavu, has called for increased private sector investment in rural communities to accelerate inclusive economic growth and advance the government’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Shandavu said investment in telecommunications infrastructure was critical to stimulating economic activities, improving business efficiency and expanding access to digital services, particularly in rural districts.

He was speaking in Namwala district when he officially opened an MTN Connect Store, a facility expected to provide telecommunications services closer to the people and enhance access to reliable communication services.

Mr Shandavu commended MTN Zambia for extending its investment to Namwala.

He said partnerships between the government and the private sector are important in promoting local economic development and creating opportunities for communities.

He further said improved digital connectivity would enable local entrepreneurs and small-scale businesses to access wider markets, facilitate financial transactions and improve communication with customers and business partners.

And MTN Southern Province Regional Manager, Ndumba Ndumba, said the establishment of the Connect Store would enhance access to telecommunications services and improve the way individuals and businesses conduct their daily activities.

Mr Ndumba said the facility would provide customers with convenient access to MTN services while supporting business operations and promoting digital inclusion in the district.

He further disclosed that MTN had also installed a telecommunications tower in Namwala to strengthen mobile network coverage and improve internet connectivity.

The investment is expected to complement the government’s efforts under the Grow Zambia Agenda, which places emphasis on stimulating economic growth, encouraging private sector participation and ensuring that development opportunities reach communities across the country.
