World.title: Vast Majority of Women Suffer Violence Without Reporting It
World.content:
Actress Samantha Ruth Prabhu is participating in a campaign to end violence against women in India. Globally, only a very small percentage of women seek help or report the physical or sexual violence they have experienced to the authorities, and legal cases often fail to result in convictions or sentences. Image: UN Women India

By IPS Correspondent

HAVANA TIMES – Only seven percent of women who experience physical or sexual violence report it to the police, and barely 23 percent seek help from family members, their communities or authorities, according to a UN Women report released on Monday, November 23.

The study by the United Nations agency, based on data from 54 countries, estimated that worldwide, 840 million women and girls – nearly one in three – have experienced physical or sexual violence at some point in their lives.

Published ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, November 25, the report notes that even when women decide to come forward, justice is far from guaranteed.

Sexual violence crimes are among the least likely to result in a conviction.

Sima Bahous, executive director of UN Women, said that “too many justice systems around the world are failing women and girls who experience violence. Cases go unreported, trials fail to move forward, and rulings go unenforced.”

“Justice cannot be achieved when women and girls have no access to it or when the law fails to protect them. We must work to ensure that justice systems fulfill their fundamental responsibilities to protect survivors, uphold their rights and prosecute perpetrators,” she added.

The UN Women study reveals a system in which silence is the norm, accountability is the exception, and perpetrators are far more likely to go unpunished than women are to obtain justice.

Many women remain silent, not by choice, but to protect themselves from the risks associated with speaking out. That is why barely seven percent of victims report acts of physical or sexual violence to the police, despite it being one of the most widespread human rights violations.

Women who report abuse may lose their homes, their children and their income. They may face abandonment by their families, exclusion from their communities and threats from the perpetrators they identify.

When women decide to come forward – sometimes years after the crimes were committed – they are all too often punished for speaking out and blamed for having waited. Some are murdered by their abusers simply for seeking help.

The number of women survivors of violence seeking help is declining in most countries that track such data.

In Asia, according to UN Women, only 16 percent of survivors seek help. In Africa, the figure is 31 percent, and in Latin America and the Caribbean, 40 percent.

In European Union countries, while 64 percent of survivors speak about the assault with someone close to them, only 14 percent go to the police.

According to research cited in the report, between 63 and 97 percent of complaints worldwide do not result in a conviction. Cases get lost in the justice system; survivors are subjected to repeated questioning and intimidating situations, and perpetrators may never be brought to trial.

All too often, perpetrators in positions of power are never convicted of the crimes they commit, fostering a culture of impunity.

The same pattern is repeated in the digital sphere. Only 25 percent of women involved in public life who experienced online violence filed a complaint with the police.

It is not the perpetrators who are penalized, but the women, who are silenced and excluded from digital spaces and prevented from exercising their right to participate freely in public life.

Against this backdrop, Bahous stated that “progress is possible. Today there is greater recognition of violence against women and girls, more laws protecting survivors, and more perpetrators behind bars.”

She emphasized that “the protections women have today are the result of the struggles of generations who dared to speak out. Now we must honor their courage by delivering justice, ensuring that every law provides safety, every promise translates into protection, and every word into action.”

“Until every woman and every girl can live free from violence, without fear and without having to prove that she deserves to be believed,” the UN official added.

The theme of this year’s International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women is “UNiTE to End Violence against Women and Girls.”

First published in Spanish by IPS and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more feature reports here on Havana Times.

World.title: Milei wins Senate approval to suspend primaries, with debates mandatory only in a run-off
World.content:
Milei wins Senate approval to suspend primaries, with debates mandatory only in a run-off

27th Friday, November 2026 - 17:21 UTC Full article

The government justifies suspending the primaries on cost grounds

Argentina's Senate on Thursday approved, by 43 votes to 29, the political reform promoted by Javier Milei's government that suspends the open, simultaneous and mandatory primary elections (PASO) ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The bill, which also limits mandatory presidential debates to a run-off, now goes to the Chamber of Deputies.

The ruling party secured 21 votes from La Libertad Avanza, 10 from the Radical Civic Union and three from PRO, joined by nine senators from provincial blocs and other parties, according to La Nación. Patricia Bullrich, the ruling party's Senate leader, who was tasked with securing the votes amid tensions with Milei, defended the savings of suspending the primaries. The economy, “which today is on a very important path of stability not achieved in many years, must be brought to every Argentine home,” she told the LN+ channel. “And to think some said we didn't have the votes to suspend the PASO in the Senate...,” cabinet chief Diego Santilli wrote on social media.

Besides suspending the primaries, the reform introduces the so-called “Clean Record” rule for candidacies, changes the financing of electoral advertising on radio and television and the election of Argentina's representatives to the Mercosur Parliament, and abolishes the pre-election campaign blackout. The presidential debate will be mandatory only in a possible run-off, and penalties for candidates who skip the first-round debate are removed.

The ruling party had initially sought to scrap mandatory debates altogether, but gave way on the run-off after 12 civil society organisations, including Cippec, Poder Ciudadano and the Argentine Journalism Forum, called for them to be kept. “The debate is a public good: it offers all candidates a common space to present their proposals and allows citizens to know and compare them,” they said.

The government justifies suspending the primaries on cost grounds. Its critics argue that it favours the ruling party, because without primaries the Peronist opposition, which lacks a common candidate, would find it harder to organise its electoral offer. Some allied lawmakers had also warned that Neuquén's decision to bring forward its provincial elections to February 14 meant changing the rules with the 2027 calendar already under way.

World.title: Argentina bans online betting advertising, including in football and on social media
World.content:
Argentina bans online betting advertising, including in football and on social media

27th Friday, November 2026 - 17:08 UTC Full article

Argentina's Senate during the debate on the betting law

Argentina's Senate unanimously passed, by 72 votes, a law to prevent gambling addiction and regulate online betting, banning gambling advertising in the media, on social media, in stadiums and on billboards, and requiring football clubs to review their sponsorship deals with betting firms. The law, approved on Thursday, had been pending in the upper house for more than two years.

Argentina's Senate unanimously passed, by 72 votes, a law to prevent gambling addiction and regulate online betting, banning gambling advertising in the media, on social media, in stadiums and on billboards, and requiring football clubs to review their sponsorship deals with betting firms. The law, approved on Thursday, had been pending in the upper house for more than two years.

The text was passed unchanged from the version the Chamber of Deputies approved in November 2024. It aims to limit children's and teenagers' exposure to betting and give the state tools to tackle compulsive gambling.

The law bans the advertising, promotion and sponsorship of betting on television, radio, print, the internet, social media, podcasts and billboards, as well as at stadiums, festivals and concerts, including covert advertising. The restrictions also apply to influencers, athletes and celebrities. The Argentine Football Association, the Professional League and clubs such as Boca Juniors, River Plate, Racing and Independiente will have to adjust their deals with betting companies, although the deadline will be set by the regulations, which the executive must issue within 120 days. The only exception is for licensed gaming halls and betting shops.

Under-18s will be banned from betting, and platforms must verify each user's identity and age through facial recognition linked to the national population register, not only when opening an account but at every login and when collecting a prize. Welcome bonuses and loyalty schemes are banned, and only debit cards or digital wallets with available funds may be used, with daily limits similar to those for cash machines. Credit cards and accounts receiving social benefits will not be accepted. A National Self-Exclusion Register is also created, to which close relatives can add a person.

The law sets heavy fines, 50% higher when minors are involved, and amends the Criminal Code to punish unlicensed gambling operations with three to eight years in prison. Judges will be able to order illegal sites to be blocked, and the Central Bank must prevent banks and wallets from processing payments to clandestine platforms.

The Catholic Church, which had called for the law's approval after Pope Leo XIV's recent visit, welcomed the decision. The Bishops' Commission for Social Pastoral Care received it with “deep gratitude” in a statement entitled “A step towards caring for our youth”.

World.title: US Air Force cloud platform hacked, Reuters reports
World.content:
US Air Force cloud platform hacked, Reuters reports

27th Friday, November 2026 - 17:06 UTC Full article

US Air Force

Cloud One, the US Air Force's cloud computing platform, suffered a computer intrusion that threatens the security of sensitive tactical, logistical and personnel data, three sources familiar with the incident told Reuters on Friday. It is the latest in a series of security breaches at US federal bodies.

Cloud One, the US Air Force's cloud computing platform, suffered a computer intrusion that threatens the security of sensitive tactical, logistical and personnel data, three sources familiar with the incident told Reuters on Friday. It is the latest in a series of security breaches at US federal bodies.

According to two of the sources, the intrusion was detected a month ago during system upgrade work and forced service interruptions on the platform. So far the attackers have not been identified, and the scope of the intrusion and whether information was stolen remain unknown.

Cloud One, launched in 2017, is one of the US military's largest cloud platforms, according to the sources, and combines resources from four providers: Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet. It supports numerous applications, including those handling personnel, payroll, logistics and maintenance data, the Air Force's cloud-based command and control system, which collects data from air defence radars across North America, and a system that tracks bombs and missiles at more than 200 Air Force installations worldwide. “A breach here is a very serious matter,” one of the sources said.

The Air Force declined to comment on its security, vulnerabilities or the operational status of its networks. “We continuously take prudent measures to protect the Department's information, systems and operational capabilities,” it said.

The revelation comes days after an intrusion was reported in an open-source intelligence analysis network of the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which exposed unclassified information, and following security breaches at the FBI and the Department of Agriculture. It also coincides with a series of failures that authorities attributed to technical causes rather than cyberattacks: the global Microsoft outage on November 12, the nationwide ground stop of all US flights for about four and a half hours on November 13, which the government blamed on outdated telecommunications equipment, and the outage of the National Security Agency's classified internal network on November 17.

World.title: Earth exceeds 2C of warming for seven consecutive days for the first time
World.content:
Earth exceeds 2C of warming for seven consecutive days for the first time

27th Friday, November 2026 - 04:35 UTC Full article

The record coincides with the failure of the UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya, which ended on November 22 without a main political agreement

The planet's average temperature exceeded pre-industrial levels by more than 2C for seven consecutive days, something that had never happened before, the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the European Earth observation programme, has confirmed. On Monday, November 23, the largest daily anomaly ever measured was also recorded: 2.25C above the 1850-1900 period.

The 2C threshold was reached on ten days in November — the 3rd, 4th, 13th and from the 18th to the 24th — seven of them consecutively. On November 23, the global average temperature was also 1.34C above the 1991-2020 average. These are not the highest absolute temperatures, which usually occur in July and August, but the largest deviation from normal for this time of year. Until now, 2C had been exceeded on only two days in November 2023 and four in February 2024. The data are preliminary, although Copernicus does not expect changes of more than 0.02C.

Exceeding that threshold for a few days is not the same as breaching the 2015 Paris Agreement, which aims to limit warming to 1.5C and keep it well below 2C, measured as an average over many years. “While this does not mean the long-term 2C threshold set by the Paris Agreement has been exceeded, it is a clear preview of where our climate is heading,” warned Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. “El Niño is temporary; the underlying warming caused by greenhouse gas emissions will persist unless we reduce those emissions.”

Copernicus considers it very likely that 2026 will end as the second-warmest year on record, with a 20% chance of equalling or surpassing 2024, and expects it to be the second calendar year in which warming exceeds 1.5C. Its director, Carlo Buontempo, has warned that there is a fairly high chance of at least one year exceeding 2C before 2030.

The record coincides with the failure of the UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya, which ended on November 22 without a main political agreement after several oil-producing countries refused to allow the final text to mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

World.title: Lula picks banker Luiz Carlos Trabuco to run the Finance Ministry in his fourth term
World.content:
Lula picks banker Luiz Carlos Trabuco to run the Finance Ministry in his fourth term

27th Friday, November 2026 - 04:30 UTC Full article

Trabuco, who comes from a humble background and has been a personal friend of Lula for years, has worked at Bradesco, the country's second-largest private bank, since the age of 17

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has chosen banker Luiz Carlos Trabuco, 75, chairman of Banco Bradesco's board, as finance minister for his fourth term, which begins on January 5. Trabuco accepted the post on Thursday night, according to the magazine Veja, although the appointment has not yet been officially announced.

He is the first known name in the new cabinet, which reflects the importance of the task ahead, including implementing the fiscal adjustment. Trabuco, who comes from a humble background and has been a personal friend of Lula for years, has worked at Bradesco, the country's second-largest private bank, since the age of 17.

Markets welcomed the news. The São Paulo stock exchange rose 6% on Thursday, its biggest gain since Lula's re-election on October 25. Over the past month the index had lost 18% of its value and the real had fallen 15% against the dollar, amid investor distrust over the public finances. Last week the Central Bank sold US$1 billion from its reserves to curb the rise of the US currency.

Congress has just approved the government's spending containment plan, with savings of about 60 billion reais, around US$10.6 billion, and the government has pledged to maintain the social benefits Lula announced at the end of the campaign. Public debt has risen sharply during the current term, the fiscal deficit is around 9% of gross domestic product and the benchmark interest rate stands at 13.75%, one of the highest in the world. Last week the Finance Ministry cut its 2027 growth forecast to 1.8%.

The ministry was led for almost the entire current term by Fernando Haddad, of the Workers' Party. According to Reuters, Lula plans to announce a first batch of ministers next week, on his return from the Mercosur summit in Montevideo.

World.title: Live Streaming Creators Multiply Across Uruguay and Argentina as the Platform Economy Widens in Mercosur
World.content:
Live Streaming Creators Multiply Across Uruguay and Argentina as the Platform Economy Widens in Mercosur

27th Friday, November 2026 - 01:46 UTC Full article

On a weekday morning in Buenos Aires, a surprising number of people under 35 are not listening to the radio or watching breakfast television. They have a YouTube tab open instead, where a group of hosts in a brightly lit studio are chatting, reading viewer messages out loud and laughing at their own jokes. Across the River Plate in Montevideo, a 24-year-old is setting up a ring light in her bedroom to stream a cooking show to a few hundred followers, some of them in Rosario, some in Porto Alegre.

Both scenes say something about how quickly live streaming has moved from a niche hobby to a real part of the media and work landscape on both banks of the river.

Argentina's Streaming Channels Grow Up

Argentina is where the shift is most visible. Over the past few years, digital-native channels such as Luzu TV, Olga and Blender have built audiences that would have seemed unthinkable for an internet project not long ago. Luzu and Olga now each have more than two million subscribers on YouTube, and their daily shows run on a schedule much like a traditional broadcaster, complete with hosts, guests, sponsors and commercial breaks.

The rivalry between the two biggest channels has become a story in its own right, followed in the entertainment press with the same intensity once reserved for the battle between Telefe and El Trece. In July this year, after the World Cup coverage wound down, Olga moved ahead of Luzu in monthly YouTube views.

What's striking is how far these outfits have travelled from the image of a few friends with a webcam. Several are branching out into scripted series and theatre, and their business models increasingly resemble those of television networks. Most of their hosts, though, are not trained journalists and don't present themselves as such. The appeal is the relaxed, conversational tone and the feeling that viewers are part of the show.

Uruguay's Advantage: The Pipes

Uruguay's streaming scene is smaller, as you would expect in a country of around three and a half million people, but it sits on some of the best connectivity in the Americas. State-owned Antel has spent years pushing fibre optic cable deeper into the country, and in June 2026 it announced that every town with more than 1,000 inhabitants was now connected to fibre, a first on the continent.

For creators, that matters more than it might sound. Stable upload speeds mean a young musician in Tacuarembó or a gamer in Salto can go live without the stream freezing every few minutes. Some of the more interesting Uruguayan streams come from small towns, with hosts talking about rural life, football, local food or the slow rhythm of the interior.

Many Uruguayan streamers lean on the much larger Argentine audience next door. The shared accent, humour and cultural references make the crossover feel natural, and a creator who catches on in Buenos Aires can suddenly find their audience several times bigger.

Why the Numbers Keep Rising

Several forces are at work.

Young audiences are drifting away from linear television and radio, and advertisers have noticed. Brands that once bought only TV spots now set aside part of their budgets for streaming shows and individual creators.

Economics also looks different in this part of the world. In Argentina, where inflation and currency swings have long squeezed household incomes, the chance to earn in foreign currency through global platforms, sponsorships or international fans is a powerful draw. For a student in Córdoba, a few hundred dollars a month from streaming can make a real difference.

And there's simply more variety now. Alongside entertainment and gaming, viewers can find streams on personal finance, language learning, cooking, fitness and politics. Live shopping is beginning to appear too, with small businesses showing products on camera and answering questions in real time.

A Wider Mercosur Market

The growth isn't confined to the two countries. Brazil already has one of the largest creator economies in the world, and Paraguayan creators are building their own followings. Within Mercosur, that creates an unusually connected audience, divided mostly by language rather than borders.

Some of that cross-border contact happens away from big broadcasts entirely. Younger users in particular are mixing streaming with one-to-one video chats, meeting people from neighbouring countries to practise Portuguese or Spanish or just compare notes on music and football. Some do it through Omgfun online, where conversations are matched by shared interests and live translation helps when vocabulary runs short. The platform economy, in other words, is about everyday connection as much as ad revenue.

The Challenges Ahead

Not everything about the boom is smooth. Audience measurement is still a work in progress, and industry analysts in Argentina have warned that some viewer counts may be inflated by bots. Most creators earn modest, irregular incomes, and the pressure to go live every day can lead to burnout. Questions about labour rights, taxation and platform payouts are only starting to be discussed by regulators in the region.

There's also the matter of dependence. Many creators rely almost entirely on a single platform, and a change in algorithm or payment rules can wipe out a big chunk of their income overnight.

What Comes Next

Even so, few people expect the trend to reverse. Better connectivity, a young population comfortable on camera and a growing advertising market point in the same direction. On both sides of the River Plate, live streaming is no longer a curiosity. It has become a workplace, a stage and, for many, a new way of talking to the rest of the region.

World.title: Milei becomes the first head of state to visit Alliana in Paraguay after Peña's fall
World.content:
Milei becomes the first head of state to visit Alliana in Paraguay after Peña's fall

26th Thursday, November 2026 - 22:33 UTC Full article

Milei and Alliana in Asunción

Argentine President Javier Milei travelled to Asunción on Thursday to back Paraguayan President Pedro Alliana, becoming the first foreign head of state he has received since replacing Santiago Peña, who was removed from office and jailed over the collapse of Ueno Bank. The same day, Paraguayan prosecutors said they had detected funds from the bank in Argentina.

Argentine President Javier Milei travelled to Asunción on Thursday to back Paraguayan President Pedro Alliana, becoming the first foreign head of state he has received since replacing Santiago Peña, who was removed from office and jailed over the collapse of Ueno Bank. The same day, Paraguayan prosecutors said they had detected funds from the bank in Argentina.

Milei was received with honours at the López Palace, the seat of Paraguay's government. “Welcome to Paraguay, President Milei! May this visit allow us to keep building a future of prosperity for our brotherly peoples,” Alliana wrote on social media, highlighting that the two countries are united by “the affection of two peoples who have grown up together”.

Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, who accompanied Milei, gave a press conference with his Paraguayan counterpart, Rubén Ramírez, whom he described as a “friend”. Quirno said the two governments have long shared “the ideas of freedom and the protection of private property”, and that Buenos Aires had offered its cooperation in dealing with the crisis caused by the collapse of Ueno Bank, which left almost three million savers without access to their deposits.

Paraguay's deputy prosecutor for international affairs, Manuel Doldán, told ABC Cardinal radio that “some funds” from Ueno had been detected in Argentina, so Argentine authorities had been asked to freeze assets and property linked to the bank, and a formal request for cooperation had been sent. “We are requesting the identification of bank and financial accounts, corporate, accounting and asset documents, which will also allow us to see how the financial ecosystems were handled there,” he said.

The visit coincided with an intense legislative day in Argentina. The Chamber of Deputies passed into law the reform of the Central Bank's charter by 141 votes in favour, none against and 99 abstentions, a week after the session scheduled to approve it collapsed for lack of quorum. The reform bans the bank from printing money to finance the Treasury and strengthens the tenure of its authorities. Deputies then moved on to debate the 2027 budget, while the Senate discussed suspending next year's open primary elections, known as PASO.

Milei and Alliana will meet again next week in Montevideo at the Mercosur summit of heads of state, together with the host, Yamandú Orsi, and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Relations between Argentina and Brazil are at their lowest point: this week Brasília permanently withdrew its ambassador from Buenos Aires and decided not to invite Milei to Lula's inauguration, after Quirno cast doubt on Brazil's electoral process.

World.title: Edmundo González announces his return to Venezuela after more than two years in exile in Spain
World.content:
Edmundo González announces his return to Venezuela after more than two years in exile in Spain

26th Thursday, November 2026 - 22:31 UTC Full article

Venezuelan opposition leader Edmundo González

Venezuelan opposition leader Edmundo González, a candidate in the July 2024 presidential election, announced on Thursday that he will soon return to Venezuela, after more than two years in exile in Spain, to take part on December 5 in the pilgrimage of the Virgin of Coromoto, the country's patron saint, in the city of Guanare.

Venezuelan opposition leader Edmundo González, a candidate in the July 2024 presidential election, announced on Thursday that he will soon return to Venezuela, after more than two years in exile in Spain, to take part on December 5 in the pilgrimage of the Virgin of Coromoto, the country's patron saint, in the city of Guanare.

“I will soon be in Venezuela to accompany the pilgrimage of our patron saint, the Virgin of Coromoto. What better time to return? After so long away from home, I am moved to think that I will be with you again,” González wrote on X. He said he had “much to thank Venezuelans, Spain” and his family for.

Opposition leader María Corina Machado had announced his return the day before at an event at the Central University of Venezuela. “He will be here soon,” she said. González replaced Machado as candidate in 2024 after the authorities barred her from running. The opposition claims González won, citing the tally sheets it collected, while the National Electoral Council proclaimed Nicolás Maduro the winner without publishing detailed results.

González left Venezuela in September 2024, with an arrest warrant against him, after negotiations with siblings Jorge and Delcy Rodríguez held at the Spanish embassy in Caracas. His son-in-law was detained for more than a year and released in early 2026.

He will return to a very different country, after Maduro's removal from power in the January 3 US military operation. Delcy Rodríguez has since governed as acting president and has promised elections under a renewed electoral authority, though without setting a date. Machado returned to Venezuela after ten months abroad, and in recent weeks close aides such as her adviser Carlos Blanco and her campaign chief, Magalli Meda, have also come back.

González's return coincides with a rapprochement between Rodríguez's government and Washington: last week US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela in Caracas.

World.title: Peso regains some ground after nearing 20 to the dollar in a week of losses
World.content:
After seven consecutive days of decline, the Mexican peso appreciated early on Friday, though trading volume is typically much lower on Black Friday than on a standard business day.

The peso fell to its worst level since April 2015 on Thursday, closing at 19.72 to the U.S. dollar, while depreciating 7.01% during the seven-day losing streak. It has fallen nearly 14% over the past three months and was down 9.54% on the year.

The peso initially climbed 0.64% to 19.57 shortly after opening, but had weakened to 19.657 by 5 p.m.

Banco Base expects the peso to end its losing streak and trade between 19.49 and 19.69 per dollar in a session of reduced liquidity, due to the partial reopening of U.S. capital and bond markets after the Thanksgiving holiday.

Mexico’s currency had not experienced such a prolonged negative stretch since the period from Aug. 31-Sept. 8, 2023, although the depreciation then was less severe (5.07%).

Analysts attribute the losing streak to investors unwinding carry-trade positions and shifting into safe-haven assets.

The carry-trade is a strategy where an investor borrows money at a low interest rate (in this case, the U.S. dollar) and invests it in an asset offering a higher rate of return (the Mexican peso), thus profiting from the interest rate gap.

However, Mexico’s central bank (Banxico) has embraced a policy of monetary easing. And when it cut its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.25% in early November just two months after the U.S. Federal Reserve raised its rate from 3.75% to 4%, the interest rate gap narrowed to 225 basis points, a historic low.

At the same time, markets are pricing in potential U.S. Federal Reserve hikes (it is widely expected to raise its rate again at its Dec. 8-9 meeting), expecting the yield cushion that made the peso attractive to narrow even further.

Meanwhile, persistent U.S. inflation, strong U.S. growth and broader risk-off sentiment have boosted demand for the U.S. dollar as a safe haven.

Some strategists expect elevated volatility heading into the Fed’s upcoming policy meeting and see potential for the peso exchange rate to surpass 20 to the dollar before stabilizing or drifting lower toward 18.50 in 2027.

However, headline inflation in Mexico neared 4.0% in the first half of November, which alongside tariff and trade uncertainty, complicates Banxico’s policy path, though it is not expected to lower its rate at its Dec. 17 meeting.

With reports from Reforma, El Financiero and La Jornada

World.title: Working poverty in Mexico hits its lowest level on record
World.content:
Listen to this article

Working poverty in Mexico fell to its lowest level since the indicator was first measured in 2005, thanks to wage recovery and steady economic growth.

Working poverty — defined as someone whose labor income is too low to buy a basic food basket, as determined by national statistics agency INEGI — decreased to 30.5% in the third quarter, a decline of 1.4 percentage points from the second quarter.

The 30.5% figure bettered the previous record low figure, which came in the first quarter of 2026, when it stood at 30.7%.

In year-on-year comparison, labor poverty — as it is also known — decreased by 3.9 percentage points, its largest drop since the third quarter of 2021, when it fell by 5.3 percentage points as the Mexican economy recovered from the COVID-19 pandemic.

Higher labor incomes supplied by a strong third-quarter economic performance helped improve working poverty, following a spike recorded in the second quarter.

In addition to the recovery of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in these two periods, the increase in the minimum wage mandated in January deserves credit for the improvement in INEGI’s Labor Poverty Trend Index (ITLP).

GDP grew 0.9% quarter-over-quarter and 3.3% year-over-year in the third quarter, the largest annual increase since the second quarter of 2023, while the minimum wage has increased by 154% since 2018.

In 2018 the percentage of the population in working poverty was at 40%. It has declined since then except for spikes in 2020 and 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Still, according to the economic observatory and research group “Mexico, ¿cómo vamos?,” the figures for working poverty indicate that 40.1 million people in Mexico live in households whose labor income is insufficient to purchase the basic food basket.

“It’s not something to celebrate just yet, because 30.5% of people don’t earn enough to eat,” says Rogelio Gómez Hermosillo, executive president of Citizen Action Against Poverty. “It’s good that it’s at the lowest point … but what more can we do?”

INEGI’s ITLP also breaks down the data by rural and urban populations.

While declining from a high of 62.6% in the third quarter of 2013, working poverty among rural residents was at 43.1% in Q3 2026. For urban residents, it was down from a COVID-induced high of 41.8% in Q3 2020 to 26.9% in the most recent report.

With reports from El Economista, Excelsior and La Jornada

World.title: Authorities rescue 4 Bengal tigers behind a former Mazatlán nightclub
World.content:
Authorities in Mazatlán found four Bengal tigers in a gated lot behind a former nightclub this week, marking the latest big-cat seizure in a country where wildlife trafficking persists.

Federal officers also seized four pavorreales (peacocks), five vehicles, a trailer and the property in the Francisco I. Madero neighborhood, an area that includes a zona de tolerancia (red-light district). It’s about six to eight kilometers inland from Mazatlán’s beachfront hotel zone.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by OstokSanctuary (@ostoksanctuary)

The operation began Monday when National Guard members in the state of Sinaloa received a citizen complaint about constant roars. After officers confirmed the roars as well as bird sounds, the area was secured and a federal prosecutor obtained a judicial warrant.

According to reports, the animals went to the Ostok Sanctuary, north of Mazatlán, at the request of the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa). Ostok used to have another site near Culiacán, the capital of Sinaloa, but it shut down last year and its roughly 700 animals were relocated because of nearby cartel violence.

This week’s transfer occurred Tuesday after the sanctuary’s team sedated the tigers: a white cub about 5 months old, a yellow cub about 7 months old and an adult pair.

All the animals were reportedly in good health.

Ostok Sanctuary President Ernesto Zazueta said the animals were found in “a place that they apparently used for experiments with animals or some kind of handling, because there was a wall full of photographs,” the news source EFE reported.

Prosecutors are investigating a possible crime against biodiversity, the newspaper El Debate Sinaloa reported. No reports mention arrests, and the tigers’ legal fate is undecided.

It was not Sinaloa’s first such case. In April 2025, Ostok rescued two Bengal tigers, a white tigress and a yellow tiger from an abandoned lot in the Golden Triangle, a mountainous region known for organized crime.

Wildlife trafficking is ‘out of control’ in Mexico

Throughout the country, animal trafficking remains widespread. A 2022 Center for Biological Diversity study concluded that “Wildlife trafficking in Mexico is out of control.”

Seizures include not only Bengal tigers, but many other animals, as well. Just this week, Profepa reported rescuing 70 turtles and a chameleon being moved illegally in Chihuahua state, 88.9 Noticias reported.

In Tlaxcala state, Profepa reported that police seized six wild birds and arrested two people for illegal possession of wildlife at a livestock market. The birds were two yellow-headed parrots, whose sale is prohibited, and four American kestrels; the vendors did not have documents proving the birds’ legal origin.

Profepa reported 1,119 Facebook and Instagram posts for possible illegal wildlife sales from May 2025 to June 2026, the agency said in a news release.

Titled “Profepa strengthens actions to detect and combat the illegal sale of wildlife on social media,” the release noted that Profepa worked with Meta — the platforms’ parent company — and that 640 of the posts, or 57%, were removed or resolved.

With reports from Ríodoce, El Debate Sinaloa and EFE

World.title: It’s confirmed: Gas stations and toll booths across Mexico will stop accepting cash
World.content:
As expected, the Finance Ministry (SHCP) has determined that gas stations and toll booths are the first segments of the economy that will be restricted to only accepting electronic payments.

The new Digital Economy Law required the SHCP to identify priority areas in which the use of cash would be eliminated, and it selected the two sectors that were already conducting pilot programs.

An SHCP directive published Friday defined the “strategic sectors” (hydrocarbons and infrastructure) and outlined the respective activities subject to the Digital Economy Law — sale to the public of gasoline and diesel, and collection of tolls.

The date that the new requirements will go into effect has yet to be announced. The publication of this order in the government’s Official Gazette gives these strategic sectors 15 business days to establish “the conditions, requirements, obligations and operations” for the receipt of digital and electronic means of payment.

According to the SHCP, digital and electronic means of payment are understood to be: QR codes and NFC devices; debit and credit cards; fund transfer orders (including direct debit); and any device, card or interface that allows the making of payments and transfers of resources.

The SHCP statement says the decision to declare gas stations a strategic sector is designed to discourage tax evasion and “tax-related fuel theft,” and close existing loopholes regarding the illegal sale of fuel.

The statement explains that handling cash makes it difficult to trace the true origin of fuel sold at retail. Electronic payments, on the other hand, leave a traceable footprint.

The government also believes that eliminating cash at public service stations can reduce the risks and costs associated with handling cash for the stations and station attendants.

With regard to toll booths, the SHCP said the transition to a digital economy will eliminate “operational frictions that translate into longer waiting times, traffic congestion and limitations in the capacity to process traffic flows, while also reducing crossing times and improving the efficiency of public transport service.”

For example, the SHCP cited a study that found that the average wait time at toll booths to enter Mexico City is nearly 15 minutes, a delay that would be reduced to 2.40 minutes by paying electronically.

With reports from El Economista, Informador and Forbes México

World.title: Sheinbaum to press US on SpaceX launches after Starship debris hits Tamaulipas beaches
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Thursday during her daily morning press conference that her administration intends to discuss with the United States the frequency of Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches from Texas, following complaints of their debris reaching the coasts of Tamaulipas.

The president said takeoffs from Starship, one of the company’s bases near the border with Tamaulipas, require the use of a portion of Mexican airspace, which needs clearance from the country’s aeronautical authority.

El 8 de octubre denunciamos a SpaceX por los daños ambientales que sus lanzamientos provocan en las costas de Tamaulipas. PROFEPA ya dio trámite a nuestra denuncia: exigimos que se investigue el impacto de estos residuos en el mar, la fauna y la pesca, ¡que SpaceX responda por los daños! — Jorge Álvarez Máynez (@AlvarezMaynez) November 27, 2026

Therefore, she said, Mexican authorities are looking for a diplomatic meeting between the aerospace authorities of both countries to “establish permission for the use of Mexican airspace including the frequency of such use, and, if necessary, to discuss the potential relocation of the launch site.”

Sheinbaum noted that, for now, the number of launches is low. However, she cited a future goal of up to 400 flights per year, which would necessitate determining the frequency with which Mexico might grant permits.

According to Sheinbaum, such an increase could affect air traffic due to the restrictions applied during each takeoff.

“What would this imply for Mexican airspace?,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that a meeting with the U.S. Embassy has already taken place, and clarified that these matters should be addressed with the U.S. government rather than with SpaceX, as the latter is a private company whose operations affect national airspace.

Sheinbaum clarified that the negotiations with the U.S. government are independent of the investigations into the waste on Mexico’s Gulf Coast, and that the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa) will determine any potential liability on the part of the company.

Meanwhile, SpaceX said last week that external partners indicated the small amount of debris discovered along the Tamaulipas shoreline is not directly linked to the company’s aerospace activities.

Regarding images that have circulated on social media showing suspected space debris on the coast of Tamaulipas, SpaceX said that most of the posts are “intentionally misleading.” It also added that independent tests conducted on the materials within Starship and the Super Heavy booster confirm that they “do not pose any chemical, biological, or toxicological risks.”

With reports from The Associated Press and El Financiero

World.title: A bitter indulgence: The reality of Mexico City’s street-cart potato chip vendors
World.content:
It’s a cloudy day, and sales have been very slow.

Elvia knows that with weather like this, it will be difficult to end her shift on a high note. At 32, she’s spent the last three years selling potato chips from a pushcart, a classic Mexico City street treat.

Although her stall sits on a bustling sidewalk along Parque México, in the heart of the capital’s affluent Condesa neighborhood, there hasn’t been much activity since lunchtime.

Competition is tough, particularly in tourist areas, where artisans, ice cream sellers, musicians and other street vendors all vie for relatively meager wages.

“It’s not like this in the summer,” Elvia says. “When it’s hot, people seem more inclined to buy potato chips.”

Elvia comes from a family of potato-chip street vendors — a trade that gained popularity in Mexico City during the 1940s and ’50s, and has since spread to the rest of the country.

An affordable indulgence

A “Mexicanized” take on U.S.-style French fries, this version consists of deep-fried julienned potatoes topped with a variety of hot sauces, chamoy, a sort of pickled pork skin known as cueritos and — for a more refined palate — bone marrow.

Three potato types are commonly used: Alpha, Atlantic and Fianna. Varieties like Atlantic and Fianna contain higher starch and less water, allowing them to crisp and brown properly when fried.

The potatoes are prepared using a double-frying method, which makes them crunchy on the outside and soft on the inside. As a result, they don’t taste like your average, mass-produced potato chips.

In addition to the traditional salt flavor, potato chips are also commonly found marinated, jalapeño-flavored or in mixed assortments. Generally, people order them with hot sauce, lime and salt.

Since street-cart potato chips and other classic fried snacks are so readily available, they punctuate many people’s childhood memories. You can easily find them outside subway stations, hospitals, parks, schools and government offices — essentially, anywhere with a high volume of foot traffic.

A complicated arrangement

At Mexico City’s Central de Abasto — where both small- and large-scale merchants purchase supplies for many businesses in Mexico City’s informal economy — potatoes start at just 12 pesos per kilogram, according to the Central de Abasto Price Monitor, which fluctuates daily.

On average, 1 kilogram yields 12 medium-sized bags. In Mexico City, small bags generally cost between 10 and 20 pesos, while large ones can go up to 50 pesos.

Taken at face value, owning a cart that sells potato chips (or other classic fried snacks found in Mexico City) can be a great business.

The profit, however, does not go to vendors like Elvia.

“The cart isn’t mine,” Elvia tells me. “It belongs to the man I work for.”

Unlike other vendors, she doesn’t have to purchase the supplies from Central de Abasto. They come with the cart, which Elvia rents and retrieves from a storage area every day.

This arrangement means vendors have to pay a percentage of sales to their employers. In Elvia’s case, she only keeps 25% of what she makes during an eight-hour workday.

When her shift ends, she’s not allowed to continue working. She must return the cart to the storage area until the next day, when she’ll retrieve it once again and bring it to the new location assigned to her.

In addition to the rental and supply fees, many street vendors face the daily burden of paying “piso,” “protection money” police officers and others demand in exchange for being allowed to work.

Elvia is one of the lucky ones. She hasn’t had to pay piso to operate. But given its nature, other potato vendors understandably did not want to grant us an interview.

One woman simply dismissed me, saying, “I’d rather not — customers keep coming, and we have to attend to them.” A logical explanation, of course. But her tone betrayed something more guarded, an impulse to protect herself.

A profession with a long tradition (and little legal protection)

When asked if she has an official permit, Elvia shrugged: “My boss handles that.”

In reality, street vendors in Mexico City are required to obtain a “Permit to Engage in Commerce on Public Thoroughfares” from the relevant borough authority.

The Mexico City government promoted these permits to regulate the industry and protect its employees, who are rarely covered by the law or supported by their employers.

However, vendors like Elvia don’t deal with the paperwork. That’s left to the person who assigns them the spots where they will operate for the day.

Elvia is not the only one facing this lack of state protection. Street vendors — selling fruit, aguas frescas, tamales and bread from baskets — work every day with few safeguards. Similarly, the capital’s other endemic trades contend with few labor protections, and some have even organized to demand greater protections from the state.

Elvia, however, has little faith that an advocacy group will organize on her behalf.

Since there is no union for street vendors in Mexico, “I can only rely on my family,” Elvia says. “My nieces and cousins also do this kind of work.”

For now, she’ll simply have to continue renting her cart, doling out the majority of her profits and hoping she’s never required to pay piso.

“It’s the only thing we have left,” Elvia says. “This is the only way we earn a living.”

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Mexico files formal complaint over DEA’s Sinaloa tip lines: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

✉️ Mexico submits formal complaint over DEA tip lines : Sheinbaum said Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco submitted the complaint to U.S. Ambassador Ron Johnson over the DEA’s WhatsApp, Signal, Threema and email tip lines for Sinaloa. She said Thursday that the establishment of the tip lines amounted to U.S. “interference” in Mexico.

: Sheinbaum said Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco submitted the complaint to U.S. Ambassador Ron Johnson over the DEA’s WhatsApp, Signal, Threema and email tip lines for Sinaloa. She said Thursday that the establishment of the tip lines amounted to U.S. “interference” in Mexico. 🇲🇽🇺🇸 Dealing with Trump administration “is not hard” : Sheinbaum said it is “not hard as long as you’re clear about your principles,” adding that “there are limits in the relationship.” She said there is communication and coordination on trade, immigration and security, and that “I have a team that deals with all of that.”

: Sheinbaum said it is “not hard as long as you’re clear about your principles,” adding that “there are limits in the relationship.” She said there is communication and coordination on trade, immigration and security, and that “I have a team that deals with all of that.” 🌎 G20 summit is not the “last chance” for a trade deal: Asked whether the Dec. 14-15 summit at Mar-a-Lago is Mexico’s last chance for a deal with the U.S. before 2027, she said “No, it’s not the last [chance],” noting that Trump still has two years left in office. “Of course we hope to reach an agreement this December, but that will depend a bit on the proposals that are presented,” she said.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Sheinbaum on Friday spoke about her government’s relationship with the Trump administration at the end of a week in which Washington rankled Mexico City with two moves.

The first was the deportation of Inés Gómez Mont, a former Mexican television host, to Spain rather than Mexico, even though she is wanted in Mexico for alleged tax fraud and embezzlement.

The second was the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration’s announcement that it had established “dedicated tip lines” to receive information on Sinaloa Cartel narcos and corrupt Mexican officials.

On Wednesday, Sheinbaum questioned why U.S. authorities didn’t send Gómez Mont to Mexico, given that “they know” there is an outstanding warrant for her arrest here. On Thursday, she said that the DEA’s establishment of tip lines aimed at collecting information on Mexican citizens was “a matter of interference.”

Despite these irritants in the bilateral relationship — and various others — Sheinbaum asserted on Friday that dealing with the Trump administration is not difficult as long as she remains faithful to her principles.

She frequently says that the Mexico-U.S. relationship is based on four principles, namely respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity; shared and differentiated responsibility; mutual trust; and coordination without subordination.

#Mañanera La Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum afirmó que la relación con Estados Unidos debe basarse en la coordinación y cooperación, no en la subordinación, y con respeto a la soberanía nacional. Ante la decisión de la DEA de habilitar canales para recibir denuncias sobre… pic.twitter.com/eME3yx2JsA — REFORMA (@Reforma) November 27, 2026

In Sheinbaum’s view, the U.S. government violated some of those principles when CIA officers took part in a drug lab raid in Chihuahua without her government’s knowledge or authorization, and when it became involved in a police academy project in Querétaro.

Mexico submits ‘formal complaint’ to US over DEA tip lines

Sheinbaum said that Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco submitted a formal complaint to U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ron Johnson about the DEA’s establishment of its WhatsApp, Signal, Threema and email tip lines for Sinaloa.

“The ambassador said he was going to review it,” she said.

In a social media post on Wednesday in which he announced the Sinaloa tip lines, DEA Administrator Terry Cole said that numbers for Jalisco and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) would be posted on Thursday.

Dealing with the Trump administration ‘is not hard,’ says Sheinbaum

A reporter said she imagined that managing the relationship “with Washington” is “very hard because there is something new every day, and I understand that you find out about most things on social media.”

“It’s not hard as long as you’re clear about your principles,” Sheinbaum said.

“Is there a guiding light?” the reporter asked.

“Of course,” Sheinbaum responded.

“There are principles that you defend,” she said.

“And there is communication and there is coordination [with the U.S. government]. There is the trade issue and the immigration issue and the security issue, but I have a team that deals with all of that,” Sheinbaum said.

“So as long as you’re clear about your principles, and there are limits in the relationship, there’s no reason why [dealing with the U.S.] should be hard,” she said.

Sheinbaum: G20 summit is not the last chance to reach a trade deal with US

A reporter asked the president whether the 2026 G20 Leaders’ Summit, to be held at the Mar-a-Lago Club in Florida on Dec. 14 and 15, is the “last chance” for Mexico to reach a trade deal with the United States before 2027.

“No, it’s not the last [chance],” Sheinbaum responded.

She highlighted that U.S. President Donald Trump still has two years left in office and stressed that “there is always dialogue” between Mexico and the United States.

“In January, the situation in the United States is going to change a bit because a new Congress and new Senate and new governors will come in,” Sheinbaum said.

“… But the direct relationship with the U.S. government and President Trump continues in all the areas in which we are working,” she said.

“Of course, we hope to reach an agreement this December, but that will depend a bit on the proposals that are presented,” Sheinbaum said.

Mexico and the United States have been seeking to resolve a range of trade-related issues following the U.S. government’s decision in July not to renew the USMCA free trade pact for an additional 16 years to 2042. Trump is particularly concerned about the United States’ large trade deficit with Mexico, while the Mexican government is pushing for a reduction of U.S. tariffs that currently apply to Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles.

Sheinbaum and Trump both said in October that a trade deal is “very close.”

José Medina Mora, a Mexican businessman and president of the Business Coordinating Council, said on Monday that a deal between Mexico and the United States could be announced at the upcoming G20 Leaders’ Summit, at which Sheinbaum is set to hold a second bilateral meeting in as many months with Trump.

World.title: El Jalapeño: SpaceX insists scorched rocket parts on Mexican beach could have been left by careless picnickers
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MATAMOROS, Tamaulipas — Aerospace manufacturer SpaceX issued a formal statement Tuesday denying any connection to thousands of scorched, aerospace-grade polymer fragments that washed ashore on Playa Bagdad, located approximately 3 miles south of the company’s Starbase launch facility and directly downwind of a rocket that exploded on live television last week.

Company spokespeople maintained that the white composite paneling, gray thermal tape and blue industrial adhesive currently covering the Tamaulipas shoreline could have originated from any number of local coastal activities, including artisanal fishing, beachside tourism or spontaneous atmospheric combustion. In a social media post, the company asserted that reports linking the wreckage to its recent launch were “fabrications or deliberately intended to deceive,” adding that any hypothetical booster lining that might have hypothetically drifted across the Rio Grande poses zero chemical, biological or toxicological risk to the sea turtles currently attempting to crawl over it.

“Simply because an object falls from the sky in the exact trajectory of our disintegrating launch vehicle, lands a mile south of our launchpad and bears a serial number matching our proprietary booster lining does not establish a causal link,” said a senior aerospace communications strategist who requested anonymity to protect him from any potential litigation. “Frankly, we are disappointed by the rush to judgment before anyone has ruled out rogue beachgoers.“

Environmental inspectors with Mexico’s Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection, known as Profepa, spent the morning cataloging 1,500 distinct fragments of carbon-fiber reinforcement alongside empty beer cans and flip-flops. Local conservationists noted that while tourist litter typically consists of polystyrene coolers and plastic bottle caps, the newly arrived debris features heat-shielding tiles engineered to survive atmospheric reentry at 17,000 mph.

“We are keeping an open mind during the investigation,” said an environmental technician stationed near the mouth of the Rio Bravo. “It is entirely possible that a family on holiday from Monterrey brought several metric tons of liquid-oxygen-resistant rubber sheeting for a weekend picnic and simply forgot to pack it out.”

SpaceX confirmed it remains in close contact with Mexican authorities and stands ready to assist with cleanup efforts the moment investigators prove the debris did not wash up from an unrelated, competing spaceport operating out of Brownsville.

World.title: Drone Attack Kills Police Officer in Bolívar
World.content:
A drone attack killed a police officer in Bolívar on Friday. It came two weeks after an attack on an army base in the same department.

File photo. The command building of the Metropolitan Police of Bogotá, Colombia, December 2017. Photo: EEIM, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Security: Colombia

Drones dropped explosives on the police station in Arenal, in southern Bolívar department, on Friday 27 November 2026 and killed Subintendente Óscar Mauricio Díaz. A subintendente is a mid-ranking police officer.

The national police director, a major general, wrote on X on Friday: “To his family, my support. We will honour his memory and will not rest until justice is done.”

The authorities still have to establish the circumstances and who is responsible. The Arenal station is a repeat target, attacked twice earlier this year, in March and July.

The March attack used drone-borne explosives. In July the station was damaged and at least three police officers were hurt.

Bolívar Governor Yamil Arana said on 11 July that the attack was apparently the work of the ELN, the National Liberation Army, Colombia’s largest remaining guerrilla group. On 7 November an attack on the military base of Santa Rosa del Sur, a town in southern Bolívar, killed three uniformed personnel and wounded 16 people by the Army’s count, with other reports giving higher figures.

Defence Minister Jorge Mora said it was retaliation by the ELN for the capture of a rebel leader known as “Carrito”, a leader of an armed group called the Frente de Resistencia Guamocó.No statement so far says who carried out the Arenal strike. The authorities have not linked it to any group or to the earlier attacks.

President De la Espriella, a conservative who took office on 7 August 2026 promising a hard line against armed groups, condemned the attack on X “with absolute firmness”.He called it a terrorist attack carried out with explosives launched from a drone.”

Attacking our Public Force is attacking Colombia,” the president wrote on Friday, using the term for the army and police. He ordered intelligence and investigation capabilities to be deployed.

Other attacks hit the police on the same day and earlier in the week. On Friday an explosive near a road in a rural area of Los Patios, next to the border city of Cúcuta, wounded four police officers who are out of danger (see Colombia explosive wounds four police near Cúcuta).

On Monday 23 November explosive drones aimed at the Cúcuta police headquarters fell on nearby homes and wounded three civilians, including an 18-month-old baby. The ELN claimed that attack (see rebels claim drone attack on Cúcuta police).

No direct effect on US investors or travellers has been established. None of the statements mentions peace talks with the ELN, so the record is silent on whether talks are on or off the table.

The police have not said how many drones were used. The Colombia news page carries the wider record.

Drone-borne explosives hit the police station and killed a police officer. The authorities are still establishing the circumstances.

World.title: Peru Says Rain-Hit Ballots Are Safe
World.content:
Peru's election office says no regional office in the flooded north was damaged. Only the national election court can move the 6 December vote.

Photo: Bernard Gagnon / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

Elections: Peru

Peru’s election office said on Friday 27 November 2026 that its offices and ballot material in the rain-hit northern regions of Piura and Tumbes are undamaged. The statement came nine days before the regional runoff on Sunday 6 December 2026.

Heavy rain from El Niño, the Pacific warming pattern that brings floods to Peru’s north coast, flooded streets in Piura on Thursday 26 November, and the question is whether the vote can go ahead. The office, ONPE (Oficina Nacional de Procesos Electorales), runs the count and the logistics of every Peruvian election.

Key Facts Who. ONPE, Peru’s election office, says its offices in rain-hit Piura and Tumbes are undamaged.

What. Ballot material reached all 63 regional offices; seven offices in rain areas were checked.

Where and when. Piura and Tumbes, northern Peru; regional runoff on Sunday 6 December 2026.

Power Index. Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 53.9 points (November 2026 edition).

As of. 28 November 2026, 04:20 GMT.

Peru’s election office says no regional office in the flooded north was damaged. Only the national election court can move the 6 December vote.

ONPE checked seven of its 63 regional offices in rain-affected areas: Sullana, Piura, Castilla, Tumbes, Morropón, La Esperanza and José Leonardo Ortiz. The readings were taken up to 9:00 a.m. Lima time on Friday, and none of the seven reported damage.

Paul Cárdenas, adviser to ONPE’s national head, said on Friday: “The heads of the offices have reported that the offices have suffered no damage.” He added that the schools inspected in flooded zones can still serve as polling sites.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 53.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The runoff covers 15 regions, where 12,474,107 registered voters will choose governors and vice governors on Sunday 6 December from 7:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., ONPE said. It is needed because no ticket reached 30% of valid votes in the first round on 4 October 2026, while ten other regions were decided outright (see regional runoffs explained).

The JNE (Jurado Nacional de Elecciones), Peru’s election court, moved the date from Sunday 29 November to 6 December after ONPE asked for more time. Rain has since become the main risk, and the response has come in three steps: a decree that locked in the 15 runoffs, ONPE’s ballot rescue plan for rains and early shipment of the material.

ONPE said on 25 November that shipping began on Friday 20 November from its warehouse in Lurín, south of Lima and took five days, by road, air and river. The kits cover 42,929 polling tables at 5,417 voting sites, with 100 spare ballots per collection centre.

Table boxes were double-wrapped in plastic and film against water, ONPE said, and each vehicle carried an ONPE commissioner, satellite tracking and a police escort. Cárdenas said on Friday that the material reached all 63 offices about two days earlier: “We took the decision to send out the electoral material in good time,” he said, because of how El Niño is advancing.

The headquarters of the National Elections Jury (JNE), Peru’s electoral court, in central Lima, 2024 (Photo: Omar Vega Ramos, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

Most polling sites are schools of the Education Ministry, and Cárdenas warned that rain can leave them unusable “from one moment to the next”. ONPE monitors the situation daily with data from executive-branch agencies, he said.

Piura had heavy rain for a second day running on Thursday 26 and Friday 27 November, and the national weather service Senamhi said on 27 November that it would continue through the weekend. Senamhi’s forecast beyond the weekend is not known.

Every regional office has a generator, ONPE said, and it has coordinated with Osinergmin, the energy-sector regulator, so that power cuts are avoided or fixed fast. If the risk materialises, ballots and tally sheets of high-risk offices move to a contingency computing centre at ONPE headquarters in Lima.

If roads are blocked, the material travels by sea with the Peruvian Navy from the ports of Callao, Salaverry, Pimentel or Paita. ONPE rated five offices critical in runoff regions: Tumbes, Sullana, Paita and Castilla in Piura, and Chiclayo in Lambayeque.

Critical means the computing centre sits on the first floor, the risk is high and the office lies in a declared emergency zone. ONPE announced this contingency plan before Friday’s check.

Cárdenas said that a postponement is not ONPE’s decision, because only the JNE can take it. ONPE will tell the court what is happening on the ground, he said.

The JNE has made no decision on postponement, and ONPE’s reading is as of 9:00 a.m. on Friday, before the weekend rain. The people affected are voters and officials in two northern regions near the border with Ecuador.

The next dated step is the vote itself on Sunday 6 December. It stays on unless the JNE decides otherwise, and ballots can still be moved by sea if roads close.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the 6 December vote still go ahead in Piura and Tumbes?

ONPE says its offices and ballot material there are undamaged, so the vote is on. Only the JNE can postpone it.

What happens if roads are blocked by rain?

ONPE has a plan to move ballots and tally sheets of high-risk offices to a computing centre in Lima. If roads are cut, the Navy would carry them by sea.

Who is affected by the rain and the vote?

Voters and election officials in two northern regions near the Ecuador border. There is no direct effect for readers elsewhere.

World.title: Brazil Retail Bond Sales Jump 47% in October
World.content:
Rate-linked bonds took almost half of October’s sales while the Selic holds at 13.75%.

File photo, 2011. A panorama from the TV tower shows the Monumental Axis, the Esplanade of the Ministries and Lake Paranoá in Brasília. (Photo: Leandro Neumann Ciuffo, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Economy: Brazil

Brazilians bought R$10.56 billion (about US$1.90 billion) of government bonds through the Treasury’s retail platform in October, 47% more than a year earlier, Brazil’s Treasury said on 27 November. The platform, Tesouro Direto, lets individuals buy federal bonds through brokers and has run since 2002.

Almost half of the money went into bonds that follow the Selic, the central bank’s policy interest rate, now 13.75% a year. For a US investor or a holder of Brazilian ADRs (US-listed shares of Brazilian companies), it shows where ordinary Brazilian savers put new money while rates stay high.

Rate-linked bonds took almost half of October’s sales while the Selic holds at 13.75%.

The Tesouro Direto programme began in 2002. The Treasury’s October report counted 37,097,172 registered investors, up 9.9% in 12 months, of whom 3,987,860 were active investors, up 22.4%.

Copom, the central bank’s rate-setting committee, held the Selic at 13.75% on 4 November, saying the decision was consistent with bringing inflation to around its target. It was the committee’s 282nd meeting, and the next one is on 8–9 December, with the decision due on 9 December.

Selic-linked bonds made up 48.4% of October sales, the Treasury said on 27 November, led by Tesouro Selic, a bond whose return follows the Selic, at R$3.85 billion (about US$0.70 billion). Tesouro Reserva, a Selic-linked bond launched in May 2026 with Banco do Brasil, the state-controlled bank, added R$1.26 billion (about US$0.23 billion), or 11.9% of sales.

Inflation-linked bonds, which adjust with consumer prices, took 29.1% of sales and fixed-rate bonds 22.4%, the Treasury said. Within the inflation-linked group, Tesouro Renda+, a retirement-income bond launched in 2023, took 7.2% of all sales.

Sales beat redemptions by R$2.87 billion (about US$0.52 billion) in October, the Treasury said, lifting the stock of bonds in the programme to R$285.25 billion (about US$51.5 billion). That is 41.93% more than the R$200.97 billion (about US$36.3 billion) of October 2025.

October was not the peak: the Treasury’s all-time monthly record is August 2026 at R$15 billion (about US$2.71 billion). Sales were 20.37% above September’s R$8.77 billion (about US$1.58 billion).

Small tickets dominate: 80.2% of October’s sales operations were for up to R$5,000 (about US$902), and the average sale was R$8,634.05 (about US$1,558). Another 350,550 people registered in the month.

By maturity, 43.9% of October sales were in bonds due within five years, 36.2% between five and 10 years and 19.9% beyond 10 years. The Treasury’s report also counts 1,222,698 sale operations in October.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Tesouro Direto?

It is the Treasury’s platform for individuals to buy federal government bonds, open since 2002. Investors buy through brokers.

What does a Selic-linked bond do?

Its return follows the central bank’s policy rate, so it pays more when the rate is high. Buyers tend to be less exposed to price swings when rates change than holders of fixed-rate bonds.

Why do these sales matter outside Brazil?

They show where Brazilian households put their savings at a policy rate of 13.75%. The Treasury’s report counts 37,097,172 registered investors.

World.title: Brazil Keeps Green Power Flag for December
World.content:
With the rainy season under way, fewer costly thermal plants are needed, so December bills carry no flag surcharge.

The turbine hall of the Belo Monte hydropower plant on the Xingu River in Pará state, photographed in October 2023. Photo: Túllio F / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Economy: Brazil

Brazil’s electricity regulator, the National Electric Energy Agency (ANEEL), kept the green tariff flag for December, so power bills carry no surcharge, it announced on Friday 27 November 2026. It is the third month in a row without an extra charge, after October and November.

ANEEL says the reason is rain: fuller reservoirs mean fewer expensive thermal plants have to run. Consumers therefore pay no flag surcharge on top of the base tariff for the month.

What. Green flag kept for December, so no surcharge is added to power bills.

When. Decided on 27 November 2026 and applies from 1 to 31 December.

Brazil’s tariff-flag system, introduced in 2015, colours each month by the expected cost of generating power for the national grid. Green adds nothing to a bill, while yellow and red add a surcharge for every 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh, the unit on a power bill) used, according to ANEEL’s flag page.

In its statement on 27 November, ANEEL said, in our translation from Portuguese: “With the rainy season, reservoir levels have improved.” It added that running thermal plants, which produce more expensive power, “becomes less necessary”.

The flag for December 2025 was yellow, after red level 1 in November 2025. This year’s green flag therefore replaces a surcharge that households paid a year ago.

The grid operator ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) projected for the week of 14–20 November that reservoirs in the Southeast and Centre-West would end November at 58.6% of capacity, up from 55.2%. Inflows into those reservoirs were forecast for November at 148% of the long-term average.

The picture is uneven across the country. The same projection put reservoirs at 88.8% of capacity in the South, 53.5% in the Northeast and 48.2% in the North, with November inflows forecast at 68% of the long-term average in the Northeast and 54% in the North.

File photo. The spillway of the Itaipú dam, a hydroelectric plant on the Paraná River on the Brazil–Paraguay border. (Wikimedia Commons)

ONS’s December operating bulletin forecasts power demand 6.7% above December 2025, at 89,981 average megawatts. Inflows are forecast at 118% of the long-term average in the Southeast and Centre-West and 230% in the South.

The Northeast and North are forecast at 60% and 50% of their long-term averages. Those two regions are therefore forecast to stay below normal inflows.

The saving for a household is the avoided surcharge: ANEEL’s flag page lists R$1.89 (about US$0.34) per 100 kWh for yellow, R$4.46 (about US$0.81) for red level 1 and R$7.88 (about US$1.42) for red level 2. We convert at the central bank’s selling rate of R$5.543 per US$ on 27 November 2026.

ANEEL’s calendar sets the January flag announcement for Wednesday 23 December 2026. ONS’s December forecast has Southeast and Centre-West reservoirs ending the month at 56.6% of capacity, the level of 27 November and below the 58.6% projected earlier for the end of November.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a tariff flag in Brazil?

It is a monthly colour code that adds a surcharge to power bills when generating electricity costs more. Green adds nothing.

Why did ANEEL choose green?

Rain has improved reservoir levels, so cheaper hydroelectric plants can carry more of the load. Thermal plants, which cost more to run, are needed less.

Could the flag change again?

Yes, because ANEEL sets the colour every month, and a drier spell could bring a surcharge back. The next decision covers January.

World.title: Brazil Justice Reportedly Offers Court Names
World.content:
A reported suggestion from one justice has put two names in play for Brazil's empty Supreme Court seat. Nothing is official, and the Senate calendar points to 2027.

Imagens de Brasília - Fachada do Palácio do Congresso Nacional O Palácio do Congresso Nacional é um dos pilares da arquitetura monumental de Niemeyer que dão forma à capital inaugurada em 1960. Está erguido na Praça dos Três Poderes, que tem este nome por também abrigar o Palácio do Planalto (sede do Poder Executivo) e o Palácio do Supremo Tribunal Federal (instância máxima do Poder Judiciário). Construído em terreno elevado, é visto de longe como culminância da avenida Eixo Monumental, que abriga a Esplanada dos Ministérios e atravessa a cidade de norte a sul. Sede das duas Casas do Poder Legislativo e um dos mais famosos cartões postais do Brasil, o Palácio do Congresso Nacional é composto por duas cúpulas e duas torres de 28 andares, que abrigam a Câmara dos Deputados e o Senado Federal. Foto: Pedro França/Agência Senado

Politics: Brazil

Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino reportedly gave President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva at least two names for the empty seat on Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court, in a private talk on Wednesday 25 November 2026. The names are Estela Aranha, a minister of the Superior Electoral Court, which runs Brazil’s elections, and Ney Bello, a federal appeals judge, according to a column by Milena Teixeira in the news portal Metrópoles on 26 November 2026.

Dino has not confirmed the report, and we found no public statement from him. Lula has announced no nominee.

Key Facts Who. Justice Flávio Dino reportedly suggested Estela Aranha and Ney Bello to President Lula.

What. The Senate hearing for any nominee is expected in 2027, says committee chair Otto Alencar.

A reported suggestion from one justice has put two names in play for Brazil’s empty Supreme Court seat. Nothing is official, and the Senate calendar points to 2027.

The Supreme Federal Court (STF) is the final judge of Brazil’s largest political and business disputes. Who sits on it therefore matters to investors and companies in the United States as well as to Brazilians.

The seat fell vacant when Luís Roberto Barroso, then an STF justice, announced early retirement at a plenary session on Thursday 9 October 2025. He was 67, eight years short of the mandatory limit of 75, and said it was “hora de seguir outros rumos” (time to follow other paths).
