WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The STF’s own news service reported that his retirement decree was published on Wednesday 15 October 2025 and took effect on Saturday 18 October. Lula’s first choice to replace him, Attorney-General Jorge Messias, never took the seat.

File photo: President Lula, left, at the swearing-in of the Supreme Federal Court’s new president on 29 September 2025. (Lula Oficial, CC BY-SA 4.0)

The Senate plenary rejected Messias on Wednesday 29 April 2026, with 42 votes against and 34 in favour, and Agência Senado, the Senate’s news service, reported his reaction that day. Forty-one votes were needed to approve him.

Article 101 of the Constitution sets the court at 11 ministers, so ten justices now sit. It asks for citizens of notable legal knowledge and unblemished reputation, over 35 years old, and the president appoints only after an absolute majority of the 81 senators, meaning 41 votes, approves the choice.

Teixeira reported that Dino spoke privately with Lula on Wednesday 25 November, after a meeting at which Lula discussed setting up a Ministry of Public Security, a planned new federal ministry. Aranha was Dino’s digital rights secretary when he ran the Justice Ministry, and Bello sits on the Federal Regional Court of the 1st Region, an appeals court based in Brasília.

The column says Bello and Dino are friends and academic partners, a bond formed in the northeastern state of Maranhão. It adds that Dino backed Bello’s bid for a seat on the Superior Court of Justice (STJ), Brazil’s top court for non-constitutional law, in 2024.

Diário do Centro do Mundo, a Brazilian news portal, wrote on 28 November 2026, citing a column by Bela Megale in the newspaper O Globo, that Lula has signalled to allies he tends to choose a woman. That is a reported tendency, not a decision, and the same portal names Edilene Lôbo, another minister of the electoral court, as a second woman gathering support.

Other names circulated on 27 November 2026, according to Bahia Notícias, a Brazilian news site. They include Daniela Teixeira and Regina Helena Costa of the STJ, Maria Elizabeth Rocha, president of the Superior Military Court, and Rodrigo Pacheco, a former Senate president who now sits on the Federal Audit Court (TCU), the government’s spending watchdog.

Senator Otto Alencar, chair of the Senate Constitution and Justice Committee, said on Thursday 26 November 2026 that time is short. “Nós só temos três sessões na CCJ este ano”, he said, adding that the report, the hearing and the plenary vote still have to fit in: “Ao que tudo indica, ficará para o ano que vem” (Everything indicates it will be left for next year).

The hearing is therefore likely in 2027, and it depends on Lula sending a name first. After the Messias vote, the Senate has already shown it can block a president’s choice.

Lula has not said whether he has decided, and the presidency has set no date for a formal nomination. Dino has not confirmed his role, so the two names remain a report until one of them speaks.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction platform, lists a market titled “Will Lula announce nomination of a Supreme Court minister by…?”, with US$40,048 traded across all its deadlines. Its 31 December outcome stood at 98% at 11:14 p.m. Eastern time on 27 November, and prices like these are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Lula chosen a new Supreme Court justice?

No. Lula has announced no nominee, and the two names rest on press reports that Dino has not confirmed.

Why is the seat still empty?

The Senate rejected Lula’s first nominee in April, and no second name has been sent. The Senate calendar for this year is nearly over.

When could a new justice join the court?

Only after Lula names someone and the Senate holds a hearing and a vote. The committee chair expects that to happen next year.

What to See & Do

SATURDAY IN SÃO PAULO

TODAY’S PICK — FREE ART IN LUZ Spend Saturday at the Pinacoteca, then walk to the Mercadão Start at the Pinacoteca de São Paulo in Luz. It opens at 10am, closes at 6pm, and entry is free on Saturdays (paid entry on other days it is open). Allow two hours for the galleries and the sculpture garden. The building is one of the city’s oldest art museums and sits beside Luz station. If you have energy left, the Museu da Língua Portuguesa is in the same station complex. It is open 9am to 4:30pm and costs R$25; check the museum’s own site for free days. For lunch, walk or ride to the Mercado Municipal (Mercadão) in Centro. It is open 6am to 6pm on Saturdays and entry is free. The single metro journey costs R$5.40. Luz station is on the metro and train network, so you need no car.

OUTDOORS — IBIRAPUERA Parque Ibirapuera is open from 5am to midnight every day and entry is free. It is the easiest place to walk, run or sit on the grass. If the sky stays clear, go in the late afternoon. MAC USP, on the park’s edge, is open 10am to 9pm and is free, so it works as a rain shelter.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — PAULISTA AND POMPEIA We have not verified café wifi or weekend hours this week, so we name no café. A cleaner option is to plan your laptop time around the museums that are open. Sesc Pompeia in Pompeia is open 10am to 5pm on weekends and entry is free. Japan House São Paulo, on Avenida Paulista, is open 10am to 7pm at weekends, also free, and is a calm place to sit between meetings.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — STREET ART AND CITY VIEWS For a louder mood, head to Beco do Batman in Vila Madalena. The open-air street is always open and free. Or go to the Farol Santander in Centro. It is open 9am to 8pm and costs R$45.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Sala São Paulo, in Luz, offers guided visits at no charge, and its concerts are ticketed. For an easy evening, Vila Madalena around Beco do Batman is a short walk for dinner. Stick to busy, well-lit streets and book a ride app home late at night.

01 A rebound with a fever

Wall Street bounced firmly. The Nasdaq Composite rose 2.31% to 24,130, the S&P 500 gained 1.60% to 7,297 and the Dow added 1.18% to 50,775 (RT, Friday 27 November close).

The VIX fell 11.16% to 23.81 (RT, Friday close). That is a calmer reading, but it is still well above the sleepy levels of a confident market.

Gold also climbed, up 1.94% to US$3,637 an ounce. Rising together with stocks and yields, it points to investors hedging as well as chasing the rally.

02 The 5% line in the bond market

The US 10-year yield rose to 4.936%, up 1.48% on the day (RT, Friday close). The dollar index gained 0.36% to 104.035 (RT, Friday close).

Data gave the Fed little reason to hurry. The Dallas Fed trimmed mean PCE, a gauge of underlying US inflation, eased to 2.8% from 3.0%, but the goods trade deficit widened to 149.5 billion dollars against 133 billion expected.

Wholesale inventories rose 0.9% and retail inventories excluding autos rose 0.6%. The Fed balance sheet fell to US$6.73204 trillion from US$6.74145 trillion in the week to 23 November (RT economic calendar, RT).

03 Brazil in the crossfire of dollar and yields

For Brazil, the message is uncomfortable. The IGP-M, which tracks wholesale prices and feeds into rents and contracts, rose 1.24% in November against 0.94% expected, though it eased from 1.47% in October.

The central bank held the Selic at 13.75% on 4 November, after a cut in September. Copom meets again on 8-9 December, and a US 10-year yield near 5% makes another cut harder to justify.

The fiscal picture offered some relief. The central government balance for October came in at a surplus of R$52.27 billion (about US$9.4 billion at 5.5582 reais per dollar, RT close) against R$47.55 billion expected (RT economic calendar, RT).

Europe looks softer. Eurozone business confidence slipped to -0.01 from 0.08 in November (RT economic calendar, RT).

Spanish inflation fell to 4.1% and French inflation to 2.9%, both below forecasts, while eurozone economic sentiment slipped to 95.8 against 97.2 expected and industrial sentiment dropped to -5.1. In the US, the weekly report of the US Energy Information Administration (EIA, eia.gov/petroleum/supply/weekly) showed commercial crude stocks at 418.9 million barrels, up 1.1 million.

Gasoline stocks rose 1.7 million barrels to 217.7 million, so fuel demand is not tightening the market. Elsewhere in Latin America, Chile’s unemployment rate rose to 10.0% against 9.8% expected.

Mexico’s October trade surplus was only US$0.298 billion against US$2.077 billion forecast, although the seasonally adjusted surplus was US$2.068 billion against US$0.823 billion in September (RT economic calendar, RT).

World.title: Costa Rica’s 911 Can Now Locate Android Callers Automatically
World.content:
Costa Rica’s 911 emergency system now automatically receives the location of callers using compatible Android phones, making it easier for responders to find people who do not know their exact address or cannot describe their surroundings. The service was highlighted during the government’s weekly press conference on Wednesday, November 25, as part of efforts to strengthen public safety and improve emergency response. The 911 Emergency System first announced it on November 16.

The technology works on Android smartphones with native Google services. When a person calls 911 from one of these devices, location information is transmitted automatically to the emergency system. It is separate from the 911 mobile app, which lets users share their location and chat with operators.

The service is particularly relevant in Costa Rica, where conventional street addresses are not always available and locations are frequently described using landmarks and points of reference. For visitors unfamiliar with local geography, it could prove especially valuable during emergencies in remote communities, rural areas or unfamiliar destinations.

The initiative involved Costa Rica’s three mobile network operators, Kölbi, Claro and Liberty, along with Google, Apple, the Ministry of Science, Innovation, Technology and Telecommunications (MICITT), the Superintendency of Telecommunications (SUTEL) and the data protection agency Prodhab.

Although Apple took part, the service is not yet available on iPhones. Authorities expect to add iOS compatibility in a later phase and have not announced a date. Kathya Villar Bonilla, director of the 911 Emergency System, said the tool complements emergency response but does not replace communication with operators. Those experiencing an emergency should continue calling 911, answering operators’ questions, providing any location references they can and following instructions.

While some 911 operators speak English, callers should not assume English-language assistance will always be immediately available. Knowing a few basic Spanish phrases could prove useful, including “¿Habla inglés?” (Do you speak English?) and “Necesito ayuda. No sé exactamente dónde estoy” (I need help. I don’t know exactly where I am).

The accuracy and availability of the technology depend on several factors, including mobile coverage, device compatibility, operating system and environmental conditions. The emergency system said location information is transmitted only while an emergency call is active and is used exclusively to assist the response. Once the call ends, the data is not retained and the device is not tracked.

The 911 system registered its database with Prodhab under Law 8968, Costa Rica’s personal data protection law, and handling of the information is subject to confidentiality and authorized-access controls. Villar said protecting people is at the center of the institution’s work, and that the tool helps responders locate emergencies and strengthens the assistance provided to the population.

World.title: ICE Opens Solar Plant in La Carpio Powering Equivalent of 30,000 Homes
World.content:
Costa Rica’s state electricity company has opened its first new power plant in seven years, a solar farm in western San Jose that the utility says will produce enough electricity each year to cover the consumption of more than 30,000 homes. The Costa Rican Electricity Institute (ICE) inaugurated the San Antonio Solar Plant yesterday in La Carpio, in the La Uruca district of the capital. The plant has an installed capacity of just over 10 megawatts and has been feeding the national grid since August, according to the institute.

The $13 million project uses 21,300 panels on about 11 hectares (27 acres) of land that once housed a thermal backup plant of the same name. That fuel-burning plant shut down in 2019, and ICE began building the solar farm on the site in October 2025. San Antonio is only the second solar plant ICE owns. The first, Miravalles in Bagaces, Guanacaste, came online in 2012. The utility now operates 31 plants across hydroelectric, geothermal, wind, solar and thermal sources, though solar still supplies only a sliver of the country’s electricity.

ICE Executive President Marco Acuña led the ceremony alongside First Vice President Francisco Gamboa. Acuña said the electricity mix continues to mature and that the project’s cost was competitive, adding that the institute would not build any plant that costs more than the industry average.

He attributed the seven-year gap to the administration of former President Carlos Alvarado, which he said had concluded Costa Rica did not need more electricity. Feasibility studies, contracting and construction can take more than three years for a single project, he said. The timing matters. Costa Rica relies on hydroelectric dams for most of its power, and the dry season is starting just as El Niño is expected to peak in December. Less rain means lower reservoirs and more reliance on costly thermal backup, and there is already a plan to spread El Niño power costs over three years of electricity bills.

Solar panels produce the most in exactly those dry, cloudless months, which takes some of the load off the dams. ICE describes solar as a complement to steadier sources such as hydroelectric and geothermal power, since its output varies through the day and peaks around noon.

At 10 megawatts, San Antonio is a modest addition. Acuña said ICE will now concentrate on two far larger projects. The 90-megawatt Abangares plant in Guanacaste, built with the Coopeguanacaste cooperative, is due in December 2027, and the Las Delicias plant in Montes de Oro, Puntarenas, is scheduled for mid-2028. Together they would add 150 megawatts, according to the institute.

Private developers have also been awarded about 200 megawatts of solar capacity that will join the grid over time, ICE said. The institute is separately moving ahead with the Borinquen geothermal plant in Guanacaste. For now, the new plant’s contribution is small against national deman but its significance is that it ends a long pause in public generation projects at a moment when drought is testing how much the grid can lean on water.

World.title: Costa Rica Records Historic Arribada of 347,000 Sea Turtles in Ostional
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Ostional National Wildlife Refuge in Guanacaste has recorded an extraordinary mass nesting event involving approximately 347,000 female olive ridley sea turtles, lasting more than 50 days. The phenomenon, which began in September 2026, has drawn the attention of environmental authorities and researchers because of its exceptional duration and magnitude.

According to the Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE), available historical records contain no documented nesting event with comparable characteristics in Ostional or elsewhere in the world. Known as an arribada, this natural phenomenon occurs when large numbers of female sea turtles emerge from the ocean to lay their eggs on the same beach.

Although Ostional experiences multiple arribadas throughout the year, the duration of this event distinguishes it from previous nesting episodes. Park rangers from the Tempisque Conservation Area, part of the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), worked alongside researchers from the Foundation for the Balance between Conservation and Development (FUNDECODES) to monitor nesting activity day and night.

Historical figures released by MINAE illustrate the magnitude of the event. In 2021, the busiest month, September, recorded approximately 307,000 female turtles, while November 2022 registered around 206,000. The busiest nesting months in 2023, 2024 and 2025 recorded approximately 111,000, 160,000 and 190,000 females, respectively.

Costa Rica has recorded 11 arribadas in Ostional so far in 2026. The event that began in September stands out because of its prolonged duration and the number of turtles involved. The cause of the unusual behavior has not been determined. One hypothesis proposed by environmental authorities is that turtles originating from different regions of North and South America converged in Ostional during the same period.

MINAE said further scientific research and analysis of the monitoring data will be needed to establish whether this explains the phenomenon.Carlos Pizarro, administrator of the Ostional National Wildlife Refuge, emphasized the importance of continuous monitoring to understand the event and compare the findings with historical records.

Environmental authorities also recognized the contribution of the local community to protecting nesting beaches and supporting conservation efforts. Ostional is internationally recognized as one of the most important nesting sites for olive ridley sea turtles (Lepidochelys olivacea), and researchers there are also studying the turtles’ exposure to pollution.

Anyone going to the beach during an arribada must enter with an authorized local guide, a rule covered in our Guanacaste turtle season article. Touching turtles and disturbing nests are not allowed, and flash photography is prohibited during nighttime nesting.

World.title: Red Cross Loses Poás Volcano Parking as It Weighs Ending Mountain and Water Rescues
World.content:
The Costa Rican Red Cross no longer runs the parking lot and restrooms at Poás Volcano National Park, one of the country’s main natural attractions, after the contract passed this month to a private consortium. The change takes a source of income from an organization that says it may have to stop mountain and water rescues to stay afloat.

The National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) put the service out to tender in April. The award went to VolcAN Group, a consortium of three individuals, according to the public procurement filed. The contract covers 256 parking spaces for cars, motorcycles, buses and minibuses, along with the restrooms.

SINAC said, through the Environment Ministry’s press office, that the Red Cross was not selected because it did not submit all the required documentation. The Red Cross objected and appealed and SINAC said those challenges were reviewed and resolved by the Comptroller General’s Office, and the award stands.

The Red Cross had managed the Poás parking area for four years. It has not said publicly how much the contract brought in. It continues to provide similar services at the Barva Volcano section of Braulio Carrillo National Park and the Prusia section of Irazú Volcano National Park.

SINAC’s page for the park lists parking at 2,750 colones (about $6.17) for cars, 1,250 colones ($2.80) for motorcycles and 5,000 colones ($11.21) for buses and minibuses, paid by card at the entrance booth. The park sits on one of Costa Rica’s two most active volcanoes and is among several protected areas with new rules this high season.

The lost contract comes during the worst financial stretch in the organization’s recent history. Its financial statements show losses of 524 million colones (about $1.18 million) in 2022, 704 million colones ($1.58 million) in 2023, 865 million colones ($1.94 million) in 2024 and 936 million colones ($2.1 million) in 2025.

From January through July of this year it had already lost 943 million colones ($2.11 million). By June, 66 of its local committees and boards were operating at a loss. General manager Walter Fallas said in October that the scenarios under review include moving some local committees to daytime-only shifts, which would lengthen response times at night, and suspending water and mountain rescues. He said those operations tie up crews and equipment for long periods and generate overtime the organization cannot fund.

Fallas said the Red Cross is also considering ending its support for the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) in recovering bodies and its emergency response in indigenous territories. Some stations could close, he said, though he ruled that out for the remainder of 2026. No date has been set for a decision on the rescue services.

The Red Cross responded to 537,919 incidents in 2025, roughly one every minute. During its mid-year vacation operation, from July 4 to 19, it handled 28 water emergencies and four mountain emergencies, by its own count. The organization says it needs about 30 billion colones ($67.3 million) a year to operate and took in about 24.6 billion colones ($55.3 million) in 2025.

The Finance Ministry announced a transfer of 1.5 billion colones ($3.36 million) in October, an amount the Red Cross says falls short of its needs. A bill that would exempt several of the organization’s funding sources from the fiscal spending cap is pending in a legislative committee.

For now, Red Cross crews continue to respond to emergencies nationwide, including on beaches and mountain trails and can be reached through 911.

World.title: Three Popular Places in Costa Rica I’ve Never Visited
World.content:
I have lived more than three decades in Costa Rica. That seems like enough time to get to know every corner of the place. After all, it is not a big country, about the same size in area as my home state of West Virginia. But the truth is that ninety percent of my life here has been spent within a triangle whose three points are San Isidro de el General, Dominical and Quepos/Manuel Antonio.

Throw in the Puerto Jimenez area where I have a small undeveloped parcel of land, and the San Jose area, because there are always times when it is necessary to head to the capital, and it’s more like 99 percent.

As for the other one percent– I had the good fortune to work for two major travel sales companies between 2012 and Covid and got to see most of the rest of the country a couple days at a time. The well-known tourist destinations, from Arenal to the Guanacaste Gold Coast, to most of the Nicoya Peninsula, and down through the Southern Pacific region to the border with Panama, all checked off.

But there are a few places I have never visited, and wonder if I ever will. And I also wonder– am I really missing anything? Here are 3 popular locations I don’t know, and possibly never will:

1) Monteverde

2019 was my final year in the travel business and my company gifted me a two night stay at a new Monteverde boutique hotel for 2020. However Covid put an end to my gift, and as my commission-only job morphed from preparing and selling travel itineraries to dealing with unhappy customers who wanted a cash refund and not a future credit, I was soon voluntarily unemployed.

But Monteverde is not the only cloud forest in Costa Rica. I can leave my house, drive one kilometer, make a right hand turn and head 45 kilometers up the mountain to the Cerro del Muerte and its own high elevation cloud forest.

2) Cahuita/Puerto Viejo

I have been to Tortuguero, experienced boating in through the canals and the funky little town on a narrow strip of land with water on all sides. But I never made it to the south end of the coast.

I do have experience with Caribbean culture as I lived on St Croix in the US Virgin Islands for two years before coming to Costa Rica. I enjoyed my time on St Croix, yet departed feeling like I had gotten all the Caribbean experience I would need for the rest of my life.

3) Santa Teresa

Recently I saw a clip on Facebook entitled Sights of Santa Teresa. In thirty seconds of shots of people walking, cycling, cruising slowly on ATVs, not a Tico in sight. I know it’s a popular surf spot and Tom Brady has a place somewhere near there. But to be honest, it seems like a place for people who want to come to Costa Rica without experiencing Costa Rica.

Three places that perhaps under different circumstances I would have landed upon and made home. Am I missing anything by never knowing them? You tell me.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Tax Office Will Send Notices Only to a Digital Mailbox From Jan. 1
World.content:
Starting Jan. 1, Costa Rica’s tax authority will stop delivering notices to your door, by mail or by fax. If you are registered as a taxpayer, official notices will go only to a digital mailbox in TRIBU-CR, the Finance Ministry’s online tax system and your deadline to respond will start running whether or not you open them.

The change comes from Law 10.982, published Nov. 17 in the official gazette La Gaceta. It makes the mailbox the single official channel for collection notices, requests for information and other tax procedures. The timing is the part to understand. You are considered notified on the business day after a notice lands in your mailbox. Your period to respond begins the business day after that.

The ministry will send you a text message or email when something new arrives. That alert is a reminder, not the notice itself, so a wrong phone number or a message caught in a spam folder does not stop the clock. The rule applies to anyone registered with the tax administration, including companies, self-employed professionals and people who declare rental income.

To read your notices, log in to the Virtual Office, known as OVi, at ovitribucr.hacienda.go.cr with your TRIBU-CR credentials. Before Jan. 1, log in once to confirm you can get in, and check that the phone number and email on file are current so the alerts reach you. After that, open the mailbox on a regular schedule even if no alert has arrived, because the law counts the days from the deposit, not from the moment you read it.

If an accountant handles your taxes, agree now on who checks the mailbox and how often. Francisco Ovares, president of the College of Public Accountants, recommended that companies and accountants review how they communicate with the tax administration. He said the reform aims to simplify procedures but must guarantee legal certainty and due process.

There are limited exceptions. In certain assessment, penalty and appeal proceedings, you can designate an email address for notices. If that email bounces, the notice goes to the mailbox instead.

People who are not registered, have no mailbox and have no email on file will still be notified in person or through a notice published in La Gaceta.

If age, health, a disability, where you live or your economic situation makes the system hard to use, you can go to designated tax administration offices for help setting up the mailbox.

The same law changes other rules. Advance income tax payments will be calculated on the tax you owed the previous year or the average of your last three fiscal periods, whichever is higher. Three quarters of that base is split into three equal installments due on the last business day of June, September and December.

If you are just starting a business, the advance payments begin the following fiscal period. The ministry may also use its own land and construction valuation tools when it reviews property transfers, real estate capital gains and the luxury home tax. The mailbox rule arrives weeks before another change. Rules requiring businesses and professionals to register the SINPE Móvil numbers they use to get paid take effect Jan. 18.

World.title: The Drive From Some Costa Rica Destinations to the Airport Now Tops Five Hours
World.content:
If your Costa Rica trip ends on the Osa Peninsula, in Tamarindo or in the southern highlands, plan on most of a day to get back to the main international airport in San Jose. The drive from San Vito de Coto Brus to Juan Santamaría International Airport now averages 5 hours 28 minutes, the longest of any canton in the country.

That is longer than the roughly four-hour nonstop flight from Costa Rica to Atlanta. The figures come from the 2026 National Competitiveness Index, published by the Competitiveness Promotion Council. It measures the average drive from the main town of each of the country’s 82 cantons to the airport in Alajuela, using Google Maps data collected every day of the year.

The readings are taken at 7 a.m., noon and 5 p.m., so they reflect real traffic, not the best-case time your map app shows late at night. Here is what the index shows for some of the places visitors go most. From the Osa, on the southern Pacific, the drive averages 4 hours 7 minutes, the sixth-longest in the country. From Carrillo, the canton that includes Playas del Coco and Playa Hermosa, it is about 4 hours.

From Santa Cruz, the area that includes Tamarindo, it is about 3 hours 48 minutes. From Quepos, next to Manuel Antonio National Park, it is 2 hours 49 minutes. Those are averages from each canton’s main town, not from your hotel. If you are staying at the beach or down a gravel road, add the time it takes you to reach that town first.

Monteverde has no figure. It was left out because it only got its own local government in 2024 and does not yet have comparable data. If you are in Guanacaste, flying out of Liberia changes the math. The average drive to Daniel Oduber International Airport is 32 minutes from Carrillo and 59 minutes from Santa Cruz.

Even that has slowed as the Santa Cruz drive is about 10 minutes longer than it was in 2022. Víctor Umaña, executive director of the Center for Tourism Studies, said congestion on Route 21 between the Liberia airport and the beaches can stretch a 20.5-kilometer (12.7-mile) trip to as much as an hour and a half.

The trend is national as the rive times to Juan Santamaría in San Jose rose in 78 of 82 cantons between 2022 and 2026, and the countrywide average went from 1 hour 40 minutes to 1 hour 51 minutes. Inside the greater metropolitan area, the average went from 32 to 43 minutes. Escazú is now 40 minutes from the airport on average, and central San José is 37.

The main reason is more cars on the same roads. Vehicles carrying the mandatory insurance grew 17% between 2022 and the end of 2025, to about 2.09 million. The same index found that traffic jams in Costa Rica doubled in a year. Andrés Fernández, an economist at the council, said the longer trips affect both travelers and businesses, and that the indicator shows whether travel times are getting worse regardless of distance.

For your own planning, treat the average as a minimum and add at least an extra hour on top of it, because a single crash or closure on a two-lane highway often has no detour. If your flight leaves before midday and you are more than three hours away, spending the last night near the airport removes the risk.

Check for roadwork before you leave. Route 1, the main highway from Guanacaste and the central Pacific into Alajuela, has night lane closures near Naranjo for about two weeks.

World.title: UN Expert Albanese Spends Night in Costa Rica Airport as Court Gives Immigration 24 Hours
World.content:
Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, spent last night inside Juan Santamaría International Airport after Costa Rican immigration authorities refused her entry. Hours later, the Constitutional Court ordered that she not be removed until it rules on her case.

Albanese, an Italian lawyer, arrived yesterday afternoon on a flight from Paris. She had been invited by the University of Costa Rica (UCR) to receive an honorary doctorate at a ceremony scheduled for this morning. Omer Badilla, director general of the General Directorate of Migration and Immigration, said in a video statement sent to media that the immigration police applied a rejection under the General Law of Migration and Immigration because Albanese is the subject of an international alert for alleged links to terrorist acts.

He did not say which body issued the alert or what acts it referred to. The directorate said separately that the refusal rested on national security grounds and that Albanese had been placed at the disposal of the airline that flew her in, so it could arrange her departure.

Albanese has denied any link to terrorism. Speaking to local media from the terminal, she called the accusation ridiculous, said not even the United States had gone that far, and asked authorities to present proof or apologize. She said she had been told informally that the decision was related to agreements with Washington.

The U.S. government sanctioned Albanese in July 2025 over her work as rapporteur, a move criticized at the time by UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk. Israel barred her from entering its territory in February 2024.

Late Thursday, the Constitutional Chamber, known as Sala IV, admitted a habeas corpus petition challenging the refusal. In a resolution signed last night by Magistrate Luis Fernando Salazar Alvarado, the court ordered immigration authorities to ensure Albanese does not leave Costa Rica until the case is decided, unless she chooses to go freely, with legal counsel and after being warned of the consequences.

The court gave the immigration director and the head of the Professional Migration Police 24 hours from notification to file a sworn report with certified copies of the relevant documents. Under the Constitutional Jurisdiction Law, disobeying the order is punishable by three months to two years in prison or a fine. Magistrate Anamari Garro Vargas was assigned to the case.

One petition was filed by Frente Amplio lawmaker Joselyn Sáenz, who argued that U.S. sanctions are not binding on Costa Rica and do not by themselves justify a rejection under national immigration law. Her filing asks whether the refusal is tied to those sanctions or to Costa Rica’s commitments under the Shield of the Americas security framework with Washington and requests that Albanese be allowed to contact her lawyer and the Italian consulate.

The UCR administration called the situation extremely serious, asked immigration authorities and the Foreign Ministry to explain the legal basis for the decision and requested due process for Albanese. The university’s governing council said it deeply regretted the situation and reaffirmed its commitment to academic freedom.

Türk said he was very concerned and urged Costa Rican authorities to reconsider urgently and allow her entry. Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, publicly praised the decision.

The case comes as President Laura Fernández, who took office in May, has moved Costa Rica closer to Israel and the United States. Last week the country shifted its stance on UN votes on Israel and the Palestinians and in May the government said it could open an embassy in Jerusalem. UN special rapporteurs have raised concerns about Costa Rica before, including a 2025 warning that the country’s judicial independence was at risk.

It was unclear early this morning whether Albanese would be able to attend the ceremony. The court’s ruling, expected once immigration authorities file their report, will decide whether she can enter or must leave and may clarify how far foreign sanctions and unexplained security alerts can shape who is allowed into the country.

World.title: Three Egyptian businessmen busted at Sandhill checkpoint for immigration offences; One granted bail, another faces deportation
World.content:
Three Egyptian businessmen busted at Sandhill checkpoint for immigration offences; One granted bail, another faces deportation

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Three Egyptian businessmen appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday on separate immigration charges, with one being granted bail, another remanded to prison and the third ordered to be removed from Belize.

The men were identified as Ahmad Ismael Gaber Namma, Hossam Galal Elsayed Bakr of the Maya Mopan area of Belmopan, and 35-year-old Mohammed Altia Mohamed Attia Farag of Otro Benque, Orange Walk Town.

According to the Belize Immigration Department, the three men were detained at a checkpoint in Sandhill Village on Wednesday, November 25, 2026.

Namma appeared before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison, where he pleaded guilty to failing to comply with the conditions of his visitor’s permit, which expired on November 18.

Namma expressed interest in obtaining an extension but indicated that he was prepared to return to Egypt if the court decided otherwise.

The Immigration Department successfully applied for his removal from Belize. Namma was fined $1,000 plus $5 in court costs, which he paid immediately. However, he was remanded to the Belize Central Prison pending the preparation of his deportation documents.

Meanwhile, Bakr and Farag appeared before Magistrate Tehra Brown. Bakr was charged with failing to produce a valid permit to an immigration officer upon demand, while Farag was charged with failing to comply with the conditions of his visitor’s permit, which expired on October 28.

No pleas were taken from either man after the Immigration Department requested an adjournment to verify the authenticity of their marriage certificates. Both men claim to be married to Belizean women.

Their attorney, Ian Gray, argued that their marriages and community ties to Belize demonstrated that they were not flight risks.

However, the Magistrate denied Bakr bail amid concerns over his alleged illegal entry into Belize, while Farag, who entered the country legally, was granted bail of $2,500 plus one surety of the same amount.

As part of his bail conditions, Farag must report to the Orange Walk Police Station three times a week, on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. He successfully posted bail.

Both men’s passports have been confiscated by the Immigration Department.

Bakr and Farag are scheduled to return to court on December 4, 2026, when immigration officials are expected to provide an update on the verification of their marriage certificates.

World.title: Ministry of National Security, Energy and Ports to host Energy Fair and Marketplace
World.content:
Ministry of National Security, Energy and Ports to host Energy Fair and Marketplace

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of National Security, Energy and Ports (MNSEP) will host its Energy Fair and Marketplace 2027 on Thursday, January 28, offering the public an opportunity to explore energy solutions, innovations and products aimed at promoting energy awareness and sustainability.

The event will take place at the Caribbean Motors Showroom in Belize City from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., with free entrance for all attendees.

World.title: Belize welcomes 108 new citizens, celebrating stories of hope and belonging
World.content:
Belize welcomes 108 new citizens, celebrating stories of hope and belonging

By Zoila Palma: On November 26, 2026, Belize welcomed 108 new citizens during a citizenship ceremony where Minister of Immigration, Governance and Labour, Kareem Musa, reaffirmed the constitutional restrictions preventing Guatemalan nationals from obtaining Belizean citizenship through registration while Guatemala’s territorial claim against Belize remains unresolved.

The new citizens came from Central America, North America, South America, the Caribbean, Europe, Africa, the Middle East and Asia.

Among the recipients were American entrepreneur Debbie Baldwin, popularly known as “Miss Debs” for her burger and mobile food business, and German-born textile artist and author Ingrid Cayetano, wife of Belizean artist and Punta Rock pioneer Delvin “Pen” Cayetano.

El Salvador accounted for the largest number of recipients with 38, followed by Honduras with 35. Together, the two countries represented nearly 68 percent of the new citizens.

During his address, Musa acknowledged the political instability, civil conflicts, economic challenges and gang violence that have influenced migration throughout Central America. He said Belize has provided generations of families with an opportunity to find safety, employment, education and a peaceful environment in which to raise their children.

He also addressed concerns surrounding Guatemalan nationality, citing Section 29(3) of the Belize Constitution, which restricts citizenship by registration for nationals of countries that do not recognize Belize’s independence, sovereignty or territorial integrity. None of Thursday’s recipients were Guatemalan nationals.

Musa reiterated that Belize remains committed to protecting its territorial sovereignty while pursuing a peaceful resolution of Guatemala’s claim through the International Court of Justice. Oral hearings in the case are scheduled for February 2027.

He also highlighted the journeys of two Honduran recipients, Anthony Henrriquez and Janeth Romero, whose experiences reflect the challenges and sacrifices faced by families who migrated to Belize in search of better opportunities.

Henrriquez was ten years old when he crossed Belize’s western border after his mother left Honduras to find a safer future for her children. More than two decades later, he is a husband, father of two daughters and bartender in Caye Caulker. He described Belize as “little in size but big in heart,” adding, “I love Belize. It is my home and the home of my daughters.”

Romero, who moved to Belize in 2013, established a small business selling personal care products to support her family and said obtaining legal status helped her family access healthcare. She has settled in Orange Walk and hopes to improve her English to communicate more effectively within her community.

Musa said citizenship offers individuals the opportunity to participate in Belize’s democratic processes, exercise their rights and contribute to decisions affecting their communities.

He also emphasized the responsibilities that come with citizenship, including respecting the law, protecting the environment and upholding Belize’s constitutional principles and territorial sovereignty.

World.title: Climate Change Department and UNEP’s Climate Finance Analyst discuss climate transparency efforts
World.content:
Climate Change Department and UNEP’s Climate Finance Analyst discuss climate transparency efforts

By Zoila Palma: On November 27, 2026, the Climate Change Department met with UNEP’s Climate Finance Analyst to advance Belize’s climate transparency efforts through the Enabling Activity Project and the Capacity Building Initiative for Transparency (CBIT).

These initiatives are important in strengthening national capacity, improving climate data and reporting systems, and enhancing Belize’s ability to monitor and communicate progress on climate action.

The Climate Change department says that through continued collaboration and capacity building, Belize is taking meaningful steps toward greater climate transparency, accountability, and informed decision-making for a more climate-resilient and sustainable future

World.title: Argentina locks politicians out of the printing press. Could Belize learn from it?
World.content:
Argentina locks politicians out of the printing press. Could Belize learn from it?

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Argentina has done something many countries only talk about.

It has taken the money printer out of the hands of politicians.

On Thursday, November 26, the Chamber of Deputies approved a new central bank charter by 141 votes to none, with 99 abstentions. It now heads to the executive for promulgation.

The change is easy to explain.

Argentina’s central bank can no longer finance the national government, the provinces or the municipalities.

Not a little. Not in an emergency. Not at all.

Its primary mission is now to preserve the value of the peso, with the older employment and development goals removed.

How did Argentina get here?

By doing the opposite for years.

Government after government spent more than it earned and covered the gap with freshly printed pesos, which fuelled currency crises and pushed inflation into triple digits.

Ordinary people paid for it. At the supermarket. At the pump. In salaries that bought less every month.

President Javier Milei made ending that practice a central promise. This law puts it in writing.

It is not a total victory for him. A future president could still remove the central bank governor with the support of 37 of 72 senators, a much lower bar than the two thirds of both chambers Milei wanted.

Now bring it home.

Belize has never had Argentina’s kind of inflation. There is a reason.

Our dollar is pegged to the US dollar at two to one. It has been for decades.

That peg is a promise. And a promise like that has to be backed by US dollars sitting in reserve.

Print too many Belize dollars and the promise gets harder to keep.

Here is why.

Belize imports most of what it uses. Fuel. Vehicles. Machinery. A lot of what is on the dinner table.

Extra Belize dollars created to fund government spending end up chasing imports. Imports are paid for in US dollars. The reserves go down.

Push that far enough and the peg itself is at risk.

That is not theory. It is the story of country after country.

And Belize is not without pressure today.

The public debt is about $4.68 billion. This year’s interest bill is $189 million. Fuel costs are high. US dollars are tight enough that Belize Electricity Limited says it has had to wait on the banks to pay its supplier in Mexico.

The Central Bank of Belize is allowed to extend credit to the government within limits set by law.

Those limits are the guardrails.

Argentina spent years driving without any, and has now welded them in place.

Belize still has its guardrails and still has its peg.

The lesson from Buenos Aires is to keep both.

World.title: Applications open for January 2027 intake of Edinburgh Napier University online degrees
World.content:
Applications open for January 2027 intake of Edinburgh Napier University online degrees

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Applications are now open for the January 2027 intake of online degree programmes from Edinburgh Napier University, offered through SEI Degrees.

The programmes are delivered fully online and are described as 100 percent flexible and 100 percent relevant, allowing students to study from Belize while continuing to work.

Degrees are available at both the undergraduate and postgraduate levels, including MBA, MSc, BA and BSc programmes, with a wide variety of specialisms.

Edinburgh Napier University, based in Scotland, is promoted as being among the top 5 percent of universities worldwide and is AACSB accredited, an international accreditation for business schools.

The online format offers Belizean professionals a route to a United Kingdom degree without the cost of relocating abroad.

World.title: Bulridge Ltd. leads planting of 300 seedlings in Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve
World.content:
Bulridge Ltd. leads planting of 300 seedlings in Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Bulridge Ltd. has led the planting of approximately 300 seedlings in a degraded area of the Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve as part of its ongoing forest restoration efforts.

The activity took place last Saturday, when the company headed into the reserve in the Cayo District with a group of volunteers from The Office Gurus Belize.

Together, the team transplanted the seedlings into an area in need of restoration.

Bulridge said the work contributes to continuing efforts to restore the forest.

The company thanked The Office Gurus team for their time and effort, and credited photographer @jbarrera_ph for documenting the day.

“Every seedling makes a difference,” Bulridge said.

The Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve is one of Belize’s best known protected areas, recognised for its pine forest, rivers and waterfalls.

World.title: Market Bag: Prices dip as Uncle joins Observer at ‘Curry’
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Shoppers will find further relief in food prices this week at the Coronation Market, where several popular produce items are being sold at lower prices.

When the Market Bag team visited the downtown Kingston landmark Thursday, sweet peppers were selling for $350 per pound, while Scotch bonnet peppers were going for $300 per pound. Tomatoes were priced at $200 per pound, carrots for $350 per pound and onions for $250 per pound.

Meanwhile, Irish potatoes were being offered at $250 per pound; sweet potatoes, $400 per pound and pumpkin for $300 per pound.

Lettuce was being sold for $500 per pound, while sorrel remained at $600 per pound.

Joining Market Bag for a special market visit was digital content creator Hakeem Bryan, popularly known as “Uncle”, who admitted that he has been struggling to keep up with rising food prices.

“It’s terrible. Because wah day lettuce rise to the moon, wah day tomato rise to the moon. And mi ah say, yo, mi a go stop eat lettuce, mi a go stop eat tomato,” Bryan said.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: Traffic takedown
World.content:
A father holds his daughter as he watches a representative of the Island Traffic Authority remove the licence plate from his vehicle on Old Harbour Road on Thursday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

A push by the Island Traffic Authority (ITA) to make Jamaica’s roads safer ahead of the Christmas season was welcomed by some motorists but criticised by others as an early-morning enforcement drive on Old Harbour Road left 42 motorists without licence plates by midday on Thursday.

The operation, conducted jointly by the ITA and the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) at the St Catherine-Clarendon border, forms part of the traffic authority’s ‘Fatal Five Road Safety Intervention Strategy’ which targets the five leading causes of traffic crashes

— speeding, improper overtaking, improper lane use, pedestrians in the roadway, and unsafe right turns.

According to ITA figures, 373 of the 415 vehicles inspected up to midday Thursday were found to be roadworthy. The remaining 42 vehicles were found to be in breach of some road rules, resulting in the drivers being ticketed and given 24 hours to complete repairs before being barred from the road, after the vehicles were stripped of their licence plates.

ITA Manager of Corporate Communications and Public Relations Dontae Matthews told the Jamaica Observer that while the initiative targets the five leading causes of fatal crashes, it includes other areas designed to make travelling on Jamaica’s roads safer.

He said the ITA will be conducting an audit of roads and making recommendations on issues such as road markings and pedestrian crossings. The ITA will also be expanding its public education on the use of the roads and enforcement activities such as the one conducted on Thursday.

According to Matthews, although the initiative is being rolled out to meet the festive season, it will continue into 2027.

He said the ITA hopes the intervention will continue to drive down road fatalities in Jamaica, which recorded 281 fatal crashes, resulting in 324 lives lost up to November 26 this year. This represents a four per cent reduction compared with the corresponding period in 2025.

“It will go into the next financial year as well, and we will be assessing the data over time, and we’ll be making tweaks if the five causes of fatalities change… amendments will be made, and we will target those five reasons as well… So, the Christmas season is very important, but we will be taking it beyond it, into the new year, and we’re hoping for a reduction in road fatalities,” said Matthews.

But the ITA’s enforcement activity did not find favour with all road users, several of whom complained that the checks were unfair and disrupted their daily business.

Visibly upset as she stood beside her car, a motorist identifying herself only as Rosa recounted how the traffic stop derailed her day. Police had pulled her over and removed her licence plates after deeming the tint on her windscreen an infraction.

Rosa told the Observer that the police denied her and her partner the chance to fix the issue on the spot, leaving them stalled for several minutes en route to getting medical care for their sick daughter.

“If it’s the tint, why them never just let us tear it off? Because I’ve seen police do that before and them allow you to just tear it off. And if you a go charge me, charge me, but now them tear off mi licence plate, have mi here so for how long before they could take it off, with mi sick baby inna the car,” charged Rosa as she pointed to her partner holding the child in his arms.

“I was on the way to the doctor, and before them hurry up and take off the licence plate them have mi here a spin round with the baby. Mi can’t tek dem something here!” she complained.

While Rosa did not dispute the infraction, admitting the tint extended several inches too far onto her windscreen, she argued there were far better ways to remedy the situation.

“Mi tint up and mi wrong, I understand that. But they could have made me just tear it off. They didn’t give me no option,” she said.

Her frustration was echoed by another motorist who received a $10,000 ticket and had his licence plates removed also due to a tint infraction. He claimed the stop was unfair and introduced disorder to his planned day.

“They didn’t give me an option, they just gave me this ticket and remove my plate. This is now hindering me from going to Kingston to conduct my business. Now this a go cost me $6,000 to get back my plate, plus the $10,000 ticket, that’s $16,000. I don’t even factor in the gas and the toll fee that I’m going to have to add to that. It’s just unfair,” he said.

Another motorist chimed in, telling the Observer that he was on his way to have his windscreen fixed. That windscreen issue resulted in the removal of his licence plates. The driver argued that a more productive exercise would be addressing the potholes damaging vehicles across the island and pressing the Government to fix the roads.

“Right now this don’t make no sense, because they don’t even ask mi any question, dem just do wha’ dem a do. They need to be fixing the potholes weh a chop people tyre and a mash up people vehicle,” he charged.

But some motorists were pleased with the operation, insisting that more needs to be done to ensure safety on the roads. Among those applauding the ITA was Dr Charlton Collie, who told the Observer that he was impressed by the process.

“It’s in the interest of the drivers, because it is in protection of them, so I think it’s very important, and I appreciate what they are doing, because I could be at a disadvantage if a motorist with their defective vehicle hits mine, and that could result in a loss of life,” he said.

“I appreciate what they’re doing because I hardly [ever] see anything like this. So, really, it is up to us to do better on the roads,” added Collie.

His sentiment found resonance with Ricardo Williams, another motorist who was stopped due to a tint infraction but was given a warning to have it removed. He thanked the ITA for the opportunity to have his issue corrected, and admitted that the intervention was necessary.

“Yes, my tint was about six inches so we are going to have it rectified, so I’m wrong there. I understand that and mi respect what’s going on here today,” said Williams.

World.title: Project blue for Kingston Harbour
World.content:
Scores of plastic bottles and other waste prevented from entering the Kingston Harbour through a private sector led-initiative. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

PRIME Minister Dr Andrew Holness has expressed pleasure at the success of an ongoing project to prevent millions of kilogrammes of plastic and other solid waste from entering Kingston Harbour over the past six years.

According to Holness, this fits well with the Government’s plans for the redevelopment of downtown Kingston.

The prime minister was taken on a tour of sections of the Kingston Harbour on Thursday, and was briefed on the work of the project that — since it was launched four years ago — has prevented some eight million kilogrammes or 8,000 metric tonnes of waste from entering the harbour.

The forces behind the Kingston Harbour Clean-up Project — which has cost more than $1 billion since its launch — include non-profit organisations the Ocean Clean-Up, GraceKennedy Foundation, and Clean Harbours Jamaica.

The project has accomplished the commendable feat by setting up unique barriers at strategic locations where discharge from drains and gullies would enter the harbour. These barriers trap the waste, then special teams using boats and other units remove the garbage, which is then taken to land where it is sorted and disposed of.

Barriers have been placed at the mouths of nine gullies which drain into the harbour — Sandy, Shoemaker, Mountain View, D’Aguilar, Tivoli, Balmagie, Rae Town, Barnes, and the Kingston Pen.

“There is a plan to redevelop the waterfront of the Kingston Harbour. The plan is very ambitious. It involves a harbour walk, which starts just at almost where the craft market is, coming all the way around to where the airport is. We intend to create a walkable and runnable harbour, a linear garden, open spaces, and public spaces for the citizens to be able to interface, interact, recreate, conduct business meetings and gatherings on the waterfront,” said Holness as he indicated how a cleaner harbour will interact with the downtown Kingston redevelopment plans which have been many years in the making.

Holness commended the entities leading the project for seeing the importance of a clean harbour and taking steps to fix the problem of pollution.

“The funding is largely private, and that ought to be noted, but the effort of Government in the facilitation of, and in the support, has an economic value to make the project effective. All partners share the concern about non-degradable and some degradable waste entering the harbour. This project, taking out eight million kilogrammes of waste out of the harbour is a significant impact,” the prime minister added.

Minister of Water, Environment, and Climate Change Matthew Samuda pointed out that as a result of the project, and other initiatives that are to come, “We are well on the way to making Kingston Harbour blue again.”

Samuda pointed to a lecture that was given recently by Professor Mona Webber, which zoomed in on the impact that non-degradable waste, especially, has on mangroves.

He noted that the work to remove waste from the harbour has already started producing measureable results.

“It’s the first time we have had the level of growth and survival rate that we are seeing with the new mangroves that are being planted along the coastal area for protection. It is a measurable impact that even the UN Marine Biology Department is seeing,” said Samuda.

Meanwhile, Nisha Bakker, director of partnerships at Ocean Clean-Up, said the results of the studies and surveys being done to see the full extent of the positive impact of the clean-up are not yet available.

However, she pointed out that there are some obvious and very positive effects on fish populations.

“We’re seeing mangrove restoration and improved biodiversity. We hope by the longer term that this will also be positive for real estate value and economic growth,” she said.

Frank James, chief executive officer of GraceKennedy Group, described the project as one of the greatest examples of public-private partnership.

“That beautiful harbour that we are looking at has eight million kilogrammes less waste than it would have without this project,” said James as he expressed gratitude to numerous government agencies which have facilitated the mission.

He underscored that outside of the fact that GraceKennedy sees the national good in having its foundation partner on such a project, he couldn’t help but acknowledge that the harbour is basically the company’s backyard.

“As you know, the Kingston Harbour is really our backyard, so it is very personal for us as well. But, importantly, we recognise that the harbour is bigger than us. You will note the name of the project does not have GraceKennedy in it. It is the Kingston Harbour Clean-up Project. We are very happy to have the Ocean Clean-Up, who have been really tremendous in the amount of funding and expertise that they have brought to the table and also Clean Harbours Jamaica, the people who make it happen every day on the ground.

“The project directly impacts, livelihoods of people. We are talking about the fisheries industry, which is a key part of it. We are talking about marine life, the mangroves. We need nothing more than Hurricane Melissa to demonstrate the importance of the mangroves in protecting the seashore and making sure we are able to protect the land and also that we build a marine biodiversity,” added James.

World.title: Victory!
World.content:
Ras-I.

While his own album, Heart of Love, did not advance to the final six in the Best Reggae Album category for the 69th Grammy Awards, reggae artiste Ras-I believes Jamaica has already secured a meaningful victory.

When the nominations were announced, the singer said his attention was drawn less to the absence of his name and more to the fact that all six nominees were Jamaicans.

“Dat a di first victory right deh so,” he said, explaining that his immediate reaction was to congratulate those who had earned nominations. “It’s only six spots and some 119 albums were submitted. So, just to even be in the conversation is a win. Congrats to Runkus, who is my bredda inna music and inna life. Mi glad say somebody from our generation inna di mix, so it’s a nice balance.”

For Ras-I, the all-Jamaican showing is a reminder of the island’s enduring influence on reggae and the creative work being produced by its artistes. It is also a moment that invites celebration beyond individual accomplishments, particularly in an industry where international recognition can carry significant weight.

That appreciation for Jamaica’s musical reach also informs his support for calls to establish a separate Grammy category for dancehall.

“It would be nice to have a dancehall category, because dancehall is very impactful, we can’t deny that. I mean, look at all the greats the genre has produced,” he said.

The argument for a dedicated category speaks to the distinction between two of Jamaica’s most influential musical exports, both of which have helped shape the global soundscape. While reggae has long enjoyed its own Grammy category, dancehall’s cultural and commercial footprint has continued to expand, with generations of artistes carrying the genre to audiences well beyond the Caribbean.

For Ras-I, recognising that impact through a dedicated category would provide another avenue for Jamaican music to receive the international acknowledgement it deserves.

He also believes the conversation surrounding Grammy recognition should extend beyond the familiar names that dominate Jamaica’s local music landscape. In recent discussions about the nominations, some music fans have questioned the inclusion of artistes who may not enjoy widespread recognition at home. Ras-I, however, cautions against using local popularity as the sole or main measure of an artiste’s relevance or international standing.

He pointed out that reggae’s audience stretches across continents, meaning an artiste who appears relatively unfamiliar to Jamaican listeners could have an established fan base in other markets.

“The world is a big place, so you not knowing someone round deh so, nuh mean say another 200,000 or 2 million people nuh know him across the world. And Grammy votes nuh stop with Jamaicans, and sales nuh stop inna Jamaica. In fact, sales barely happen inna Jamaica,” he said.

Rather than dismissing unfamiliar names, he encouraged listeners to take the opportunity to discover the music and the artistes behind it.

“So, it alright if yuh nuh know who a man is. You can go search and find out just like yuh woulda search and find any drama weh a gyaan pan di socials. Go look fi some good music. Why you wouldn’t say, ‘Who name Runkus, make me go check out dis?’ Yuh might be surprised. Yuh goodly love the album,” Ras-I charged.

His observation raises a wider point about how music is consumed and evaluated in an increasingly connected industry. An artiste’s visibility in Jamaica does not necessarily reflect the size of their audience elsewhere, just as a lack of local familiarity does not automatically diminish the quality or reach of their work.

Ras-I’s response to this year’s Best Reggae Album nominations reflects a perspective that extends beyond the need for personal gratification. For him, this year’s list of nominees represents reggae’s continued evolution and an opportunity to discover new voices.

World.title: CARBON CHARGES THREATEN CARIBBEAN TRADE
World.content:
CARICOM businesses and consumers could incur an additional US$3.6 billion in shipping costs between 2028 and 2035 under proposed global regulations to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the maritime industry, with alternative plans from Japan and Tuvalu carrying significantly different price tags.

The projected burden is outlined in a new study by the Caricom Private Sector Organisation (CPSO), which assesses the economic implications of the International Maritime Organization (IMO)-proposed Net-Zero Framework (NZF) for the region.

Released ahead of the 85th session of the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85), which opens in London on November 30, the study measures, for the first time, the potential impact of the framework on each of 12 Caricom member states.

The CPSO estimates that, under the framework approved by the committee in April 2025, shipping costs for imports into the region could increase by 14 per cent by 2035, adding US$761 million to the bill in that year alone.

According to the CPSO, the study also examines four alternative proposals submitted ahead of the November 30 to December 3 meeting, including options from Japan, Tuvalu, Brazil, and Liberia.

Under Japan’s proposal, the additional shipping costs to Caricom between 2028 and 2035 could amount to approximately US$3 billion, below the US$3.6 billion projected under the approved framework. Tuvalu’s proposal, however, could push the additional cost to US$4.8 billion, CPSO said in a news release on Thursday.

The preliminary estimates for the proposals from Brazil and Liberia are considerably lower, at approximately US$700 million and US$500 million, respectively. However, the CPSO cautions that neither guarantees that the region will receive compensation for the financial burden it incurs.

Japan’s proposal is among the alternatives seeking to reshape the framework’s approach to reducing shipping emissions and managing the associated financial costs, with greater emphasis on a lower-cost compliance pathway. Tuvalu’s proposal, meanwhile, takes a more ambitious approach to emissions reduction and the associated financial mechanism, with a potential for higher charges on shipping activity.

The CPSO’s modelling suggests that, despite differences in the financial implications, all five options would increase shipping and import costs for the Caribbean.

Dr Patrick Antoine, chief executive officer and technical director of the CPSO, said the organisation endorses efforts to achieve net-zero emissions in shipping but cautioned that vulnerable economies should not be forced to bear a disproportionate share of the costs.

“The CPSO supports net-zero shipping. However, we do not support a text that charges, in full, a region facing disproportionately negative impacts and leaves what comes back to be decided later. There can be no IMO-NZF without safeguards for Caricom,” the release quotes Antoine.

Under the framework as approved, the study projects that shipping costs could rise by roughly one-third by 2035, compared with 2027, taking normal freight growth into account. The landed cost of imported goods could increase by approximately 2.5 per cent, before the additional expense is compounded by Customs duties and taxes.

The implications could be particularly severe for Caribbean economies, where imports account for between 28 and 47 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP).

The study estimates that real imports into the region could be US$2.9 billion, or 9.5 per cent, lower in 2035 than they would otherwise have been. Food imports alone could decline by US$312 million.

The CPSO argues that the region is especially exposed because shipping operators serving Caribbean markets have limited options for switching to cleaner fuels in the near term. There is no established regional bunkering network for these fuels, while feeder vessels serving the islands have little representation in shipyard order books.

Consequently, shipping lines are likely to absorb the additional regulatory charges and pass them on to importers through freight surcharges, as they have done with carbon-related costs imposed by the European Union since 2024.

The study notes that nine international shipping associations, in a November 18 statement, also highlighted the current lack of commercially viable alternative marine fuels.

According to the study, the economic impact is expected to vary across the region, with tourism-dependent island economies facing potential declines of between 6.6 per cent and 9.5 per cent in real imports.

It said that for smaller islands served by limited shipping routes, the risk extends beyond higher freight charges to the possibility of shipping lines reducing or withdrawing services altogether.

The estimates focus on imports, but the CPSO points out that exports would also be exposed to the additional charges because they are transported on the same vessels.

Another concern is the distribution of revenue collected under the proposed framework. The study estimates that Caricom’s payments in 2030 could represent approximately two per cent of the revenue expected to flow into the IMO’s Net-Zero Fund, despite the region accounting for just 0.12 per cent of global imports.

However, the rules governing how the fund’s resources will be distributed have yet to be established.

The framework is expected to return for consideration at the IMO’s resumed extraordinary session on December 4. The CPSO is therefore urging negotiators to ensure that any final agreement, including a possible compromise, protects Caribbean consumers from further increases in the cost of living and safeguards food security.

It is proposing three conditions for supporting any framework that incorporates a fund or investment facility.

First, the rules must formally recognise the disproportionate economic impact on Caribbean small island developing states (SIDS), guarantee a dedicated share of funding for them, and allow a phased implementation of requirements on shipping routes serving the region.

Second, the fund must return to Caricom at least the amount collected from its imports and exports, preferably through a regionally controlled mechanism such as the Caribbean Development Bank.

Third, negotiators should prioritise the option carrying the lowest net cost to the region, keeping the proposals from Japan, Brazil, and Liberia under consideration.

Beyond the immediate financial risks, the CPSO believes the transition to cleaner shipping could create opportunities for the Caribbean once the necessary vessels and fuel infrastructure are established.

The study estimates that a dual-fuel feeder vessel could generate savings of between US$200 and US$250 for every tonne of conventional fuel it replaces. However, the technology and supporting fuel supply arrangements are not yet sufficiently established in the region.

“This is an investment agenda as much as a negotiating position,” Antoine said. “Caricom can be a supplier of cleaner marine fuels, not just a payer of carbon charges. But the infrastructure, the ships, and the finance have to come first, and the private sector is ready to assist with bridging the gap that exists.”

World.title: UNITED FRONT!
World.content:
Jamaica striker Khadija Shaw (left) and United States player Alana Cook battle for possession during the 2022 Concacaf Women’s Championship match at the BBVA Bancomer stadium in Monterrey, Mexico, on July 7, 2022. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica will go into 2031 with no experience of hosting a tournament on the scale of a FIFA Women’s World Cup. However, Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts says they will have a helping hand with US Soccer providing assistance throughout the preparation process.

On Monday, Jamaica, USA, Mexico and Costa Rica were confirmed as co-hosts at FIFA’s Extraordinary Congress in Zurich, Switzerland.

The 2031 Women’s World Cup will be the first edition to feature more than 100 games following the expansion from 32 to 48 teams.

While multi-country hosting has become the norm in recent years, the 2031 tournament will mark the first time four different nations come together to stage a FIFA World Cup.

Jamaica will be the first Caribbean country to host a senior World Cup but unlike its co-hosts, the island has limited experience staging major international football tournaments. Its most significant hosting assignment came in 2019 when the National Stadium welcomed a double-header during the Concacaf Gold Cup group stage.

Ricketts, however, told the Jamaica Observer that US Soccer, who has hosted several World Cups including last summer’s men’s tournament, will be offering their support, as the country prepares to host in less than five years’ time.

The JFF boss previously told the Observer that US Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone was key in Jamaica joining the 2031 World Cup bid.

“US Soccer and the JFF have established a very good relationship,” Ricketts said. “So much so that we have a game against the US on the 13th of December and I would have posed the question to them, what city are you going to play? Because we want to play somewhere where we have a strong Jamaican representation, and they chose Fort Lauderdale.”

“So we do have a good relationship and they are expecting us to depend on them for a lot of support in this regard. So like I said, we have a good relationship, Tom King [managing director of Administration] and, of course, Cindy and myself do have a very good relationship and we are working closely and are expecting to come up trumps.”

US Soccer CEO JT Batson says Jamaica’s inclusion in the bid was important to driving the continued success of women’s football.

“I think one of our goals of an inclusive 2031 Women’s World Cup was as an instigator of investment in obviously our countries but also across the region and ultimately the world,” he said. “For Jamaica and Costa Rica to show the world that they can host a Women’s World Cup and obviously field great teams, that is obviously a motivator in programmes and countries all over the world, so that was a big driver in terms of why we approached it the way we did.”

With projected revenue exceeding US$4 billion and more than four million fans expected to attend. Ricketts believes Jamaica will play a central role in the 2031 showpiece.

“People are just super, super excited and indeed exciting and interesting times ahead. Even around the Caribbean, I’ve been getting tons of calls and congratulatory comments from my colleagues around the Caribbean because we are representing the Caribbean, representing the world,” he said.

“Jamaica is a brand and we’re hoping that people from the diaspora and people all over the globe will just come to Jamaica, people who would not have known Jamaica but would probably have known of Jamaica, we’re just expecting them to come and enjoy some reggae music, enjoy the beaches, enjoy some food and just enjoy some football and see what Jamaica is about.”

Cone believes the four host nations will produce the greatest-ever tournament in women’s football.

“The opportunity is much bigger than any one of us,” she said. “Together with FIFA, we want to deliver the biggest and most impactful Women’s World Cup in history and use its success to accelerate the growth of women’s soccer around the world. Our ambition is to create a tournament that not only inspires millions of players, but helps give them the opportunities to play, grow and pursue their dreams.”

The National Stadium in Kingston is expected to host at least three games, which would be the Reggae Girlz group stage matches.

World.title: Heineken + F1 + Porsche = Party
World.content:
Padd0.0ck Club ExP.Perience takes over a section of Barbados Avenue, New Kingston, in front of the Porsche Showroom, Kingston for big screen F1 viewing.(Photo: Rory Daley)

Porsche Jamaica and Heineken combine forces to give Formula One fans an adrenaline-filled night as their Padd0.0ck Club ExP.Perience event took over a section of Barbados Avenue, New Kingston, on Saturday, November 21.

“The event was awesome. I loved the energy, the spirit, and the enthusiasm for F1,” Holly Bostock, managing director, Red Stripe, told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

Her words were mirrored by Shauwn Gracey, sales manager, Porsche Jamaica.

“What you see tonight is a result of three great brands coming together in Heineken, Porsche, and F1,” he said.

The centre of attraction was a large screen viewing party of the Las Vegas Grand Prix. The Heineken brand is a global sponsor of F1. Bostock said the aim was to elevate the viewing party experience similar to that in Las Vegas, and it was definitely a party atmosphere as specially invited guests arrived to music from DJ Tyler and DJ Quan.

With food and drink included, patrons mixed and mingled, not just with their F1-obsessed compatriots, but with the latest Porsche models in and outside of the showroom, including the up-for-auction one-of-one 911 Carrera built to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the brand in Jamaica.

For those wanting a bit more interactivity, the Porsche racing simulator was on hand to scratch the itch of driving any of the popular models virtually.

“Heineken always loves to host a good viewing party of our international sponsorships, whether that be UEFA Champions League or F1. We did another F1 viewing last year, so we’re committed to doing these exciting exclusive events,” said Bostock.

Once race time started — after a technical hiccup — all eyes were glued to the screens, including the massive one set up outside of the showroom on the street. The Las Vegas Grand Prix turned out to be one of the most exciting, with multiple lead changes and drama until the very end. The race was won by four-time Formula One World Drivers’ Champion Max Verstappen, marking his 75th F1 victory, his third time winning the race, and his fourth race win of the 2026 season.

“Heineken approached us, said they were looking for a partner to host the Las Vegas F1 viewing party, and when you think about high-performance cars, you think about Porsche. So, it was a no-brainer for us. The connection was easy and effortless. From the moment they came to us, we thought let’s do it,” Gracey said.
