World.title: Portmore ministers oppose AI data centres without consultation, impact studies
World.content:
In this Scotland File photo A young demonstrator holds a placard outside the Scottish Parliament Building after a march through Edinburgh on November 14, 2026, against the building of data centres and the growth of AI. (Photo by STEVE WELSH / AFP)

ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — The Portmore Ministers’ Fraternal, a Christian group based in Portmore, St Catherine, has expressed it does not support the proposal to establish artificial intelligence (AI) data centres in the city in the absence of consultation with the citizens and stakeholders of the municipality and thorough, publicly available environmental impact assessments.

The fraternal’s statement on Thursday follows the recommendation by Member of Parliament for St Catherine East Central Alando Terrelonge, that Portmore become home to AI data centres during his contribution to the State of the Constituency Debate in the House of Representatives on November 17.

While acknowledging the importance of technological advancement, youth empowerment, employment creation and economic development, the fraternal said proposals with potentially significant consequences for the environment, public infrastructure and community well-being must be informed by sound evidence, transparency and meaningful public participation.

“Citizens and stakeholders of Portmore have not been consulted on this proposal. The people who live, work, worship and raise families in the municipality must have a meaningful voice in decisions that could affect their quality of life and the resources upon which they depend,” the group said.

Citing international experiences with data centres, the group noted concerns about the demands data centres can place on electricity systems and water resources, alongside their implications for emissions, infrastructure costs and surrounding communities.

“The extent of these impacts depends on the scale, location, technology and operating arrangements of each development. These concerns warrant careful examination before any commitment is made to establish such facilities in Portmore,” the group added.

It is calling for:

– Thorough, independent environmental impact assessments and baseline surveys addressing water availability, energy requirements, cooling systems, noise, emissions, waste management, drainage, flood risk and the cumulative effects of any proposed facilities.

– Meaningful consultation with citizens and stakeholders, including residents’ associations, churches, community organisations, businesses, young people, environmental specialists and the municipal authorities. Consultation must occur early enough to influence decisions.

– Public disclosure of relevant project information, including proposed locations, the scale of development, water and electricity sources, environmental safeguards, anticipated employment opportunities and any costs or obligations to be borne by the public.

– Clear evidence that essential services and community well-being will be protected, with enforceable safeguards, independent monitoring and accountability arrangements.

The group maintained that these assessments and consultations must precede decisions on siting, approval and construction. It added that their findings must help determine whether data centres are appropriate for Portmore and, if so, under what conditions.

The group shared that it believes that the holistic development of Portmore must encompass economic opportunity, environmental stewardship, social well-being and the protection of present and future generations.

“Promised benefits must be carefully weighed against potential costs and risks to the community,” it said adding that The Portmore Ministers’ Fraternal stands ready to engage constructively with the political directorate, relevant public agencies, technical experts, investors, citizens and other stakeholders in shaping a responsible and inclusive development agenda for Portmore.

World.title: 9 things you need to read ahead of the Spanish election
World.content:
If a PP-Vox coalition comes to fruition, it’ll mark the first time the far right has governed in Spain since the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.

From understanding the key political players and parties, to watching Sunday’s results like a pro, here’s everything you need to know. (Click on the headlines to read the full reports.)

Picture taken in 1936 of Spanish soldiers loyal to the young Republic acclaimed by the crowd as they arrive in Madrid from Vilcavaro to fight against the nationalist troops of General Franco. | AFP via Getty Images

Ninety years after the outbreak of the civil war, Spain’s campaign for the Nov. 29 election has unmistakable echoes of 1936.

Politicians are resurrecting the rhetoric of a conflict that still runs deep in the polarized national psyche, with Sánchez leading crowds in chants of “¡No pasarán!” (“They shall not pass!”), the slogan immortalized by the left-wing forces that resisted Franco’s three-year siege of Madrid.

Both far-right leader Santiago Abascal of Vox and Madrid’s regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso of the PP have, in turn, referred to their left-wing opponents as the “Popular Front,” used by the coalition of communist, socialist and republican forces that governed Spain on the eve of the outbreak of the civil war.

The election is also set to reshape politics in the northern industrial region of the Basque Country, where the bitterly divisive question of independence is boiling up again.

World.title: ‘An advocate for Russia’: Kushner’s Putin comments spark outrage in Europe
World.content:
“This is extremely dangerous—not only for Ukraine but also for the security and national interests of the United States,” Oleksandr Merezhko, chair of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee and a lawmaker from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party, told POLITICO.

The interview offered a rare window into Kushner’s thinking as he touched on his roles in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza and his belief that “America’s most valuable export is really capitalism.”

Kushner, who described Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev in the interview as an “incredible friend,” was less complimentary toward Zelenskyy, saying he had “wrongly” attacked Trump in the past.

The remarks come at a fragile moment for Kyiv’s relations with the White House. Zelenskyy is still pressing for deliveries of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles and U.S.-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi this month brought no breakthrough.

There have been persistent tensions between the U.S. and Ukrainian leaders, and Trump on Wednesday unilaterally tweaked a joint statement with NATO chief Mark Rutte to urge Ukraine, as well as Russia, to avoid expanding the war.

“I have long argued that Witkoff and Kushner need to be replaced,” Merezhko said, referring additionally to Steve Witkoff, Trump’s other peace envoy. “They view Ukraine not even as businessmen seeking deals with Russia, but through the eyes of Putin himself.”

World.title: We’d be ‘stupid’ not to: Poland defends $300M military AI deal with Palantir
World.content:
Maven uses AI to analyze military data, supporting everything from logistics to the identification of battlefield targets.

Palantir celebrated the deal on X, calling Maven “the vanguard of next-generation AI warfare” and saying it was proud to stand with Poland in defending a “sovereign Europe.”

The company, which has drawn criticism for its work with U.S. immigration authorities and the Israeli military, faced protests in Warsaw earlier this month over concerns about data security and technological independence.

“All the keys, servers and information are — and will remain — exclusively in the possession of the Polish Armed Forces,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

Defense authorities in Denmark, Finland, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and Sweden already use Palantir software, though not all use Maven.

Some are seeking to reduce that dependence. The Dutch military said in late October it wanted a European alternative by 2028, while France and Germany agreed in July to explore developing their own defense software.

World.title: Meta’s UK rollout for Muse AI agent exposes it to more liability
World.content:
Muse, an AI agent that takes actions on users’ behalf, was introduced in the U.K. this week — several months after its launch in the U.S. — following talks with British regulators.

The Competition and Markets Authority, which enforces consumer law in the U.K., said Meta had made changes to Muse’s terms of service in the U.K. following “weeks” of engagement to “make them fairer for consumers” and ensure they reflect U.K. consumer law.

Meta declined to comment on detailed regulatory discussions. It says Muse can lend a “helping hand” on everything from chasing a refund and renewing car insurance to doing the Christmas shopping — but publicly acknowledges the tool “can and will still make mistakes.”

The AI agent, which is the first to be launched by a Big Tech company in the U.K., can also make payments on behalf of users with their approval.

The U.S. terms of service cap liability at $250 except for claims “arising from Meta’s gross negligence, willful misconduct or fraud.”

They absolve Meta of liability “to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law” for any losses or damages caused by Muse “taking any unintended, erroneous or unauthorized action.”

World.title: Asia-Pacific trade bloc opens accession talks with UAE, Philippines and Indonesia
World.content:
Accession talks with Uruguay, which have been running since early this year, are well advanced and could “potentially” be concluded early next year, a diplomat granted anonymity to discuss the plans told POLITICO.

Trade ministers are meeting in Hanoi, Vietnam, for the 11th CPTPP Commission meeting, hosted annually by a rotating chair.

The U.K. became the first country without a Pacific coastline to join the bloc in 2024. Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico and Singapore were among its founding members in 2018. Decisions are taken by consensus.

The U.K. is expected to sign a trade deal soon with the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes the UAE. But London has yet to strike trade deals with the fast-growing Indonesian and Philippine economies.

Negotiations with the three nations “are all complicated and will require serious effort to get across the line,” said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation think tank. “This includes capacity building for some applicants to make certain that everyone is clear on what the CPTPP requires, as well as careful work to ensure that member concerns are addressed.”

The bloc is emerging as a “Plan B” as efforts to reform the World Trade Organization falter. China, Taiwan, Ecuador, Ukraine, Cambodia and Argentina have also applied to join.

World.title: The man who coined ‘Brexit’ likes the sound of ‘Breturn’ and ‘Brejoin’
World.content:
Since arriving in Downing Street, Burnham has argued that Brexit “has not worked” as he tees up tighter ties with the EU. He has said that he hopes to rejoin within his lifetime — but insisted Monday that it would be “unthinkable” to do so without a referendum.

“If you’re looking for something catchy, there’s a couple of options: Let’s Breturn or Brejoin,” Wilding said when asked what the moniker for a future campaign should be. “But really, Burnham doesn’t want to go back to the past, he wants to go to the future, and the faces and arguments of 2016 will be dumped.”

“There will be a tonal change where Burnham caters his argument towards the younger vote and the business vote — seizing these cohorts will be vital to electoral success,” the strategist added.

Wilding coined Brexit in 2012 when he penned an article on Britain’s place in Europe.

“Unless a clear view is pushed that Britain must lead in Europe at the very least to achieve the completion of the single market, then the portmanteau for Greek euro exit might be followed by another sad word, Brexit,” he wrote for news outlet Euractiv , now known as Rapporteur. His writing is cited as the earliest evidence of the word Brexit in the Oxford English Dictionary.

The term was subsequently adopted as the accepted shorthand for the U.K. leaving Europe and was plastered on buses and billboards during the 2016 referendum campaign on Britain’s membership.

World.title: Dépendance aux Big Tech américaines : où en est la France par rapport à ses voisins européens ?
World.content:
"L'explication est d'ordre économique : dans un grand pays, le marché domestique est mieux à même de soutenir des alternatives ou des technologies nationales, qui impliquent des investissements importants et des économies d'échelle élevées", a détaillé Vili Lehdonvirta.

Pourquoi la taille compte

En Europe, la carte de la dépendance aux technologies américaines suit des tendances similaires, reflétant la taille du marché et le niveau de revenu. Cependant, elle est également plus contrastée en raison d'un ensemble hétéroclite de choix nationaux qui complique les efforts de l'UE visant à réduire ces dépendances stratégiques.

"Dans l’ensemble, on a cette configuration où les petits Etats membres ont recours au cloud américain et pas les grands Etats membres", a décrit Vili Lehdonvirta. "Le cloud est un exemple de technologie qui nécessite un investissement initial important, et ensuite, plus on opère à grande échelle, plus elle est efficace."

La méthodologie de l’étude présente certaines limites pour évaluer le degré de dépendance globale, car elle se concentre uniquement sur l’hébergement des services nationaux destinés au grand public, et non sur les systèmes locaux ni sur l’utilisation plus large de la technologie au sein de l’administration. Par exemple, Vili Lehdonvirta indique que les entités municipales — tels que les conseils d'école ou les systèmes de billetterie des piscines — sont plus susceptibles de recourir à des technologies américaines, la souveraineté numérique ne relevant pas de leurs compétences.

La taille et les revenus ne font pas tout non plus : les choix politiques déterminent également si les pays développent ou non des fournisseurs nationaux.

Au Royaume-Uni — la cinquième puissance mondiale —, 50,9% des sites gouvernementaux dépendent de technologies américaines, selon l'étude. Vili Lehdonvirta rappelle que l'exécutif britannique "a décidé, il y a environ quinze ans, de mettre le paquet sur le cloud dans le cadre d’une directive du gouvernement s’appliquant à tous les ministères et agences gouvernementales". En l’absence d’alternatives nationales, "très rapidement, tout a migré vers le cloud américain. Aujourd’hui, il serait difficile de revenir en arrière, même s’ils le souhaitaient", souligne-t-il.

World.title: ‘Islam is Sharia’: Germany’s far-right leader attacks Le Pen on Muslims and Europe
World.content:
“Yes, I’m keeping my fingers crossed for Ms. Le Pen,” Weidel said during an interview with a new weekly video podcast from WELT published Friday. WELT, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.

But Weidel bristled at Le Pen’s call this week for a “Europe of nations” to replace a “German Europe.” The leader of France’s far-right National Rally party had “perhaps misunderstood something, or doesn’t see how the money flows,” Weidel said, referring to Germany paying the largest portion of the EU budget.

The relationship between the two parties has been cold since Le Pen cut ties with the AfD in 2024, after one of the AfD’s leading politicians told an Italian newspaper that not every SS member was automatically a criminal.

Among Europe’s “patriotic” parties, “it is not the AfD that is isolated, but increasingly the National Rally, if it carries on like this,” she added.

Weidel also rejected Le Pen’s contention in a television appearance in October that Islam, unlike Sharia, is compatible with the French Republic: “Islam is Sharia and Sharia is Islam.” Le Pen has worked to rid the party of the racist and antisemitic reputation it developed under her father, Jean-Marie, who was convicted multiple times for racist comments and downplaying the Holocaust.

On the subject of expelling migrants from Germany, Weidel outbid her AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla, who recently put the number of people who should leave Germany at 2.6 million.

World.title: Uganda begins Africa's first mRNA Ebola vaccine trial
World.content:
Uganda has begun clinical trials of an experimental vaccine targeting the Ebola strain responsible for the ongoing outbreak in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the country's virus research institute announced on Friday.

 

The outbreak, caused by the less common Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has killed more than 5,700 people, with over 11,000 cases recorded since May, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). No vaccines or treatments are currently approved for this strain.

Trials of two experimental vaccines are scheduled to begin on Monday in eastern DRC, the epicentre of the outbreak, targeting people who have been in contact with infected individuals and those considered at high risk of infection.

Uganda has already begun testing one of the two vaccines, developed by US pharmaceutical company Moderna using the mRNA technology widely used during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Uganda Virus Research Institute said in a statement it had "launched Africa's first mRNA Phase I clinical trial... in collaboration with Moderna of an investigational vaccine against Bundibugyo ebolavirus".

The study will involve 224 healthy volunteers aged between one and 65 to assess the vaccine's safety and its ability to trigger an immune response.

Uganda, which shares a long and porous border with eastern DRC, managed to contain the spread of the virus after recording imported cases earlier this year.

The country was declared Ebola-free in August after recording 20 infections and two deaths.

Children wash their hands during an initiative aimed at raising awareness about preventing the spread of the Ebola virus at a primary school in Bunia, Congo, Friday, Nov. 13, AP Photo

Gavi secures 1.5 million doses of experimental Ebola vaccine

Meanwhile, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, has signed a purchase commitment with India's Serum Institute for 1.5 million doses of the other experimental vaccine, developed in collaboration with the University of Oxford.

The alliance aims to have "hundreds of thousands" of doses ready for distribution if clinical trials prove successful and the vaccine is approved by the WHO and DRC government.

"We're investing in it, hoping that the signals will be positive, and if that is the case, we'll have gained months and months on the deployment," Emanuele Capobianco, Gavi's director of global health security, told AFP.

Capobianco said he hoped for trials to conclude "within the first half of 2027" and even "within the first quarter" in a more optimistic scenario.

Gavi also holds a stockpile of 500,000 doses of Ervebo, an existing vaccine against the Zaire strain of Ebola, which is being tested to determine whether it is also effective against Bundibugyo.

World.title: Europe Tonight: How do opposing Spanish parties expect to address housing or imiigration issues?
World.content:
Spain is getting ready to vote in snap general elections on Sunday. According to the latest polls, the results could unseat Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, and a new right-wing coalition could be installed in Spain, a change that could significantly impact the balance of power in the EU.

 

Our Euronews presenter Felicia Pochhammer welcomed Javier Martínez-Cantó, a Research Fellow at the Spanish National Research Center, on our new weekly evening show to discuss major campaign issues in Spain, such as how different parties are proposing solutions to issues that have dominated the election campaign, including housing and immigration. As well as, in the case that Pedro Sánchez actually manages to stay in office, what signal would that send out to the rest of the Union?

World.title: Estonia will close border with Russia 'to secure Europe,' foreign minister says during Baku visit
World.content:
Estonia will close its border with Russia on 1 December, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna confirmed in Baku on Friday, stating that “we are not happy about that, but we need to respond and we need to secure Europe as well.”

 

Speaking to reporters at the official opening of the Estonian embassy in Azerbaijan's capital, Tsahkna said his country's decision addresses growing security concerns over Russia’s actions against European countries.

He warned that Estonia, which shares a border with Russia, has also faced an increase in Russian sabotage and attacks targeting Europe.

Tsahkna travelled to Baku as Estonia increases its diplomatic presence in the South Caucasus, describing his country's new embassy in Baku as a long-term commitment.

"Every embassy for us has a huge value," he said, while describing the decision to open a diplomatic mission in Azerbaijan as "well calculated".

"Our nations, we have a long history together, the same understandings, lots of personal relations, but also the same challenges and interests to the world," Tsahkna said.

He added that an intergovernmental commission meeting earlier this month helped move cooperation towards practical projects involving public institutions and private companies.

Trading energy and development in the Middle Corridor

Tsahkna said that Azerbaijan's role in regional and European energy security, as well as the development of the East-West Middle Corridor connecting Asia and Europe, are among Estonia's key interests.

"We see Azerbaijan as a huge opportunity of learning how you're dealing with energy," the foreign minister said.

According to the Estonian foreign minister, the historic peace process and the normalisation between Azerbaijan and Armenia open new perspectives across the South Caucasus, which until recently was dominated by Russia.

Estonia also opened an embassy in Armenia earlier this year, demonstrating its strategic interest in boosting its diplomatic presence in both countries and the wider region.

Tsahkna outlined Estonia's interest in digitalisation, AI and other technology sectors in Azerbaijan, as well as opportunities emerging from the EU's expanding global trade partnerships.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of Estonia, Margus Tsahkna at Press Conference, 27 November 2026 Euronews

Following a bilateral meeting with Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev, the Estonian foreign minister said that the EU was keen to develop a more practical, long-term cooperation with Azerbaijan, particularly in trade, energy and regional connectivity.

"Estonia definitely supports the visa liberalisation process between Azerbaijan and the European Union," Tsahkna said.

Tourism and education also featured in Tsahkna's address as he called for stronger educational and people-to-people ties, welcoming more Azerbaijani students to Estonia and encouraging greater tourism between the two countries.

"We are very happy to host your students, your people to Estonia more and more and to see more Estonians as well coming to Azerbaijan," he said.

Ukraine remains central to security discussions

Tsahkna said he arrived in Baku directly from Kyiv, describing how "the last night I was there, Kyiv was under heavy ballistic missiles attacks," adding that developments in different regions were interconnected.

A staunch supporter of Ukraine, Estonia will co-host next year's Ukraine Recovery Conference with the war-torn country.

Azerbaijan's assistance has reportedly exceeded $50 million (€45.6 million), and its first humanitarian shipment arrived right after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, including food and medicine.

In addition, Azerbaijan's State Oil Company (SOCAR) has gas stations across the country providing free fuel for emergency services vehicles.

Tsahkna stressed the importance of international assistance to help Ukraine withstand the coming winter, thanking Azerbaijan for the humanitarian support it provides to the war-torn country.

From Azerbaijan's perspective, Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov underlined the growing cooperation between the two countries.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Jeyhun Bayramov at Press Conference, 27 November 2026 Euronews

The opening of Estonia's embassy comes at a time of intense cooperation between the EU and the South Caucasus countries on energy diversification, transport connectivity and regional security.

For Tallinn, deeper engagement with Baku is part of a broader effort to strengthen ties with a region increasingly interconnected with Europe's economic and geopolitical priorities.

World.title: Azerbaijani and Armenian civil societies seek 'new history' in new round of peace talks
World.content:
Scores of representatives from Azerbaijan and Armenia's civil societies gathered in the Armenian town of Dilijan on Thursday and Friday for the fifth round of their "Peace Bridge" programme talks,

 

The 60 representatives in attendance marked the largest turnout since the two-track dialogue platform was established in 2025, in the historic peace agreement between the two countries.

Azerbaijan and Armenia's civil society representatives focused on roads and infrastructure between the two countries, as well as economic, social and humanitarian affairs, education, and political and geopolitical issues during their new meeting, this time in Armenia, as part of the normalisation process between the two former enemies.

Armenian Security Council Secretary Alen Simonyan told the gathering that roads are "the main link for cooperation between Armenia and Azerbaijan". The joint group also discussed the requirements for bilateral normalisation with Armenian Deputy Foreign Minister Vahan Kostanyan.

Participants during a Peace Bridge Initiative roundtable discussion APA, November 2026

From Azerbaijan's side, Deputy Chairman of the Board of the Centre for Analysis of International Relations and Multiculturalism Farhad Mammadov said that "there are certainly issues on which we disagree, but we hold an honest and sincere dialogue on all of them."

"We try to explain what concerns our society, the issues and reasons involved, and what we can achieve," Mammadov said.

"These problems have objective and subjective causes, and if we cannot resolve every problem quickly, we focus on matters where we can take concrete steps."

"No topic is off limits. We can ask each other questions and receive answers," Mammadov said, describing the spirit of the discussion.

"We will also consider how to overcome differences and give greater substance to peace policies," Azerbaijan's representative said.

Participants of the Peace Bridge Initiative hold a smaller breakout group discussion APA, November 2026

Meanwhile, Armenian Council President Areg Kochinyan, who also served as coordinator, said the expanded format allowed both sides to tackle sensitive topics openly and draft concrete recommendations for their governments.

Kochinyan said that the civil society dialogue is distinct from official state negotiations, but it plays a vital role in reshaping public attitudes after decades of conflict.

"Through this dialogue, rather than simply overcoming the reality shaped by decades of conflict, hostility and hatred, we are trying to create a new normal, new realities and a new history alongside the past," Kochinyan said.

"We are discussing a peace agenda focused on the future and on creating conditions in which our societies can live as neighbours in peace and mutual understanding," he added.

From initial talks to committees

Established under the auspices of both governments following the 8 August 2025 Washington Summit, where Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan signed the peace process declaration mediated by US President Donald Trump, the Peace Bridge platform began in late 2025 with small groups of permanent experts from each country.

The initiative gained momentum through reciprocal visits, starting with an initial meeting in Yerevan between 21 and 22 October 2025, followed by a roundtable in Baku between 21 and 22 November 2025.

In February of this year, the third meeting in Yerevan marked a symbolic step when 19 Azerbaijani experts crossed the delimited and demarcated land border on foot between the Azerbaijani village of Ashagi Askipara and the Armenian village of Voskepar.

Participants, including Areg Kochinyan, Vahan Kostanyan, Farhad Mammadov, during a Peace Bridge Initiative roundtable discussion APA, November 2026

A fourth gathering took place in Azerbaijan's Gabala district between 10 and 12 April 2026, focusing on direct contacts between non-governmental organisations and media representatives.

The fifth forum comes days after Armenia and the US began preparatory construction on the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) transit corridor in Syunik province, a key link aimed at connecting mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan and reinforcing wider East-West trade routes across the South Caucasus.

By expanding to 60 delegates and formalising six specialised committees in Armenia, coordinators aim to generate concrete policy recommendations, ranging from cross-border trade and environmental monitoring to youth exchanges and media cooperation, that can support official peace efforts across the South Caucasus.

World.title: Relatives say jailed Iranian twins beaten and tortured, one faces execution
World.content:
Family members of two Iranian sisters detained following the January 2026 uprising said the twins — one sentenced to death and the other to 25 years in prison — were severely beaten and tortured in prison despite international calls for their fair treatment and release.

 

21-year-old twins Taraneh and Rumina Rahimi were arrested in Isfahan on 24 January during protests that the UN said were met with severe government repression, leaving thousands dead.

Taraneh was sentenced to death and Rumina to 25 years in prison. Both sisters have denied all charges.

Their cousin, Massoud Nurmohammadi, who is based in the US and has spoken to multiple international media outlets, said Taraneh can no longer walk properly due to blows inflicted on her legs during detention, and that an untreated bone injury caused an ear infection that has affected her balance.

The two sisters were shortlisted for the European Parliament's Sakharov Prize in October 2026.

Rights groups have warned that Tehran has executed at least 39 people in connection with the demonstrations and placed more than 120 others on death row.

Enforced disappearance, torture, rape threats

Amnesty International said the sisters were held in enforced disappearance for more than three months after their arrest, with their family unable to determine their whereabouts.

When their mother was finally permitted to visit, the twins' faces were severely swollen and bruised, and their hair had been pulled out to the extent that she could identify them only by their voices, according to Amnesty.

Amnesty International also said Taraneh was tortured and refused to sign a forced confession until interrogators threatened to rape her sister in front of her.

The confession alleged she had carried a bladed weapon during the protests, and was used as the basis for the death sentence. There is no independent evidence to support the allegation.

Their cousin said that the sisters' lawyers filed a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation. Iran's judiciary assigned the complaint to the same official the sisters had accused of carrying out the abuse.

One of their lawyers has since been detained. A second withdrew from the case. The family has appointed new legal representation to pursue the appeal.

In less than two months, Iranian judges sentenced at least six women including Rahimi to death or upheld existing death sentences against them following trials Amnesty International described as unfair.

Iran Human Rights (IHR), a Norway-based organisation, documented at least 121 death sentences handed down in connection with the January 2026 protests in a report published on 16 November.

"Behind these death sentences, there are horrifying narratives of torture that cannot be imagined," IHR director Mahmoud Amiri-Moghaddam said.

"Young protesters have been sentenced to death based on confessions taken from them under torture and after grossly unfair trials in revolutionary courts. Even the few lawyers who dare to truthfully defend their clients face threats, harassment and serious risks to their personal safety."

European Parliament condemns sentences

On 8 October, the European Parliament approved a resolution on the human rights situation in Iran by 541 votes to 11, with 25 abstentions, condemning what it described as unprecedented violence by security and judicial authorities against civilians since January 2026.

MEPs expressed concern over attacks on human rights activists and journalists, and trials of protesters based on confessions obtained through torture.

The resolution called for the death sentences against Iranian protesters, including Taraneh Rahimi, to be overturned, and cited Rumina Rahimi's prison sentence.

A court in Qom this week sentenced Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi and eight other members of her band to 74 lashes each, two years banned from leaving the country and two years excluded from artistic activity after they performed a concert without observing mandatory veiling rules.

The Qom Provincial Criminal Court charged the group with undermining public decency by producing and disseminating vulgar and unethical content online.

World.title: Serbia’s student movement puts forward Professor Saičić as its presidential candidate
World.content:
The student movement in Serbia has decided to put forward Professor Radomir Saičić, a distinguished chemistry professor and academician, as its candidate for the upcoming presidential election, scheduled for December 27. His candidacy is hardly a surprise. Saičić had been mentioned from the very beginning as one of the leading figures who could represent the students in the presidential race.

 

He is, however, a rather different kind of political figure from those who have dominated Serbia’s political scene for years. A deeply religious, exceptionally quiet and reserved man, Saičić is widely respected in academic and professional circles. He is not a conventional politician, nor someone known for seeking public attention or political confrontation. His reputation rests primarily on his academic achievements, personal integrity and the respect he commands among his colleagues. That is precisely what makes him an appealing choice for a movement that has repeatedly presented itself as an alternative to the country’s established political elite.

“I entered the movement believing that a change of government makes sense only if it also brings a change in the system of values, including the way those in power treat citizens. That is why I will advocate a sovereign Serbia in which the Constitution is respected and every citizen can live with dignity” Saičić said and added:

“As President, I will respect the limits of my constitutional powers, publicly explain my decisions, and demand the same accountability from other holders of public office. It is time to restore dignity to the office of the President of Serbia. Faith gives me the moral strength and the obligation to keep my word. Science teaches me to ask questions and seek evidence, while life has taught me to take responsibility when things are most difficult. I am ready to take that responsibility now.”

The political significance of his nomination goes beyond the choice of an individual candidate. The students appear to be deliberately seeking someone who can embody a break with the political culture of the past 14 years: a figure associated with expertise, personal modesty and moral authority rather than political ambition or a cult of personality.

The presidential election will take place on December 27, while December 6 is the final deadline for submitting presidential candidacies, according to the official electoral timetable.

Vučić considers boycotting the elections

One of the biggest uncertainties surrounding the election is whether the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which dominated Serbian politics under Aleksandar Vučić for more than a decade, will even participate. The party has yet to make a final decision, while Vučić himself has openly expressed his preference for staying out of the presidential race. Such a boycott could reflect the party’s reluctance to risk another potentially humiliating defeat following its loss in the October parliamentary elections. It would also raise questions about the legitimacy of an election in which the country’s former ruling party might refuse to take part.

Vučić said that opinions within the SNS were divided, but made clear that he personally favoured ignoring the presidential election.

“There are different views: some want to support an independent candidate, others want the SNS to put forward its own candidate, while some, like me, want us simply to ignore the elections and let them boast that they have taken everything and won 94 per cent of the vote.”

He also described the forthcoming presidential election as: “The most meaningless elections in history.”

Daily arrests and review of contracts signed by the SNS Government

Meanwhile, Serbia remains in a highly tense and politically uncertain atmosphere. Although the previous government is formally still in office, pending the formation of a new administration, arrests and investigations involving senior figures from the former Vučić administration are continuing. The developments have further polarised an already divided society, with the former president accusing the new parliamentary majority of political persecution, while the student movement insists that accountability and the rule of law must finally apply to everyone, regardless of political connections.

For the student movement, the presidential campaign is expected to focus on the rule of law, the fight against corruption and the restoration of public confidence in state institutions. One of its central promises will be a comprehensive review of contracts and agreements concluded by Vučić and his governments, particularly those involving major public investments and the use of public resources. The students are expected to argue that the country needs transparency, institutional accountability and independent oversight, rather than decisions made behind closed doors.

Perhaps the most important political message of Saičić’s candidacy is the attempt to redefine the very nature of political power in Serbia. For the past 14 years, the country’s political system has increasingly revolved around one man, with institutions often reduced to instruments of presidential authority. The students are promising a different model: a functioning state in which institutions serve citizens, public officials are accountable and political authority is exercised within constitutional limits.

Saičić’s challenge, therefore, will be to turn the moral credibility of the student movement into a credible political alternative. His quiet personality and academic background may be precisely what the movement believes Serbia needs at this moment. But the presidential election will also test whether the students’ unprecedented parliamentary victory can be translated into a broader mandate for institutional and political change.

World.title: Spain election: Will Vox be the kingmaker, and will housing decide the vote?
World.content:
Spaniards are getting ready to cast their ballots on Sunday following months of social and political unrest.

 

The campaign for this snap general election, called by prime minister Pedro Sánchez in July, sees centre-right Partido Popular (People's Party) ahead in the polls, with Eurosceptic party Vox in third.

The conservatives are unlikely to secure enough seats to govern alone, and that could make Vox's support decisive. In 2023, the PP won 137 seats and Vox 33, only 6 seats short of an absolute majority.

The party is pushing for stricter migration rules, national preference in access to certain benefits, and a rollback of some environmental and social policies.

What conditions could Vox lay out to join a coalition with PP?

“Vox is going to obtain lots of electoral support" tells Euronews Pedro Riera Sagrera, Professor of political science at University Carlos III, Madrid.

"And as a consequence, I think that they are going to be strong enough to basically force the formation of a coalition government between the two of them."

Vox's influence will depend not just on how many seats it wins, but on how other parties vote or abstain.

If the PP needs Vox to take power, the far-right leader Santiago Abascal could use that leverage to demand concessions.

Joining the government, with cabinet positions, or staying outside it while supporting PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo in parliament, seems the likeliest scenario.

A deal could include policy commitments, particularly on immigration, one of Vox's central campaign issues.

Could a deal also include regional alliances?

Feijóo has made it clear that he prefers to govern alone, with parliamentary support from Vox only when needed.

In a November interview with national media, he described his goal as securing support agreements with the far-right party.

But he has not ruled out a coalition which might also include regional agreements as an alternative to cabinet positions.

Vox has already secured vice-presidencies and ministerial portfolios in several Spanish regions, though some political experts cast doubts about the stability these agreements might provide.

If the two parties fall short of a majority, other political groups could vote against Feijóo or negotiate support for an alternative candidate.

Abstentions could also prove decisive in the second investiture vote. And if no candidate wins Congress's confidence within two months of the first vote, another election must be called.

Housing crisis: Is it the most important issue of this election?

Vox has vowed to tackle Spain's unsustainable housing shortage and to give Spanish nationals priority access to social housing.

According to a poll by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), housing emerged as the most important issue in the country, ahead of migration and the economy.

Many European countries are struggling with housing, but, in Spain, the situation has become critical.

The Bank of Spain says that over the past 45 years, the financial effort needed to buy a house has grown by 89%, compared to only 10% in the euro area.

In other words, while house prices and incomes have increased more or less in tandem across much of Europe, in Spain the property tag has grown way bigger than salaries.

What's driving Spain's housing crisis and how to fix it?

Mostly, a massive housing shortage that’s been building up since the 2008 financial crisis.

The country has accumulated a housing supply gap of around 750,000 homes, putting enormous pressure on the market and inflating prices.

And that’s certainly not because Spain’s population is booming.

Lack of housing workers, delayed licences and planning, but also building restrictions enforced by local authorities are the main culprits, according to José García-Montalvo, Economics Professor at Barcelona's UPF.

Cutting red tape isn't the only solution. According to Ramon Bastida, Director of the Sustainable Housing Department at UPF, there are also practical ways to speed up the process.

For example, off-site construction, which means pre-producing parts of buildings in factories and assembling them on site.

But the housing crisis is also affecting renters. Spain's fees grew by 44% in the past five years, on average, with dramatic increases in places like Malaga (+86%), or Madrid (nearly 60%), according to property platform Idealista.

No wonder most young Spaniards don't leave their parental home until they turn 30, according to Eurostat, the last to fly the nest in the EU, only behind young Greeks (31), Croatians (31.5) and Slovaks (31).

Watch Euronews Verify

Join Euronews Verify live on TV, Euronews' website, and on digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram) every weekday at 6:40 pm Brussels time. In just under 11 minutes, our new format goes beyond the headlines to make sense of what's happening, fact-checking and untangling the day's most pressing issues to explain why they matter to you.

World.title: EU enlargement back in focus: Montenegro, Moldova and Greece's 2027 role
World.content:
The new geopolitical reality has put EU enlargement back at the centre of the debate. From the Western Balkans to Eastern Europe, the accession of new members is no longer just a matter of institutional and economic convergence.

 

It is also a question of security, influence and Europe's strategic direction. Montenegro is aiming to become the EU's 28th member by 2028, while Moldova is trying to advance on its European path despite the challenges posed by the conflict in Transnistria.

Enlargement's return to the agenda is directly linked to the war in Ukraine and growing concern over Russian influence in the wider region. For Brussels, integrating candidate countries now has a broader strategic dimension: it will determine where the limits of Europe's political and economic influence lie in the years ahead. These issues were discussed at a conference in Athens, co-organised by the Irish presidency and the think tank ELIAMEP.

Montenegro: the 2028 goal and unresolved issues with Croatia

Montenegro is the most advanced of the Western Balkan candidate countries. It aims to complete accession negotiations and become the EU's 28th member state in 2028.

Predrag Zenović, Montenegro's chief negotiator for EU accession since December 2023, was optimistic about the timetable. "We see Montenegro as the EU's 28th member state by 2028," he told Euronews.

Podgorica's timetable foresees closing all negotiating chapters in 2026, signing the Accession Treaty in 2027 and joining in 2028.

However, unresolved bilateral issues with Croatia remain a significant obstacle. Asked whether the dispute could go to international arbitration, Zenović said the two sides are examining various proposals to settle their differences. He expressed confidence that the need to maintain accession momentum would prevail.

"There has to be some kind of mutual understanding on both sides," he said, arguing that both Zagreb and Podgorica recognise the importance of enlargement and the limited time available.

Moldova: the European perspective and the Transnistria question

For Moldova, too, the European path has a clear security dimension. The presence of Russian troops in the breakaway region of Transnistria is one of the main threats to the country's territorial integrity.

The Moldovan government is seeking the peaceful reintegration of the region, starting with economic integration. Cristina Gherasimov, Moldova's Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration, told Euronews that the region now follows the same customs code as the rest of the country. Since September, it has also begun gradually introducing VAT and excise duties on certain categories of goods.

"Moldova will always continue to pursue the peaceful reunification of the country," she said, stressing that on security issues the country needs the support of its European partners.

The key question is how far the presence of Russian troops could affect Moldova's EU accession. Gherasimov argued that the Transnistria conflict should not become an obstacle to the process, since the decision on the country's European future belongs to its citizens.

"Whether Moldovans join the European Union or not is their choice, not Russia's choice," she said.

She also described Moldova's efforts to counter disinformation and pro-Russian narratives, which, she said, foster fear and mistrust of the European perspective. Despite this pressure, she maintained that support for EU accession remains strong in Moldovan society.

Greece and the challenge of the 2027 presidency

In this new geopolitical environment, Greece wants to play an active role in speeding up enlargement, as it is due to hold the Presidency of the Council of the EU in the second half of 2027.

Athens has considerable diplomatic capital in this area. A key reference point is the 2003 Thessaloniki Summit, which reaffirmed the European perspective of the Western Balkans.

According to Dr Ioannis Armakolas, senior researcher and programme director at ELIAMEP and Associate Professor of Comparative Politics of South-East Europe at the University of Macedonia, enlargement is expected to be a key priority of the Greek Presidency. Expectations are high, he notes, both in the Western Balkans and in candidate countries such as Moldova and Ukraine.

"Greece has this symbolic diplomatic capital because of the famous Thessaloniki Summit of 2003. Therefore, there is an expectation that something important will happen during the Greek Presidency," he says.

One of the most ambitious goals is to complete Montenegro's accession process during the Greek Presidency. Armakolas believes this is achievable, provided the country closes its negotiating chapters on time and resolves its outstanding issues with Croatia. Athens could also help advance other enlargement files, from Albania and Serbia to Moldova and Ukraine.

The question, then, is not only how many countries will manage to walk through the door of the European Union, but also whether the Union itself can turn the geopolitical need for enlargement into a credible, concrete political plan.

World.title: Polls open in Taiwan's closely watched local elections
World.content:
Polls have opened for local elections in Taiwan. While campaigners have stayed away from the topic of China and focused on issues like transport and childcare, Beijing has repeatedly weighed in.

Taiwan's voters begun choosing mayors and county chiefs in local elections on Saturday that may gauge the mood ahead of the island's 2028 presidential elections.

Polls close at 4 p.m. (0800 UTC/GMT) and results are expected by early evening. Winners will serve four-year terms.

Most candidates are from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) or the Nationalist Party, also known as the Kuomintang or KMT. The latter has traditionally performed better in local elections and favors closer ties with China.

President Lai Ching-te has campaigned for candidates from his DPP.

Closely watched in Beijing

China is paying close attention, despite not currently featuring as a key campaign issue. Taiwan's government warned its people to be vigilant against fake news on social media, citing a Chinese disinformation campaign.

Taiwan's 22 cities and counties are currently focused on issues such as transport, childcare and the environment. While these issues do not directly impact the China policy, Beijing has repeatedly weighed in.

Shen's rallies have seen throngs of supporters in Taipei, with frenzied demand for his campaign ribbons, badges and other goodies Image: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

China denounced the governing Democratic Progressive candidate for Taipei's mayoral race, Puma Shen, who is wanted by Chinese police for alleged "separatist activities." He entered the mayoral race as an underdog but has managed to ride a political wave that drew huge crowds to his campaign rallies.

Earlier this month, Shen said Chinese police had never contacted him and that whoever wins, Taipei's election would be a victory for democracy in the face of pressure from Beijing.

If Shen wins, he would be the capital city's first DPP mayor in nearly 30 years. This result could be seen as "quite shameful" in Beijing, according to Austin Wang, political science professor at the University of Nevada.

Why China is watching Taiwan's local elections so closely To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China claims Taiwan as part of its territory under its "One China" principle and has recently increased pressure on Taiwan to accept its sovereignty claims, threatening force to seize the island.

Taipei's incumbent and KMT member, Mayor Chiang Wan-an has campaigned against Shen, also pulling in thousands of supporters to his rallies. In the last election, KMT thrashed DPP, winning 14 of the 22 cities and counties while the DPP won only five. Chiang is also seen as a potential future presidential candidate.

What impact could the vote have on presidential elections?

Analysts have cautioned that the local elections are not a reliable barometer of how people might vote for the presidential elections in 2028. Still, Saturday's results could influence the selection process for the KMT presidential candidate.

Results of local elections are generally announced on the voting day itself Image: Ann Wang/REUTERS

The DPP is likely to rally behind President Lai for a reelection.

The most likely KMT candidates are Taichung's outgoing Mayor Lu Shiow-yen and parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu.

KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun, who's pro-Beijing stance has even alienated her from many in the party, is also viewed as a potential challenger for the party's nomination. However, she could face pressure to step down if KMT performs poorly in the local elections.

World.title: Spain's Sanchez makes final appeal to voters before election
World.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez told people to turn out in large numbers so the country does not go "backwards." Polls suggest an end to his eight-year leftist leadership of Spain.

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Friday hit the campaign trail one last time before Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday, telling people to "vote, vote, vote" to make sure the country doesn't go "backwards."

Opinion polls point to a change in government, with the conservative People's Party (PP) slated to come out on top, bringing an end to Sanchez's eight years of leftist leadership.

Spain's general election this Sunday is also crucial because it kicks off a round of elections on the continentand because it is yet another test of the region's shift to the right.

The PP would potentially have to rely on support from the far-right anti-immigration Vox party to form the next government in Spain.

There's also a chance that the election ends in a hung parliament, with neither the right-wing coalition nor the left bloc securing a majority.

Pedro Sanchez's immigration-friendly policies made him an outlier in Europe where populist parties have surged to power Image: Isabel Infantes/REUTERS

Sanchez has so far campaigned on a platform of having boosted the Spanish economy when its European Union partners were struggling.

He has pointed to his policies of having increased the minimum wage and having lifted pensions in line with inflation.

But people are frustrated that the cost of living has soared and that they're not able to enjoy the fruits of economic growth, with many unable to leave their parents' house because of very high rental prices.

Spain’s housing crisis becomes main election issue To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sanchez doubles down on attempt to appeal to leftist voters

Sanchez said during his final rally in Madrid that the "elections are about moving Spain forward, not moving it backwards."

He doubled down on an attempt to appeal to left-leaning voters, telling them that a right coalition government, with far-right members in parliament, would reverse the years of social progress and gut public services.

Oscar-winning Spanish film director Pedro Almodovar was also at the rally this evening.

Sanchez wore a red T-shirt that said "the power of the people," telling people that a "progressive majority is within our reach."

Sanchez has also become the standard-bearer for Europeans frustrated with the Trump administration.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo dismisses Sanchez's campaign of 'fear'

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who has said that he wants to maintain good relations with US President Donald Trump, dismissed Sanchez's campaign of "fear."

Feijoo won the most seats during elections in 2023, but he was not able to form a government.

"And when a government has nothing to offer but fear, it means it has nothing else left to offer," he told supporters at his campaign finale in the southern city of Seville.

Alberto Nunez Feijoo's pitch to voters has largely focused on improving government management and the competence of public officials. Image: Matteo Secci/ZUMA/picture alliance

"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," said Feijoo, who built his career running central public bodies and the northwestern Galicia region.

He has advocated for tough immigration policies and stronger border management.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the Vox party, favors a much tougher approach, with his party having advocated for mass deportations.

Addressing a closing rally at a bullring in the eastern city of Valencia, Abascal told supporters not to "vote out of fear. Vote with courage."

"What we are up against is a criminal mafia led by a ruthless boss, a liar," he said, referring to the corruption scandals that have surrounded Sanchez and his government.

World.title: US disables ship in Gulf of Oman under Iran blockade
World.content:
The United States said it was continuing "to strictly enforce the blockade" of Iran's ports. Meanwhile, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador over a strike that killed two Italian technicians.

The United States military on Friday announced it had fired at a ship in the Gulf of Oman that it said was violating Washington's blockade of Iranian ports.

A US aircraft fired "precision munitions" in the stern of the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer, US Central Command (CENTCOM), said, adding that it "continues to strictly enforce the [US] blockade."

CENTCOM oversees US forces in the Middle East.

The statement said that "the ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled" and stressed that "the civilian crew was unharmed."

It said that the ship had left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas.

The US blockade has disabled six ships and redirected 158 others.

Washington launched its blockade of Iranian ports in mid-July following the collapse of an agreement with Tehran.

The war broke out in February after the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, which prompted Tehran to impose its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.

Kuwait summons Iran ambassador over strike on military site

Meanwhile, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador after a Thursday drone strike killed two Italian technicians at a Kuwaiti military site.

A Kuwaiti citizen and a Pakistani citizen were also injured and hospitalized in the attack.

Iran has denied responsibility for the strike.

Iran denies role in drone strike that killed 2 Italians in Kuwait To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kuwait's Foreign Ministry said Deputy Foreign Minister Hamad Al-Mashaan condemned the "continued Iranian attacks" and said Kuwait reserved its right to self-defense.

The two technicians worked for Rheinmetall Italia, a subsidiary of the German defense firm Rheinmetall.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the strike, calling on "all parties to exercise restraint."

Guterres is "deeply concerned by the continued escalation in the region," according to his spokesman, Stephane Dujarric. "Renewed hostilities would have devastating consequences for the region and beyond."

World.title: Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill
World.content:
Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.

However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.

Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.

Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.

What did the Supreme Court say about the law?

Chief Justice Richard Wagner said that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society."

Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.

"This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he said.

CAQ ruled Quebec in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ), which also supported Bill 21, formed government.

The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.

Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.

Opponents of Bill 21 argue that it unfairly targets Muslims and other religious minority groups Image: Sean Kilpatrick/empics/picture alliance

Critics argue secularism bill weakens rights protections

Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

"This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.

He said the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.

Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to "Islamophobia as a state policy."

World.title: Germany news: Lawmakers approve debt-laden 2027 budget
World.content:
The checkered skipper's large, powerful head, stark colorscheme and low, rapid flight are among its more distinguishing features Image: Rosemarie Kappler/Zoonar/picture alliance

The checkered or arctic skipper, carterocephalus palaemon, has been named the 2027 butterfly of the year by BUND, the German Federation for the Environment and Nature Conservation.

As so often, the animal has a more literal and descriptive moniker in German, where it's known as the gelbwürfelige Dickkopffalter, or "yellow-checked thick-headed butterfly" — an homage to two of its most distinguishing features, its coloration and its large head.

BUND said that with its choice for 2027 it wanted to "raise awareness about the loss of valuable water-based ecosystems." It said that the loss of transitional areas between woods and open land with long grasses were crucial to both the butterfly and the caterpillars and were being lost.

"Forest and path edges are often mowed short. With this, the butterflies' feeding and wintering locations are lost. The climate crisis is also weighing on the checkered skipper: for the caterpillars' development, carterocephalus palaemon needs damp living spaces or at least a damp microclimate."

The species is not classified as endangered in Germany at present, but its numbers are in decline.

World.title: Spanish rider Marc Marquez announces MotoGP retirement, days after clinching record 8th world title
World.content:
Marc Marquez took fans and his team by surprise when announcing this weekend's race in Valencia will be his last. The 33-year-old won a record eight MotoGP titles, including his rookie and retirement seasons.

Marc Marquez, one of the most successful motorcycle racers of all time, announced on Friday that he would retire from MotoGP world championship after this weekend's season finale in Valencia.

The 33-year-old Spaniard's decision comes just a few days after he clinched his eighth top-tier motorcycle racing championship, equaling the record of Italian great Giacomo Agostini set in 1975 and surpassing the seven career titles of Marquez's own childhood hero and later rival Valentino Rossi.

"Thank you to everyone who's been part of the journey. I hope you've enjoyed it as much as I have. This will be my last race in MotoGP. We made history," Marquez said in a video recorded in the Valencia garage and shown during Friday's free practice.

He did not issue any firm comments about what he planned next, saying: "I first need to understand what I need in my next life."

Marquez held a sign of thanks from his team 'for pushing us to the limit and making history with us' Image: Matteo Averna/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Why did Marquez say he was retiring now?

The move came as a surprise, not least given that earlier this year Marquez had signed a contract extension with his Ducati team that was set to run until 2028.

The 33-year-old, who has battled with repeated injuries and surgeries in the latter half of his career, said he made the decision after last month's Japanese Grand Prix in light of the physical and mental toll of his battles for fitness.

"Sometimes you need to understand the situation, but it's true that the situation this year was on the limit," he said. "When I signed the contract in March, as always, I was super optimistic and I didn't know that I would have another surgery on my right shoulder [in May]."

Marquez said that at times this season, chasing a massive deficit after his early-season injury to come back and win the championship, he had begun to "feel the fear" in the saddle, and even noticed brief recurrences of the double vision he struggled with a few years ago.

"It was one of the main reasons why I controlled the risk and why I crashed less this second part of the season," he said.

Marquez claimed a record eighth MotoGP title this year, against all the odds given how far behind he fell while injured early in the season Image: Oscar Gonzalez/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Who is Marc Marquez?

Marquez burst onto the scene in MotoGP in 2013, highly touted after winning two world titles in junior series before graduating to compete in the top tier.

Aged 20, he won the championship in his rookie season, and went on to win the title in six of his first seven seasons with Honda, establishing himself as motorcycle racing's dominant force by 2019.

But Marquez suffered a serious crash at the 2020 season-opener in Jerez, broke his arm and endured an extremely rocky road to recovery.

He underwent four operations, was forced to abandon several comeback attempts and was battling with blurred vision, all while his Honda bike was no longer the class of the field, forcing him to push it too hard to try to stay at the front.

Instead of retiring during this bleak spell, something Marquez said he considered, he switched to the smaller Gresini team where he slowly rediscovered his belief and his race-winning pace by ending a drought of more than 3 calendar years with a win in Aragon in 2024.

He then secured a factory weat with Ducati for the 2025 season, and went on to claim a seventh MotoGP title — matching his childhood idol Valentino Rossi's modern-era record.

This season's campaign, culminating in an eighth championship, was arguably unlikelier still. After his early season crash in France, leading to surgery on his shoulder and a foot injury, Marquez returned trailing his championship rivals by 102 points.

But he won six of the subsequent nine races, sealing the championship last weekend in Portimao in Portugal. When he went up to collect his trophy, organizers superimposed a silhouette of a goat (as in "Greatest Of All Time") behind him as he climbed onto the podium.

MotoGP organizers put forward their case for Marquez as a potential 'GOAT' after he wrapped up his eighth (and now final) title last weekend Image: Jose Breton/AP Photo/picture alliance

Marquez himself has however shied away from that title, saying instead that he hoped to be in the discussion as "one of the greatest" in the sport's long history.

World.title: France seeks German man in Channel migrant boat probe
World.content:
A German businessman is accused of supplying equipment to smugglers organizing migrant crossings from France to the United Kingdom. However, he can't face formal charges until he is extradited to France.

France has issued an arrest warrant for a German businessman as part of an investigation regarding the migrant deaths in the English Channel.

Joint investigation by several media outlets including French daily Le Monde and the BBC showed that Marvin R.* of MaRe Boote, managing director of a small firm in western German town Werne, is suspected of being one of the main suppliers of inflatable boats smugglers use to journey across the Channel.

According to the media reports, the 35-year-old businessman is accused of supplying smuggling gangs with inflatable boats, engines and life jackets worth hundreds of thousands of euros.

Although the number of arrivals has since fallen, the crossings remain a major political issue in Britain Image: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP

UK authorities estimated that boats or engines linked to MaRe Boote were responsible for three in every 10 detected crossings during the first four months of this year, the BBC and Le Monde reported.

Arrested and released in Germany

The prosecutor in the northern French city of Lille, Samuel Finielz, confirmed late on Thursday that "five people had been arrested and a German national was briefly detained in his country."

According to Finielz, this is part of the investigation about Channel crossings and sinkings since May last year.

The five others are now held in pre-trial detention and were suspected of offenses including "assisting illegal entry and residence as part of an organized criminal group, involuntary manslaughter, involuntary injury and endangering the lives of others," Finielz told the media.

'Migration paradox': How borders, aid drive human movement To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Lille authorities in May issued an arrest warrant against "the German national implicated in this case," he said, on charges of manslaughter and endangering the lives of others.

Marvin R. was arrested and released by German authorities and now required to appear before a French court before January, the prosecutor added.

The BBC wrote that Marvin R. is contesting extradition to France. He can not be formally charged until he is extradited to France, it noted.

How many migrants cross the English Channel?

Migrants frequently cross the English Channel from France to the United Kingdom in small rubber dinghy boats. It is a dangerous journey as the Channel is one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year and there have been many deaths.

New EU migration pact: Will the bloc deliver on promises? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges us to refrain from revealing the full names.

World.title: Divisions deepen between EU member states after tense budget summit
World.content:
An EU leaders summit on the bloc's seven-year budget fell apart amid divisions over how to fund Ukraine. The budget proposal also includes a 3% tax on US tech companies, in a bid for the EU to generate additional funds.

EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday night.

Squabbles and thinly veiled public barbs meant they left without a deal and didn't even attempt to resume discussions on the planned second day.

There is a self-imposed deadline to find agreement before the end of 2026 on the budget which covers the 2028-2034 period. But experts say there is no cause for alarm, yet.

"Every time there are long-term EU budget negotiations, there are breakdowns, chaos, recrimination and a lot of political theater and drama," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an EU economist and expert at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels.

The center of that political theater this time was the prime ministers of Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — countries wanting a reduced budget — who staged a walkout during smaller, group meetings, claiming the atmosphere had not been constructive to getting a deal.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar called the whole summit "completely unnecessary," pointing the blame at the man who had decided to call it and whose job it is to meditate the talks, European Council President Antonio Costa.

Costa was diplomatic in defending his decision to bring the leaders to Brussels, telling the press: "For me it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December."

European Council President Antonio Costa was forced to defend his decision to call the summit which ended in acrimony Image: Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Germany demands more for competitiveness, security, defense

Long before the summit started, Germany had laid down an ultimatum — Berlin would only sign off on the budget if all the other EU countries greenlit an additional €45 billion ($49 billion) support loan for Ukraine to fund the country in its war efforts through 2027.

Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria and Slovakia have dug their heels in against the proposal, insisting that giving Ukraine money to buy weapons will prolong the war. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico even accused Germany of "blackmail."

Can Europe defend itself without the US? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As Europe's biggest economy, Germany's contribution amounts to around 25% of the whole budget.

In a press conference after the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said "hundreds of billions" still need to be slashed. The European Commission's original proposal of approximately €1.786 trillion had already been reduced by €204 billion (down 10.2%).

"Europe needs to exercise a sense of proportion," said Merz. "The budget cannot grow indefinitely, and the burden of financing it must be distributed fairly."

Merz also aimed a comment toward Costa, who has been renewing the details in the budget proposal at every stage.

"The proposals that have been on the table so far are not a basis for an agreement," said Merz.

Costa did tell leaders on Thursday that he is planning to cut between €220 billion to €230 billion out of the next proposal.

Berlin's budget reduction push is backed by six other countries who together call themselves the "Sensible Seven." All pay more into the collective EU financial pot than they receive out of it.

The leaders of the 'sensible seven' — Germany, Netherlands, Denmark, Belgium, Sweden, Finland and Austria — met separately at the Brussels summit Image: Frederic Sierakowski

They are opposed by 17 EU member states who insist the total budget should grow, led by France and Italy. These countries call themselves the "Friends of Cohesion" — a nod to the EU cohesion funds which are used to share wealth from the EU's richer regions and nations to its poorer ones.

In the current proposal, agriculture, fisheries and cohesion spending falls from 59.1% to 42.4%, while money for economic competitiveness, security, and defense rises from 17.7% to 27.7%. This rebalancing is a key German demand.

EU looking elsewhere to raise funds

The EU is also searching for a way to add money into the budget that doesn't come from national contributions. The current proposal includes a controversial EU-wide digital tax which could chart a course for a major battle with the US.

The idea, originally put forward by French President Emmanuel Macron, is for a 3% tax on revenues of online advertising, online marketplaces and on the monetization of user data. The money, to be paid directly into the EU's budget, is estimated to bring in €5 billion per year.

But the proposal is ringing alarm bells in Ireland, where US tech giants like Google, Meta, Apple, Microsoft and LinkedIn have their European headquarters.

"A digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who could still veto the proposal.

Protecting the EU's top triple-A rating

There is a fear in some European capitals that without being able to generate its own funds, future EU loans could downgrade the European Commission's unblemished standing on international markets.

The EU has around €860 billion in outstanding debts it took out for its pandemic recovery funding and to support Ukraine. Its triple-A credit rating could be downgraded if Marine Le Pen, the far-right front-runner in France's presidential election, wins in the spring and follows through on her promise to reduce French contributions to the EU budget.

If France's far-right challenger wins the spring 2027 election, it could change the whole shape of the EU budget negotiations Image: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

EU member states that favor a financing model through national contributions rather than through tax revenue "understand very well what will happen if the EU loses its triple-A rating," said Bruegel's Kirkegaard. "Interest rate costs will go up even more. Who has to pay for that? Net contributing countries, like Germany, the Nordics, the Dutch, which is why they are much more open to this than in the past."

Other European tax experts believe that prior examples of these digital taxes show the costs outweigh the benefits.

"We analyzed the states which have a digital services tax [DST], and we've seen that economic cost exceeds the revenue generated," said Cristina Enache, an economist at the Brussels-based nonprofit Tax Foundation Europe. "Spain has a DST and the expected revenue was twice or three times larger than what they actually are collecting."

Enache called the tax proposal "politically impossible."

EU leaders know that the clock on their end-of-2026 deadline is ticking, and will return to the same conference rooms in late December hoping for a more conducive atmosphere to strike a deal.

World.title: ¿Quién va a ganar las elecciones? La probabilidad de cada mayoría según las encuestas
World.content:
