World.title: PM Radev, Finance Ministry, try to shift blame as Bulgaria faces possible fine over excessive deficit
World.content:
Prime Minister Roumen Radev and his Finance Ministry have tried to shift blame on to previous governments as Bulgaria faces a possible fine because of its inaction to address the excessive deficit.

Radev’s comments at a November 25 regular meeting of the Cabinet came nine days after he told his ministers to stop blaming previous governments.

The Bulgarian government information service quoted Radev as telling the November 25 meeting: “Yesterday, the European Commission slapped a resounding slap on everyone who over the years spent recklessly without attracting investments, who borrowed without developing the economy, lied about the real deficit to get us into the euro zone, and led the finances to an excessive deficit and catastrophe”.

According to Radev, the European Commission’s good forecast for next year “is a clear confirmation that the course taken by the government to restore state finances is correct”.

“So we will not fulfill the nihilistic dreams of the opposition to stop our European funding and payments under the RRP (Recovery and Resilience Plan),” Radev said.

Radev said that the government “will continue with the reforms and the elimination of inherited inefficient and corrupt practices in public enterprises”.

“Since the beginning of the year, foreign direct investment has increased by more than 100 per cent, and this percentage is increasing even more,” he said (In fact, going by Bulgarian National Bank data, as reported by The Sofia Globe, the increase in FDI in January – September 2026 is about 66 per cent on an annual basis).

A statement by the Finance Ministry on November 24, when the European Commission announced its recommendation that Bulgaria should be fined, offered similar arguments.

“Today’s assessment by the European Commission (EC)—part of the European Semester’s Autumn Package—points to a significant deviation from the recommended trajectory for net expenditure for 2026, as well as the risk of sanctions for failing to comply with the Council’s recommendation of July 10 2026,” the Finance Ministry said.

“This situation is a direct consequence of accumulated systemic problems and the political crisis of recent years—issues for which all political forces bear shared responsibility,” the ministry said.



According to the Finance Ministry “it is important to clarify that such a sanction has no bearing on the fifth payment under the Recovery and Resilience Plan, nor is it expected to block funds from European sources”.

“The government will continue to restore the state’s financial stability, while strictly safeguarding key social commitments, support for vulnerable groups, and predictability for citizens and public services,” the ministry said.

“The responsibility now lies with the National Assembly—we expect all political parties to demonstrate statesmanship during the adoption and implementation of the 2027 Budget, so that the flawed practices leading to EU sanctions may be consigned to the past once and for all,” it said.

Of the eight governments that Bulgaria had between January 2017 and January 2026, while Radev was president, he appointed four as interim administrations. Of those four, one was in office for 308 days, from 2022 to 2023. It was headed by Gulub Donev, who currently is Radev’s Finance Minister.

Assen Vassilev, leader of opposition party We Continue the Change and a former finance minister, alleged that Radev was lying, saying that the evidence was in the reports of the European Commission on the economy and finances of Bulgaria in the years before 2026.

Vassilev said that the European Commission report clearly states that the 2026 Budget is the one with a problematic deficit.

This budget was written by the Radev Cabinet and adopted by the Progressive Bulgaria MPs – even though the opposition in the form of We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria had warned that it could lead to European sanctions for refusing to optimise spending.

“If there weren’t 1.5 billion euro more for expenses to support the administration, we could easily have a 4.1 per cent deficit, which with the derogation for military spending would have allowed us not to enter an excessive deficit procedure,” Vassilev said.

The derogation to which he was referring is an EU decision that allows a deficit above the three per cent ceiling in the euro zone if the expenditure that leads to it is in the field of defence. The exception is due to the threat to European security from Russia and the war it is waging in Ukraine.

The European Commission said that it also has concerns about the draft Budget for 2027 and will monitor Bulgarian finances closely in the first six months after January 1 due to the risks facing the economy.

Vassilev said that the European Commission’s reports on Bulgaria for each year are public and none of them have mentioned an excessive deficit or a problem with the financial framework.

So far, Bulgaria has not been sanctioned for unbalanced finances, as the Commission is now threatening.

Vassilev said that next year’s Budget, currently at first-reading stage in Parliament, is “even worse” than the criticised Budget 2026, because “it hits the foundation of the economy, investments and consumption and will bring us a recession”.

He again called for the draft Budget to be withdrawn by the Finance Ministry and revised. And for a new version to be submitted “by different Finance Minister”.

(Photo: government.bg)

World.title: European Parliament approves 2027 EU budget
World.content:
In a vote on November 25, the European Parliament gave its final greenlight to the last annual budget of the 2021-2027 EU long-term budget framework.

In the 720-member European Parliament, the 2027 budget was adopted by 406 votes to 184, with 69 abstentions.

In a deal reached on November 11, the European Parliament and member state governments agreed to set the overall level of commitment appropriations (legal promises to pay in the same year or later) at 199.7 billion euro, and payment appropriations (actual payments made to beneficiaries) at 211.5 billion euro.

In commitment appropriations, this sets the 2027 budget at 0.99 per cent of the EU’s gross national income (GNI).

The European Parliament secured an additional 300 million euro for its priorities compared to the European Commission’s proposal, boosting investment in research, transport and energy networks, Erasmus+, civil protection, border management, military mobility, the EU’s neighbourhood, and humanitarian aid. The deal also includes stronger cybersecurity and security capabilities for the EU institutions and delegations.

Key increases compared with the European Commission’s proposal include 39 million euro for the EU’s Southern and Eastern Neighbourhood, 30 million euro for humanitarian aid and 30 million euro for border management and migration.

MEPs secured more research funding through Horizon Europe with 21.5 million euro extra, and for transport and energy networks an additional 22.5 million euro.

For education, the Erasmus+ programme receives an additional 14 million euro and the civil protection mechanism is reinforced by 13.5 million euro.

Further increases support military mobility (10 million euro), and climate and environmental action (10 million euro).

The 4.9 billion euro NextGenerationEU over-run costs are to be dealt with as agreed previously through a “cascade mechanism”, designed to manage the borrowing costs and protect flagship programmes.

The amount allocated to servicing the Ukraine Support Loan debt is set at 650 million euro, in line with the European Commission’s proposal.

The European Parliament, Council and Commission have also acknowledged in a joint statement the possibility of covering the loan’s debt service costs by mobilising the Ukraine Support Loan special instrument in 2027.

As The Sofia Globe reported previously, the Council of the European Union formally adopted on November 23 the EU’s budget for 2027.

World.title: Vukovar Resolution: It’s Up to Serbia to Confront its Past
World.content:
November the 28th, 2026 – MEP Karlo Ressler has stated that now the Vukovar Resolution has been adopted, it is up to Serbia to confront its past.

The European Parliament has formally adopted a resolution on the 35th anniversary of the fall and destruction of Vukovar, and Members of the European Parliament paid tribute to surviving Vukovar residents with applause. Index reports that the initiator of the resolution, MEP Karlo Ressler, spoke in a Media Servis Interview of the Week about the importance of the resolution for Croatia, relations with Serbia, and other current European topics.

“We won’t remain silent about what happened in Vukovar. We cannot compare it with Operation Storm (Oluja). The reactions from Serbia are not encouraging,” Ressler stated.

The Vukovar Resolution, which was adopted by a large majority, emphasises that the memory of Vukovar’s sacrifice belongs not only to Croatia, but to the whole of Europe, and that it serves as a lasting reminder that defending peace, human rights, and fundamental European values requires constant vigilance, sacrifice, political courage, and dialogue.

Ressler described the atmosphere in the European Parliament during the tribute to the people of Vukovar. “When you see the people of Vukovar who went through that Calvary of Vukovar, who personally bore the greatest sacrifice and burden in their lives, you see in an even deeper, more human way how important it is to speak about Vukovar today as well, and I think this is the least we can do for those people who truly gave everything for our freedom,” he noted.

“It’s important that we have woven our memory of Vukovar into the broader European cultural and civilisational heritage,” Ressler added.

minor changes requested by the liberals

The resolution was also supported by other Croatian MEPs, and minor amendments were introduced into the text at the request of the Liberals. Ressler claims that not a single key provision was abandoned in the process. “We did not want to agree to anything that would be substantive. I think it is important to speak about Vukovar and what happened completely clearly and without any relativisation or similar,” he emphasised. “We insisted that Vukovar be clearly recognised first and foremost as a symbol of Croatian resistance to Milošević’s Greater Serbian aggression, that horrific crimes took place in Vukovar—clearly including Ovčara, as well as a whole series of other murders, systematic looting, persecution of the Croatian population, and rapes that formed part of ethnic cleansing. That is something clearly stated there,” he continued.

The resolution also calls for the opening of war archives, which is one of the key issues in the search for missing persons from the Homeland War. Croatia is still searching for 1,725 missing persons.

“any kind of calculation speaks to something much deeper”

Representatives of the student movement in Serbia, which defeated Aleksandar Vučić in recent elections, stated in reaction to the resolution that reconciliation requires acknowledging all suffering and that Operations Flash and Storm must not be omitted from a comprehensive view of that historical period. Ressler assessed that such messages from Serbia are not encouraging. “Any kind of calculation around paying tribute to Croatian defenders, and tributes to the victims of Vukovar and Ovčara, speaks to something deeper, something civilisational. It truly saddens me that such a situation exists, but I would separate two things,” he remarked. “So, as the European Parliament, we bowed to that sacrifice. On the other hand, it is up to Serbia, to the incoming leadership, and generally to the entire society, to confront what happened in the 90s,” Ressler believes.

pupovac’s statement

SDSS President Milorad Pupovac warned that the resolution could negatively affect relations between Croatia and Serbia, recalling that members of the student-civic movement had previously criticized the politicization of wartime suffering. Ressler rejected such a stance. “No, I cannot accept such theses suggesting that we should, say, keep quiet about what happened in Vukovar, that we should be patient until the 50th anniversary or find some better timing,” he said. “We’re paying tribute to the sacrifice of Vukovar, to the heroic defenders, and that is what we will continue to do. Therefore, I do not think we should put this in the background in order to somehow appease the incoming government in Serbia. That is not our task,” he stated.

historical facts exist whether people like them or not

Asked whether Europe had hitherto been too restrained in naming those responsible for the wartime events in Croatia, the HDZ MEP stated that there had been tendencies to equalise guilt. “Veselin Šljivančanin on one side and the Vukovar defenders and Blago Zadro on the other cannot be in the same sentence or placed in the same context. It simply does not work that way. Historical facts exist, and a large part of it is documented,” he noted.

“Some kind of equalisation of guilt, like putting Vukovar, Flash, and Storm in the same basket, these are completely incomparable things, and I think such tendencies did exist. I am not saying they are not sometimes present today as well, but that is something we are fighting against,” Ressler concluded.

World.title: Who is Robert Palić Who Was Shot (Again) Yesterday in Zagreb?
World.content:
November the 28th, 2026 – Who exactly is the controversial entrepreneur Robert Palić who was shot for the second time in Zagreb yesterday morning? From Thai businesses to arrests in Belgrade and luxury cars, his story is a colourful one, to say the least.

Controversial entrepreneur Robert Palić was shot for the second time yesterday morning in Dubrava in Zagreb. His turbulent biography has been marked by all kinds of ventures, links to Mamić, arrests and a multi-million tax affair. Paula Bosancic reports for 24sata that the hotelier, restaurateur, luxury car dealer, long-time Dinamo fan, a man whom the media linked to Zdravko Mamić, and an entrepreneur who for years sat in the dock because of a multi-million tax affair. Robert Palić was wounded again yesterday morning in Dubrava, the second time in a span of about twenty months. As has since been learned, Palić was once again hit in the legs. He was taken to hospital, where he received medical help, and according to reports, he is not in a life-threatening condition.

Palić was seriously wounded for the first time on the 19th of March 2025. After recovering he was given police protection, and he arrived at the Zagreb County Court, where he was being tried for irregularities in the import of luxury cars, accompanied by plain-clothes police officers. At the end of December last year, after years of denying guilt, he suddenly changed his defence strategy. He admitted guilt, reached a settlement with USKOK and avoided going to prison. He received a prison sentence replaced by community service and a fine of €150,000. Less than eleven months later he again ended up in hospital with gunshot wounds.

Robert Palić is an entrepreneur whose biography has for about fifteen years been intertwined with Croatian football, expensive cars, exotic destinations, criminal investigations and violence?.

he attacked a uefa investigator

The public first got to know Robert Palić better back in August 2010, and it was in the premises of Zagreb’s Dinamo. Croatian football was then being shaken by a match-fixing scandal, and one of the most exposed people in the whole story was the controversial UEFA investigator Robin Bokšić. Palić called a press conference at which he accused Bokšić of still owing him €1,200 for accommodation in his hotel in Crikvenica. But he did not stop only at the unpaid bill. He also made a series of much more serious accusations against the man who was investigating irregularities in Croatian football.

“I simply want it to be known who UEFA is sending to Croatia,” Palić said at the time, as reported by 24sata. He presented himself as a long-time Dinamo fan, hotelier and restaurateur. The media later also described him as a man close to the then head of Dinamo, Zdravko Mamić. At that moment Palić was already an established entrepreneur in tourism and hospitality, and according to contemporary media reports, in addition to the hotel in Crikvenica he also had a hotel in neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Palić’s business interests ranged from hospitality and hotel management through car trading to real estate. Family members were also involved in the business. A particularly interesting part of his business biography relates to the purchase of a share in a palace in Smičiklasova Street in the centre of Zagreb. The property was owned by Rudar, a company of the former Croatian tycoon Josip Gucić, who had once planned to open a hotel there. Co-ownership of the property was acquired by Palić’s company Fi-Bo trade, founded immediately before the purchase with share capital of only 20,000 kuna. The company director was Palić’s son-in-law Antun Berišić.

A whole series of trading companies were linked to members of his family, including Sports Concept Seven, Nekretnine Sopnica, Aktiv-konto and ZAG-Nekretnine. For years Palić also did business on the Croatia–Thailand route, where he spent part of the year. Despite the criminal proceedings against him, he occasionally appeared in the media as a tourism entrepreneur. During the summer of 2024, for example, he commented on the poor tourist season in Crikvenica.

“We have five hospitality facilities in the first row by the sea, we have a small family hotel that has also been operating for 20-odd years,” he said at the time. He claimed that his business was at least 40 percent weaker than the previous year and that he employed 85 workers from different parts of the world.

arrested in belgrade

At the beginning of 2018, Robert Palić found himself at the centre of a major USKOK investigation on suspicion of tax fraud in trading luxury cars. At the moment when Croatian investigators launched arrests, Palić was in Thailand. A wanted notice was issued for him, on the basis of which he was subsequently arrested in Belgrade and extradited to Croatia. USKOK also requested the blocking of his assets. The Zagreb County Court ordered temporary security measures on properties in Zagreb and Crikvenica and a boat. The value of the properties written about at the time amounted to around 12 million kuna. Palić did not spend long in investigative detention. After being released he continued doing business while USKOK prepared an indictment against him and his associates. The indictment against a total of nine people was raised in October 2019. Among the accused were also members of his family.

croatia’s most expensive collision…

Robert Palić hit the headlines again back in 2019, but this time not because of the court proceedings. He was involved in a spectacular traffic accident in Zagreb’s Dubrava in which two extremely expensive sports cars were seriously damaged. Palić was driving an Audi R8 Spyder 5.2 FSI Quattro with Czech registration plates, a car with a ten-cylinder engine and 525 horsepower. The price of a new example with additional equipment exceeded 1.5 million kuna.

A BMW M3 driven by the then 26-year-old Mihael Ćibarić collided with his Audi. After the collision the BMW hit a traffic light and two more parked cars. Both drivers ended up in hospital with serious bodily injuries. Ćibarić was already known to the public as one of three brothers linked to an attack on an employee of Dubrava Clinical Hospital in 2018. Because of the value of the destroyed sports cars, the media described the accident as one of the most expensive collisions in Croatia. Central to Palić’s criminal file are two companies, Elite cars 7 and Paresis, through which he traded in used luxury vehicles. These were expensive Mercedes, BMW and Porsche models, including Mercedes-AMG GT, BMW 740 D and Porsche Macan.

According to the USKOK indictment, from the beginning of 2015 until January 2018, Palić organised a group that, through fictitious transactions and unreliable business documentation, unjustifiably reduced VAT payment obligations. How much money was circulating through those companies is shown by the fact that Paresis alone during 2017 generated more than 18.5 million kuna in revenue, while the reported profit amounted to only 56,888 kuna. The company was later deleted from the court register. According to the original indictment, the state budget was damaged by almost 6.6 million kuna. The amount of damage established in the later settlement was lower and amounted to approximately 4.94 million kuna, or €655,146. For years Palić rejected the accusations, and the court proceedings dragged on. When he was first shot in March 2025, the trial was still ongoing.

police protection

On the morning of the 19th of March 2025, Robert Palić was seriously wounded near the Mrak café in Zagreb’s Dubrava area, which he regularly visited. Because of multiple gunshot wounds to the legs he underwent surgery, and after leaving hospital he had to undergo rehabilitation. Because of his health condition the trial at the Zagreb County Court was also postponed. At the time the media wrote a great deal about the possibility that the shooting represented a warning to Palić. However, the motive for the attack was never publicly confirmed, nor was it established that the shooting was connected with his business or the criminal proceedings.

When he appeared in court again on the 26th of May 2025, Palić had police protection. He was accompanied into the courtroom by plain-clothes police officers. Several months after the shooting the police achieved the first significant breakthrough in the investigation. Darko Dakić, then 47 years old, was arrested on suspicion of assisting the perpetrator of the attack on Palić. As Večernji list wrote, Dakić was already known to the police. Back in 2010, he had been arrested on suspicions linked to attacks on entrepreneur Josip Galinec and journalist Dušan Miljuš. However, the criminal complaint against him and other suspects in those cases was dismissed due to lack of evidence. In the investigation of the attack on Palić, Dakić exercised his right to remain silent. The police also released surveillance camera footage and asked for the public’s help in identifying the direct perpetrator. Despite the arrest of the suspected accomplice, the identity of the attacker and the motive for the shooting remained unknown to the public.

a very sudden settlement with uskok…

Nine months after the first shooting a major turnaround occurred in Palić’s court proceedings. On the 29th of December 2025, after years of trial during which he denied guilt, Palić decided to admit the criminal offences and conclude a settlement with USKOK. Of the total of nine accused, eight agreed to the settlement. Robert Palić and his sons Roberto and Ivan were each sentenced to 11 months in prison, with the prison sentences replaced by community service. In addition, Palić received a secondary fine of €150,000, his son Roberto €40,000 and Ivan €10,000. At the time the judgement was pronounced Palić had already paid €86,436 of his fine. He is also obliged to compensate the state for damage of €655,146 within two years and to settle €3,476 in court costs. The total financial obligations imposed on him by the settlement thus exceed €808,000. Prison sentences replaced by community service were also imposed on his son-in-law Antun Berišić and Smiljan Karamatić. Both also received fines of €40,000 each. The other accused who admitted guilt received suspended sentences and financial sanctions.

World.title: Croatian Craft Owners Now Face Fines of up to €30,000
World.content:
November the 28th, 2026 – Croatian craft owners are now facing eye-watering fines of up to €30,000. Here’s who the new EU rules apply to.

The latest regulations cover a range of products, from coffee, chocolate and car tyres to furniture, paper and firewood, and the deadlines for adaptation depend on the size of the company and the type of product. Poslovni reports that Croatian craft owners, traders, importers and manufacturers who deal in certain types of goods will face the application of new European rules aimed at preventing products linked to deforestation and forest degradation from being placed on the market. For non-compliance with the prescribed obligations, craftsmen and persons performing an independent activity face fines of up to €30,000.

At its session held on the 25th of November, the Croatian Government submitted to the parliamentary procedure the final proposal for amendments to the Act on the Implementation of the European Regulation on Products Linked to Deforestation and Forest Degradation. The amendments align Croatian legislation with newer European regulations, change the list of covered products, specify the obligations of participants in the supply chain and adapt the misdemeanour provisions.

what can croatian craft owners now be fined for?

According to the current law, whose provisions the Croatian Government has now proposed to amend and supplement, for certain misdemeanours craftsmen and persons performing an independent activity are prescribed fines of €7,000 to €30,000. Among the misdemeanours covered by this range of fines are failure to fulfil the prescribed obligations when placing goods on the market, preventing the competent authorities from carrying out checks, and failure to implement ordered corrective measures. The final proposal of the law further aligns the misdemeanour provisions with the rules applicable to economic operators lower in the supply chain, the simplified regime for micro and small primary economic operators, and the obligations of authorised representatives.

Fines of €2,000 to €10,000 are provided for Croatian craft owners and persons performing an independent activity if, when they are obliged to do so, they fail to establish a system for collecting the necessary information, documents and data, fail to establish a system for risk assessment and mitigation, fail to establish or maintain a due diligence system, or fail to make the prescribed information and documentation available to the competent authorities.

For legal persons, fines of one to four percent of total annual turnover at the level of the European Union in the financial year preceding the imposition of the fine are prescribed, while responsible persons in legal persons may be fined amounts from €1,000 to €5,000.

the new eu rules apply to seven basic categories

The European regulations apply to seven basic categories of goods – cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood – as well as a range of products derived from those raw materials. Among the products listed in the final proposal of the Croatian law are as follows: beef and certain meat products, coffee, coffee extracts and concentrates, chocolate and food products containing cocoa, soya and palm oil, new car tyres and certain rubber products, wooden furniture, parquet, building joinery and prefabricated wooden houses, firewood, briquettes and pellets, certain paper and cardboard products, wooden pallets and packaging and certain types of soap and chemical products produced from oil palm.

Not all products within the listed categories are covered. The application of the regulations depends on the tariff code of the product, its properties and the prescribed exemptions. For example, for certain categories, used products, products obtained from recycled material and packaging that serves exclusively to protect or transport another product are exempted.

the rules aren’t the same across the board…

The purpose of the European regulation on deforestation-free products is to ensure that the goods covered by the regulations have not been produced on land on which deforestation has occurred after the 31st of December 2020 and that they have been produced in accordance with the relevant legislation of the country of origin. The largest part of the obligations to verify the origin of goods and exercise due diligence applies to economic operators who first place the covered products on the market of the European Union or export them. For traders and economic operators lower in the supply chain, different obligations are provided, including the collection and retention of prescribed data on suppliers and business customers.

For micro and small primary economic operators who meet the prescribed conditions, a simplified regime has also been introduced, which includes a one-time submission of a simplified declaration instead of the regular submission of due diligence declarations.

for some, the deadline is the end of december…

According to official information from the European Commission, the bulk of the obligations begins to apply on the 30th of December 2026 for medium and large economic operators and traders. For most micro and small enterprises that meet the conditions for deferred application, the deadline is the 30th of June 2027. However, that deferral does not apply to everyone. For micro and small economic operators who deal in products covered by the previous European Timber Regulation, the start of application of the new rules is also the 30th of December 2026. For certain newly included product categories, an additional adaptation period is provided, until the 30th of December 2027.

In addition to financial fines, non-compliance with the regulations can have other consequences for business. Competent inspectors can, depending on the irregularities established, prohibit the placing of goods on the market, order their withdrawal or recall, temporarily seize products and order their disposal if the irregularities cannot be remedied in any other way. The costs of implementing certain measures, including the storage, safekeeping, transport and disposal of goods, are borne by the economic operators or traders themselves. Supervision will, depending on the type of product, be carried out by market, veterinary, agricultural, sanitary, forestry and phytosanitary inspection, with the participation of other competent authorities.

The proposed amendments to the Croatian law will enter into force on the eighth day after publication in the Official Gazette, after they are adopted by the Croatian Parliament. The deadlines for the start of application of individual European obligations are regulated separately by European regulations.

World.title: Croats are Leaving Germany, But It Doesn’t Mean They’re Returning to Croatia
World.content:
November the 28th, 2026 – The government may be full of self-praise because Croats are leaving Germany, but it doesn’t necessarily mean they’re returning to Croatia. In addition to that, the way Croatia and Germany deal with statistics is very different.

About ten years after the major wave of Croatian emigration to Germany, the migration trend has become more blurry. Slobodan Muftic reports for Index that the data from the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) show that from the beginning of January to the end of September this year, 7,012 Croatian citizens moved to Germany, while 16,955 left the country. A closer look at the statistics, however, shows that the reason is not so much a mass return of Croats from Germany as the fact that fewer and fewer of them are going there.

Destatis records that in the pandemic year 2021, 28,457 Croatian citizens moved to Germany, while last year the figure was only 11,352. At the same time, the number of Croatian citizens leaving Germany has for years ranged between 22,000 and 25,000. The negative migration balance is therefore increasing primarily because Germany is attracting fewer and fewer new Croatian immigrants.

not all of them are going back to croatia

“As soon as an economic crisis and existential uncertainty appear, people who are not permanently emigrated return. The European Union no longer needs as much labour, because the European economy is currently not particularly prosperous. These are normal and expected fluctuations. In any case, it is obvious that the major emigration wave from Croatia has been stopped,” academic and demography expert Anđelko Akrap explained.

But who are the people actually leaving Germany today? Are working-age people and families with children who emigrated after Croatia’s accession to the European Union returning to Croatia, or primarily members of older generations of emigrants after retirement? And how many of them choose life in a third country instead of returning to Croatia? “According to Eurostat data for 2024, of the total number of Croatian citizens who left Germany, almost 80 percent were aged 15 to 64. Around ten percent were persons aged 65 and over, and the same proportion were children under 15,” said Monika Balija Vincek, assistant professor at the Croatian Studies.

It would be premature to conclude that all of the almost 17,000 Croatian citizens who left Germany this year returned to Croatia. Although Croatian data also confirm that the migration trend has reversed, our Central Bureau of Statistics (DZS) records significantly different figures from the German Destatis.

differences in the methodology between german and croatian statistics

For example, according to German statistics, last year 20,504 people moved from Germany to Croatia, regardless of citizenship, while Croatian statistics recorded only 9,628 arrivals from Germany, of whom 8,334 were Croatian citizens. Part of these differences stems from different methodology. German statistics record registrations and de-registrations of residence regardless of its duration, while Croatian statistics, based on data from the Ministry of the Interior, cover persons who change their country of residence for at least one year.

As such, a Croatian citizen who every year goes to Germany for several months of work and then returns can regularly appear in German but not in Croatian statistics. Furthermore, some Croatian citizens live and work in Germany for years without ever having de-registered their residence or reported a temporary departure abroad to the Croatian Ministry of the Interior. When such persons return to Croatia, it is possible that their return is not administratively recorded at all.

“Given that German statistics record the departures of Croatian citizens regardless of the country of destination, we cannot calculate how many of them returned to Croatia and how many went to other countries. Likewise, among the mentioned 8,334 Croatian citizens who moved to Croatia there may also be persons who moved to Croatia for the first time, so it is not necessarily a matter of 8,334 returnees,” explains assistant professor Balija Vincek.

not all of them have any intention of going back to croatia

Some Croatian citizens are probably moving from Germany to Austria, Switzerland, Bosnia and Herzegovina or other countries. Special account should be taken of Croatian citizens originating from BiH who went to work in Germany with Croatian documents but never lived in Croatia. Their return to BiH is recorded as the departure of Croatian citizens from Germany.

Demographer and university professor Tado Jurić, in his July analysis for Večernji list, warns that the increasing number of departures of Croatian citizens from Germany does not necessarily mean a mass return to the homeland. He claims that two-thirds of returnees do not end up in Croatia but, after Germany, continue their lives in other European countries. At the same time, the number of new emigrants from Croatia is decreasing, mainly due to exhausted migration potential. In his opinion, the period of mass one-way emigration has ended and a period of multi-directional migrations is beginning.

eurostat’s data makes it even less convincing

“From Eurostat data for 2024 it can be inferred that among Croatian citizens who have been leaving Germany in recent years, the old gastarbeiter generations do not predominate. According to the results of our recent survey of more than 600 Croatian citizens in Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, among respondents who had already taken steps towards returning to Croatia, almost 70 percent had moved to Germany in 2014 or later,” emphasises assistant professor Monika Balija Vincek. An interesting insight into the reasons for the return of Croats from Germany is also provided by Balija Vincek’s research published in 2023 in the Croatian Geographical Bulletin. It covers nine returnees aged 28 to 41 who spent between two and six years in Germany.

“i’ll go back to germany again if i need to”

Eight of them had planned a return even before leaving Croatia, and five returned after achieving the goal for which they had emigrated – raising enough money to buy property, repay a loan or start their own business. The remaining four cited attachment to family and friends in Croatia, dissatisfaction with life in Germany and difficulties integrating into the local society as the main reasons for return.

It is particularly interesting that eight of the nine respondents did not rule out the possibility of going abroad again if economic conditions in Croatia forced them to do so. Although it is a small and non-representative sample, the research points to problems with housing policy, job insecurity and living standards in Croatia, as well as the fact that the return of emigrants does not necessarily have to be permanent. “In the conversations I had with returnees from Germany, some mentioned that because of potentially unfavourable conditions on the labour market and an unsatisfactory standard of living in Croatia they would again consider leaving, and more recent research also highlights difficulties upon return or after return. We know, therefore, that for some a new departure is still a possibility, but for now we do not have data on how many of them actually leave again,” Balija Vincek said.

Or as one of the respondents in the research, then a 41-year-old who returned and opened a craft business in Croatia, explained: “I went to Germany to repay a loan, so if the same thing happens again, I will definitely go abroad again.”

World.title: Vukovar Resolution: We Know Who in Serbia Has Information on Missing Persons
World.content:
November the 27th, 2026 – The Vukovar Resolution was formally adopted yesterday, and now the focus is who exactly in Serbia has information on those still listed as missing.

The European Parliament has adopted a resolution marking the 35th anniversary of the fall and destruction of Vukovar. Index reports that the document pays tribute to the victims, condemns the glorification of war criminals and calls on Serbia to open its archives in order to clarify the fate of the missing. The resolution, however, has drawn opposition from the Student Movement that is taking power in Serbia, instead of serving as an incentive for confronting the past. The topic was discussed on HRT’s programme Otvoreno.

what does the vukovar resolution actually mean?

MEP Karlo Ressler (HDZ) said that this was a cross-party initiative supported by all Croatian MEPs. “That was a precondition for broad support from all European colleagues. Thirty-five years after the fall of Vukovar it was important to speak about this openly in the European Parliament,” he said. He believes the main goals of the resolution have been achieved.

“I think we’ve achieved the main tasks with this resolution, and they concern conveying the message that Vukovar is a symbol of the resistance of a small number of defenders against a superior aggressor. We pay tribute to all Croatian defenders and all civilian victims, but we also open the issues of the missing and other questions arising from the Homeland War,” Ressler stated. He added that the resolution calls on the Serbian authorities to prevent the glorification of convicted war criminals. “The state funeral of Ratko Mladić is explicitly mentioned, but the horrific crimes at Ovčara are also clearly mentioned. The camps to which Croatian defenders were taken are named,” Ressler said. He emphasised that it is important to speak about Vukovar on the basis of clear historical facts. “Vukovar is a topic that unites us in Croatia, but it also has strong lessons for the entire European continent,” he concluded.

“serbia isn’t providing useful information”

Croatia is still searching for 1,725 people, of whom 320 are from the Vukovar area. Ana Filko, director of the Directorate for Detained and Missing Persons at the Ministry of Croatian Veterans, stated that Croatia has to date received no content-wise usable information from Serbia for finding the missing.

“We’ve identified concrete documentation. We’ve identified specific units, mainly rear engineering units that participated in the sanitation or concealment of graves. We’ve also identified which persons are located in the territory of Serbia and who may have that knowledge. We have forwarded that knowledge to the Serbian commission, but we have not received a concrete response,” Filko explained. She stressed that a “vow of silence” is one of the key problems in the search for the missing. “It is linked to the fact that these persons are not prepared to give information out of fear of a certain retaliation from the Serbian side, but also to the fact that finding the missing is linked to uncovering the crime committed,” she said.

Filko added that Croatia does not depend on Serbia in the search, as the results show. In the past ten years, 343 missing persons have been identified without any help from Serbia. “They could speed up the process in order to alleviate the agony of the families. We cannot change the past, but we can influence the future of every family. We will not give up until we find the last missing person,” she said.

Nataša Kandić, founder of the Humanitarian Law Centre, believes that an important message is at the end of the resolution, but that it communicates poorly with everything that was said before. Ressler replied to her: “We wanted to achieve that we are clear, that we do not speak about the suffering of Vukovar in abstract, general terms. We speak about murders, rapes, the persecution of the Croatian population after the occupation of the city, we speak about the causes of the war. It is important that 35 years after Vukovar there is no relativisation around this and we are now trying to weave it into the common European memory.” The resolution also mentions Boris Tadić’s visit to Ovčara in 2010, when he apologised for the crimes. Kandić said that this apology remains forever.

“That is recognition of how much the crimes and the destruction of Vukovar are a shame that belongs not only to the JNA but also to the citizens of Serbia who were mobilised, who were taken, many against their will,” Kandić said. She added that she would have liked the paragraph on joint responsibility to have been expanded in the resolution and for all countries to come together.

a call to serbia’s new government

Sandra Rapčak Škomrlj, president of the Association of Children of Fallen and Missing Croatian Defenders of the Homeland War, said that the mere change of power in Serbia does not mean a change of rhetoric. “We know that they rebelled when they found out about the resolution.

The new authorities must be aware that without resolving the past we cannot build the future,” she said and called on the Serbian authorities to cooperate. “Someone must answer for the war crimes committed. I call on them to bring those who committed the crimes to justice, to open the military archives so that they can provide information about the missing, and not for future generations to take on the burden of the past,” Rapčak Škomrlj stated.

Through the association, families have for years been filing lawsuits for the payment of war reparations from Serbia. More than 20 lawsuits have been filed and war reparations have been paid, while some proceedings are still ongoing. “We invite all those whose loved ones were killed and identified at Ovčara to contact us if they wish to file a lawsuit,” she said.

World.title: €100 Million Investment for New Jadrolinija Fleet Launched
World.content:
November the 27th, 2026 – A €100 euro investment for a new Jadrolinija fleet has now been launched, with 10 brand new vessels planned.

Part of the tenders for the construction of new ships has already been published and is in the implementation phase. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the Minister of Maritime Affaits, Transport and Infrastructure Oleg Butković stated this week that the recapitalisation of Jadrolinija is now ready. He added that the accompanying contracts will soon be signed for the implementation of the shore power supply system for ships at the Brajdica and Zagrebačka obala container terminals in Rijeka.

fleet modernisation

“Jadrolinija is going into recapitalisation, that is ready. We are going in two directions – with the recapitalisation of Jadrolinija and with the World Bank. Part of the tenders for the construction of new ships has already been published and is in the implementation phase, so Jadrolinija expects to sign contracts for the construction of new ships next year,” Butković revealed. Unofficially, it has been learn edthat the recapitalisation of Jadrolinija should be worth up to €100 million. It is closely linked to modernisation and should secure Jadrolinija’s financial position until 2043. It is a combination of different sources. Jadrolinija Management Board President Robert Blažinović revealed to us that the tenders should be published by the end of November.

“I think that within the next ten days or so we will also proceed to contracting the construction of the first ship,” Blažinović told us. This was preceded by a competitive procedure with negotiations for construction and design. Jadrolinija’s strategy of building ships with alternative propulsion and electric propulsion is well known, and the locations where they will sail have been determined in advance – the Šibenik, Zadar and Dubrovnik areas. The ships with alternative and electric propulsion will sail in the waters around Šibenik, Zadar and Dubrovnik.

alternative fuel vessels

Blažinović revealed that the Ministry of Transport has established very active cooperation with the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). It has been known for some time that the company has a mandate letter with the IFC, which is working with Jadrolinija on preparing a sustainable financing model for the fleet renewal programme, as well as on assessing projects from the financial, technical, environmental and organisational aspects. We’re talking about a programme that can cover up to ten new ships and represents one of the largest investment phases in the recent history of this state-owned company. At the same time, the possibility of co-financing from EU funds in the segment of green technologies is also opening up, where maximum co-financing can be secured.

“The new ships should bring greater energy efficiency, reliability and comfort, with capacities adapted to the needs of individual lines. At the same time, we must continue investing in the existing fleet, digitalisation and the knowledge of our employees in order to maintain a leading position in maritime passenger transport and continue building the trust of passengers that we have been gaining for eight decades. The greatest challenge will be to align the scope of the necessary investments with the financial sustainability of operations. The green transition requires significant capital, but its implementation also depends on the availability of alternative fuels and the development of appropriate infrastructure. Jadrolinija must be business-efficient and competitive while at the same time ensuring the connectivity on which the daily life of islanders, the local economy and tourism depend. Our transformation is therefore part of a broader development strategy,” Robert Blažinović concluded.

World.title: New Pension Increases Announced for Croatian Retirees in 2027
World.content:
November the 27th, 2026 – Further pension increases have been announced for Croatian retirees in 2027, commenting on their previous growth and on the economy.

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković commented on the growth of pensions and the societal position of pensioners, emphasising that both wages and pensions have risen in the recent period, and announced additional changes that come into force from 2027. Poslovni reports that Croatia will apparently achieve economic growth of around 2.4 percent this year. During the terms of the current Government, absolute GDP has increased from €47 billion to €101 billion. Today, 1.76 million people are employed in Croatia, while the number of unemployed is around 70,000.

Plenković emphasised that as of the 1st of January 2027, the payment of income tax by pensioners is being abolished, which will further increase pensions for more than 540,000 pensioners. In November, 571,945 pensioners paid almost €20 million in tax into the budgets of cities and municipalities, or an average of €34.62 per pensioner. The opposition has warned that by tax relief for some pensioners the Croatian Government will shift the cost onto local budgets.

The state budget for 2027, presented in the Croatian Parliament, according to the Prime Minister’s words also has an important role in preserving social cohesion. The Government plans to allocate around €11 billion for pensions, which is €875 million more than this year.

wage growth will be reflected in pension growth

Plenković recalled that in recent years, Croatia has faced major external shocks and crises, as well as the devastating earthquakes in Zagreb and Banovina. €5.3 billion has so far been allocated for reconstruction. Croatia has recorded 22 consecutive quarters of economic growth, and projections for next year envisage growth of 2.1 percent. A budget deficit of 2.9 percent and a slowdown in inflation to 2.7 percent on an annual basis are also expected. Such trends should enable further growth in the wages of employees in public services, agreed with the trade unions. The wage base will increase by three percent as of the 1st of January 2027, and as of the 1st of April a meal allowance of €30 is being introduced. This will be followed by an additional one-percent increase in the base from 1 August and an increase in the meal allowance by a further €20 as of the 1st of October. Wage growth in the public sector will also be reflected in pensions through their regular adjustment.

World.title: Croatia Can Expect €15.9 Billion in Revenue From Tourism
World.content:
November the 27th, 2026 – Croatia can expect to bring in €15.9 billion in revenue from tourism alone, with the prime minister discussing the second most important visitors.

Croatia should finish this year with slightly better tourism results than it recorded last year, and the value of fiscalised invoices is growing significantly faster than the number of invoices issued. Croatia should end 2026 with approximately €15.9 billion in tourism revenue, around 22 million tourist arrivals and 110 million overnight stays, Prime Minister Andrej Plenković stated on this week at a government session.

Reflecting on the results presented during last week’s Days of Croatian Tourism (Dani hrvatskog turizma) in Poreč, the Prime Minister emphasised that positive movements were recorded this year both in arrivals and overnight stays, as well as in the value of tourist spending. According to the data presented at that event, during the first ten months 21.3 million arrivals and 109 million overnight stays were recorded, representing growth of two percent in arrivals and one percent in overnight stays compared with the same period last year.

an 18% increase in fiscalised invoices in tourism

Particularly notable is the growth in the value of fiscalised invoices in the tourism sector. In the first ten months of the year, invoices worth approximately €8.6 billion were fiscalised, which is 18 percent more than in the same period of 2025. At the same time, around 410.4 million invoices were issued, or six percent more than last year. The value of invoices is thus growing significantly faster than their number, which points to an increase in the average fiscalised amount. A distinction should be made here between fiscalised turnover and revenue from foreign tourists, which is recorded separately in the statistics of the Croatian National Bank.

croatian tourists are now right behind the germans

Plenković particularly singled out the importance of domestic guests for Croatian tourism. According to him, Croatian tourists occupy second place among the most important tourist markets, right behind guests from Germany. Data presented at the Days of Croatian Tourism show that domestic guests recorded approximately 3.1 million arrivals and 13.6 million overnight stays this year. The Prime Minister also emphasised the importance of further investments in the development of continental tourism, especially projects that connect healthcare services, rehabilitation and the tourist offer. The government expects the continuation of positive trends during the post-season as well, along with preparations for the next tourist year. Although the final financial result for 2026 still needs to be confirmed, the indicators so far point to another year of growth for Croatian tourism.

World.title: Keila family finds needle, staple in 'trick-or-treat' candy given to children
World.content:
A family in Keila discovered a sewing needle and a staple hidden inside sweets their children had collected during Halloween and St. Martin's Day trick-or-treating.

Police have launched an investigation after the family handed over the tampered candy, prompting the mother to warn other parents and restrict future visits to people they know.

As with Halloween, which has been gaining in popularity in Estonia in recent decades, the home-grown St. Martin's Day (Mardipäev) traditions include a variant of trick-or-treating in which youngsters present a song, riddle or other performance before being rewarded.

Speaking to "Ringvaade," mother of three, Mari-Liis Azojan, said her husband first spotted a staple pushed into the center of a piece of candy he had pulled from his pocket.

"Suddenly, my husband looked at me wide-eyed. A staple had been pushed into the middle of the candy," Azojan recalled, adding that the household does not use a stapler.

When she went to her children's room to help them inspect the rest of the candy stash, one of the children found a sharp sewing needle inside a second sweet. "It was a real shock," she added.

Mari-Liis Azojan. Source: ERR

The family contacted Police and Border Guard Board that evening and turned over the evidence. "We're now trying to retrace the route the children took so the police can investigate further," Azojan added.

The Health Board has previously warned that narcotics and potent prescription medication have also been found concealed inside confectionery.

Azojan said the incident left the family shaken, noting that her children no longer want to go door-to-door for traditional Estonian mumming holidays like St. Martin's Day, November 10, or St. Catherine's Day (kadripäev), which falls just over two weeks later on November 25.

"If they do decide to go, we'll arrange visits with people we know. It's terrifying to experience something like this yourself," she added.

After posting a warning on social media, Azojan said she had received messages from other parents reporting similar cases across Estonia in previous years, including a suspected incident in Tallinn's Nõmme district, also this autumn. She noted that foreign objects can even be slipped into sealed candy wrappers. The family discarded most of their remaining sweets out of caution.

World.title: Estonian insurers exclude airBaltic insolvency from policies despite bailout
World.content:
Several major Estonian insurers have updated their travel insurance terms to exclude disruptions caused by any potential bankruptcy of Latvian carrier airBaltic.

While Latvia's parliament, the Saeima, approved a €175 million state guarantee for the struggling airline on Thursday, LSM reported, insurers in Estonia say its known financial troubles make the risk effectively uninsurable.

The Latvian flag carrier, a major service provider for Estonians and with about a quarter of the market share linking to Tallinn Airport, has been wrestling with severe financial difficulties for months and would have run out of cash without the bailout.

Notices on Estonian insurers' websites show that underwriters remain unconvinced about the airline's outlook, however, with several recently adding explicit exclusions for the carrier.

"Important information! For travel insurance contracts concluded from November 24, 2026, the 'Strike, insolvency' travel disruption add-on does not cover the insolvency risk of carrier Air Baltic Corporation AS," one insurer, Salva Kindlustus, states on its website.

LHV Kindlustus introduced a similar clause on Thursday, specifying that strike, natural disaster and insolvency coverage do not apply in the event of airBaltic's insolvency or bankruptcy.

The company's product department head Alver Kivirüüt told ERR that travel insurance is primarily meant to cover sudden, unforeseen events such as pre-trip illness, lost luggage or flight cancellations.

"In the case of airBaltic's, we are dealing with publicly known financial difficulties and a resulting heightened risk of insolvency, which is why we are currently not offering insolvency coverage for this airline on new travel insurance contracts," Kivirüüt said.

For Swedbank and If Kindlustus, airBaltic's fragile situation has prompted no policy changes because carrier insolvency was already excluded from their terms.

"Travel service provider insolvency or bankruptcy has already been an excluded risk in our travel insurance terms, regardless of the specific airline," If Kindlustus travel insurance product manager Jonatan Jõks explained, adding that the insurer has in any case not been seeing a spike in customer demand for airline-insolvency coverage.

Swedbank risk insurance subdivision head Eivo Kisand noted that travel insurance is not all-risk coverage and only compensates for events explicitly listed in a policy. "For example, travel insurance does not cover trip cancellation or itinerary changes caused by a service provider's insolvency," Kisand said, meaning airfare and related expenses would not be reimbursed if an airline goes bankrupt.

Not standard in disruption cover

According to Iizi travel insurance product manager Pille Plees, policies covering airBaltic's bankruptcy are actually still available on the market, though the airline's restructuring has put carrier-insolvency clauses under sharper focus.

"Standard travel disruption coverage does not automatically include this risk, and even with broader coverage, special conditions or exclusions may apply to a specific airline," Plees said.

She noted that crises visibly shift buyer behavior — for instance after the Middle East crisis early on this year, the share of Iizi customers opting for broader travel disruption cover rose from 18 percent to 30 percent — though most travelers revert to cheaper, narrower policies once the news value dies out of such sagas.

Pleas also cautioned travelers not to assume credit card travel insurance automatically covers airline insolvency, urging policyholders to check the small print of exact terms.

The insurers stressed that the new restrictions apply only to newly issued policies and do not retroactively alter existing contracts. Kivirüüt called Thursday's Latvian state guarantee encouraging, however, adding that LHV is monitoring developments and will reassess restoring coverage once airBaltic's finances stabilize.

Wider restructuring woes

The insurance clampdown comes amid a turbulent autumn for Tallinn Airport's largest carrier, which held a 23 percent market share at the Estonian hub as recently as last month, though it had already announced in September plans to scale down routes next summer.

In September, airBaltic entered financial restructuring under U.S. Chapter 11 proceedings while securing a €350 million loan at roughly 12 percent interest, following a €30 million Latvian state bailout approved in August. Thursday's €175 million guarantee unlocks the second tranche of that loan.

The airline also announced in October plans to cut 500 to 700 jobs across its Riga, Vilnius and Tallinn bases — roughly a fifth of its nearly 3,000-strong workforce — after posting a €44.34 million loss last year. In a separate incident adding to its travails, airBaltic was among regional companies affected this month by a massive data leak at Latvian telecom provider CSC Telecom.

Estonia's own Nordica ceased operations in late 2024.

World.title: Former Prime Minister Mart Laar to advise President Ülle Madise
World.content:
Historian and two-time Estonian Prime Minister Mart Laar is set to become an adviser to President Ülle Madise from December.

Mart Laar's role will be to advise the head of state on matters concerning the number of people who sustain the Estonian language and culture, history, social cohesion and international relations.

"I value Mart Laar's experience in Estonian public affairs and international relations. He has personally been responsible for decisions whose impact we continue to feel decades later. I particularly value his advice on issues concerning the survival of the Estonian language and culture and what unites us as a people in Estonia," President Ülle Madise said.

Laar said he was happy to assist the president. "If the president wishes to seek advice on culture, collective memory and history, it would be inappropriate to refuse," Laar said.

Laar graduated cum laude from Tartu State University with a degree in history in 1983 and began working as a history teacher at Tallinn Secondary School No. 24. He later headed the Department of Historical Monuments at the Ministry of Culture and was active in the Estonian Heritage Society. He earned a master's degree in history from the University of Tartu in 1995 and a doctorate in the same field in 2005.

During the years leading to the restoration of Estonia's independence, Laar was a member of the Congress of Estonia and the Estonian Committee and took part in the work of the Constitutional Assembly. He served as Estonia's prime minister from 1992 to 1994 and again from 1999 to 2002, and as minister of defense from 2011 to 2012. He chaired the Supervisory Board of the Bank of Estonia from 2013 to 2023. Laar has served several terms in the Riigikogu and published several books and articles reflecting on affairs in Estonia and around the world.

In 2001, President Lennart Meri awarded Laar the Order of the National Coat of Arms, Second Class, for his contribution to the restoration of the Republic of Estonia. Laar has also received numerous high honors both at home and abroad.

President Ülle Madise. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

World.title: Consumer psychologist: Retailers use more tricks as shoppers grow cautious
World.content:
This year, 44 percent of people in Estonia plan to buy something during Black Friday sales, making Estonians the most eager shoppers in the Baltic states, consumer psychologist Ivar Soone said.

While purchase intent reaches 60 percent among people aged 18–29, 31 percent of respondents are cutting spending compared with last year, and only six percent plan to increase their shopping budget. Consumers limiting their spending are planning purchases more carefully because current economic conditions have weakened their sense of financial security.

Consumer caution is making life harder for retailers, however, because Estonia has a disproportionately large amount of retail space per capita. Speaking on an ERR radio program, Soone said stores are therefore turning to every possible psychological tactic.

"Especially in the current economic climate, selling is quite difficult, which is why these tricks are used extensively. Studies in Estonia have shown that simply putting a sign next to a product saying 'Sale' or 'Cheap' can increase sales by as much as 50 percent without changing the price," Soone said.

In addition to discount labels, retailers are extending the duration of promotions as they compete to reach consumers' wallets first. As a result, a one-day Black Friday increasingly becomes a Black Friday weekend, week or even month. The trend extends beyond Black Friday, Soone said. Italian Christmas cakes known as panettones appeared in stores as early as September this year, while Soone received his first Christmas gift reminder by email in January.

Ivar Soone Autor/allikas: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Artificial discounts and time pressure

In reality, discounts offered during lengthy sales campaigns may not save consumers money, as highlighted by a recent study from British consumer organization Which? The study found that in 44 percent of cases, shoppers could buy the same product elsewhere at the same price. In another 34 percent of cases, the product was available at a lower price at a different time.

Soone noted that consumers often lack a clear understanding of regular prices because a large hypermarket may stock as many as 60,000 products. People typically remember only the prices of everyday benchmark goods such as milk and bread. Retailers are quick to exploit that gap in memory. They first establish a high anchor price and then advertise a steep discount. A European Commission report found that actual discounts average just 14 percent, rather than the apparent one-third reduction often advertised.

Beyond price manipulation, retailers also rely on the scarcity effect and fear of missing out, offering discounted products only until the end of the day or while the last few items remain in stock. Retail chains use the same time pressure in everyday promotions, limiting offers from Thursday to Sunday or until supplies run out.

"When we process information, blood flows to that part of the brain. That's where the well-known advice comes from: before you get angry and say something, count to ten. It allows us to rationalize, the emotion subsides a little, and the same applies to shopping and consumption," Soone explained.

Emotional purchasing decisions are reinforced by social proof, which encourages people to follow the crowd, whether prompted by an overcrowded store or an online notice that 100 people are currently viewing the same product. Buyers are similarly lulled into complacency by prices broken into small installments because a monthly payment of €19 may appear insignificant at first glance.

The most deceptive effect, Soone said, is the false feeling that a purchase has generated a profit.

"The transaction benefit effect also comes into play, where people calculate how much they save instead of thinking about how much they actually spend. The same applies to promotions like 'Third item free!' I focus on getting something free, but no one pays attention to the fact that they are spending a pile of money," Soone said.

Three simple habits

According to Soone, three simple habits can help consumers avoid retailers' tricks. The first is to wait until the next morning before making a major purchase. If a person still feels they genuinely need the item the following day, the decision is likely to be more considered.

As a second tool, the psychologist recommended preparing a shopping list before going to the store to maintain focus on necessary purchases. Anyone can test the effectiveness of this strategy at home by comparing their receipt with the items they originally intended to buy. Soone noted that people often go to the store for bread and milk but return with 20–30 products, while forgetting to buy the bread and milk altogether.

To avoid giving in to emotion, he suggested a simple self-discipline exercise.

"You can play a game with yourself and decide that this time you won't take the bait. No matter how tempting the offer seems, you won't buy it today. Tell yourself you'll come back in the afternoon to buy it. Then you'll find out whether you still want it that badly later in the day," Soone said.

As a third measure, consumers should always ask themselves whether a new item will actually be used at home or whether they are being tempted solely by a low price.

After an emotional purchase, people often experience one of two reactions because the brain tries to avoid negative feelings at all costs. In one case, deep regret and guilt emerge, prompting people suffering from compulsive shopping to hide their new purchases from themselves. In the other, post hoc rationalization takes over, with buyers convincing themselves that an item left sitting on a shelf will someday prove useful.

After November's shopping frenzy, consumers may discover in January that prices have fallen even further. Soone acknowledged that retailers often offer better prices at the start of the year because they need to clear old inventory. Despite all the warnings, however, people should not deny themselves sensible purchases or feel guilty about them.

"I encourage everyone not to become discouraged, regardless of the weather, shopping or anything else. Shopping in moderation is still a very pleasant dopamine boost, so enjoy it," Soone said.

To keep both the dopamine boost and the family budget in balance, the consumer psychologist advised avoiding excessive purchases and not stressing too much. If a person has carefully planned a purchase and genuinely needs the item, they can occasionally reward themselves with something nice.

World.title: Andres Anvelt: Surveillance populism not proof of a surveillance society
World.content:
Lawful surveillance is essential to ensuring public safety, but the state must strike a balance between security and fundamental rights without giving in to populist claims of a "surveillance crisis," Andres Anvelt writes.

The state's obligation to catch criminals and provide people with a safe society does not automatically mean creating a surveillance society. If the ground rules are in place and people do not wake up in the morning or go to bed at night feeling that "Big Brother" is constantly breathing down their necks, then talk of a pervasive surveillance society is more a case of populism invoking fundamental rights than an infringement of those rights widely felt across society.

Over the past few decades, we have moved into the world of technology at a breakneck pace, on both sides of the line between good and evil. Criminal investigations are therefore no longer conducted solely by interviewing neighbors at crime scenes or comparing fingerprints. Incidentally, even these traditional investigative procedures have always been subject to statutory requirements, reliability checks and judicial oversight. All with the aim of establishing the truth.

That is why assertions that Estonia has entered a "surveillance crisis" strike me as populist and even deliberately fearmongering. Where do such assertions come from and why do they spread through society? Often, they have the same origins as other catchy slogans: superficial engagement on the part of readers and listeners and information overload.

The recent lower court ruling that attracted considerable media attention and awarded two individuals unusually large amounts of compensation speaks not of a surveillance crisis, but of the Estonian state's failure over the course of a decade to bring domestic law into conformity with European law.

This issue first made it onto the political agenda more than a decade ago when we discussed a newly published European Court of Justice ruling with other European justice ministers and, naturally, turned our attention to the European Commission. What next? Would there be a coordinated response? Unfortunately, none was forthcoming. In hindsight, this is understandable, as the legal traditions of European countries have historically differed so greatly that it was impossible to establish a common position then and no such position has been reached since.

Surveillance in society, meanwhile, is nothing new. Even police patrols on the streets or monitoring traffic keep an eye on all of us. In the technologically advanced 21st century, there are simply more eyes watching. The purpose of lawful surveillance is to collect information in a targeted manner to establish evidence of crimes or prevent security threats. Should those threats materialize, they could have serious consequences for our entire society and state.

However, a clear distinction must be drawn between such activities and the unjustified fishing for data that those proclaiming a "surveillance crisis" often talk about. This is precisely where the underlying problem lies: Some deny that it exists, while others seek to stir up mass hysteria around it.

A real-life example. Twenty-five years ago, two young men who had deserted from a naval academy in St. Petersburg arrived in Estonia. They had no criminal history here whatsoever. Then came bombings, killings and robberies across Estonia on a scale our society had not seen in a long time. Forensic investigators found fingerprints and even DNA here and there, but our databases yielded nothing — there was nothing against which to compare these findings.

"The police are not fishing for data; they are analyzing it. It was precisely this data analysis that led us to the criminals at the time."

One option is to use information technology to identify patterns: What unusual similarities can be found in the areas surrounding different crime scenes? This requires processing enormous amounts of data. In the initial stages of pattern analysis, this data need not be linked to identifiable individuals, since identifying specific people at that point would serve little purpose and would also be too labor-intensive. Every person-hour is worth its weight in gold. The police are not fishing for data; they are analyzing it. It was precisely this data analysis that led us to the criminals at the time.

Fishing for data would mean moving from the particular to the general, singling out a specific individual and then looking for patterns, sentiments and anomalies relating to that person without a clear investigative objective. This would be particularly unsettling in the absence of a legal basis, the necessary judicial authorization, a clearly defined beginning and end to the operation and a specific objective. That is fishing for data. If such practices became widespread in society, there would indeed be grounds to speak of a surveillance crisis.

It is important for society to strike a balance between rights and freedoms on the one hand and internal security and a sense of safety on the other. Ideally, lawmakers should arrive at that balance independently, through dialogue with society. It is more regrettable when that balance has to be sought through court rulings as these are a clear indication that someone has failed to notice something important or has chosen not to.

At the beginning of this century, when our society was recovering from the widespread crime of the 1990s and striving for greater safety, the extensive collection and analysis of data was not a problem for many people. Crime and the insecurity that accompanied it remained serious concerns. This was clearly reflected in surveys measuring people's sense of safety and perceptions of danger. The balance therefore also appeared to be right.

Now, some two decades later, with crime having receded considerably as a perceived threat in people's everyday lives, that balance appears, at least on the surface, to have shifted. Moreover, there are at times attempts to make us feel that crime has been replaced by a state surveillance policy — or a "surveillance crisis" as some would have us see it.

Once again, the particular is being extrapolated to the general. A court finds the processing of the personal data of public figures to have been unlawful (it is good that the court has done so and bad that such data processing took place) and the conclusion put forward is that a surveillance crisis is supposedly shaking the very foundations of our state's fundamental rights framework and infringing on everyone's rights. Is that really the case or is it a deliberate exaggeration?

It is also true that the state and lawmakers in particular must make a genuine effort to ensure that surveillance is not only lawful but also sufficiently transparent and subject to oversight so as to leave no grounds for reasonable suspicion or facile speculation. Otherwise, it becomes easy to portray our entire society as the collective victim of arbitrary state action.

Criminal proceedings, whose purpose is to deliver justice, must be trustworthy. If we require that evidence collected through a traditional investigative procedure, such as a crime scene examination, remain uncompromised and establish highly formalistic but unquestionably necessary procedures to ensure this, the same principle must apply when collecting, processing and storing data from the virtual world. Although activities in that realm are often physically intangible, there must be no compromises when it comes to the purpose of data collection or compliance with procedural requirements.

Compliance with these requirements must be verifiable after the fact and the purpose of every action must be justifiable. There must be no justification for fishing for data, even if it may appear to be the easiest way to "catch" someone or something.

A balance must be struck before courts are called upon to rule on surveillance issues. Otherwise, conflict is built into the system from the outset. A fresh attempt to resolve the problem is currently underway in the Riigikogu Legal Affairs Committee. A cursory examination of the effort does little to inspire confidence that a balance is within reach, but finding common ground is precisely what we elect our representatives to do. Until that happens, we will have to endure surveillance-related populism in the media, in society and in the Riigikogu itself.
