World.title: Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
World.content:
Chinese archaeologists have announced discoveries from four sites across the country, including Paleolithic campsite ruins and greater details of an aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture.

The findings, announced at a Wednesday conference held by China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration, come from four years of work at four sites along the Yangtze River. They include Taohuahe in the southwestern Sichuan province; Fanshan in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province; Lingtoushang in the eastern Jiangxi province; and Laohudun in the central Hubei province.

The discoveries were presented by Archaeology China, a government program launched in 2018 to fund long-term excavations investigating the origins of farming and civilization.

Taohuahe, discovered in 2022, has yielded over 13,000 Paleolithic-age stone artifacts, including large stone choppers, and 179 animal fossils dating from 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, researchers at the conference announced. Excavations have also revealed stone-working and storage areas, cobblestone surfaces, and a semicircular refuse pit.

Wang Youping, an archaeologist at Peking University, told domestic media that, unlike in other archaeological digs in southern China, numerous animal bones have been recovered at Taohuahe.

“Southern China’s acidic soil usually destroys bone,” Wang said. “Researchers had assumed that people in the lush south relied mainly on plants. The (presence of animal) bones suggests that meat was equally important to their work, daily lives, and evolution.”

The second site discussed at the meeting, Fanshan, was discovered 40 years ago and is the highest-ranking aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture ever found, researchers said. The Liangzhu culture, located in northern present-day Hangzhou, flourished about 5,000 years ago. UNESCO added the ruins of its walled city and system of dams and reservoirs to its World Heritage List in 2019.

Excavations that began in 2024 indicate that a walled compound enclosed the site’s cemetery mound. At least three buildings stood at its center, including a large oval structure raised on stilts, likely used for ceremonies. The compound lies on a ridge that formed part of the surrounding area’s water system, leading researchers to hypothesize that the tombs, ritual spaces, and dams were planned as a single complex.

After last year’s discovery of a courtyard wall at the Fanshan site, archaeologists uncovered a group of three related buildings this year. Wang said the wall may have formed the cemetery’s outer boundary, while the buildings may have served as sacrificial halls. He added that the culture may already have had a mausoleum system.

Researchers also announced at the conference that they have discovered Neolithic and Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) settlements at a third site, Lingtoushang. The settlements contained evidence of smelting and large quantities of copper, shedding light on close cultural exchange and how the societies exploited and controlled metal resources.

Excavation of the fourth site, Laohudun cemetery in Hubei, began this year. According to researchers, the area contains the highest concentration of Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) tombs in southern China.

At the site, archaeologists unearthed bamboo and wooden slips — writing materials used before the invention of paper — along with numerous inscribed lacquerware and wooden artifacts. The inscriptions cover a wide range of topics, including politics, military affairs, literature, medicine, folklore, and art, offering greater insight into society at the time.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Stone artifacts found at the Taohuahe site in Sichuan province. From the National Cultural Heritage Administration)

World.title: Food for feed: The price paid beyond the plate
World.content:
IMPACT. An anchovy purse seine fishing vessel, docked at a harbor in Chile, in 2021. The industry faces declining stocks and pressure from the fishmeal sector that depends on them.

Much of the fishmeal and fish oil that support imported farmed seafood consumed in the Philippines comes from global supply chains linked to pollution, labor abuses, overfishing, and food insecurity in other countries

In May 2025, a regional office of the Philippines’ fisheries agency in Visayas announced an initiative that would invite fishers to government meetings held to expand fish farming in the region.

Officials would introduce the fishers to ongoing fish breeding, processing, and distribution projects as part of a push to transform the local economy “from fish hunting to fish farming.” They emphasized that this transformation would ease stress on the ecosystem.

“Instead of constantly taking from the sea, let’s try to cultivate fish and give the ocean a chance to recover,” said community development officer Joel Lutao.

But critics worldwide have questioned whether the practice of catching and reducing whole, fresh fish to grow more seafood can ever be considered sustainable. The most popular types of farmed seafood — milkfish, tilapia, salmon, shrimp, and trout — are fed the kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it.

Two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fishmeal and fish oil. Before it reaches market, a farmed salmon, for instance, eats at some farms more than six times its weight in wild-caught fish.

The concerns about aquaculture extend far beyond the fate of the oceans. The feed that powers most of this industry comes with a huge variety of other hidden costs, according to a wide-reaching investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization based in Washington, DC.

These costs include the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, violent protests typically spurred by the horrid smell from fishmeal factories, and escalating geopolitical tensions as countries compete for scarce sources of protein.

‘There’s no fish left here’

What economists often call “externalities,” these social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury seafood is eaten.

In The Gambia and Mauritania, the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity, as fish that once sustained local communities are increasingly being diverted into fishmeal factories for export.

In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labor on ships, at farms, and in factories.

In other countries, including India and Peru, this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some of them violent, usually in the form of labor strikes and community protests sparked by the water pollution or stench from factories cooking thousands of tons of decomposing fish, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries.

WORK. Workers offload catch at a fishmeal plant in Ullal. Photo courtesy of Changing Markets Foundation

In Senegal, fishmeal has put local fishers out of work, so increasingly they are selling — or repurposing — their boats to flee to Europe, typically taking the roughly 930-mile sea journey to Spain’s Canary Islands, a route that claimed more than 3,000 lives in 2025.

“We’re fishermen, but there’s no fish left here, so we left,” said Cheikhou Omar, a 21-year-old fisher, in September 2024 as he sat on a beach in Senegal, rescued after the fishing boat he took trying to get to Spain capsized, killing two dozen.

The five-year investigation mapped roughly the entire global fishmeal industry, including more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms, and seafood retailers. The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries, visiting factories and farms and boarding fishmeal ships at sea.

Unsustainable fishing

The oceans bear an especially heavy and largely invisible burden of the fishmeal and fish oil industry. More than a fifth of wild-caught fish around the world is used for non-human consumption, especially as feed for fish, but also chickens and pigs.

The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fishmeal production, operating in the waters of at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by leading ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets.

For example, less than 30% of the fleet had publicly available location information, and under 25% had a unique vessel identification number, or ship license plate. Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.

Scientific studies classified at least half of the species landed by the assessed fishmeal vessels as “overexploited” or worse. Most of the ships in this fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish. Both gear types are associated with high levels of waste, routinely hauling in large volumes of bycatch and non-target species.

At least 165 of the ships in the global fishmeal fleet were bottom trawlers, conducting a particularly destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their paths.

The problem of unsustainable fishing is compounded by heavy government subsidies that keep too many vessels operating, accelerating pressure on already stressed fisheries.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at University of British Columbia. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”

The problem with fishmeal

As commodities, fishmeal and fish oil promise to grow in international importance.

Starting in 2022, more than half of the seafood eaten globally came from fish farms rather than wild catch. Aquaculture is a $313-billion industry and the fastest-growing segment of global food production. Most of these fish farms are powered by fishmeal and fish oil.

Fishmeal processing in the Philippines is concentrated in three cities. The first is the port city of Navotas, known as the country’s “fishing capital.” Located in Metro Manila on the island of Luzon, it has at least one fishmeal plant.

The second is Zamboanga, a city on the island of Mindanao regarded as the Philippines’ “sardine capital,” home to half a dozen fishmeal plants. The third is General Santos. The national “tuna capital,” it lies in Mindanao and hosts four fishmeal plants.

Many of these plants focus primarily on processing seafood for human consumption, but they also redirect inedible offcuts into fishmeal. This practice is widely cited as sustainable and socially beneficial, since it uses materials that would otherwise be thrown away.

Therefore, fishmeal production in the Philippines is less of a driver of food insecurity than it is in other countries that use whole edible fish. However, the Philippines suffers from severe food insecurity because of general overfishing and the export of most catch, be it small anchovies or larger species like tuna.

The far greater burden of food insecurity, social unrest, and air and water pollution is borne by the poorer countries that produce the fishmeal or fishmeal-fed seafood the Philippines imports. The country imported more seafood than it produced as of 2023.

Half of all seafood globally is farmed, and most of that is fed fishmeal. The fish farms in several of the countries that export the most seafood to the Philippines — including China, Vietnam, Papua New Guinea, Chile, and Japan — have ties to severe problems caused by fishmeal production, according to the investigation.

Hidden costs

The investigation revealed a surprising diversity of hidden costs in the global feed industry.

In Senegal, fishmeal production accelerated overfishing, eroding traditional fishing grounds and contributing to thousands of young men attempting deadly and desperate voyages at sea to Europe.

In Russia, fishmeal workers were held captive in secluded company towns in remote parts of the country, or stuck on ships far from shore.

“People have nowhere to go, no money,” one worker said in a plea to Russian President Vladimir Putin, who participated in an episode of a call-in television show about the fishmeal plant. “Please, help us,” a second worker said.

In Chile, several hundred protesters burned tires and blocked coastal highways and railway tracks, demonstrating against the early closure of the fishing season, a move partly driven by overfishing tied to fishmeal.

The investigation also unveiled the hidden role of forced labor and land appropriation in China’s growing aquaculture industry. (To be continued) – Rappler.com

The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project.

Duterte has been detained in The Hague, the Netherlands, since March 2025 after he was arrested due to crimes against humanity. His case stemmed from his drug war and the killings allegedly committed by the Davao Death Squad.

On November 30, the former president will be the first Asian head of state to face a trial due to crimes against humanity before the ICC.

Meanwhile, the Senate began plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 on November 23, with lawmakers proposing P204.634 billion in amendments that prioritize “basic needs,” including health care and education, while cutting billions of pesos in infrastructure projects.

World.title: More than a place to eat: Inside Cavite’s thriving food bazaar culture
World.content:
In Mendez, Cavite, local bazaars do more than bring the community together over food — they also help young entrepreneurs earn extra income and gain real-world business experience

For some residents, a visit to the food bazaar means satisfying a craving for takoyaki, fries, or milk tea.



For local entrepreneurs, the stalls offer something more: an opportunity to introduce their products, find new customers, and turn a small business into a growing livelihood.

What began as an initiative to give local merchants a place to sell their products has grown into a gathering of food entrepreneurs and customers in Mendez, Cavite.



For Alvin Dimaranan, one of the organizers of the food bazaars, the initiative started with a small group of entrepreneurs looking for opportunities to promote their businesses.

“We were just a few, but we pushed through,” he recalled, describing how they initially gathered around 18 merchants for the Mendez Day celebration in 2018.

Dimaranan, who is also known as Vindims, documented the preparations and opening of the bazaar through his vlogs.



The videos eventually gained traction on Facebook, reaching almost two million views over several weeks. The unexpected turnout encouraged more entrepreneurs to participate.



From its initial group of merchants, the organization has since grown to approximately 123 to 125 businesses, according to Dimaranan.

“If I want to grow a business, it could just be me,” he said. “But my concept is a food bazaar, so there should be more merchants who can benefit.”

Turning first-time buyers into regular customers

For some business owners, participating in the bazaars means reaching customers who might otherwise never discover their products.

Jhon Christian Atienza, owner of Jacob’s Milk Tea, established his business on March 8, 2023. He joined the Mendez food bazaars to introduce his products to a wider audience, gain customer feedback, and make his business more recognizable.

Through the events, Atienza said, customers who initially purchased out of curiosity eventually became regular patrons.

For him, the benefits extend beyond the sales made during the bazaar.



Some customers have also recommended his business to their families and friends, helping him reach more potential buyers through word of mouth.

He considers these recommendations valuable because they help establish relationships that continue even after the bazaar ends.

A similar experience comes from Jefferson Hondo, owner of Chambee Mendez, which opened in March 2026.

Hondo joined the bazaar to promote his store not only to Mendez residents but also to visitors from neighboring towns.



He said the exposure helped the business attract regular customers who first encountered the brand during the event.

Because people intentionally visit bazaars to explore different food offerings, Hondo said promoting the business and generating sales became easier.

For Mark Anthony Arania, owner of Leonora’s, the bazaar similarly provides an opportunity to introduce his business’ pasta dishes to more residents.

Established on July 7, 2021, Leonora joined to expand its reach within Mendez.



Arania said participation helped the business gain recognition and attract more customers.

A livelihood beyond the food stalls

While some entrepreneurs participate to expand existing businesses, others see the bazaars as a means of supporting their daily needs.

Arlyssa Siagan, owner of Kopi’s Long Fries, started her business on December 1, 2024.



As a college student, she joined the bazaar primarily to help cover her educational expenses.

The income she earned also contributed, even partially, to her family’s needs.

Beyond the financial assistance, Siagan said the experience taught her how to interact with customers and manage a business.

However, balancing entrepreneurship and academics also required sacrifices, particularly in managing her time.

She said the opportunity to participate in bazaars demonstrates how small business ventures can provide students with an additional source of income while allowing them to develop practical skills.

Meanwhile, Dela Pendon, owner of Edna’s Puto Bumbong, has been operating her business for 10 years. She joins bazaars to promote her products and encourage more customers to patronize them.

Bringing the community together

For customers Nic and Frankie, visiting the food bazaar has become part of their routine, with the two going approximately twice a week.

Aside from the food choices, they said the bazaar offers a nearby place to eat, hang out, and spend time with friends.

They also identified Jacob’s Milk Tea as one of the businesses they continued supporting after discovering it through the bazaar.

They believe these events help residents become more familiar with local businesses, encouraging them to visit restaurants and stores even when the bazaars are no longer operating.

More than providing access to different food offerings, they said, the gatherings create opportunities for residents to interact, reconnect with friends, and spend time with their families.

For Dimaranan, the benefits also extend beyond the merchants.



Organizing a bazaar creates opportunities for street sweepers, garbage collectors, barangay tanods, and local performers, including singers, bands, and dance groups.

The organizers also incorporate performances into their events, with contributions from participating merchants helping provide compensation for local talents.

Sustaining opportunities for local entrepreneurs

The local government also recognizes the bazaars as part of its efforts to support micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs).

Ronald Perey, chief of staff of the Mendez local government, said the initiative provides local food producers and entrepreneurs with an opportunity to introduce their products to the public within a shorter period.

Perey identified December 2022 as the beginning of the municipality’s involvement in recognizing and supporting the initiative under Mayor Cocoy Mendoza’s administration.

He said the LGU hopes that greater product recognition can eventually encourage businesses to increase production, expand their operations, and generate employment opportunities.

The municipality also plans to provide starting capital assistance to encourage more entrepreneurs to establish or sustain their businesses.



Perey cited the Sustainable Livelihood Program and the municipality’s investment policies as other forms of support.

However, opportunities to participate in the bazaars are not without limitations.

Hondo pointed out that organizers restrict the number of participating businesses because of limited space and the need to manage competition among vendors offering similar products. This means not every entrepreneur who wants to join can secure a stall.

Dimaranan also identified unpredictable weather, daily rental fees, and utility expenses as challenges, particularly when rain discourages customers from visiting.

Despite these difficulties, the bazaars continue to provide a shared platform for entrepreneurs to reach customers and introduce their products.

In Mendez, a food bazaar may last only a few days. But for the entrepreneurs who bring their products to the stalls, the relationships and opportunities they build can continue long after the tents come down. – Rappler.com

Neo Croox is a Rappler intern from the University of Santo Tomas.

World.title: [Vantage Point] The Legarda-Leviste solar empire: From government contracts to private billions
World.content:
In renewable energy, the true measure of entrepreneurial success is electricity delivered to the grid—not merely shares sold or paper valuations achieved.

Behind Leandro Leviste’s entrepreneurial success lies a corporate strategy that converted government-awarded development opportunities into marketable equity, generated billions in financial transactions, and left substantial contractual obligations unresolved.

Leandro Leviste was undeniably innovative, though his commercial ingenuity extended well beyond the technology of generating solar power. His corporate strategy demonstrated how exclusive renewable-energy development rights granted by the government could acquire enormous financial value even before some of the projects underpinning them delivered electricity. (READ: Leviste solar companies passed around DOE deals as franchisee incurred losses)

Did the Filipino public receive economic benefits commensurate with the private wealth those state-granted opportunities helped create?

In the first installment, Vantage Point examined the Anti-Money Laundering Council’s (AMLC) allegations concerning Senator Loren Legarda, former Energy secretary Alfonso Cusi, and Leviste in the acquisition and retention of solar development rights.

We now trace what happened after those rights were secured: how corporate assets were consolidated, how shares were monetized, and how billions subsequently moved through Leviste’s personal accounts.

The corporate strategy centered on Solar Philippines Power Project Holdings Inc. (SPPPHI), Leviste’s principal investment vehicle. In February 2022, a reported asset-for-share swap involving interests in 20 solar project companies and associated assets (See list of these companies below this paragraph) was structured around roughly 24.37 billion shares of SP New Energy Corp. (SPNEC), valued at P2.50 apiece. That translated into a transaction valuation of approximately P60.93 billion, subject to the terms and completion of the share exchange. (See list of these companies:

Solar Philippines Calatagan Corporation

Solar Philippines Tarlac Corporation

Solar Philippines Tanauan Corporation

Terra Solar Philippines, Inc.

SP Holdings, Inc.

Solar Philippines Batangas Baseload Corporation

Solar Philippines Tarlac Baseload Corporation

Solar Philippines Central Luzon Corporation

Solar Philippines South Luzon Corporation

Solar Philippines Southern Tagalog Corporation

Solar Philippines Eastern Corporation

Solar Philippines Western Corporation

Solar Philippines Visayas Corporation

Solar Philippines Central Visayas Corporation

Solar Philippines Southern Mindanao Corporation

Solar Philippines Batangas Corporation

Solar Philippines Retail Electricity, Inc.

Laguna Solar Rooftop Corporation

Solar Philippines Rooftop Corporation

Solar Philippines Commercial Rooftop Projects, Inc.

To be clear, this was not P60.93 billion in cash earnings. Still, it illustrates how development rights, corporate interests, and related assets could be packaged into marketable equity capable of attracting institutional capital. A privately held portfolio had found a direct pipeline for monetization through the stock market.

The entry of Meralco PowerGen Corp. (MGen) gave that pipeline substantial financial muscle. In 2023, its renewable-energy arm, MGreen, injected P15.9 billion into newly issued SPNEC shares—capital that flowed directly into the listed company. Subsequent deals involving existing shares and exchangeable financing arrangements, however, provided funding opportunities for Leviste’s corporate vehicles as selling shareholders or borrowers. (READ: Leandro Leviste sells another P3 billion in SPNEC shares as solar controversies mount)

By June 2025, Leviste had announced completed and agreed share transactions totaling P20.49 billion, comprising P18.26 billion involving the MGen group and P2.23 billion from earlier sales to public investors. His widely publicized P34-billion funding target included prospective deals and financing arrangements and should not be mistaken for fully realized personal cash-outs.

SPNEC investment and share transactions

Source: SPNEC June 25, 2025 PSE clarification. MGen group deals and public sales total P20.49 billion.

Monetization continued even after Leviste entered Congress. On August 20, 2026, SPPPHI offloaded another 2.4 billion SPNEC shares at P1.25 apiece, raising P3 billion in gross proceeds and paring its common-share stake from 16.30% to 11.51%. Eight days later, SPNEC’s board approved the acquisition by its wholly owned subsidiary, Terra Nueva Inc., of land from Provincia Investments Corp. and JJPNM Agro Industrial Corp.—both subsidiaries of SPPPHI.

As Vantage Point previously reported, the land acquisition disclosure omitted the purchase price, acreage, and valuation methodology. While there is no established link between the share sale and the proposed land purchases, minority shareholders deserve full transparency on the terms under which Leviste’s private firms continue transacting with the listed company as his equity stake shrinks.

The AMLC’s financial investigation adds another layer to the picture. According to reported Court of Appeals records, Leviste’s accounts logged roughly P28.07 billion in inflows and P29.82 billion in outflows, representing P57.89 billion in cumulative financial activity. Investigators also flagged 1,044 checks totaling roughly P14.99 billion issued to Leviste by his solar companies, raising concerns about the possible commingling of corporate and personal funds.

Reported financial activity in Leviste’s accounts

Source: Reported AMLC findings in Court of Appeals proceedings. The P14.99 billion in checks is not added to this total

Here, the accounting principle is fundamental. Corporations have legal personalities distinct from their shareholders. Funds transferred to an owner must rest on a clear accounting and legal basis—whether as dividends, loan repayments, advances, or other legitimate transactions. Owning a corporation does not automatically make its cash the owner’s personal property.

Leviste maintains that all transactions were lawful and undertaken in the ordinary course of business. Assessing that claim requires a line-by-line reconciliation of corporate ledgers, bank statements, tax filings, and underlying contracts. Gross transaction volume alone does not establish unlawful enrichment. (READ: Leviste denies he made money from selling franchise to Pangilinan’s Meralco group)

(Editor’s note: Tony La Viña, the spokesman of Senator Loren Legarda and Representative Leandro Leviste, has spoken up on the solar controversy in this clip: Watch:

Meanwhile, major contractual commitments went unmet. The AMLC identified roughly P10.44 billion tied to 26 terminated renewable-energy contracts. Separately, the Department of Energy (DOE) pegged its broader aggregate demands against Solar Philippines, its subsidiaries, and affiliates at P24 billion. Because the two figures cover different scopes and may overlap, they should not be combined—nor do they represent final judicial awards. (READ: DOE: Only 0.3% collected from P24 billion in penalties vs Leviste’s Solar Philippines)

Just as importantly, these reported obligations should not automatically be pinned on today’s SPNEC. Under MGen’s stewardship, MTerra Solar Phase 1 began commercial operations in August 2026, initially declaring 600 MWac under its Meralco power-supply agreement. That represents tangible project delivery, and the capital and execution risks shouldered by the new controlling shareholder deserve due recognition.

Similarly, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla’s inquiry into alleged franchise flipping demands legal precision. Solar Para sa Bayan’s congressional franchise is legally separate from the DOE service contracts held by other Solar Philippines entities, and MGen has denied acquiring shares in the franchise holder. Whether any transaction circumvented statutory restrictions remains a question for investigators to address.

The Court of Appeals’ freeze orders remain provisional safeguards, not convictions. What the government must now establish is straightforward: which corporate entities owe money, where the proceeds of monetization went, and whether the individuals behind unfulfilled obligations can be held legally accountable. (READ: Loren Legarda, Leandro Leviste face plunder, graft complaints over solar projects)

In renewable energy, the true measure of entrepreneurial success is electricity delivered to the grid—not merely shares sold or paper valuations achieved. Government development rights are instruments of national energy policy, not unconditional entitlements to private fortune. Filipinos are owed a transparent accounting of both sides of the ledger: what private enterprise gained from public privileges and what the nation received in return. – Rappler.com

Source note: This analysis draws from reported AMLC findings contained in Court of Appeals proceedings, SPNEC’s Philippine Stock Exchange disclosures and corporate filings, Department of Energy pronouncements, statements from the parties concerned, and previous Vantage Point investigations into Solar Philippines and SPNEC.

World.title: Saving reefs: Coral Triangle expedition makes its way to the Philippines
World.content:
Researchers aboard the Tara schooner are taking coral samples in Palawan and Mindoro to understand why the region's corals are so resilient

MANILA, Philippines – The Tara schooner makes its stop in the Philippines as part of its 18-month expedition in the Coral Triangle, attempting to understand why and how corals in the region are resisting climate change.

The storied schooner, built for polar drift in 1989 with its round aluminum hull, will be making stops in Araceli, Palawan, and Puerto Galera, Mindoro. It arrived in the Philippines on November 20 and docked at the Manila Yacht Club.

“It appears that coral reefs in the region seem to have a resistance and resilience potential that’s higher than everywhere else in the world, but we can’t explain really why,” Martin Alessandrini, advocacy officer of Tara Ocean Foundation, told reporters aboard the schooner on Thursday, November 26.

“It’s really a ray of hope for coral conservation, but we need to better understand it in order to better protect these corals.”

The Coral Triangle covers the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste, and Solomon Islands, and contains majority of the known coral species in the world. It is known as the Amazon of the Ocean.

After leaving France at the end of 2025, the schooner crossed the Atlantic to reach the Pacific via the Panama Canal. Its first public stopover was in Tokyo, Japan, in April 2026. Prior to the Philippines, researchers in the schooner had stopped and collected samples from the waters of Papua New Guinea and Palau.

The team in the schooner mainly works on sampling. After collection, they send the samples to different laboratories for analysis. It takes two to three years after the expedition “to produce all the data and the very first results,” said Alessandrini.

SAMPLING. Divers from the Tara schooner take coral samples in Palau.

Climate change has triggered coral bleaching events, threatening marine habitats around the world. Four global coral bleaching events have been recorded since 1998, according to a recent report from the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network, with each event “associated with a 6.5–9.9% relative loss of global hard coral cover.”

Tara Ocean Foundation, based in Paris, France, supports the expedition and has partnered with the UP Marine Science Institute and non-profit organization Blue Alliance. The expedition vessel was designed by French naval architects Olivier Petit, Luc Bouvet, and engineer Michel Franco.

Inside the schooner

The vessel is manned by six sailors and eight scientists.

Below the cockpit is a common area where the staff holds meetings. In the kitchen are at least two packs of dry yeast and a KitchenAid stand mixer.

“Yes, we make bread everyday,” Alessandrini said as he toured reporters in the vessel. “It’s a French boat, so we need bread and we need good food.”

Further along are the sleeping quarters and bathrooms. There is a bookcase at the end of the hallway, lined with works of great authors.

The storage area beyond the sleeping quarters houses the watermaker (“to produce drinking water from seawater”), generators, and food stocks in huge containers.

All diving equipment is stored at the back of the boat, where coral samples are also kept and conserved.

“We take sediments around the corals,” Alessandrini explained. “We take fragments of corals also. And we take cores of corals, which help us understand the previous climate in the region.”

Filipino on board

Three Filipino researchers are slated to join the expedition at intervals during its Philippine leg.

Vince Nikko Ordinario, 27, is the first to join the team heading for Palawan. Ordinario, a research assistant at the UP Marine Science Institute, said he will be in the vessel for 40 days.

SIGNAGE. The entrance to the cockpit is decorated with art and signages. Photo by Iya Gozum/Rappler

“I joined to help this expedition, get data, analyze,” Ordinario told Rappler in the schooner. “Then I can take it home to the laboratory. We can use the data in the laboratory.”

Two other Filipino researchers are joining in the latter half of the Philippine leg. After their stops in Palawan and Mindoro, the team would have been done with five out of the total nine sampling sites they intend to visit in the expedition.

Following the public stopover in Manila, the schooner is scheduled to stop by Kuala Terengganu, Malaysia, in July 2027 and then in Singapore in August 2027. – Rappler.com

World.title: Visayas grid placed under yellow alert anew due to plant outages
World.content:
File photo. Visayas grid on red alert, according to NGCP.

MANILA, Philippines — The National Grid Corp. of the Philippines (NGCP) on Saturday placed the Visayas power grid under a yellow alert for one hour due to insufficient operating reserves amid multiple power plant outages and reduced generation capacity.

In an advisory issued on Nov. 28, the NGCP said the yellow alert would be in effect from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m.

The grid operator reported an available capacity of 2,617 megawatts (MW) against a projected peak demand of 2,369 MW during the period.

Article continues after this 

The grid operator reported an available capacity of 2,617 megawatts (MW) against a projected peak demand of 2,369 MW during the period.

READ: NGCP: Visayas Grid under yellow alert again on Nov. 2

The NGCP said 24 power plants were on forced outage, while 19 others were operating at reduced capacities, resulting in a total of 609.5 MW of unavailable capacity.

Of the plants on forced outage, 11 had been offline since November, one since October, two since September, two since August and one since June.

Three other plants had been on forced outage since 2025, one since 2024, two since 2023 and one since 2021.

Article continues after this 

Among the factors behind the yellow alert were the unplanned outage of the Unit 2 of Therma Visayas Inc. (TVI) coal-fired power plant in Toledo City, Cebu, and the reduced capacity of TVI Unit 1.

The unavailability of Palm Concepcion Power Corp. (PCPC) and Kepco-SPC Power Corp. (KSPC) Unit 2, which are both undergoing scheduled maintenance, also contributed to the alert.

Article continues after this 

A yellow alert indicates that the power supply can still meet demand, but it warns that a plant breakdown could lead to brownouts. /dp

World.title: P17.6M worth of illegal drugs seized in weeklong Cordillera operations
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

BAGUIO CITY—Police seized more than P17.6 million worth of illegal drugs and arrested 20 suspected drug personalities in a series of operations across the Cordillera from November 16 to 22.

In a report, the Police Regional Office-Cordillera (PRO-CAR) said it conducted 23 operations during the period, including 11 buy-bust operations and nine marijuana eradication activities. The other operations involved the implementation of a search warrant, service of an arrest warrant and a police response.

The operations resulted in the destruction of 11,076 fully grown marijuana plants and 8,385 seedlings. Police also confiscated 122,000 grams of marijuana leaves and fruiting tops and 66.08 grams of shabu, valued at a combined P17,639,944.

Article continues after this 

READ: BOC seizes P291M worth of suspected shabu at NAIA

Of the 20 arrested suspects, three were classified as high-value individuals while 17 were identified as street-level individuals.

Ifugao accounted for the largest amount seized, with its provincial police office confiscating P14.64 million worth of marijuana leaves and fruiting tops. One street-level individual was arrested in the province.

Benguet police seized P2.59 million worth of illegal drugs and arrested three street-level individuals.

In Baguio, police confiscated P220,388 worth of shabu and arrested 11 suspects, including one high-value individual.

Article continues after this 

Kalinga police seized P142,732 worth of shabu and arrested two street-level individuals, while Abra police confiscated P42,160 worth of shabu and arrested two suspects, one classified as a high-value individual and the other as a street-level individual. In Apayao, police arrested one high-value individual while serving an arrest warrant.

PRO-CAR urged residents to report suspected illegal drug activities to authorities and support efforts to prevent drug-related activities in their communities. /dp

World.title: Senate wraps up deliberations on proposed P7.2T budget for 2027
World.content:
The Senate wraps up its marathon deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget early Saturday morning, Nov. 28. Photo courtesy of Senate

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate has wrapped up its week-long plenary deliberations for the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, paving the way for the period of amendments before the chamber votes on its version of the spending bill.

The Senate began its marathon deliberations for different government agencies on Monday, Nov. 23, and concluded on early Saturday, Nov. 28.

READ: VP Duterte faces Senate on OVP budget, dodges impeach questions

Article continues after this 

The proposed General Appropriations Bill for next year was sponsored by the Senate panel on finance, which Sen. JV Ejercito leads.

During the deliberations, the Senate took up the proposed budgets of the following government agencies, among others:

Congress of the Philippines (P27.89 billion)

Judiciary (P84.132 billion)

Department of National Defense (P326.9 billion)

Department of Health (P378.629 billion)

Department of Public Works and Highways (P587.9 billion)

Department of Agriculture (P175 billion)

Commission on Higher Education (P38.821 billion)

Department of Migrant Workers (P11.894 billion)

Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity (P9.034 billion)

National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (P1.738 billion)

Marawi Compensation Board (P1.247 billion)

National Amnesty Commission (P266.6 million)

Commission on Filipinos Overseas (P187.8 million)

Metropolitan Baguio City, La Trinidad, Itogon, Sablan, Tuba, and Tublay Development Authority (P45.4 million)

Department of Information and Communications Technology (P8.514 billion)

National Intelligence Coordinating Agency (P3.086 billion)

National Security Council (P1.122 billion)

Anti-Money Laundering Council (P335 million)

Film Development Council of the Philippines (P311 million)

Philippines Racing Commission (P202.8 million)

Movie Television Review and Classification Board (P69.742 million)

Optical Media Board (P53.462 million)

READ: JV, Lacson: Budget ‘bicam’ open to all, sparing none

The Senate also deliberated the proposed budgets of the Office of the President and Office of the Vice President which include P10.083 billion and P785.2 million, respectively.

Vice President Sara Duterte appeared in the Senate on Thursday to attend the deliberations.

Article continues after this 

With the plenary deliberations concluded, the Senate is set to proceed to the period of amendments, during which senators may propose changes to the allocations and provisions of the spending bill.

The chamber will then vote on its version of the GAB on second reading before proceeding to the third and final reading.

Article continues after this 

Once approved, the Senate’s version will be transmitted to the House of Representatives for reconciliation with the lower chamber’s version.

The two chambers will then convene a bicameral conference committee to reconcile differences in their respective budget proposals. The resulting conference committee report must be separately ratified by both chambers before the enrolled bill can be sent to Malacañang.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian has expressed confidence that Congress could complete the budget process and ratify the measure before Dec. 17.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. may then sign the enrolled bill into law as the 2027 General Appropriations Act. He also has the constitutional power to veto specific items in the appropriations bill./dp

World.title: P24.3M smuggled cigarettes seized in Negros warehouse raid
World.content:
INQUIRER.net stock images

MURCIA, Negros Occidental — A warehouse in Barangay Santa Rosa yielded more than P24.3 million worth of suspected smuggled cigarettes after law enforcement operatives raided the facility on Friday morning, Nov. 27.

Operatives seized 429 master cases of cigarettes during the operation in Purok Ipil-Ipil, following intelligence reports that illicit tobacco products were being stored in the area, the Police Regional Office Negros Island Region (PRO NIR) reported.

No caretaker or owner was present during the inspection of the warehouse and its vicinity. However, police have identified a person of interest for further investigation.

Article continues after this 

READ: P2.4M in contraband cigarettes seized, 2 arrested in Batangas

Authorities recovered 310 master cases of JHAZZ American Blend, 31 boxes of JHAZZ Menthol, 77 master cases of Kentucky Select, and 11 boxes of assorted cigarette brands from the warehouse and a Toyota Avanza found at the site.

Based on the Bureau of Customs’ (BOC) valuation of P57,300 per master case, the confiscated cigarettes were worth a total of P24.35 million, the PRO NIR said.

Initial inspection showed that the cigarettes lacked government permits and mandatory graphic health warnings, potentially violating laws on tobacco regulation, taxation and economic sabotage.

These include Republic Act No. 10643, or the Graphic Health Warnings Law; Republic Act No. 8424, or the National Internal Revenue Code; and Republic Act No. 12022, or the Anti-Agricultural Economic Sabotage Act of 2024.

Article continues after this 

The PRO NIR said the seized items were inventoried in the presence of required witnesses, with the proceedings documented using body-worn alternative recording devices in compliance with Supreme Court guidelines.

The confiscated cigarettes are being kept at the Murcia Municipal Police Station pending turnover to the BOC’s Customs Intelligence and Investigation Service. /dp

World.title: 3 hurt in 7-vehicle smashup in Pagadian City
World.content:
Emergency responders attend to the aftermath of a seven-vehicle collision along Rizal Avenue in Barangay Sta. Lucia, Pagadian City, on Friday noon, Nov. 27, 2026, leaving three people injured. Photo courtesy of Daryl Aya-ay

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur—Three people were injured in a seven-vehicle collision triggered by a runaway delivery truck along Rizal Avenue in Barangay Sta. Lucia in this city Friday noon, Nov. 27.

Police Capt. Derf Jay Maquinta, spokesperson for the Zamboanga del Sur Police Provincial Office, said the crash occurred at 12:10 p.m. near the corner of Duterte Street.

Initial investigation by the Pagadian City Police Station showed that a white Isuzu Elf drop-side truck, loaded with about 200 boxes of assorted dried fish, was negotiating an uphill stretch when it lost engine power and suffered brake failure.

Article continues after this 

READ: Driver dies as car falls from 4th floor of Makati building 2

The truck driver jumped out of the cab before the vehicle rolled backward, ramming a yellow Bajaj-type tricycle locally known as a “bao-bao” and five parked vehicles—a blue Honda Civic, a red Nissan March sedan, a white Chevrolet Trailblazer, a white Ford Ranger Raptor, and a white Mitsubishi Pajero.

The tricycle driver and his two passengers sustained injuries and were rushed by Pagadian City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office responders to nearest hospital for treatment.

Police are conducting further investigation to determine liability in the incident. /dp

World.title: Unlocking the genetic secrets of the Philippines’ lesser-known eagle
World.content:
A pair of South Philippine hawk-eagles engages in courtship near their nest at Mahagnao Volcano Natural Park in Burauen, Leyte, as observed by a team led by Philippine Eagle Foundation biologist Tristan Luap Senarillos. (Photo: Philippine Eagle Foundation)

MANILA, Philippines — In the forests of the southern Philippines lives another endangered eagle that has received far less scientific and public attention than the critically endangered Philippine eagle.

The South Philippine hawk-eagle (Nisaetus pinskeri), found only in the Philippines, is considered the country’s second most threatened eagle, with an estimated 600 to 800 mature individuals remaining in the wild and its population continuing to decline.

Now, Filipino scientists have unlocked part of the bird’s genetic history, providing a scientific foundation for future research and conservation efforts to prevent its extinction.

Article continues after this 

Researchers from the University of the Philippines (UP) Diliman and the Philippine Eagle Foundation (PEF) sequenced and analyzed nearly the entire mitochondrial genome of the endangered raptor.

Their findings, published on Oct. 26, 2026, in the international scientific journal PLOS ONE, offer new insights into the species’ evolutionary history and its relationship with other birds of prey.

“Every species has a unique story written in its DNA,” said Cynthia P. Saloma of UP Diliman, one of the scientists behind the study.

“By studying the DNA of the South Philippine Hawk-eagle, we are learning more about its history and its connections to other eagles. This knowledge can help us make better decisions about protecting endangered wildlife,” she added.

Unlocking the eagle’s genetic history

At the center of the research is the mitochondrial genome, a set of genetic instructions found in mitochondria, the structures within cells responsible for producing most of the energy needed for cellular functions.

Article continues after this 

Unlike most DNA, which is inherited from both parents, mitochondrial DNA in birds is generally passed down from mothers to their offspring, making it a valuable tool for tracing evolutionary relationships.

Dhan Mikhail Perdon conducted much of the study’s bioinformatics analysis as part of his undergraduate thesis at UP Diliman’s National Institute of Molecular Biology and Biotechnology.

Article continues after this 

Working with fellow researchers from the Philippine Genome Center, Perdon identified 18,654 DNA building blocks in the South Philippine hawk-eagle’s mitochondrial genome and compared its genetic sequences with those of other birds of prey.

The researchers found that the species is more closely related to the changeable hawk-eagle (Nisaetus cirrhatus), which is found across parts of Asia, than to other hawk-eagles included in the study.

Despite their close evolutionary relationship, the two species occupy different geographic ranges and habitats.

While the South Philippine hawk-eagle depends on forests on a handful of Philippine islands, the changeable hawk-eagle has a much wider geographic distribution and can also inhabit forest edges and cultivated areas.

The researchers also found that analyzing multiple genes together provided a clearer picture of evolutionary relationships among eagles than examining a single gene.

Overlooked and endangered

Beyond its genetic findings, the study draws attention to a broader conservation challenge: Many of the world’s most threatened birds of prey remain among the least studied.

Christopher McClure, executive vice president of conservation and science at The Peregrine Fund, highlighted these research gaps in a 2019 study on global raptor conservation priorities.

The study underscored the lack of scientific information on tropical birds of prey despite their high risk of extinction.

The Philippine Eagle Foundation promotes public awareness of the South Philippine hawk-eagle and the importance of protecting its forest habitat.

“Some of the world’s most threatened birds of prey are also among the ones we know the least about. The South Philippine Hawk-eagle is a good example. While it may not be as well-known as the Philippine Eagle, its survival is no less important,” McClure said.

The conservation scientist also co-authored a 2023 study identifying priority conservation areas and estimating the global population of the critically endangered Philippine eagle.

For lesser-known raptors, he said, understanding their genetics, population sizes, breeding habits, habitat requirements and threats is essential to developing effective conservation strategies.

“What is exciting about this study is that Filipino scientists are helping bring a poorly studied and endangered eagle out of the shadows,” McClure said.

“I hope this discovery inspires more research, greater public awareness, and stronger conservation efforts. We should not wait until a species is on the brink of extinction before giving it the scientific attention it deserves,” he added.

From rescued birds to scientific discoveries

The genetic research was made possible partly by South Philippine hawk-eagles under the care of the Philippine Eagle Center in Malagos, Davao City.

Researchers obtained blood samples during routine veterinary examinations, with trained animal keepers and veterinarians ensuring the birds were handled safely.

Although widely associated with efforts to save the Philippine eagle, the center also cares for other threatened birds of prey.

The PEF was also the first institution in the world to successfully breed the South Philippine hawk-eagle in captivity.

RELATED STORY: Philippine eagle faces higher risk of extinction, study finds

Jayson Ibanez, PEF director for operations and a co-author of the study, said the dwindling population of the South Philippine hawk-eagle underscored the need for greater conservation attention.

“With only a few hundred mature birds believed to remain, we cannot afford to ignore this species. This research gives us new knowledge that can help us understand these birds and plan how to protect them,” Ibanez said.

Beyond the laboratory

While the study provides a starting point for understanding the eagle’s genetic history, several questions remain about the survival of its remaining populations.

Researchers hope to examine DNA samples from more South Philippine hawk-eagles across their geographic range to determine the extent of genetic differences among populations and whether groups inhabiting separate forests remain genetically connected.

Further research could also help determine whether some populations are becoming too small and isolated to survive in the long term.

Such information could guide habitat protection and help identify areas requiring greater conservation attention.

For Ibanez, however, the next challenge lies beyond the laboratory — in the forests where these endangered birds live.

“DNA can tell us about an eagle’s past, but protecting its future is still up to us,” Ibanez said.

“We need to find where these eagles still live, protect their forest homes, and work with local communities to keep them safe. Saving the Philippine Eagle should also mean saving the other endangered eagles that share our forests.”

World.title: Church of the Risen Lord in UP Diliman declared Important Cultural Property
World.content:
The Church of the Risen Lord at the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City is now included in the country’s registry of cultural properties managed by the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) after being declared as an Important Cultural Property. Photo from NCCA Facebook.

MANILA, Philippines—The National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) declared the Church of the Risen Lord at the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City as an Important Cultural Property in recognition of its “architectural, artistic, spiritual, and social value.”

In a Facebook post on Friday, the NCCA said it also acknowledges architect Cesar Concio’s “skillful reinterpretation and ingenious adaptation of international design movements to the Philippine climate” in designing the church.

“The Church of the Risen Lord stands as a significant work of Filipino Tropical Modernism and has retained the spirit of its era despite few modifications. It remains a powerful testament to how architecture, by blending function and beauty, elevates the human spirit and fosters a deeper sense of collective belonging,” the commission said.

Article continues after this 

“As an Important Cultural Property, the Church of the Risen Lord is recognized as an enduring legacy of the Filipino people, worthy of continued protection and stewardship,” it added.

The declaration comes following a petition filed on Oct. 15 by the UP Christian Ecumenical Ministry, which owns and manages the church.

In its petition, the ministry said it was seeking the declaration of the church as an Important Cultural Property on the basis that it “serves as a central point of spiritual and social connection for the diverse Christian population of the UP Diliman Community.”

It also cited Concio’s “use of Modernist forms in creating a spiritually moving space that connected with the landscape,” which had “evoked spiritual transcendence and visually communicated faith.”

“Beyond its primary role as a place of worship, the Church of the Risen Lord serves as a dynamic hub for artistic, cultural, and intellectual production and encounter,” the ministry added.

An Important Cultural Property is defined as a site that has “exceptional cultural, artistic, and historical significance to the Philippines, and has been officially declared as such by law or the pertinent cultural agency or agencies.” /cdv

World.title: Ilocos Norte logs 53 new dengue cases in a week
World.content:
SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — Ilocos Norte recorded 53 new dengue cases from Nov. 15 to 21, bringing the province’s total to 3,229 from the first to the 46th morbidity week of 2026, according to the Provincial Epidemiology and Surveillance Unit (PESU).

The new infections were reported across the province’s 21 municipalities and two component cities, Laoag and Batac.

Pagudpud logged the highest number of new cases with 12, followed by Laoag City with nine, PESU data showed.

Article continues after this 

READ: Misamis Oriental town halts F2F classes over rising dengue cases

Ilocos Norte also reported five dengue-related deaths during the period covered by the latest PESU data.

Health authorities urged residents to continue observing preventive measures to curb the spread of dengue and prevent further case increases.

These include removing stagnant water that can serve as mosquito breeding sites, keeping homes and communities clean, and protecting themselves from mosquito bites. /dp

World.title: More Multinationals Exit Myanmar as Economic Turmoil Deepens
World.content:
At least four more international brands announced their withdrawal from Myanmar this month, as deepening post-coup turmoil triggers a fresh exodus of foreign investment.

They joined a broader retreat of multinational businesses since the 2021 military takeover, driven by regime import and currency controls, soaring production costs, power outages, and international sanctions.

On Thursday, Singapore-based Pezzo Pizza announced it would close all branches in Myanmar starting today (Nov. 27), ending 10 years of operations. The company entered the market in 2016, operating five branches across Yangon and Mandalay.

The announcement came a day after The Manhattan Fish Market shuttered its last Yangon outlet, at Myanmar Plaza, ending the Malaysia-based seafood chain’s 12-year presence.

On Nov. 13, Japanese automaker Isuzu announced it had ended Myanmar repair and maintenance operations after liquidating its local service unit.

Meanwhile, British consumer goods giant Unilever will exit Myanmar after 16 years by selling its shares to Centig Holding, a subsidiary of local partner Europe and Asia Commercial (EAC), with the deal expected to close in 2027.

While the four companies gave no reason for their exit, the World Bank 2026 report notes that Myanmar’s private sector is operating in “a highly challenging and uncertain environment” driven by conflict, macroeconomic pressures, policy reversal and weakening state capacity. It adds that firms are facing “higher cost, greater compliance risks, [and] weaker incentives to invest, expand and innovate.”

According to a Myanmar Peace Monitor report released on Nov. 27, the post-coup flight of foreign investment encompasses nearly 40 multinational companies across 16 countries ranging from neighboring Thailand, Malaysia and India to the U.S., UK, Spain, Germany, Austria, Italy and Norway. It said the withdrawals were being driven by the spread of armed conflict and a collapsing business environment.

The departing businesses span major sectors such as oil and gas, mining, banking, telecommunications, real estate, and manufacturing, including 12 global clothing brands whose exit has dealt a severe blow to local garment workers.

“More companies are monitoring the situation and planning exit strategies,” a Myanmar policy analyst told The Irrawaddy, blaming currency controls and raw material shortages triggered by regime import controls.

“Foreign investors can’t endure these losses any longer,” he said, adding that he expects the situation to worsen amid rising unemployment, soaring inflation and shortages of basic goods.

World.title: Beijing Shields Myanmar Regime After Genocide Ruling, Naypyitaw Begs for Energy Investment, and More
World.content:
Myanmar seeks more Chinese energy investment at Belt and Road forum

Naypyitaw’s reliance on China for energy investment, fuel supplies and electricity infrastructure is deepening all the time, with Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin using his latest trip to China to seek yet more investment across the sector.

At the Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministers’ Conference in Qingdao on Nov. 25-26, Ko Ko Lwin met officials from China’s National Energy Administration (NEA), urging them to help Myanmar meet its electricity and energy needs. Discussions covered new offshore gas exploration, hydropower projects, cross-border power lines, solar and wind projects, and energy storage batteries.

Much the same topics were on the agenda when Ko Ko Lwin traveled to Kunming and Beijing in April to secure lower rates for fuel imports from a number of Chinese firms. Myanmar relies on imports for 97 percent of its gasoline and diesel needs, a dependence that had already taken a serious toll on the cash-strapped regime before the Middle East crisis triggered shortages and price hikes.

Regime officials are also asking Chinese state enterprises to invest in refinery projects linked to the Myanmar–China oil pipeline network. In April the regime signed a deal with China’s North Petro-Chem to increase production at the Htaukshabin-Kanni oil field in Magwe Region’s Minbu.

It has also revived the Thanlyin No. 1 Oil Refinery near Yangon with Chinese assistance, potentially enabling it to bypass jet-fuel sanctions and sustain air operations. The facility’s expected output of up to 150,000 metric tons of jet fuel annually roughly matching Myanmar’s imports last year.

China defends Myanmar regime after ICJ genocide ruling

China has publicly defended Myanmar after the International Court of Justice (ICJ)’s landmark ruling that the country committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing “noted” the ruling but argued that the Rakhine issue should be handled cautiously given its “complex historical, ethnic and religious dimensions.” He urged the international community to avoid “complicating” the issue and reiterated China’s support for dialogue and the repatriation of displaced Rohingya.

China also raised concerns about what it called judicial “overreach” and questions of jurisdiction by international courts.

The ruling stems from a case brought by the Gambia over the Myanmar military’s 2017 clearance operations in northern Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighboring Bangladesh.

Guo also defended the Chinese judge on the ICJ, Xue Hanqin, who voted in Myanmar’s favor, saying she had “acted independently in her personal capacity.”

As a permanent member of the UN Security Council, China has consistently pushed back against international pressure on Myanmar over the Rohingya crisis, arguing that it should be resolved through dialogue and cooperation between Myanmar and Bangladesh rather than external intervention.

However, the ruling, the first finding of state responsibility for genocide in the ICJ’s 81-year history, places China in an awkward position while it continues to shield Naypyitaw from international pressure and deepens ties with a military regime now found guilty of one of the world’s worst atrocities in recent decades.

China drawn deeper into Myanmar–Thai river pollution dispute

China has promised to dispatch experts to help investigate river pollution affecting Mekong tributaries in Thailand due to unregulated Chinese-invested mining across the border in Myanmar.

The announcement came after a meeting in Bangkok on Tuesday where Thailand urged China to help halt mining operations in Shan State for at least six months as the Kok, Sai, Ruak and Mekong rivers flowing into northern Thailand are contaminated, threatening human health and livelihoods.

Thailand’s Pollution Control Department has repeatedly found arsenic, lead, cadmium and other heavy metals above safety limits in the rivers, tracing the pollution to unregulated gold and rare-earth mines in Shan State. Most of them are run by Chinese people in areas controlled by China-linked armed groups like the United Wa State Army (UWSA).

Thailand and Myanmar agreed to conduct their first joint testing of the Kok and Sai next month. But while pledging to participate in the investigation, Beijing stopped short of agreeing to the proposed shutdown and cautioned against drawing “premature conclusions.”

Instead, the Foreign Ministry spokesman claimed Chinese companies operating overseas are required to comply with local laws and environmental regulations—except that these are non-existent in the lawless borderlands of Myanmar.

Still, China seems to feel it can no longer completely dodge the issue as Thailand has brought it up at every high-level meeting, no matter how amiable, in recent weeks amid growing outrage and protests at home.

Chinese scammers move with the times

Shaken up by major crackdowns on Myanmar’s border scam hubs, online fraud networks now infest other parts of the country, from upscale condominiums in the commercial capital Yangon to remote corners of Shan State.

Since mid-November, the military regime has reported a series of raids that netted more than 570 suspected online scammers and gambling operators, over 400 of them Chinese.

In Yangon, the raids in Yankin, Mayangone and Thaketa townships resulted in nearly 230 arrests. Nearly half of them were Myanmar nationals who reportedly worked voluntarily for their Chinese bosses. In Thaketa, arrests included a Chinese ringleader wanted by China’s Public Security Ministry, but in Yankin the boss escaped, throwing his workers under the bus.

In southern Shan around the same time, some 330 Chinese scammers and around 20 Myanmar women were arrested in Kyethi and Mong Kung townships. In Kyethi, they were nabbed with a cache of rifles and pistols.

Now some major border scam centers have been dismantled under pressure from Beijing, operators appear to have dispersed across the country, running smaller, more mobile operations. But in Myawaddy near the Thai border, big compounds still thrive under the protection of regime-aligned ethnic militias.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Garment Sector Braces for EU Bombshell After Genocide Verdict
World.content:
International labor unions’ calls for the European Union to strip Myanmar of its duty-free trade privileges after the International Court of Justice’s genocide ruling have sent shockwaves through local export industry. Operators warn that withdrawing benefits would have severe impacts on the country’s garment industry and hundreds of thousands of workers.

In a Nov. 24 letter to EU leaders, IndustriALL Europe and IndustriALL Global Union called on Brussels to withdraw Myanmar’s Everything But Arms (EBA) trade preferences and terminate the EU-funded MADE in Myanmar program.

IndustriALL Europe and IndustriALL Global Union represent over 50 million industrial and garment workers in more than 140 countries. Both have pressed for stronger action against Myanmar’s military regime over labor rights abuses since the 2021 coup.

The EBA grants tariff-free entry to European markets for all exports — barring weapons and ammunition — from least-developed countries, including Myanmar. The scheme underpins Myanmar’s US$ 3-billion annual garment export trade with Europe. MADE in Myanmar, meanwhile, is an EU-backed initiative aimed at improving labor standards and working conditions in the country’s garment industry.

Local garment manufacturers said international labor groups have pushed for withdrawal of Myanmar’s EBA privileges for years, but warned the move could devastate an industry on which hundreds of thousands depend.

“If the EU decides to suspend the scheme, we will have to find alternative markets. We can no longer rely on a single export destination,” one garment operator told The Irrawaddy.

Labor organizations argue that EBA and MADE in Myanmar help channel revenue into the coffers of an illegitimate military regime and should therefore be withdrawn. The EU has yet to respond their calls.

Local factory owners, however, say the industry’s difficulties stem more from domestic challenges since the coup — including foreign-exchange controls, rising production costs, shortages of raw materials, and financial transaction difficulties after Myanmar’s inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist.

The garment industry targeted $5 billion in export earnings for the 2026-27 fiscal year ending March, but industry sources say that goal is increasingly out of reach.

“With just a few months left, we have barely achieved half the target ,” said a Yangon-based garment business owner in Yangon.

Myanmar’s garment sector employs 450,000 to 500,000 workers, mostly women, and relies heavily on the Cut-Make-Pack (CMP) model, under which foreign brands pay factories to process their raw materials. Most exports go to Japan and the EU.

Before the 2021 coup, more than 70 percent of Myanmar’s garment exports went to the EU. That share has since fallen to around 50 percent after manufacturers began shifting production to other countries.

Industry sources say more than 20 manufacturers, including suppliers for major international brands such as H&M, have either closed or plan to leave Myanmar this year.

The Myanmar Garment Manufacturers Association (MGMA) has urged the EU to consider the potential impact on workers before making any decision, warning that broader trade restrictions could further weaken the export sector and threaten jobs across the industry.

World.title: Thailand Tests Find High Lead, Arsenic in River Shellfish
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thai authorities have found dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in shellfish and other species in rivers contaminated by suspected mining pollution from neighboring Myanmar, an official said Thursday.

The findings, from nearly two years of testing, prompted authorities to urge residents to avoid eating 10 species including shellfish and river snails.

The warning came earlier this week, but with no details of the contamination levels found or the testing processes.

An official from Thailand’s Fisheries Department, speaking on condition of anonymity as they were not authorized to talk to media, told AFP that over 500 samples were taken from five rivers, and 18 had heavy metals at levels over safety limits.

The details came as Thai officials held talks in Bangkok to try to address growing public fears about river contamination from mining operations in war-torn Myanmar.

Heavy metals including mercury, lead, cadmium and arsenic were found at levels exceeding safety standards in 10 species, the Fisheries Department official said.

In some, arsenic was detected at nearly four times the permitted limit and lead at nearly six times the limit.

The affected species include freshwater shrimp, river snails, freshwater mussels and horse mussels, as well as local fish that feed on them, the official said.

The official said the tests involved samples from the Mekong and Salween rivers, which flow through Thailand and Myanmar, and three other rivers in Thailand’s north, the Sai, Kok and Ruak.

No contamination was found in farmed aquatic species, the official added.

Local residents in Thailand’s north and northeast have for months complained about river contamination from mines in Myanmar, but the issue has gathered growing public attention in recent weeks.

Tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district near the Myanmar border were suspended this month after officials found arsenic levels in the local waterworks to be 30 times higher than safe limits.

Campaigners, experts and politicians trace the pollution back to mining in Myanmar, where the long-running civil war has led to unregulated exploitation of natural resources.

In a bid to spur action, residents this week prepared traditional dishes with locally caught food from affected areas and invited politicians, attempting to highlight the risks they now face.

There are fears contamination could spread further down the Mekong, which supports millions of people across several countries.

“Fish are harder to find and even if you find, people won’t buy it,” said Saengwaree Suvirakan, a farmer from Chiang Mai, who joined a protest in Bangkok this week.

World.title: Myanmar’s Putschist President Shrugs at ICJ Genocide Verdict
World.content:
Myanmar’s putschist president, Min Aung Hlaing, hit back at the International Court of Justice (ICJ)’s genocide ruling on Wednesday, telling his cabinet that the regime will not implement “unacceptable” measures.

“As a responsible country, we will carry out measures we consider necessary but will not comply with those that should not be followed,” he said.

The World Court ordered Myanmar to implement several measures after ruling on Nov. 19 that it committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in Rakhine in 2016-17: Prosecute the perpetrators, provide reparations, ensure safe repatriation, guarantee non-repetition, and pass laws criminalizing genocide.

The junta chief claimed the ruling had damaged Myanmar’s national dignity, dismissing the case brought by the Gambia as a one-sided accusation.

“I will not accept anything that harms the country,” said the self-appointed president, who as military chief oversaw the 2016-17 Rakhine “clearance operations” now ruled as genocide. He also stands accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity following the coup he staged in 2021.

Legal experts noted that the ICJ ruling is legally binding, meaning the losing party cannot selectively choose which parts of the judgment to accept or reject.

“It was a final judgement from the international court — not a statement, recommendation or instruction,” human rights lawyer Zar Li Aye told The Irrawaddy.

“As per UN charter 94 (1), every member state is legally obliged to comply with orders from the International Court of Justice,” she stressed.

She added that Myanmar risked being found guilty of violating additional international laws if it failed to comply with the ICJ’s decision.

The ruling has drawn widespread international backing from Western and regional governments, the EU, UN officials, and major human rights organizations, which welcomed the landmark decision as a decisive step toward accountability for the Rohingya community.

Permanent members France and the UK requested a closed-door UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday to press members on Myanmar’s compliance with the ruling. The outcome of the meeting remains unknown.

Meanwhile, the judgement has triggered a chorus of denial from the regime and its allies. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected it as “a great disappointment delivered with dissenting opinions” and “not decided unanimously by judges,” referring to the 9-6 ruling.

However, it remains unclear what effect the judgement will have on the regime’s international standing.

“We may see no direct impact from the ICJ’s decision in the short term,” Myanmar political researcher Sai Kyi Zin Soe told The Irrawaddy.

“We expect to see different responses from different countries, depending on how Myanmar responds and to what extent it complies with the court’s decision,” he said.

World.title: Myanmar’s Economy Reeling as Kyat Nosedives
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of the kyat is tearing across Myanmar’s economy, disrupting imports, driving up production costs and raising fears of further economic shocks.

The kyat market rate steadily weakened since last month before nosediving to reach over 5,400 kyats to the dollar on Thursday.

Exporters as well as importers say their businesses are increasingly unprofitable, exacerbated by regime restrictions.

One exporter told The Irrawaddy that although businesses are officially allowed to exchange 85 percent of their export earnings at market rates, banks are often unable to offer them, plus the regime requires the remaining 15 percent to be converted at the fixed rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar, resulting in significant losses.

Rising operating costs and volatile exchange rates are forcing some exporters to scale back overseas shipments. Traders are also struggling to determine how to price imported goods as foreign-currency costs fluctuate sharply.

“Importers are finding it difficult to set prices because the dollar rate is so unstable. This problem needs to be resolved immediately or domestic consumption will also be affected,” said a trader.

The latest decline is due to several factors, not least that the regime has announced it will borrow over 2 trillion kyats from the Central Bank to pay plug the hole in its budget—essentially telling the bank to print money. The rubberstamp Parliament has already approved an additional budget for the Central Bank to churn out fresh banknotes.

At the same time, the regime recently issued new import licenses, driving up demand for dollars. Another factor at play is planned salary increases for civil servants in the next fiscal year.

The regime also relaxed the fixed exchange rate for remittances from overseas workers from 3,600 kyats per dollar to 4,600 kyats in a bid to encourage them to go through official banking channels—but that backfired and was read as a sign of weakness by the market.

Other currencies have soared apace, with 100,000 kyats falling from 700 Thai baht earlier this month to around 600 baht.

That is bound to make Thai consumer goods and clothing forbiddingly expensive, to say nothing of imported medicines, cooking oil and industrial raw materials.

As usual when the situation runs away from it, the regime is targeting currency traders to try and frighten the market into submission. Yangon money traders say officers from the Bureau of Special Investigation are roaming the markets in search of anyone to fine and arrest.

World.title: Myanmar’s Democratic Opposition Urges ASEAN to Shun ‘Genocidal’ Junta Leaders
World.content:
Myanmar’s democratic opposition has urged ASEAN not to reintegrate regime leaders accused of war crimes and responsible for genocide, following an ASEAN-backed stakeholders’ dialogue in the Philippines.

The two-day meeting, hosted by the ASEAN chair in Tagaytay on Nov. 22-23, brought together representatives from the National League for Democracy (NLD), the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), resistance organizations and civil society groups.

CRPH spokesperson Sithu Maung said participants warned against any ASEAN move to recognize Myanmar’s de facto military regime.

“We reiterated that ASEAN should no longer provide space for military leaders who have committed war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide,” he said, referring to recent remarks by Min Aung Hlaing that his administration is reconsidering ‌the country’s relationship with the regional bloc. The putschist president spoke out after ASEAN leaders at last week’s Manila summit reaffirmed the ban on regime leaders attending high-level regional meetings.
