One of the changes proposed in the draft Constitution is the introduction of jury trials. A separate law will determine the categories of cases in which citizens can serve as jurors, as well as the procedures governing their participation.

Speaking about the problems in the judicial system, Pashinyan cited the cases against former president Robert Kocharyan. In particular, he referred to the fact that Kocharyan remained free and put a question to journalists:

“Do you think Robert Kocharyan should be free? I believe he should not be free. I have said so openly. I made that statement in Republic Square in front of tens of thousands of people. And tens of thousands of people applauded this position.”

The prime minister is convinced that the people themselves should make decisions about all aspects of the “life of the state”.

New constitutional provision on revoking citizenship is “a preventive measure”

Journalists asked Pashinyan whether the new constitutional provisions allowing the authorities to revoke citizenship could become an instrument of political pressure.

The prime minister replied that the most reliable way to neutralise this risk was to have an independent judiciary that “would guarantee that this cannot happen”.

“As for other cases — for example, if a person with dual citizenship is convicted of espionage — why should we preserve and protect their citizenship and continue to grant them civil rights?”

According to Pashinyan, the state must protect itself, particularly given the existence of dual citizenship.

“Imagine a situation in which a person with dual citizenship is caught acting as an agent of a foreign intelligence service and is subsequently convicted. Why should we not empower a court to revoke that person’s citizenship? This would serve as an additional preventive measure against treason or espionage.”

Article 24 of the draft Constitution provides that a person may lose their citizenship by court order in certain circumstances, including crimes against the foundations of the constitutional order or state security. The current Constitution does not allow the authorities to revoke citizenship on these grounds. Moreover, it explicitly states that the Republic of Armenia cannot deprive a citizen of their citizenship.

Citizens should decide on changes to state symbols in a referendum

Addressing the absence of descriptions of Armenia’s state symbols in the draft Constitution, Pashinyan said that a law would define them and that voters would approve it in a referendum.

“We have no specific proposal. We are saying that this law will be adopted in a referendum. Citizens themselves must decide what they consider to be their flag, coat of arms and national anthem.”

The prime minister believes that the authorities must do everything possible to ensure that citizens feel an organic connection with the state and its symbols.

One journalist asked: “Are you going to say now that if we do not remove Mount Ararat from the coat of arms, war will break out?”

“No, I will not threaten anyone,” Nikol Pashinyan replied.

The current Constitution describes the colours of the Armenian flag and their order, as well as the main elements of the coat of arms. The draft Constitution contains no descriptions of the flag or coat of arms. It states that the symbols of the Republic of Armenia are its coat of arms, flag and national anthem. A law, which voters will approve in a referendum, will define their descriptions or lyrics.

Pashinyan on Armenia’s new Constitution

World.title: Abkhazia introduces law to curb dumping by Russian tour operators
World.content:
The authorities in Abkhazia plan to introduce an anti-dumping law aimed at protecting small hotels from organised price-cutting by large Russian tour operators.

Abkhazia’s parliament has already passed the bill, titled “On Amendments to Certain Legislative Acts of the Republic of Abkhazia to Prevent the Monopolisation of the Tourist Accommodation Services Market”, in its first reading.

For several years, a trend has emerged in which large Russian tour operators buy up hotel rooms in Abkhazia at low prices ahead of the tourist season. They then sell them to tourists at even lower rates, offsetting the losses through other services.

The tour operators themselves describe this kind of dumping — offering a hotel room with three meals a day for 200 roubles ($2–3) — as a “special offer” designed to attract tourists to Abkhazia.

Small hotels suffer the most. They cannot afford to adopt such pricing policies and find themselves at a competitive disadvantage. As a result, they incur losses, and some even go bankrupt, selling their properties or renting them out to the same large tour operators.

Under the new bill:

Hotels will have to register contracts containing fixed room quotas with the Ministry of Tourism.

The register will record the number of rooms and the purchase price.

If a tour operator sells a room for more than 30% below its purchase price, the Ministry of Tourism will be able to issue a formal complaint.

If the violation is not rectified, sales may be suspended or the contract terminated.

The bill also introduces the concept of a “high season”, covering the period from 1 June to 1 September, during which all promotional discounts will be prohibited.

Abkhazia’s Tourism Minister Astamur Logua stressed that the aim was not to ban discounts, but to prevent dumping and market monopolisation.

If passed, the new rules could come into force on 1 January 2027.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Alarm bells in Iranian economy: What do Pezeshkian’s admissions signify?
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 28. Iranian official representatives have recently made serious statements regarding the country's economic challenges. This implies that the situation in Iran has reached a somewhat critical stage, necessitating the population's adaptation to the current circumstances.

Over the past few days, while visiting the Razavi Khorasan Province in northeastern Iran, President Masoud Pezeshkian has, in several speeches, drawn attention to these economic issues, calling for national unity and urging the public to practice frugality.

For example, in a televised address to the public from Razavi Khorasan Province yesterday, the Iranian President noted that the options available to compensate for disruptions in the country's maritime trade are limited.

Pezeshkian stated that 75–80% of Iran's trade is conducted via maritime routes, emphasizing that shifting such a volume of trade to alternative channels is no easy task.

He pointed out, however, that nearly 50% of the lost capacity has already been recovered through alternative means, and that efforts to identify further alternatives to restore the remaining lost capacity are ongoing.

The President of Iran noted the necessity of strengthening the country's capacity to sustain trade and meet its needs by leveraging the potential of neighboring countries and developing railway and road infrastructure.

“Supporting low-income families in the face of rising living costs is of great importance. To date, the government has allocated 8.5 quadrillion rials (approximately $4.34 billion) through the implementation of a commodity voucher scheme, intended to help offset the price increases of essential goods, such as wheat, barley, rice, tea, and cooking oil. This support covers both the provision of essential goods and access to healthcare services, as the government strives to improve the situation of low-income families. Despite these measures, the country’s revenues have declined; existing restrictions on oil sales and foreign trade have contributed to a reduction in government income,” he stated.

Spokesperson for the Iranian government, Fatemeh Mohajerani, noted during a press conference in Tehran that wartime conditions have led to an increase in inflation and production costs within the country. She noted that the war carries two clear implications: inflation and economic stagnation. The country is currently embroiled in a full-scale war. Wartime conditions, trade restrictions, and rising logistics costs are exerting significant pressure on the national economy.

The severity of the economic situation is further underscored by data from the Statistical Center of Iran, which indicates that the annual inflation rate, measured up to October 22, 2026, reached 76.8% compared to the same prior period.

Overall, it cannot be said that there is a clear outlook for the development of Iran’s economy and trade at present. Supporting domestic production requires the import of goods, strengthening imports requires the export of goods, and boosting exports requires access to various markets. Currently, the naval blockade imposed on Iran in the south, around the Strait of Hormuz, is dealing a severe blow to the country’s exports. Having robust infrastructure at the country’s border crossing points is considered a fundamental prerequisite for increasing trade, specifically the import and export of goods, with countries that share land borders. The lack of substantial infrastructure at the border crossings with neighboring countries acts as a barrier to the growth of trade.

World.title: Estonian technologies could support Azerbaijan’s green energy transition - Margus Tsahkna (Interview)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 28. Estonian technologies could support Azerbaijan’s green energy transition, Estonian Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna said in an exclusive interview with Trend, as he visited Baku on November 27.

Talking about the purpose of his visit to Azerbaijan, the minister noted that the primary objective is the official opening of the Estonian Embassy in Baku.

“When I visited Azerbaijan last autumn, I told President Ilham Aliyev that I would propose opening an Estonian embassy here, and I am delighted that one year later that commitment has been fulfilled.



The opening of our embassy is a clear sign of the growing partnership between Estonia and Azerbaijan. Over the past years, we have significantly expanded cooperation in areas such as trade, digital development, innovation, education and green energy. Establishing a permanent diplomatic presence in Baku will enable us to deepen political dialogue, support business contacts more effectively and create new opportunities for cooperation between our countries,” said Tsahkna.



He believes that the embassy is not only an investment in bilateral relations but also a reflection of Estonia's long-term commitment to the South Caucasus region.

“We want to continue building a practical and forward-looking partnership that delivers benefits to both our countries,” the minister added.



Promising sectors for Estonian businesses in Azerbaijan



Tsahkna noted that Interest among Estonian businesses in Azerbaijan has been steadily growing.

“This was clearly demonstrated during the fourth meeting of the Estonia-Azerbaijan Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation held in Tallinn earlier this month and my visit to Baku with a 15-member business delegation last October,” the Estonian FM said.



He pointed out that information and communication technologies (ICT) remain one of the strongest areas of cooperation.

“Estonian companies have already established a presence in Azerbaijan's digital sector, and there is considerable interest in contributing to the country's ongoing digital transformation. Estonia has internationally recognised expertise in e-governance, digital identity, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and e-learning, all of which offer promising opportunities for practical cooperation,” he added.



At the same time, as Tsahkna noted, Estonia sees significant potential in the energy sector, particularly in renewable energy and green-transition projects.

“Estonian companies can contribute innovative technological solutions, digital tools and specialised expertise,” the minister said.



Cooperation in renewable energy, energy efficiency, digital energy solutions



“We see substantial opportunities for cooperation in all of these areas. The green transition is one of the defining economic and technological transformations of our time, and both Estonia and Azerbaijan are actively pursuing ambitious goals in this field,” said Tsahkna.



He noted that Estonia is home to a growing ecosystem of clean-technology companies that combine digital innovation with sustainable solutions.

“Our expertise ranges from energy-efficiency technologies and smart-grid solutions to digital monitoring systems and data-driven energy management. Azerbaijan's investments in renewable energy create considerable opportunities for partnerships. We believe that combining Azerbaijan's energy potential with Estonia's digital expertise can create innovative solutions that support sustainability, energy security and economic growth. The opening of our embassy in Baku will help facilitate these connections,” he explained.

Estonia’s perspective on Middle Corridor’s strategic importance

The foreign minister noted that Azerbaijan is a strategically important partner for Estonia and for Europe more broadly.

“Due to its geographic location, Azerbaijan plays a key role in strengthening connectivity between Europe, the South Caucasus and Central Asia.



The development of the Middle Corridor has the potential to diversify trade routes, improve supply-chain resilience and create new economic opportunities for businesses across our regions. As a member of the European Union, Estonia welcomes initiatives that strengthen cooperation between the EU and Azerbaijan and enhance regional connectivity,” Tsahkna added.

Estonia’s view on peace and connectivity in the South Caucasus

The minister pointed out that Estonia consistently supports efforts to advance peace and normalise relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

“A lasting and sustainable peace agreement would benefit not only the two countries directly involved but also the wider South Caucasus region. Estonia welcomes the progress made in implementing the 2025 Washington agreements, including the opening of trade with Armenia.



Greater stability in the region strengthen links between the South Caucasus and Europe, creating opportunities across a variety of areas. We hope that the current momentum towards normalisation continues,” Tsahkna concluded.

World.title: OEUK highlights asset-level methane measurement practices for Turkmenistan (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 28. Measuring methane emissions at individual oil and gas facilities, rather than relying solely on standard emission estimates, is among the UK practices discussed with Turkmenistan.

Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) said this in an exclusive interview with Trend, outlining the technical approaches and regulatory practices discussed during a recent study visit by a Turkmen delegation to the United Kingdom.

"We were delighted to host the delegation from Turkmenistan and share UK expertise and experience in monitoring, verifying and reducing methane emissions from oil and gas production, including industry experience with OGMP 2.0, the UN-led framework for improving the measurement and reporting of methane emissions from the oil and gas sector. This is a valuable opportunity to share practical approaches to methane management and support wider international efforts to reduce emissions," said Caroline Brown, OEUK’s Environment and Emissions Manager.

According to OEUK, the discussions covered methods used by the UK offshore energy industry to identify, measure and reduce methane emissions from individual production facilities, including oil and gas wells and offshore platforms, as well as transport infrastructure such as pipelines.

One of the approaches discussed was the use of Leak Detection and Repair (LDAR) programmes. These involve regular operator inspections using portable gas detection equipment and optical gas imaging to identify leaks.

The programmes also include procedures for identifying fugitive emissions, classifying leaks, prioritising repairs and checking whether the repairs have been completed effectively.

OEUK said that monitoring and reporting systems can combine operational data to create emissions inventories for individual production assets and support corporate reporting. Emissions data can also inform operational decisions, helping companies not only measure emissions but actively reduce them.

The discussions also covered efforts to reduce flaring and venting through improved operational practices, more accurate measurement, and continuous performance improvement.

Another key topic was the Oil and Gas Methane Partnership 2.0 (OGMP 2.0), the flagship oil and gas methane reporting and mitigation programme of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP). OEUK said that the framework, together with asset-level emissions inventories and monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems, formed a dedicated part of the discussions.

According to the organisation, companies seeking to align with OGMP 2.0 principles need to develop methane measurement and monitoring programmes across their assets and establish inventories based on asset-specific data rather than relying solely on generic emission factors.

The latter approach estimates emissions using standard or average assumptions instead of measuring them at a particular facility or source. For example, calculations may be based on the volume of gas produced, the number and type of equipment in operation, or the hours a compressor operates, multiplied by a standard emissions factor.

OGMP 2.0 reporting is moving towards greater use of source-specific and measurement-based information. At higher reporting levels, companies use measurements and other source-specific methods to estimate emissions from individual assets, then compare and reconcile these estimates with measurements taken at the site level.

OEUK also identified effective MRV systems, the integration of methane management into operational processes, including leak detection and repair, and governance systems for consistently recording, analysing and reporting emissions as important steps towards alignment with the framework.

The organisation said the UK's experience also highlighted the importance of cooperation between energy companies, regulators, industry bodies and technology providers in reducing methane emissions.

Key elements of this approach include clear regulatory expectations, consistent monitoring and reporting frameworks, strong engagement between industry and government, transparent exchange of good practices and technical experience, and continuous improvement based on measured performance.

According to OEUK, cooperation between industry and regulators can improve environmental performance while helping put emissions reduction measures into practice.

For reference, Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) is a non-profit trade association representing companies operating across the UK's offshore energy sector. Its membership spans the oil and gas industry, offshore wind, hydrogen and carbon capture and storage. The organisation has a history of more than five decades and serves as a representative body for businesses across the sector.

OEUK brings together more than 450 member organisations, including energy producers, engineering and contracting companies, equipment manufacturers and specialist service providers. It represents the interests of its members in engagement with the UK government, regulatory authorities and other stakeholders, while promoting the exchange of technical expertise and industry best practices.

Methane emissions management is among the areas covered by OEUK's work on environmental performance and emissions reduction. The organisation supports industry efforts to improve emissions monitoring and reporting, enhance operational practices and promote the adoption of technologies and approaches aimed at reducing the environmental impact of offshore energy production.

The study visit to the United Kingdom was conducted by representatives of relevant ministries and agencies of Turkmenistan from October 12 to 16, 2026, with the support of the European Union's Policy Dialogue and Climate Action 2024-2029 project, co-funded by the EU and the German Federal Foreign Office and implemented by GIZ. The delegation included specialists working in areas related to the country's energy sector and methane emissions management. During the visit, they met with UK government bodies, industry representatives, research institutions and technology providers, including Offshore Energies UK, and visited industrial facilities such as Shell's St Fergus gas plant and the CATS gas terminal. The programme focused on British regulatory approaches, technologies for monitoring and reducing methane emissions, and the application of the EU Methane Regulation, particularly in the context of Turkmenistan's potential energy cooperation with the European market.

World.title: Iran's Azadegan oil field boosts output by 5,000 bpd after pump upgrade
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 28. Crude oil production at Iran’s Azadegan oil field (known as Majnun in Iraq), a joint venture with Iraq, has increased by more than 5,000 barrels per day following the installation of a fourth downhole pump.

According to the National Iranian Oil Engineering and Construction Company (NIOEC), this was announced by company representative Esmaeil Gholampour.

"The operation to install the fourth downhole pump was completed within 12 days," he said.

Gholampour added that the third downhole pump had previously been installed in Well No. 141. At that time, production at the Azadegan oil field increased by 800 barrels of crude oil.

A company representative noted that the installation of the fourth pump reduced the time required for downhole pump installation operations. "Several years ago, this operation sometimes took up to 50 days. However, thanks to a series of measures implemented, this timeframe was first reduced to 25 days. Currently, installing a pump in 12 days is considered a record," he added.

Gholampour stated that shortening the time required for pump installation, along with increased production from the wells, is considered an effective step toward expanding Iran’s production capacity and improving operational processes at the Azadegan joint oil field.

According to Trend's calculation, based on data from the National Iranian Oil Engineering and Construction Company (NIOEC), the installation of the first downhole pump at a well in the Azadegan oil field increased crude oil production from 435 to 1,710 barrels per day.

The Azadegan field, located in Iran and covering an area of 1,500 square kilometers, contains approximately 32 billion barrels of crude oil. The Azadegan oil field on the Iranian side is divided into southern and northern sections. On July 5, 2022, an agreement was signed between the National Iranian Oil Company, state-owned and private banks, and drilling companies to increase production at the field. The value of the agreement was $7 billion, and it was scheduled to be completed within two years. Production is planned to reach 570,000 barrels per day. Approximately 420 wells are planned to be drilled at the field.

World.title: Azerbaijan's electricity exports to Russia rise 11.9% in nine months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 28. Azerbaijan exported 95.075 million kWh of electricity to Russia from January through September 2026, earning a total of $4.027 million.

According to Trend's calculations based on a report from the State Statistics Committee, the value of electricity exports to Russia increased by $429,000, or 11.9%, compared to the same period in 2025. Export volumes also rose by 12.467 million kWh, or 15.1%.

Meanwhile, Azerbaijan imported 58.578 million kWh of electricity from Russia during the first nine months of 2026, worth $2.270 million.

Compared to the same period last year, the value of these imports decreased by $149,000, or 6.2%, while their volume fell by 9.830 million kWh, or 14.4%.

Overall, Azerbaijan exported 341.135 million kWh of electricity to Russia, Georgia and Iran from January through September 2026, with a total value of $17.603 million. Compared to the same period in 2025, the value of these exports fell by $36.234 million, or approximately 3.1 times, while their volume decreased by 599.357 million kWh, or approximately 2.8 times.

During the same period, Azerbaijan imported 161.042 million kWh of electricity from these three countries, worth $7.886 million. Compared to the same period last year, the value of imports increased by $1.966 million, or 33.2%, while their volume rose by 26.508 million kWh, or 19.7%.

According to the latest data from the State Statistics Committee, the electricity, gas and steam production, distribution and supply sector in Azerbaijan produced goods and provided services worth 2.627 billion manat ($1.55 billion) from January through September 2026.

During this period, total electricity production amounted to 20.03 billion kWh, down 2.3% compared to the corresponding period of the previous year.

Thermal power plants accounted for the largest share of electricity generation, producing 15.170 billion kWh during the reporting period, a decrease of 9.5% year-over-year.

The highest growth was recorded at wind power plants, which generated 841.3 million kWh of electricity, 27.1 times the amount recorded in the corresponding period of the previous year.

Electricity production at solar power plants also continued to grow. From January through September, these plants generated 533.2 million kWh, up 10.1% year-over-year.

Meanwhile, power plants fueled by biomass and waste incineration generated 168.2 million kWh of electricity, an increase of 5.8% compared to the same period last year. Electricity generation from hydropower sources also increased.

Production figures for the water supply, wastewater treatment and waste management sector were also released. From January through September 2026, this sector produced goods and provided services worth 511.5 million manat ($300.88 million).

During the reporting period, the volume of water treated and distributed totaled 506.4 million cubic meters, up 4.8% compared to the same period last year.

World.title: Uzbekistan's foreign trade turnover rises 6.3% to $65.4B in nine months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 28. Uzbekistan's foreign trade turnover reached $65.4 billion in January-September 2026, increasing by $3.9 billion, or 6.3%, year-on-year, with China and Russia remaining the country's largest trading partners, according to the National Statistics Committee.

China ranked first, accounting for $15.2 billion of Uzbekistan's foreign trade turnover during the reporting period. Russia followed with $10.5 billion, while Kazakhstan ranked third with $4.3 billion.

Türkiye placed fourth with $2.2 billion, followed by Afghanistan with $1.6 billion. The Republic of Korea and the United Arab Emirates each accounted for $1.4 billion.

France and Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China, each recorded $1.3 billion in trade turnover with Uzbekistan. Kyrgyzstan rounded out the top 10, with $1.1 billion.

According to Trend's calculations based on the committee's figures, China and Russia together accounted for $25.7 billion, or approximately 39.3% of Uzbekistan's total foreign trade turnover.

The 10 largest trading partners collectively generated $40.3 billion in trade turnover, equivalent to approximately 61.6% of the national total. The National Statistics Committee reported their combined share at 61.5%, with the slight difference likely reflecting rounding in the published figures.

Based on the reported annual increase of $3.9 billion, Uzbekistan's foreign trade turnover in January-September 2025 is estimated at approximately $61.5 billion.

World.title: Two oil tankers hit naval mines and catch fire near Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 28. Two oil tankers struck naval mines and subsequently caught fire in the area of the Strait of Hormuz.

This was reported by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

One of the vessels reportedly struck a mine near Oman's Port of Khasab, while the other was hit in the eastern part of the Strait of Hormuz.

According to the IRGC, one of the tankers struck a mine at the entrance to Oman's Port of Khasab, while the other hit a mine in the eastern part of the strait while following a route not authorized by Tehran. It was noted that both vessels had attempted to pass through the strait undetected by switching off their Automatic Identification Systems (AIS).

The IRGC warned that the route in question is heavily mined and that US military aircraft would be unable to protect vessels attempting to pass through this route.

World.title: Iran's Homa gas gathering center ready to help boost gas supply
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 28. Iran's Homa gas gathering center is ready to contribute to the country's gas supply, according to Mazyar Khorshedinia, an official at the South Zagros Oil and Gas Production Company, the Ministry of Petroleum reported.

"The Homa gas field produces 10 million cubic meters of gas per day. The gas extracted from this field is transported to the Homa gas gathering center," he said.

Khorshedinia added that 23 wells are currently operational at the Homa gas field. The extracted gas is transported to the gathering center through a 6-inch pipeline and, after collection, is sent to the next gas processing facility through a 24-inch pipeline, followed by a 26-inch one.

The company official said that the necessary maintenance work at the Homa gas field had been completed on time ahead of the winter months.

"At the insistence of Iran's Ministry of Petroleum, all maintenance work at the Homa gas field and gathering center is being carried out by startup companies as part of their operations. So far, no problems have been reported as a result of the startups' activities," he said.

The Homa gas field is located in southern Iran, near the city of Khonj in Fars Province.

According to information provided to Trend by Iran's South Zagros Oil Zones Company, four gas fields - Tabnak, Homa, Shanol and Varavi - are producing gas in Iran's Parsian operational area. The area has a total production capacity of 76 million cubic meters of gas and 25,600 barrels of gas condensate per day.

Gas consumption in Iran rises sharply during the winter months, leading to certain restrictions on gas supply.

World.title: What to expect with Victoria's election count tonight
World.content:
Barring an unprecedented polling miss, Victorian Labor is set to be defeated after 12 years in government.

The Coalition is likely to form majority government, in an election that could deliver one of the most complex results in Australian political history.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog.

The final makeup of parliament remains anyone's guess, including the number of One Nation MPs — and how influential they'll be in the next parliament.

Here are some pointers on how to follow the results tonight.

Where can I see the 2026 Victorian election results?

You can follow the results using the live results service on the ABC's website.

We will be bringing you the latest figures and helping you make sense of the numbers from the ABC Election Centre in Melbourne.

The state election results will be complicated by One Nation's rise and record-low polling for Labor. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

When will results start coming in?

More than 1,700 polling centres across Victoria will close at 6pm AEDT.

The first figures are expected to come in within an hour of polls closing.

When will the election be called?

If the polls are correct, we may be able to project which party will have the best chance of forming government early in the night.

But the results in each one of the 88 Legislative Assembly districts may not be known until the full distribution of preferences are completed in the second week of December.

To give us an indication of the result before that process is completed, electoral commissions do two-candidate preferred counts.

This means the Victorian Electoral Commission (VEC) must pick the two candidates they believe will come first and second.

That used to be an easy job — but it's not so simple this election.

More than 1,700 polling centres across Victoria will close at 6pm before counting begins. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

One Nation's rise and record-low polling for Labor make it much harder to make those decisions.

If it looks like the VEC's prediction is not correct, the ABC will estimate preference flows to project the two-candidate preferred figure.

Those estimates are based on our analysis of historical voting patterns.

Which are the seats to watch?

To win majority government, the Coalition will need to win 16 additional seats and not lose any of the ones it holds.

Liberal leader Jess Wilson, who holds the seat of Kew, hopes to be Victoria's next premier. (AAP: Con Chronis)

Its biggest barrier to achieving those gains could be One Nation.

Despite the Coalition's improvement in the polls through the campaign, One Nation is still in contention to win Coalition seats and snatch gains in marginal Labor seats.

The Nationals-held seat of Morwell is considered among One Nation's best hopes of winning any seat in Victoria and the seats of Hastings and Bass on Western Port Bay, narrowly held by Labor, are not far behind.

The same is true of Pakenham in Melbourne's outer east, where state leader Warren Pickering is running.

One Nation's leader in Victoria, Warren Pickering, is running to win the seat of Pakenham. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

If One Nation is doing well, the Coalition's other path to majority government runs through Melbourne's north and west.

The Coalition hasn't won a seat north or west of the Yarra since 1996 so if it is leading in safe Labor seats like Greenvale, Tarneit or Eltham then it is probably on track for a very good night.

Premier Ben Carroll appears highly vulnerable in his seat of Niddrie in Melbourne's north-west, so many within Labor will be keeping an eye on which leadership contenders hold on.

Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams holds the safe Labor seat of Dandenong and her opponent for the deputy leadership position in July, Steve Dimopoulos, holds Oakleigh.

Labor losing either of those seats would represent an utter electoral disaster.

Labor's deputy leader Gabrielle Williams and leader Ben Carroll hold the seats of Dandenong and Niddrie. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

What should I know about the upper house?

Voters in Victoria are also casting their vote for the Legislative Council, the state's upper house.

While the final composition of the upper house is going to be hard to determine on the night, the abolition of the group voting ticket system, which helped elect micro-party representatives with very small proportions of the vote, could make life easier for the next government.

What Victoria's upper house might look like after the state election Expect to see a huge number of new faces on the red benches of the Legislative Council and a lot of current members defeated at the ballot box.

Keep an eye out for whether the Coalition seems to be on track for a second seat in the Northern Metropolitan region or a third seat in Northern Victoria.

That would indicate the party are going to be in a strong enough position to avoid tricky multi-party negotiations and instead can go to any of Labor, One Nation, or the Greens to pass legislation.

A good night for both One Nation and the Greens would be winning a seat in every region, while a great night would be picking up even more.

These results will be confirmed on Wednesday, 16 December.

World.title: MotoGP circuit to claim fewer trees as transplant solution offered
World.content:
South Australia's state government has reduced the number of trees to be removed for the controversial MotoGP circuit, with 94 olive trees to be "transplanted" across the Adelaide Park Lands.

The change means the total number of trees destroyed for the sporting event will be reduced to 288.

The olive trees are currently located between Wakefield Road and Bartels Road and will be transplanted to existing olive groves within the Park Lands.

Premier Peter Malinauskas said the project was worthy of pursuit, after seeking expert approval from arborists.

"That is a big difference to where we were previously," Mr Malinauskas said.

The state government says the species is 'hardy' and will have a high survival rate when transplanted. (ABC News)

The premier said arborists provided a "high confidence" the hardy species would have a "very high survival rate".

"Some can be transplanted quickly subject to the identified locations, but others will be put into temporary storage arrangements in pots", Mr Malinauskas said.

The reduction in tree casualties comes after a long-running feud between activists and the Malinauskas government and a call from dozens of celebrities to halt the tree removal.

Two legal challenges almost placed roadblocks in the way of the MotoGP circuit construction, but those challenges fell over in the Supreme and Federal courts.

The premier confirmed the olive tree transplanting work would start next month.

The state government said it engaged extensively with the Adelaide City Council before confirming a solution.

Protesters watch as trees in Adelaide's parklands are removed for the MotoGP circuit construction in November. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Adelaide City Council Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith welcomed the news saying the olive trees had historical significance.

"They really have followed the path of settlement in South Australia," she said.

"Clearly it's technically difficult … but we understand it's possible and it can be done."

The state government said that, including the olive trees, a total of 182 trees would be transplanted within the Park Lands.

New renders were released today to show which olive trees will be transplanted between Bartels and Wakefield roads.

The government released a new map in November 2026 to show which trees (in dark green) will be transplanted. (Supplied: SA Government)

Outside of the motorsport event period, the government said this section of the Park Lands would feature 124 mature trees in planter boxes to become a new tree-lined connection for people walking and cycling between the city and the eastern suburbs.

World.title: Culture preserved in new Aboriginal language dictionaries
World.content:
Two Aboriginal languages from Western Australia's Pilbara have been recorded and preserved in dictionaries for the first time, including one language with only three remaining fluent speakers.

The first drafts of the dictionaries were developed as part of a project by Puutu Kunti Kurrama and Pinikura (PKKP) Aboriginal Corporation to preserve Pinikura and Puutu Kunti Kurrama languages.

With both languages passed down through oral tradition, the dictionaries are the product of two years of collaboration between linguists and the remaining local speakers.

Pinikura traditional owner Terry Drage helped linguists with pronunciation.

"You can get a linguist to come in, and they will pronounce it their way," he said.

"And then that pronunciation, if we keep going with that type of pronunciation, then you lose [it]."

Terry (left) and Mitchell Drage believe the dictionaries could have an important role in the future. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

Terry's brother, elder Mitchell Drage, is also a big advocate of the project.

Only three people speak Pinikura fluently, and Mitchell Drage would like that to change.

" To me, it also says to the younger generation that our old people did have a language, and we need to maintain that as a record for the young people to hear. "

Writing an oral language

Linguist Breanna Kelly found documenting a language traditionally passed down orally one of the hardest parts of compiling the dictionary.

"A lot of the work that we do involves asking people questions to try and have them say some sentences back to us," she said.

"But we try to get information in different styles as much as we can, whether that's us just asking questions or whether it's more of a conversation, occasionally a bit of a role play."

Breanna Kelly hopes community members can use the dictionaries alongside online resources to learn the languages. (ABC Pilbara: Amy Rossbach)

Ms Kelly said the team worked with present-day speakers and historical resources.

"It's been challenging but really fun," Ms Kelly said.

"I've enjoyed picking up little bits of language along the way."

PKKP launched Pinikura and Kurrama language dictionaries at its 2026 AGM. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

'It's our responsibility'

Burchell Hayes, a Puutu Kunti Kurrama descendant, said shame around getting the language wrong can be a barrier for younger Kurrama people wanting to learn it.

"We want them to identify themselves as Kurrama and be proud of who they are and be confident to be able to speak that language without that shame factor creeping in," Mr Hayes said.

He said it was why the first draft of the Kurrama dictionary is a good base, but not the final product.

Burchell Hayes says the release of the Kurrama dictionary is a proud moment. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

The next drafts of the dictionaries are already underway, with plans to improve on the first editions by gathering feedback from community members.

Terry Drage believes these first drafts have been a big first step.

"It's a legacy that's been handed down to us," he said.

"And now it's our responsibility to pass it on as well."

World.title: Workers who lose their jobs to AI say they're also addicted to using it
World.content:
Until a few months ago, Oksana had her pick of acting jobs in China.

The 26-year-old was booked back-to-back to work on short-drama projects, usually bite-sized serialised videos made specifically for mobile viewing.

But this year, that work has all but disappeared because of the rise of videos produced with artificial intelligence (AI).

"Many of the companies I used to know and work with have switched to AI and no longer shoot live-action dramas," she said.

"Now getting a role is very hard.

"If I wanted to, I previously could have kept shooting until I dropped dead.

" This year, that's no longer the case. The short drama industry is completely different. "

How fast has the shift happened?

In 2026, more than 90 per cent of China's new micro dramas were generated by AI, including the actors, voices and scenes.

They were nearly non-existent the year before.

Rather than a whole crew and set, micro dramas can be made by very small teams on computers in a studio. (ABC)

Government figures show about 1,600 new AI micro dramas launched every day for the first half of 2026.

The AI videos have become so popular that even someone like Oksana, who has lost her job to the technology, is "obsessed" with them.

"These AI dramas really are good, truly good," she said.

"With those two or 300-episode short dramas, once I click in, I forget about getting out.

"Even when I go to sleep each night, I leave the sound on and fall asleep listening.

"My head is a bit of a mess every day now, and I can't focus on anything else."

Micro dramas for macro audiences

The micro drama episodes often focus on fantasy, underdog-style or romantic storylines alongside time-travelling and urban dramas.

The episodes are usually free and end on cliffhangers designed to keep people watching, with viewers having to pay to see the rest of the series.

One of China's biggest hits of 2026, drawing 6.08 billion views, is a series where a woman wakes up in the Tang dynasty and gains power by slaying demons that roam the city.

AI-generated videos of pets and anthropomorphic fruit are also finding large audiences.

AI micro drama developer Zhu Zhili said the technology allowed companies to produce entertainment content quicker, cheaper and with more advanced storylines.

"Before, we needed to hire real actors, build sets, go into studios, and so on," he said.

Zhu Zhili says AI makes production much more efficient. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

"Now, with AI, we only need a very small team working together on computers in a company or studio to produce a short drama that previously would have taken enormous manpower and resources to shoot.

"We can just use AI to do the pictures, storyboard generation, generative audio, generative music, and generative voiceover.

"So the efficiency is very, very high now."

AI creators have reported dramas may cost about one-tenth of traditional live-action shoots.

But Mr Zhu said despite the large volume of new dramas being made, turning a profit could still be difficult.

"In the first half of this year, China produced a total of 220,000 AI short dramas, which is an enormous number," he said.

"But on the other hand, only about 1,000 of them truly broke out, meaning they succeeded, passed 100 million views, or made money, a share of less than 0.4 per cent."

Zhu Zhili uses AI for pictures, storyboarding and generative audio, music and voiceover. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

China has ambitious goals to have AI agents, devices and applications reach 90 per cent penetration in key sectors by 2030.

The government's current five-year plan also lists micro dramas as an emerging form of "cultural business" to be actively developed.

The AI entertainment industry's development has moved at breakneck speed since the release of powerful new AI video software, like tech group ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 model.

But Chinese social media is full of stories and complaints by former actors who are now out of work.

"Then this year, after AI became widespread, nearly all my peers stopped getting call sheets. I've been at home without work for several months too," said user Liu Yuzhan, who now works as a delivery driver.

Oksana admits she is addicted to the micro dramas herself. (ABC)

Oksana says it's a similar story among her industry friends, but she believes there will always be an appetite for real human acting in longer-form content.

"Many of my peers have switched to livestreaming because of the current environment and can no longer work as professional actors," she said.

"But AI content gets tiresome if you watch it for long.

"It can never replace live actors, or the imperfections in their acting and their subtle emotions.

"AI is formulaic and can't convey emotion."

World.title: Alleged machete attack on NT woman by partner prompts police search
World.content:
Police are searching for a 22-year-old man who allegedly chased down and struck his partner with a machete in a remote Northern Territory community in the early hours of this morning.

In a statement, NT Police said it received several reports of an attack around 12:45am in the North Arnhem community of Maningrida.

Police said they were told by witnesses that the 22-year-old man allegedly chased the young woman, also aged 22, through a local park.

When the woman fell, the man allegedly struck her with a machete, resulting in "serious injuries" to her left arm.

Police said witnesses helped her into a nearby home and stopped the man from following her inside.

However, the man then allegedly struck a 43-year-old woman with the blunt end of the machete.

"[The 43-year-old woman] suffered minor cuts and sought medical treatment," an NT Police spokesperson said.

The injured 22-year-old woman was taken to the Maningrida clinic and then transported, via CareFlight, to the Royal Darwin Hospital for treatment.

Police said they were still "working to locate the offender" and investigating a "suspected breach of a domestic violence order".

"Anyone who witnessed the incident or has information about the man’s whereabouts is urged to contact police on 131 444," the police spokesperson said.

World.title: Calls for AI road signs after increased cassowary road deaths
World.content:
Cassowary advocates in Far North Queensland are questioning why a successful AI road sign trial hasn't been rolled out, as road deaths of the endangered bird almost double this year.

Figures from the Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation showed at least 22 cassowaries have been killed on Queensland roads so far in 2026.

It is a jump from between 11 and 13 road deaths each year since 2022.

Tropical Vets director Graham Lauridsen, who treats injured cassowaries, said the region had a cluster of fatalities earlier this year.

"There was a spate of deaths, sort of one after the other every week there for probably six or so weeks," Dr Lauridsen said.

Locals living on cassowary country had hoped a solution was in sight.

As hatching seasons comes to an end, more chicks and dads are expected on the roads. (Supplied: Jeff Larson)

In July 2025, the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) announced a trial, using artificial intelligence (AI) to detect cassowaries and activate a warning sign, had been successful.

The technology was installed for three months on the Kennedy Highway at Kuranda, north-west of Cairns, with 97 per cent accuracy in identifying the birds and a 31 per cent decrease in birds fatally struck, the department said.

After the trial, the Cassowary Recovery Team (CRT), a network of groups, experts and government staff who work with the birds, held a workshop to identify five road strike hotspots where signs could be installed.

Liz Gallie, on the Cassowary Coast about 140 kilometres south of Cairns, said she understood the signs would be rolled out there next.

The government announced the trial of the AI signs was a success last year. (Supplied: TMR)

"We were very excited that this is going to move forward … and so we're waiting and nothing is happening," the president of Mission Beach Cassowaries said.

In correspondence seen by the ABC, Ms Gallie wrote to the minister in September with a reply in October saying more trials were needed but no plans had been made.

"We know where they're getting killed, we've got the technology, we just need it at Mission Beach," she said.

Liz Gallie said every cassowary death affected the Mission Beach community. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

Ms Gallie said every cassowary death affected members of the community.

" We just keep hearing when they're killed and it's like, 'Oh, not another one' — it hurts. "

Project stalled

Dr Lauridsen, who is also part of the CRT, said he also understood there had been no further plans to utilise the AI technology, but now was the time to act as hatching season ended.

Liz Gallie says cassowaries are also a major tourism drawcard for the region. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

"This time of year, there's chicks on the road," he said.

"As soon as it can happen, it will absolutely have the potential to save lives."

Dr Lauridsen said better reporting and a healthier population after several years without major cyclones may partly explain the rise in reported deaths.

Graham Lauridsen said there had been a spate of cassowary road incidents this year. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

But he said that was no reason to halt efforts to protect the birds.

"If you stop, you'll regress, we'll be back where we were," he said.

"We know that cassowaries are going to have to cross the road perhaps more than they've done before.

"Having that technology where we know the hotspots are would be great."

Graham Lauridsen said the birds were likely drawn to roads due to people feeding them. (Supplied: Graham Lauridsen)

Dr Lauridsen said the AI signs avoided the complacency drivers developed with static signs.

The signs also helped mitigate costs toward cassowary conservation and rehabilitation, he added.

Community awareness

A TMR spokesperson said investigations were ongoing into how the AI road signs could be "incorporated into ongoing work to increase cassowary safety", but there was no further funding allocated or trials planned.

"The Queensland government is continuing to implement a community awareness program, including two [static] roadside billboards on the Bruce Highway near Tully and Innisfail, encouraging drivers to slow down and be aware of cassowaries," the spokesperson said.

The AI road signs detect traffic, which triggers the sign to flash a warning. (Supplied: TMR)

Jax Bergersen from the Kuranda Conservation Community Nursery said everyone involved in the CRT was frustrated after having high hopes for the signs.

"I'm afraid nature, the environment, is the thing that's put at risk," she said.

World.title: The tactics that secured North Melbourne's third AFLW premiership
World.content:
As rain bucketed down, North Melbourne confirmed its AFLW dynasty with an historic third consecutive premiership.

While it may seem repetitive to talk about the Roos' record-breaking run, what they had to compete with in 2026 makes this third flag that little bit more special.

For the first time since 2023 they lost a game, and challengers consistently came closer than in the previous two years.

The looming feeling that senior players could potentially hang up their boots also added a sense of occasion to the victory.

And then the weather showed up. The rain was going to be the great equaliser, allowing fellow grand finalist Melbourne to gather some confidence.

But by dominating three specific phases of the game, North Melbourne made history on Friday night, securing a three-peat.

The fast start that set up the victory

Throughout 2026, North Melbourne hasn't been an overly strong first-quarter team.

Generally, the opening terms were largely arm wrestles, almost like the Roos were playing with the opposition, giving them hope, before taking it away.

Roos are 'finally able to say' the words they have refused all season North Melbourne claims a historic three-peat after a near flawless but challenging season.

But on Friday night, the fast start was necessary. With rain already falling, and more on the radar, any early lead was going to be seriously valuable, so the Roos ensured they were the team in front.

Tess Craven knocked through the first goal of the game within 21 seconds, and captain Jasmine Garner kicked a second six minutes in. They went direct, gained ground with kicks, and got deep entries to unsettle Melbourne's typically staunch defence.

Both goals for the Roos came from stoppage, which was a worrying sign for Melbourne so early on. Last time these sides met, it was off turnover — not stoppage — that North Melbourne had set itself apart.

But this time around, the Roos tipped those scales in their favour.

Score sources North Melbourne Melbourne Points from intercept 15 13 Points from stoppage 29 5

Best on ground medallist Garner set the tone early in the piece. In the first quarter alone, Garner's stats included seven disposals, four inside 50s, and the goal, laying the foundations for how North Melbourne was going to attack the game.

While it took Melbourne some time to adapt to what the game was throwing up, North Melbourne just got to work.

The Demons over-possessed the footy in slippery conditions, opting for the handball too often, instead of getting boot to ball to win all-important territory.

Holding steady as the Dees fought back

Once Melbourne managed to get into the game, the Roos had to simply batten down the hatches and absorb the blows being thrown their way.

But crucially, just as in the first quarter, North Melbourne had already taken advantage of its early momentum on the scoreboard, with a classy Eilish Sheerin goal 39 seconds into the next term.

The Demons shifted to more of a kicking game in the second quarter, got into more dangerous positions, and Tayla Harris's contested marking reared its head. With this shift, they kicked what would be their only two goals of the match.

Quarter Kicks, handballs, tackles North Melbourne Melbourne Quarter 1 Kicks 46 40 Handballs 24 36 Tackles 17 23 Quarter 2 Kicks 35 39 Handballs 34 14 Tackles 17 19 Quarter 3 Kicks 48 36 Handballs 21 36 Tackles 18 24 Quarter 4 Kicks 43 38 Handballs 17 18 Tackles 15 18

That shift in style was borne out in the stats, with Melbourne's ratio of 39 kicks to 14 handballs in the second quarter helping to throw North Melbourne's movement out of whack.

While the second quarter was Melbourne's lowest-disposal quarter of the match, it was the side's most effective. Notably, both of the goals came from intercepts.

Roos create AFLW history with three-peat North Melbourne defeats Melbourne by 26 points in the grand final to claim a historic third consecutive AFLW premiership.

Pressure was also a major consideration in the second term, with Melbourne recording a pressure factor of 2.30 across the quarter — a rate at the upper end of the elite category — which rose to 2.38 in the third term.

But, crucially for the Roos, they maintained a lead even when the Demons threw their best at them. And the third quarter became a stalemate, in which North Melbourne maintained its arm's-length lead. The Roos' deep defence was staunch, repelling repeated forward entries and preventing Melbourne from scoring further goals.

Midfielders Garner (eight intercepts) and Ash Riddell (seven) were important in this respect, sliding behind the ball post-stoppage, while winger Amy Gavin Mangan, half-forward Jenna Bruton, and half-back Eliza Shannon (all six intercepts) got busy defensively.

In doing so, they lulled the Demons back into over-possession of the footy, taking their kick rate way back down to 50 per cent.

Essentially, the middle two quarters were a tale of the Roos just taking the hits and remaining on their feet.

Five-minute burst seals the premiership

While the game largely felt like it was in the balance for the duration, a five-minute patch in the last quarter turned a six-point lead into a 26-point victory for North Melbourne. It was a classic demonstration of the Roos' brand, taking the game away in a flash.

Melbourne controlled territory for the bulk of that term, attempting to break through the numbers in its attacking arc but unable to convert for the major that would have really rattled the Roos.

Instead, North Melbourne again absorbed the blows — and then the fast break happened. A long rebounding kick unlocked the Roos' speed, which had been a worry for Melbourne all evening and in the end proved the difference.

It allowed the Roos to set up an attack once again, create a stoppage inside 50, and secure a crucial goal off the boot of Bella Eddey.

And that goal was the dam wall breaking. It put the Roos up by 13 points, and opened the floodgates for two more goals via Blaithin Bogue, taking the game from a thrilling nailbiter to a comprehensive North Melbourne victory.

This is the Roos' style: absorb, absorb, absorb — then land the felling blow.

Throughout the season they have consistently dominated late in games.

They kicked the last three goals in their preliminary final, and continued the trend by kicking the last three goals in the grand final.

Prior to the game, one question for Melbourne was whether it could prevent that final flurry and hold on.

On Friday night, North Melbourne provided an emphatic answer.

World.title: Culture of fear, revenge revealed at WA's legal industry regulator
World.content:
Lawyers waiting more than a year for a practising certificate.

More than 2,000 of them having to fulfil extra conditions because of a regulator's mistake.

Others too afraid of retribution to give evidence under their own names.

These are some of the scathing findings of a bombshell report into the Legal Practice Board of Western Australia (LPBWA) released this week by a parliamentary committee that made it clear the statutory authority was scarcely fit for purpose.

Lawyers cite a culture of fear and retribution. (ABC News)

The board is supposed to decide who is admitted to practice law, issue annual practising certificates and resolve disputes and complaints about lawyers' conduct.

It is supposed to uphold "trust and confidence in the Western Australian legal system".

But the committee's findings suggest exactly the opposite.

And when the regulator is held in fear by the people it regulates, it's clear that there is a significant cultural problem.

'Culture of fear'

Complaints about the LPBWA have been circling for years, according to those in the industry.

Five peak legal bodies in WA last year separately warned of their "unprecedented loss of confidence" in the board, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry.

Five WA legal bodies made a joint submission to the parliamentary inquiry. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Their submission, all 218-pages of it, described "chronic delays" across much of the board's work, "inappropriate and highly damaging investigation and prosecution processes" and a "failure to engage, communicate and respond to enquiries and applications".

"The concerns raised also include, worryingly, reports of a culture of fear of the board by some members of the legal profession, including a fear of victimisation and retribution," committee chair Kate Doust told parliament on Thursday as she tabled the report.

" The committee also received evidence of disturbing and distressing mental health impacts on a number of individuals who have had various interactions with the board. "

These included reports of "constant mental anguish" waiting for matters to be resolved, severe post-traumatic stress disorder and suicidal ideation.

One member of the legal profession who gave evidence said the board is "very lucky someone has not topped themselves".

Lawyers slam regulator in inquiry submission In a scathing rebuke of their own watchdog, WA lawyers claim the state's Legal Practice Board is causing them psychological harm, amid calls for urgent reform.

In another example, a lawyer reportedly told a board staff member how they were unable to get a required letter from their supervisor because they were giving birth.

According to the lawyer, they replied, "What, did they die?"

The committee put forward 60 recommendations, including an independent probe into governance by an appropriate body, such as the Public Sector Commission.

A parliamentary inquiry has been examining WA's Legal Practice Board and its role in regulating the profession. (ABC News: Jack Stevenson)

And it questioned whether the current structures and practices are "fit for purpose for a modern regulator".

"The committee is also of the view that it remains to be seen whether these changes will be effective in restoring trust and confidence in the board," Ms Doust said.

Board troubled by findings

In its evidence, the board noted its "genuine concern" over evidence of interactions that have "adversely affected the mental health of legal practitioners".

"The board is profoundly troubled by reports of suicidal ideation and past attempts at self-harm," its evidence read.

It acknowledged its performance had not always been of an acceptable standard, noting various regulatory and communication shortcomings.

LPBWA executive director Libby Fulham said the board "welcomed the inquiry" and is "considering the committee's recommendations and findings".

WA's legal watchdog faces parliamentary inquiry The tables will be turned on the Legal Practice Board of WA as it faces a parliamentary inquiry amid a "detailed list" of complaints.

It's clear the board has a huge task ahead at addressing broader issues.

Law Society CEO Kate Wellington said the failings identified need to be "remedied now", while a state government spokesperson labelled some of the evidence about the board's culture and operation "incredibly concerning".

Integrity in the balance

Addressing these longstanding issues properly and with transparency will be paramount to restoring confidence in the board.

A parliamentary inquiry has been examining WA's Legal Practice Board and its role in regulating the profession. (ABC News: Hugh Sando)

"This is not just an issue for the legal profession," Community Legal WA CEO Chelsea McKinney said.

"Every Western Australian has a stake in a justice system that is fair, accessible and trustworthy. The rule of law depends on the integrity of the institutions responsible for upholding it."

Good governance and trust play a huge part.

And a time of increasing political and social fractures, that trust could not be more important.

Australian wrestling star Jermaine Haley, known by his WWE wrestling name Bronson Reed, has died due to medical complications. He was 38. World Wrestling Entertainment, the American wrestling promoter, announced Haley’s death on Saturday afternoon (Sydney time), but did not provide details. Jermaine Haley, known by his wrestling name as Bronson Reed, has died. WWE via Getty Images “WWE is devastated to announce that Jermaine Haley, also known as Bronson Reed, passed away earlier today at the age of 38 due to medical complications,” the company said. “Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.



“Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as his friends, co-workers and fans.” His death came weeks after he sustained injuries at his last performance at WWE Crown Jewel, the company’s premium wrestling live event in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on November 7. During that event, Haley was thrown onto a set of tables by fellow wrestler Oba Femi. Oba Femi in action against Bronson Reed during Crown Jewel in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. WWE via Getty Images Sports outlets reported he sustained broken ribs and a lacerated kidney following the incident, however WWE made no connection between the injuries and his death. Haley was born in Adelaide in 1988. He told The Sporting News he “dabbled in everything as a child” before getting into pro wrestling after finishing high school.



“I was always a fan of pro wrestling, since I can remember,” he told the outlet. “I had my uncle who lived with us at the time, he was a huge wrestling fan, so as a little kid at 2 to 3 years old, he was watching wrestling on TV and I guess I was sitting there watching as well. From there, I just became a fan. Related Article Wrestling WA locks in WWE for three more years, but Optus Stadium is not on the cards Matthew Farrelly, a Sydney-born professional wrestler known as Grayson Waller, paid tribute to Haley on X. “Love you brother,” he said. “Thank you for opening so many doors for myself and many others in Australian wrestling.” Australian WWE colleague Brendan Vink, known as Duke Hanson, started professional wrestling at the same time as Haley. On X, he posted: “I love you, Jermaine … Tell your people you love them.”



Haley had two stints in WWE after joining the promotion in 2019. He was released from WWE in 2021, before returning a year later. With AP Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: This film will make you think twice about your favourite children’s TV shows
World.content:
CultureMoviesCinema This film will make you think twice about your favourite children’s TV shows Nell Geraets November 28, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There is something deeply unnerving about classic children’s television shows. Productions like Here’s Humphrey or Barney & Friends display such over-the-top joy that they verge on sinister. American filmmaker Casper Kelly, creator of the mega-viral short film Too Many Cooks, first noticed that strange unease as a child watching Rankin/Bass Productions specials like Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, its stop-motion creatures “freaking him out”. Later, when his children began watching shows like Blue’s Clues, the feeling only grew. Think Barney… But a psycho killer. Roadside Attractions “The kids were very well-behaved – when a dance routine happened, they all would just start singing and dancing spontaneously, which sort of freaked me out,” Kelly says. “I was a very literal child, so I’d think, ‘How would they know to do that? Are they brainwashed? Are they being controlled?’” It was from these questions that his feature directorial debut was born. Buddy is a surreal horror-comedy about children who discover they have been trapped inside a ’90s kids’ TV show hosted by a short-tempered orange unicorn with a penchant for violence. Framed as a “knock-off Barney”, the cuddly host (voiced by Keegan-Michael Key) may initially appear jovial, but if the children refuse to play along, the consequences are deadly.



Loading “I honed in on when I was a kid watching a kid’s show … Before I had critical filters to contextualise what I was seeing. Buddy rests in an unconscious place where deep things can happen.” Many viewers have interpreted the film as an allegory for childhood predation or grooming, and the sometimes toxic environments espoused by the kids’ television industry, as was uncovered in the 2024 expose on Nickelodeon’s Dan Schneider, Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV. None of these themes are explicitly referenced in Buddy, but Kelly says he’s happy for viewers to interpret it however they wish based on their own experience with children’s content. That, he says, is the beauty of creating a film so steeped in nostalgia – everyone will connect to it differently. This isn’t your average nostalgia trip, though. Unlike the warm and fuzzies elicited from nostalgic dramas or comedies, Buddy’s nostalgia is weaponised to evoke dread and discomfort – pulling on elements in children’s TV that you always subconsciously knew were off-putting, then exaggerating them to the nth degree. Buddy takes normal cinematic nostalgia and makes it sick and twisted. Roadside Attractions





Buddy may seem jovial – just don’t get on his bad side. Roadside Attractions Buddy has since gained similar traction. After premiering at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, the film’s studio decided to promote the film by building social accounts for the unicorn, creating the impression that Buddy was a real-life long-forgotten ’90s kids’ TV mascot. Fake VHS rips and old-school commercials made some believe they remembered watching Buddy as children, thus pulling on their nostalgia before slowly trickling in split-second flashes of gore. This subverted nostalgia did so well that Buddy’s account amassed more followers on TikTok than the popular horror streamer Shudder. Though not the first cuddly-turned-creepy horror “mascot” – Five Nights at Freddy’s spawned an entire franchise off its unsettling kids’ restaurant animatronics – Buddy is arguably one of the most nuanced. Instead of a mindless killer, he’s positioned as desperate for affection, often mistaking blind compliance for love. While Buddy goes a step above, ultimately resorting to violence, he’s still an incredibly convincing, vaguely familiar children’s show mascot – and therein lies the terror. Buddy is in cinemas now. Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Another McCrae home damaged as landslide strikes troubled stretch
World.content:
NationalVictoriaLandslide Another McCrae home damaged as landslide strikes troubled stretch Hannah Hammoud November 28, 2026 — 2:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A home has been damaged after a fresh landslide struck McCrae on Saturday morning, renewing fears for residents living along the increasingly unstable hillside less than two years after a devastating slip destroyed another property nearby. Emergency services were called to Point Nepean Road about 8.05am on Saturday after part of the cliff face gave way, causing significant damage to an unoccupied home. The house was damaged on Saturday morning following the landslide. Nine News Multiple neighbouring properties have been evacuated as authorities assess the extent of the damage and the risk of further ground movement. An emergency warning has been issued, with residents and visitors urged to stay away from the area. Point Nepean Road and The Eyrie have been closed to traffic while emergency services respond.



Heavy rainfall across the Mornington Peninsula on Friday is believed to have contributed to the latest landslide, although the cause is yet to be confirmed. The latest incident has once again thrown the spotlight on the area’s history of instability. The damaged home is located close to where a major landslide destroyed a home in January 2025. That incident, on January 14, destroyed a three-storey property and seriously injured a council worker who was at the site and forced to jump to safety as the hillside gave way. Three other properties were damaged, and 19 properties were evacuated, with many residents facing lengthy uncertainty over when, or if, they would be able to return home.



The January 2025 incident was the largest of a series of four landslides and slips recorded in the area between November 2022 and January 2025. Related Article Exclusive

City life Home owners don’t have to pay to fix McCrae landslide, court finds An independent Board of Inquiry was subsequently established to investigate the causes of the January 2025 disaster and examine whether authorities had adequately responded to warnings about the hillside. Its final report, delivered in September 2025, found water from a burst South East Water main caused the January 2025 landslide. The inquiry also found that Mornington Peninsula Shire and South East Water had failed to take appropriate action in response to warning signs in the lead-up to the disaster.



Residents had raised concerns about large volumes of water flowing through the neighbourhood in the months before the major landslide. The January 14, 2025, landslide in McCrae resulted in the evacuation of 19 surrounding properties. In its examination of the events following an earlier slip on January 5, 2025, the inquiry found the shire had not appropriately escalated its response as water continued to infiltrate the already unstable hillside. The fresh landslide comes as authorities continue efforts to help residents displaced by the 2025 disaster return to their homes. On September 30, Mornington Peninsula Shire council announced it had approved plans to install two engineered protective barriers on council-owned land at Penny Lane.



Related Article City life Landslides occurred on McCrae cliff for 70 years, inquiry told The barriers, made from ballasted shipping containers, are intended to address risks associated with the 2022 and 2025 landslides and help three affected households return home sooner. Mornington Peninsula Shire mayor Stephen Batty said council is working closely with authorities to establish the extent of the incident. “Our immediate priority is the safety and wellbeing of those in the area, and the shire will exercise whatever regulatory powers are necessary to protect the community,” he said. “We ask that people avoid the area to ensure emergency services and authorised personnel can safely access the site and undertake their work.



“We acknowledge how distressing this will be for the McCrae community, particularly given the events of the past two years. The situation is still unfolding, and we will provide further information as it becomes available.” Authorities on the scene following the landslide on Saturday morning. Nine News Mike O’Neill, spokesperson for the McCrae Evacuated Residents Group, said it was frustrating to wake up to the news of another landslide in McCrae. “This is a bloody disgrace,” he said. “It highlights a lack of concern from the authorities.” “This is just another event – it doesn’t surprise me. The biggest question for me now is, how many houses and how many lives need to be put at risk before this is dealt with in the long term? So that we can all feel safe in our homes.”

Nearly 50 new homes will be built in Perth specifically for victims of domestic violence, it was announced on Saturday, aimed at bridging the gap between crisis accommodation and a new life away from abuse.

Domestic Violence minister Jessica Stojkovski made the announcement alongside Federal Member for Perth Patrick Gorman, saying there was a “bottleneck” in refuge accommodation.

Prevention of Family and Domestic Violence Minister Jessica Stojkovski Holly Thompson

“Quite often for women who are leaving family and domestic violence situation, the question is not whether they should leave; it’s where they can go,” she said.

“Ensuring that we have freed up crisis accommodation when somebody is leaving in that real urgent situation, and that we can move them into transitional accommodation once that urgency, that emergency situation has passed, is vitally important to ensuring the whole health of the system.”
