Jack Clayton offers a chuckle and wry smile when asked to recall the moment which paved his way towards earning his Baggy Green. Cricket was not a career path he envisioned when the Brisbane Lions academy prospect pondered what missing selection in the AFL draft would mean. When he picked up the bat for the University of Queensland, he was playing third-grade and was reluctant to give up his Saturday mornings when a request to be promoted to the seconds was offered. Queensland’s Jack Clayton celebrating a Sheffield Shield century at the Gabba. Chris Hyde/Getty Images Nine years to the day when he went un-drafted, and he is on the cusp of becoming Australia’s 474th Test cricketer, having been named in the squad to face New Zealand in Perth from December 9. “I certainly never thought when I gave up my footy dream that I would be in this position nine years later. At that stage, I did think I was going to go back and play footy for that season,” Clayton said on Saturday.



Related Article Analysis

Test cricket Power rankings: The quicks and spinners primed to succeed all-star Test attack “The next season, Scott Henry – our first-grade captain, who also played for New South Wales and Queensland – told me I was going to bat three for the season, and I fell flat on my face when he said that. It’s obviously been a bit of a different journey, but one I’m really proud of.” That call-up marked a sliding doors moment for Clayton, who had initially intended to attempt an AFL revival mission through the NEAFL – now the VFL – with Aspley Hornets. “I think being out of that professional set-up with footy … and just being a normal 18, 19, 20-year-old going through uni, hanging out with mates, doing all the things uni people do, gave me a lot of perspective about life, but also where sport lies in my life,” he said. “I feel like that’s helped keep me balanced and level throughout my cricket career.”



While fellow Test contenders Sam Konstas and Jake Weatherald have fought for re-inclusion in the spotlight, Clayton has been able to slowly hone his craft free of scrutiny. In an era where T20 cricket and the smash and bash mentality at the crease reins supreme, the 27-year-old is the Test arena’s traditional throwback in the mould of his childhood idol, Mike Hussey. Building his game around solid defence on the front and back foot, while seeking low-risk scoring options, he has become the anchor of Queensland Sheffield Shield side since bursting onto the scene with a gutsy century on debut. That knock of 109 was the first instance in which he demonstrated his tendency for digging his team out of a slump. At one stage on that day in February 2022, the Bulls had slumped to 6–191, before Clayton’s defiance ground the Bulls to a first innings total of 349. His century in the 2024–25 Shield final was another instance of thriving in the pressure-cooker – combining with Jack Wildermuth (111) to overturn a 166 run first innings’ deficit to set South Australia 270 to win.



Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Lyon weighing up playing future after Test snub as replacement revealed Clayton laughed “there are plenty of those moments I’ve stuffed up too”, but paid tribute to his first-grade coach Peter Clarke – now at the helm of the Sydney Sixers WBBL side – for shaping his mindset. “He was a sport psychologist for the Australian women’s team during that time, and he was really helpful for me in developing some processes around how I go about my cricket and how I compartmentalise things mentally,” Clayton explained. “I feel like that’s really helped me to make sure I stick to the process and focus on what I need to do in those situations to try and best help the team get into a position to win games.” Clayton’s call-up comes at a time when the Australian batting line-up has been hunting reinvention, culminating in the axing of Queensland teammate Marnus Labuschagne.



Despite spending much of his career batting at No.4, Clayton is poised to assume Labuschagne’s place at No.3; a challenge he will not shy away from, with his highest score of 134 coming in that same position last year. “I’d be happy to bat anywhere for Australia, one to 11 it wouldn’t bother me at all wherever I bat,” he quipped, before revealing the frank conversations he had with Labuschagne upon the latter’s return from the ill-fated tour in South Africa. “When he [Labuschagne] came back from South Africa, there was a bit of noise around me potentially taking his spot, but he was fantastic in the way he came up to me and talked about the elephant in the room straight away. Loading “He said ‘I don’t want any angst between us, I want the best for you, and I’m proud of all the stuff you’ve done and want you to be playing Test cricket and performing, and hopefully one day we can be there together’.’



Gruelling tours to India and England will follow the New Zealand battle in 2027, and there is no guarantee 37-year-old champion Steve Smith will play on beyond that. Clayton, however, was unwilling to contemplate a reality where he spearheaded the top order long-term. “As soon as you start thinking about those things in the future or things that you can’t control, I think that’s when I’ve had failures in my life. For me, it’ll be focusing on how I prepare for the first Test and how I can get myself in a situation to get out there and score runs,” Clayton said. “It won’t be going anything past the next training session, or the first session of day one, or whatever it is. I try and keep it as simple as I can in that sense, and not look too far forward in the future, and just focus on what I can do and what I can control. “What I’ve been doing in Shield cricket has been working against good quality first-class bowlers, and even international bowlers, so I’m not changing anything about the way I prepare.” Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.content:
Updated SportCricketAustralian cricket Lyon weighing up playing future after Test snub as replacement revealed Tom Decent Updated November 28, 2026 — 1:50pm ,first published November 28, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australian spin great Nathan Lyon is weighing up his playing future despite being assured by chairman of selectors George Bailey he is a strong chance of touring India as part of a blockbuster five-Test series next year. The 39-year-old is considering all his options - including retirement - but won’t make a call on that in the coming days after being left out of Australia’s Test squad to face New Zealand this summer. Nathan Lyon in action during the recent Test series against South Africa. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Lyon, second only to Shane Warne on Australia’s list of Test wicket-takers, is unlikely to play in NSW’s Sheffield Shield match against Western Australia in Sydney, starting on December 3. Lyon is frustrated at losing his Test spot to West Australian off-spinner Corey Rocchiccioli, who was named in a 13-man squad on Saturday alongside uncapped Queensland batsman Jack Clayton. Clayton is poised to bat at No.3 or No.4 in the opening Test against New Zealand in Perth from December 9.



Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket Lyon set to be axed from Australia’s Test squad, as new spinner and batter get their chance Bailey rang Lyon on Thursday evening to inform him that not only would he miss the opening Test of the summer, but he was not in selectors’ plans for any of the four matches. As Bailey told reporters on Saturday, Lyon found it difficult to hide his disappointment. Bailey was adamant Lyon’s omission had nothing to do with reports that he suggested taking red confectionery frogs onto the field against Pakistan in the UAE to help artificially shine the ball during Australia’s first Test after the infamous 2018 tour of South Africa. “Understandably, it was a tough conversation for him,” Bailey said of omitting Lyon based on form. “A tough decision. Unfortunately, he just hasn’t quite had the impact over the last few games we would have liked.



Australia’s 13-man Test squad for New Zealand series Pat Cummins (NSW/Penrith Cricket Club) (c)

Scott Boland (VIC/Frankston Peninsula Cricket Club)

Alex Carey (SA/Glenelg Cricket Club)

Jack Clayton (QLD/University of Queensland Cricket Club)

Cameron Green (WA/Subiaco-Floreat Cricket Club)

Josh Hazlewood (NSW/St George Cricket Club)

Travis Head (SA/Tea Tree Gully Cricket Club)

Josh Inglis (WA/Joondalup Cricket Club)

Michael Neser (QLD/Gold Coast Cricket Club)

Matthew Renshaw (QLD/Toombul Cricket Club)

Corey Rocchiccioli (WA/University Cricket Club)

Steve Smith (NSW/Sutherland Cricket Club)

Mitchell Starc (NSW/Manly Warringah Cricket Club) *One player will be added after round six of the Sheffield Shield “We hope it’s not the end for him. We see a path. I think he can have enormous value when you project forward to India on a tour like that with his experience. “We wanted him to take some time and not rush into any decision off the back of this.” While Bailey indicated Lyon would be given time to decide on his future, a cricket source with knowledge of the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the veteran off-spinner was weighing up all options. Lyon is contracted to Cricket Australia until the middle of next year and has spoken previously of his desire to return to India and win an away Ashes series in England.



But having been left out of Test XIs in Kingston, Brisbane and Gqeberha over the past 18 months, Lyon must decide whether he has the appetite to fight his way back into the side. The decision also leaves Lyon’s hopes of a farewell Test at the SCG, afforded to David Warner and Usman Khawaja in recent years, hanging by a thread. If Rocchiccioli struggles against New Zealand, selectors could recall Lyon with a view to getting some cricket into him before the India tour, should he play on. That does seem unlikely given the conversations behind closed doors. WA spinner Corey Rocchiccioli has been named in Australia’s Test squad. Getty Images Australia are expected to take at least three frontline spinners to India, where they have not won a Test series since 2004. While selectors have the flexibility to change the squad throughout the four-Tests, the decision to overlook Lyon for the summer represents a changing of the guard in Australia’s spin-bowling ranks.



Bailey said Rocchiccioli’s consistency at domestic level, his ability to generate bounce and the abundance of left-handers in New Zealand’s squad were factors in his promotion ahead of a likely Test debut in either Perth or Adelaide. Rocchiccioli has taken 18 wickets at 33.88 from five Shield matches this season, taking his overall first-class tally to 205 wickets at 30.62. “We’ve got some pretty strong spin depth at the moment within Australia and Roc obviously gets a chance here,” Bailey said. “With Todd Murphy, Matt Kuhnemann and Mitch Swepson, I think we’ve got some nice depth within our spin bowling ranks. They have been working hard in the background as Gaz has had this incredible career.” Meanwhile, Clayton’s selection is a reward for a prolific start to the domestic summer and puts the Queenslander on the cusp of a Test debut at No.3 or No.4, depending on where selectors believe Steve Smith is best suited. Bailey said “general discussions” had taken place about moving Smith up the to No.3, but a decision would not be made until the team assembled in Perth. Queensland batter Jack Clayton. Getty Images



The left-hander’s 449 runs at 74.83 were enough to earn him a call-up ahead of NSW’s Sam Konstas (479 runs at 68.43) and South Australia’s Jake Weatherald (509 at 56.56). Related Article Updated

Ball tampering Cricket Australia announced its Sandpapergate forum on Friday morning. It has already hit a snag “We’ve been thrilled with Sammy’s start to the year and Jake Weatherald’s been firing and back to scoring some big runs as well,” Bailey said. Lyon is among a host of casualties from last month’s tour of South Africa, with all-rounders Cooper Connolly and Beau Webster also overlooked. However, selectors have left one spot open in the squad, to be filled by a batsman following the sixth round of the Sheffield Shield, which concludes on December 6. Matt Renshaw and Travis Head look set to remain at the top of the order, while Josh Inglis is poised to add to his two Tests on home soil. Cameron Green is expected to resume bowling duties as the side’s all-rounder.



Bailey also left the door open for Cameron Bancroft to return to the Test arena, rejecting suggestions the West Australian had been overlooked in recent years because of his involvement in Sandpapergate. “I’ve articulated that to Cam on a number of occasions across the years as I think that thought has entered his mind,” Bailey said. “That has never been a discussion from our end.” Bailey was confident the fallout from the Sandpapergate revelations this month would not derail Australia’s summer. “The discussions that I’ve had with individual players and staff is that we are just excited to get to Perth and get ready for some cricket,” Bailey said. “To be honest, I think that’s where the majority of the cricket-loving public are at too.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

The hotel Risby Cove, Strahan, Tasmania Risby Cove. Check in A welcome platter of cheese and crackers awaits in the reception area. The site, which is built on the foundations of a former sawmill and is perched on the edge of Macquarie Harbour, originally belonged to Risby Timber Company. It was one of Australia’s oldest family-run firms which, from 1889, milled Huon pine. The hotel changed hands, was renovated and reopened at the end of 2025. Once the key – old school, with Huon fob – is handed over, the restfulness begins. Cue the jazz and soft-toned pendant lighting by which to sip your Josef Chromy, then wander to your suite.



The look 



In Cove Pavilion guests seeking a soak can choose from an indoor bath or an outdoor cedar hot tub. The harbour-facing deck of our Cove Pavilion features a cedar hot tub; we have a bath inside too, although the low water pressure makes for a long draw. A bioethanol fireplace is lit each evening while we’re out. A basket of board games is welcome for this stretch of early winter, but two televisions for one space is a level of extravagance I’m not convinced we need. Lighting is thoughtful and soft but there are a lot of switches, so a middle-of-the-night wake-up briefly mimics a rave with urgent, rhythmic flashes when I try to find the bedside button. Rooms feature original works by Tasmanian artists. Food + drink Risby’s serves dishes made from local seasonal produce and has a Tasmania-centric wine list.



Risby’s offers two-, three- and four-course dining and a Tasmania-centric wine list. A decadent beetroot entree is drizzled with local honey and studded with goat’s cheese; paprika-crusted tuna shines beneath pickled shaved daikon and a cloud of whipped wasabi and is best matched with zippy cocktails. A salvaged part of Strahan wharf now serves as the restaurant’s pass. An a la carte breakfast is included – expect French toast topped with brûléed banana, eggs Benedict, crunchy granola with berry compote and strong barista coffee. At Risby’s you’ll find a range of dining options and oysters from Bruny Island. Out + about We’re on the curve that leads towards Regatta Point, where the West Coast Wilderness Railway’s harbourside Strahan stop is located. Take the Cryptic Falls Express in a restored carriage behind a Drewry diesel locomotive. In premium cabins enjoy a menu curated by The Agrarian Kitchen’s Rodney Dunn, sparkling wine included, as you snake along the King River’s banks towards ancient rainforest. In town, the family theatre show The Ship That Never Was has run since 1994 and captures the history of Sarah Island; visit Sarah Island on a leisurely Gordon River Cruise.



Risby’s is located on Macquarie Harbour in Strahan, western Tasmania. Risby’s also offers 29 experiences – many inclusive and some at an additional fee, from kayak trips, crayfish-catching adventures and whisky tastings – which can be arranged with the hotel’s team before arrival. The verdict Thoughtful luxury and seclusion, with Tasmanian passion and pride in evidence at every considered juncture. Essentials



Rooms from $464, including breakfast. One of the 12 rooms is accessible. 44 The Esplanade, Strahan, Tasmania, 7468. +61 (3) 6471 7572. See risbycove.com.au The score ★★★½ Highlight Uninterrupted harbour views and the amenities on site to stay put to enjoy it.



Lowlight Related Article Tasmania Hiking a wondrous, isolated Aussie island where dreams lived and died A lack of undercover vestibules, and the sheer force of Strahan’s weather, makes jaunts between buildings a bit damp. Some ponchos or umbrellas wouldn’t go astray. The writer was a guest of Risby Cove and the West Coast Wilderness Railway.

London: British police have said the release of an unknown substance during a concert by rapper Don Toliver in Manchester last weekend was linked to attempts to commit robberies on the night of the event.

Greater Manchester Police did not provide any evidence and did not identify the substance released at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena last Sunday night (UK time) that resulted in 89 people requiring medical checks for eye and respiratory irritation. One person was taken to hospital.

The 12,000 concertgoers were evacuated soon after the incident.

People in emergency blankets after they were evacuated from the concert in Manchester last weekend. Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said something similar had occurred at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe and that police were in contact with authorities involved in those investigations. “So far, we suspect that a small group of organised criminals targeted people in the crowd to commit a series of robberies on the night,” he said.

Australian wrestling star Jermaine Haley, known by his WWE wrestling name Bronson Reed, has died due to medical complications. He was 38. World Wrestling Entertainment, the American wrestling promoter, announced Haley’s death on Saturday afternoon (Sydney time), but did not provide details. Jermaine Haley, known by his wrestling name as Bronson Reed, has died. WWE via Getty Images “WWE is devastated to announce that Jermaine Haley, also known as Bronson Reed, passed away earlier today at the age of 38 due to medical complications,” the company said. “Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.



“Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as his friends, co-workers and fans.” His death came weeks after he sustained injuries at his last performance at WWE Crown Jewel, the company’s premium wrestling live event in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on November 7. During that event, Haley was thrown onto a set of tables by fellow wrestler Oba Femi. Oba Femi in action against Bronson Reed during Crown Jewel in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. WWE via Getty Images Sports outlets reported he sustained broken ribs and a lacerated kidney following the incident, however WWE made no connection between the injuries and his death. Haley was born in Adelaide in 1988. He told The Sporting News he “dabbled in everything as a child” before getting into pro wrestling after finishing high school.



“I was always a fan of pro wrestling, since I can remember,” he told the outlet. “I had my uncle who lived with us at the time, he was a huge wrestling fan, so as a little kid at 2 to 3 years old, he was watching wrestling on TV and I guess I was sitting there watching as well. From there, I just became a fan. Related Article Wrestling WA locks in WWE for three more years, but Optus Stadium is not on the cards Matthew Farrelly, a Sydney-born professional wrestler known as Grayson Waller, paid tribute to Haley on X. “Love you brother,” he said. “Thank you for opening so many doors for myself and many others in Australian wrestling.” Australian WWE colleague Brendan Vink, known as Duke Hanson, started professional wrestling at the same time as Haley. On X, he posted: “I love you, Jermaine … Tell your people you love them.”



Haley had two stints in WWE after joining the promotion in 2019. He was released from WWE in 2021, before returning a year later. With AP Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: This film will make you think twice about your favourite children’s TV shows
World.content:
CultureMoviesCinema This film will make you think twice about your favourite children’s TV shows Nell Geraets November 28, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There is something deeply unnerving about classic children’s television shows. Productions like Here’s Humphrey or Barney & Friends display such over-the-top joy that they verge on sinister. American filmmaker Casper Kelly, creator of the mega-viral short film Too Many Cooks, first noticed that strange unease as a child watching Rankin/Bass Productions specials like Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, its stop-motion creatures “freaking him out”. Later, when his children began watching shows like Blue’s Clues, the feeling only grew. Think Barney… But a psycho killer. Roadside Attractions “The kids were very well-behaved – when a dance routine happened, they all would just start singing and dancing spontaneously, which sort of freaked me out,” Kelly says. “I was a very literal child, so I’d think, ‘How would they know to do that? Are they brainwashed? Are they being controlled?’” It was from these questions that his feature directorial debut was born. Buddy is a surreal horror-comedy about children who discover they have been trapped inside a ’90s kids’ TV show hosted by a short-tempered orange unicorn with a penchant for violence. Framed as a “knock-off Barney”, the cuddly host (voiced by Keegan-Michael Key) may initially appear jovial, but if the children refuse to play along, the consequences are deadly.



Loading “I honed in on when I was a kid watching a kid’s show … Before I had critical filters to contextualise what I was seeing. Buddy rests in an unconscious place where deep things can happen.” Many viewers have interpreted the film as an allegory for childhood predation or grooming, and the sometimes toxic environments espoused by the kids’ television industry, as was uncovered in the 2024 expose on Nickelodeon’s Dan Schneider, Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV. None of these themes are explicitly referenced in Buddy, but Kelly says he’s happy for viewers to interpret it however they wish based on their own experience with children’s content. That, he says, is the beauty of creating a film so steeped in nostalgia – everyone will connect to it differently. This isn’t your average nostalgia trip, though. Unlike the warm and fuzzies elicited from nostalgic dramas or comedies, Buddy’s nostalgia is weaponised to evoke dread and discomfort – pulling on elements in children’s TV that you always subconsciously knew were off-putting, then exaggerating them to the nth degree. Buddy takes normal cinematic nostalgia and makes it sick and twisted. Roadside Attractions





Buddy may seem jovial – just don’t get on his bad side. Roadside Attractions Buddy has since gained similar traction. After premiering at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, the film’s studio decided to promote the film by building social accounts for the unicorn, creating the impression that Buddy was a real-life long-forgotten ’90s kids’ TV mascot. Fake VHS rips and old-school commercials made some believe they remembered watching Buddy as children, thus pulling on their nostalgia before slowly trickling in split-second flashes of gore. This subverted nostalgia did so well that Buddy’s account amassed more followers on TikTok than the popular horror streamer Shudder. Though not the first cuddly-turned-creepy horror “mascot” – Five Nights at Freddy’s spawned an entire franchise off its unsettling kids’ restaurant animatronics – Buddy is arguably one of the most nuanced. Instead of a mindless killer, he’s positioned as desperate for affection, often mistaking blind compliance for love. While Buddy goes a step above, ultimately resorting to violence, he’s still an incredibly convincing, vaguely familiar children’s show mascot – and therein lies the terror. Buddy is in cinemas now. World.content:
NationalVictoriaLandslide Another McCrae home damaged as landslide strikes troubled stretch Hannah Hammoud November 28, 2026 — 2:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A home has been damaged after a fresh landslide struck McCrae on Saturday morning, renewing fears for residents living along the increasingly unstable hillside less than two years after a devastating slip destroyed another property nearby. Emergency services were called to Point Nepean Road about 8.05am on Saturday after part of the cliff face gave way, causing significant damage to an unoccupied home. The house was damaged on Saturday morning following the landslide. Nine News Multiple neighbouring properties have been evacuated as authorities assess the extent of the damage and the risk of further ground movement. An emergency warning has been issued, with residents and visitors urged to stay away from the area. Point Nepean Road and The Eyrie have been closed to traffic while emergency services respond.



Heavy rainfall across the Mornington Peninsula on Friday is believed to have contributed to the latest landslide, although the cause is yet to be confirmed. The latest incident has once again thrown the spotlight on the area’s history of instability. The damaged home is located close to where a major landslide destroyed a home in January 2025. That incident, on January 14, destroyed a three-storey property and seriously injured a council worker who was at the site and forced to jump to safety as the hillside gave way. Three other properties were damaged, and 19 properties were evacuated, with many residents facing lengthy uncertainty over when, or if, they would be able to return home.



The January 2025 incident was the largest of a series of four landslides and slips recorded in the area between November 2022 and January 2025. Related Article Exclusive

City life Home owners don’t have to pay to fix McCrae landslide, court finds An independent Board of Inquiry was subsequently established to investigate the causes of the January 2025 disaster and examine whether authorities had adequately responded to warnings about the hillside. Its final report, delivered in September 2025, found water from a burst South East Water main caused the January 2025 landslide. The inquiry also found that Mornington Peninsula Shire and South East Water had failed to take appropriate action in response to warning signs in the lead-up to the disaster.



Residents had raised concerns about large volumes of water flowing through the neighbourhood in the months before the major landslide. The January 14, 2025, landslide in McCrae resulted in the evacuation of 19 surrounding properties. In its examination of the events following an earlier slip on January 5, 2025, the inquiry found the shire had not appropriately escalated its response as water continued to infiltrate the already unstable hillside. The fresh landslide comes as authorities continue efforts to help residents displaced by the 2025 disaster return to their homes. On September 30, Mornington Peninsula Shire council announced it had approved plans to install two engineered protective barriers on council-owned land at Penny Lane.



Related Article City life Landslides occurred on McCrae cliff for 70 years, inquiry told The barriers, made from ballasted shipping containers, are intended to address risks associated with the 2022 and 2025 landslides and help three affected households return home sooner. Mornington Peninsula Shire mayor Stephen Batty said council is working closely with authorities to establish the extent of the incident. “Our immediate priority is the safety and wellbeing of those in the area, and the shire will exercise whatever regulatory powers are necessary to protect the community,” he said. “We ask that people avoid the area to ensure emergency services and authorised personnel can safely access the site and undertake their work.



“We acknowledge how distressing this will be for the McCrae community, particularly given the events of the past two years. The situation is still unfolding, and we will provide further information as it becomes available.” Authorities on the scene following the landslide on Saturday morning. Nine News Mike O’Neill, spokesperson for the McCrae Evacuated Residents Group, said it was frustrating to wake up to the news of another landslide in McCrae. “This is a bloody disgrace,” he said. “It highlights a lack of concern from the authorities.” “This is just another event – it doesn’t surprise me. The biggest question for me now is, how many houses and how many lives need to be put at risk before this is dealt with in the long term? So that we can all feel safe in our homes.”

Nearly 50 new homes will be built in Perth specifically for victims of domestic violence, it was announced on Saturday, aimed at bridging the gap between crisis accommodation and a new life away from abuse.

Domestic Violence minister Jessica Stojkovski made the announcement alongside Federal Member for Perth Patrick Gorman, saying there was a “bottleneck” in refuge accommodation.

Prevention of Family and Domestic Violence Minister Jessica Stojkovski Holly Thompson

“Quite often for women who are leaving family and domestic violence situation, the question is not whether they should leave; it’s where they can go,” she said.

“Ensuring that we have freed up crisis accommodation when somebody is leaving in that real urgent situation, and that we can move them into transitional accommodation once that urgency, that emergency situation has passed, is vitally important to ensuring the whole health of the system.”

Jack Clayton offers a chuckle and wry smile when asked to recall the moment which paved his way towards earning his Baggy Green. Cricket was not a career path he envisioned when the Brisbane Lions academy prospect pondered what missing selection in the AFL draft would mean. When he picked up the bat for the University of Queensland, he was playing third-grade and was reluctant to give up his Saturday mornings when a request to be promoted to the seconds was offered. Queensland’s Jack Clayton celebrating a Sheffield Shield century at the Gabba. Chris Hyde/Getty Images Nine years to the day when he went un-drafted, and he is on the cusp of becoming Australia’s 474th Test cricketer, having been named in the squad to face New Zealand in Perth from December 9. “I certainly never thought when I gave up my footy dream that I would be in this position nine years later. At that stage, I did think I was going to go back and play footy for that season,” Clayton said on Saturday.



Related Article Analysis

Test cricket Power rankings: The quicks and spinners primed to succeed all-star Test attack “The next season, Scott Henry – our first-grade captain, who also played for New South Wales and Queensland – told me I was going to bat three for the season, and I fell flat on my face when he said that. It’s obviously been a bit of a different journey, but one I’m really proud of.” That call-up marked a sliding doors moment for Clayton, who had initially intended to attempt an AFL revival mission through the NEAFL – now the VFL – with Aspley Hornets. “I think being out of that professional set-up with footy … and just being a normal 18, 19, 20-year-old going through uni, hanging out with mates, doing all the things uni people do, gave me a lot of perspective about life, but also where sport lies in my life,” he said. “I feel like that’s helped keep me balanced and level throughout my cricket career.”



While fellow Test contenders Sam Konstas and Jake Weatherald have fought for re-inclusion in the spotlight, Clayton has been able to slowly hone his craft free of scrutiny. In an era where T20 cricket and the smash and bash mentality at the crease reins supreme, the 27-year-old is the Test arena’s traditional throwback in the mould of his childhood idol, Mike Hussey. Building his game around solid defence on the front and back foot, while seeking low-risk scoring options, he has become the anchor of Queensland Sheffield Shield side since bursting onto the scene with a gutsy century on debut. That knock of 109 was the first instance in which he demonstrated his tendency for digging his team out of a slump. At one stage on that day in February 2022, the Bulls had slumped to 6–191, before Clayton’s defiance ground the Bulls to a first innings total of 349. His century in the 2024–25 Shield final was another instance of thriving in the pressure-cooker – combining with Jack Wildermuth (111) to overturn a 166 run first innings’ deficit to set South Australia 270 to win.



Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Lyon weighing up playing future after Test snub as replacement revealed Clayton laughed “there are plenty of those moments I’ve stuffed up too”, but paid tribute to his first-grade coach Peter Clarke – now at the helm of the Sydney Sixers WBBL side – for shaping his mindset. “He was a sport psychologist for the Australian women’s team during that time, and he was really helpful for me in developing some processes around how I go about my cricket and how I compartmentalise things mentally,” Clayton explained. “I feel like that’s really helped me to make sure I stick to the process and focus on what I need to do in those situations to try and best help the team get into a position to win games.” Clayton’s call-up comes at a time when the Australian batting line-up has been hunting reinvention, culminating in the axing of Queensland teammate Marnus Labuschagne.



Despite spending much of his career batting at No.4, Clayton is poised to assume Labuschagne’s place at No.3; a challenge he will not shy away from, with his highest score of 134 coming in that same position last year. “I’d be happy to bat anywhere for Australia, one to 11 it wouldn’t bother me at all wherever I bat,” he quipped, before revealing the frank conversations he had with Labuschagne upon the latter’s return from the ill-fated tour in South Africa. “When he [Labuschagne] came back from South Africa, there was a bit of noise around me potentially taking his spot, but he was fantastic in the way he came up to me and talked about the elephant in the room straight away. Loading “He said ‘I don’t want any angst between us, I want the best for you, and I’m proud of all the stuff you’ve done and want you to be playing Test cricket and performing, and hopefully one day we can be there together’.’



Gruelling tours to India and England will follow the New Zealand battle in 2027, and there is no guarantee 37-year-old champion Steve Smith will play on beyond that. Clayton, however, was unwilling to contemplate a reality where he spearheaded the top order long-term. “As soon as you start thinking about those things in the future or things that you can’t control, I think that’s when I’ve had failures in my life. For me, it’ll be focusing on how I prepare for the first Test and how I can get myself in a situation to get out there and score runs,” Clayton said. “It won’t be going anything past the next training session, or the first session of day one, or whatever it is. I try and keep it as simple as I can in that sense, and not look too far forward in the future, and just focus on what I can do and what I can control. “What I’ve been doing in Shield cricket has been working against good quality first-class bowlers, and even international bowlers, so I’m not changing anything about the way I prepare.” Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: Lyon weighing up playing future after Test snub as replacement revealed
World.content:
Updated SportCricketAustralian cricket Lyon weighing up playing future after Test snub as replacement revealed Tom Decent Updated November 28, 2026 — 1:50pm ,first published November 28, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australian spin great Nathan Lyon is weighing up his playing future despite being assured by chairman of selectors George Bailey he is a strong chance of touring India as part of a blockbuster five-Test series next year. The 39-year-old is considering all his options - including retirement - but won’t make a call on that in the coming days after being left out of Australia’s Test squad to face New Zealand this summer. Nathan Lyon in action during the recent Test series against South Africa. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Lyon, second only to Shane Warne on Australia’s list of Test wicket-takers, is unlikely to play in NSW’s Sheffield Shield match against Western Australia in Sydney, starting on December 3. Lyon is frustrated at losing his Test spot to West Australian off-spinner Corey Rocchiccioli, who was named in a 13-man squad on Saturday alongside uncapped Queensland batsman Jack Clayton. Clayton is poised to bat at No.3 or No.4 in the opening Test against New Zealand in Perth from December 9.



Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket Lyon set to be axed from Australia’s Test squad, as new spinner and batter get their chance Bailey rang Lyon on Thursday evening to inform him that not only would he miss the opening Test of the summer, but he was not in selectors’ plans for any of the four matches. As Bailey told reporters on Saturday, Lyon found it difficult to hide his disappointment. Bailey was adamant Lyon’s omission had nothing to do with reports that he suggested taking red confectionery frogs onto the field against Pakistan in the UAE to help artificially shine the ball during Australia’s first Test after the infamous 2018 tour of South Africa. “Understandably, it was a tough conversation for him,” Bailey said of omitting Lyon based on form. “A tough decision. Unfortunately, he just hasn’t quite had the impact over the last few games we would have liked.



Australia’s 13-man Test squad for New Zealand series Pat Cummins (NSW/Penrith Cricket Club) (c)

Scott Boland (VIC/Frankston Peninsula Cricket Club)

Alex Carey (SA/Glenelg Cricket Club)

Jack Clayton (QLD/University of Queensland Cricket Club)

Cameron Green (WA/Subiaco-Floreat Cricket Club)

Josh Hazlewood (NSW/St George Cricket Club)

Travis Head (SA/Tea Tree Gully Cricket Club)

Josh Inglis (WA/Joondalup Cricket Club)

Michael Neser (QLD/Gold Coast Cricket Club)

Matthew Renshaw (QLD/Toombul Cricket Club)

Corey Rocchiccioli (WA/University Cricket Club)

Steve Smith (NSW/Sutherland Cricket Club)

Mitchell Starc (NSW/Manly Warringah Cricket Club) *One player will be added after round six of the Sheffield Shield “We hope it’s not the end for him. We see a path. I think he can have enormous value when you project forward to India on a tour like that with his experience. “We wanted him to take some time and not rush into any decision off the back of this.” While Bailey indicated Lyon would be given time to decide on his future, a cricket source with knowledge of the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the veteran off-spinner was weighing up all options. Lyon is contracted to Cricket Australia until the middle of next year and has spoken previously of his desire to return to India and win an away Ashes series in England.



But having been left out of Test XIs in Kingston, Brisbane and Gqeberha over the past 18 months, Lyon must decide whether he has the appetite to fight his way back into the side. The decision also leaves Lyon’s hopes of a farewell Test at the SCG, afforded to David Warner and Usman Khawaja in recent years, hanging by a thread. If Rocchiccioli struggles against New Zealand, selectors could recall Lyon with a view to getting some cricket into him before the India tour, should he play on. That does seem unlikely given the conversations behind closed doors. WA spinner Corey Rocchiccioli has been named in Australia’s Test squad. Getty Images Australia are expected to take at least three frontline spinners to India, where they have not won a Test series since 2004. While selectors have the flexibility to change the squad throughout the four-Tests, the decision to overlook Lyon for the summer represents a changing of the guard in Australia’s spin-bowling ranks.



Bailey said Rocchiccioli’s consistency at domestic level, his ability to generate bounce and the abundance of left-handers in New Zealand’s squad were factors in his promotion ahead of a likely Test debut in either Perth or Adelaide. Rocchiccioli has taken 18 wickets at 33.88 from five Shield matches this season, taking his overall first-class tally to 205 wickets at 30.62. “We’ve got some pretty strong spin depth at the moment within Australia and Roc obviously gets a chance here,” Bailey said. “With Todd Murphy, Matt Kuhnemann and Mitch Swepson, I think we’ve got some nice depth within our spin bowling ranks. They have been working hard in the background as Gaz has had this incredible career.” Meanwhile, Clayton’s selection is a reward for a prolific start to the domestic summer and puts the Queenslander on the cusp of a Test debut at No.3 or No.4, depending on where selectors believe Steve Smith is best suited. Bailey said “general discussions” had taken place about moving Smith up the to No.3, but a decision would not be made until the team assembled in Perth. Queensland batter Jack Clayton. Getty Images



The left-hander’s 449 runs at 74.83 were enough to earn him a call-up ahead of NSW’s Sam Konstas (479 runs at 68.43) and South Australia’s Jake Weatherald (509 at 56.56). Related Article Updated

Ball tampering Cricket Australia announced its Sandpapergate forum on Friday morning. It has already hit a snag “We’ve been thrilled with Sammy’s start to the year and Jake Weatherald’s been firing and back to scoring some big runs as well,” Bailey said. Lyon is among a host of casualties from last month’s tour of South Africa, with all-rounders Cooper Connolly and Beau Webster also overlooked. However, selectors have left one spot open in the squad, to be filled by a batsman following the sixth round of the Sheffield Shield, which concludes on December 6. Matt Renshaw and Travis Head look set to remain at the top of the order, while Josh Inglis is poised to add to his two Tests on home soil. Cameron Green is expected to resume bowling duties as the side’s all-rounder.



Bailey also left the door open for Cameron Bancroft to return to the Test arena, rejecting suggestions the West Australian had been overlooked in recent years because of his involvement in Sandpapergate. “I’ve articulated that to Cam on a number of occasions across the years as I think that thought has entered his mind,” Bailey said. “That has never been a discussion from our end.” Bailey was confident the fallout from the Sandpapergate revelations this month would not derail Australia’s summer. “The discussions that I’ve had with individual players and staff is that we are just excited to get to Perth and get ready for some cricket,” Bailey said. “To be honest, I think that’s where the majority of the cricket-loving public are at too.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

★★★½ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews Risby Cove is a boutique experience in wild corner of Tasmania Riley Wilson November 28, 2026 — 1:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The hotel Risby Cove, Strahan, Tasmania Risby Cove. Check in A welcome platter of cheese and crackers awaits in the reception area. The site, which is built on the foundations of a former sawmill and is perched on the edge of Macquarie Harbour, originally belonged to Risby Timber Company. It was one of Australia’s oldest family-run firms which, from 1889, milled Huon pine. The hotel changed hands, was renovated and reopened at the end of 2025. Once the key – old school, with Huon fob – is handed over, the restfulness begins. Cue the jazz and soft-toned pendant lighting by which to sip your Josef Chromy, then wander to your suite.



The look 



In Cove Pavilion guests seeking a soak can choose from an indoor bath or an outdoor cedar hot tub. The harbour-facing deck of our Cove Pavilion features a cedar hot tub; we have a bath inside too, although the low water pressure makes for a long draw. A bioethanol fireplace is lit each evening while we’re out. A basket of board games is welcome for this stretch of early winter, but two televisions for one space is a level of extravagance I’m not convinced we need. Lighting is thoughtful and soft but there are a lot of switches, so a middle-of-the-night wake-up briefly mimics a rave with urgent, rhythmic flashes when I try to find the bedside button. Rooms feature original works by Tasmanian artists. Food + drink Risby’s serves dishes made from local seasonal produce and has a Tasmania-centric wine list.



Risby’s offers two-, three- and four-course dining and a Tasmania-centric wine list. A decadent beetroot entree is drizzled with local honey and studded with goat’s cheese; paprika-crusted tuna shines beneath pickled shaved daikon and a cloud of whipped wasabi and is best matched with zippy cocktails. A salvaged part of Strahan wharf now serves as the restaurant’s pass. An a la carte breakfast is included – expect French toast topped with brûléed banana, eggs Benedict, crunchy granola with berry compote and strong barista coffee. At Risby’s you’ll find a range of dining options and oysters from Bruny Island. Out + about We’re on the curve that leads towards Regatta Point, where the West Coast Wilderness Railway’s harbourside Strahan stop is located. Take the Cryptic Falls Express in a restored carriage behind a Drewry diesel locomotive. In premium cabins enjoy a menu curated by The Agrarian Kitchen’s Rodney Dunn, sparkling wine included, as you snake along the King River’s banks towards ancient rainforest. In town, the family theatre show The Ship That Never Was has run since 1994 and captures the history of Sarah Island; visit Sarah Island on a leisurely Gordon River Cruise.



Risby’s is located on Macquarie Harbour in Strahan, western Tasmania. Risby’s also offers 29 experiences – many inclusive and some at an additional fee, from kayak trips, crayfish-catching adventures and whisky tastings – which can be arranged with the hotel’s team before arrival. The verdict Thoughtful luxury and seclusion, with Tasmanian passion and pride in evidence at every considered juncture. Essentials



Rooms from $464, including breakfast. One of the 12 rooms is accessible. 44 The Esplanade, Strahan, Tasmania, 7468. +61 (3) 6471 7572. See risbycove.com.au The score ★★★½ Highlight Uninterrupted harbour views and the amenities on site to stay put to enjoy it.



Lowlight Related Article Tasmania Hiking a wondrous, isolated Aussie island where dreams lived and died A lack of undercover vestibules, and the sheer force of Strahan’s weather, makes jaunts between buildings a bit damp. Some ponchos or umbrellas wouldn’t go astray. The writer was a guest of Risby Cove and the West Coast Wilderness Railway.

London: British police have said the release of an unknown substance during a concert by rapper Don Toliver in Manchester last weekend was linked to attempts to commit robberies on the night of the event.

Greater Manchester Police did not provide any evidence and did not identify the substance released at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena last Sunday night (UK time) that resulted in 89 people requiring medical checks for eye and respiratory irritation. One person was taken to hospital.

The 12,000 concertgoers were evacuated soon after the incident.

People in emergency blankets after they were evacuated from the concert in Manchester last weekend. Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said something similar had occurred at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe and that police were in contact with authorities involved in those investigations. “So far, we suspect that a small group of organised criminals targeted people in the crowd to commit a series of robberies on the night,” he said.

World.title: A day in the life of NZ's 'chicken whisperer'
World.content:
Audio player for " How do I tell a scam from a real bank call? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/business/2856939%2Fa-day-in-the-life-of-nz-s-chicken-whisperer

How do I tell a scam from a real bank call? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

Nathan Williams describes himself as a "chicken whisperer".

While he runs the company, the chief executive and founder of eg. Free Range Eggs is also out in the shed every night, lifting each bird up to its spot in the bird aviary, so no-one sleeps on the floor.

"You can pet them and they'll all talk to each other, and the whole shed will go dead quiet and they all go to sleep, and the lights go off," he said. "We treat them like pets.

"Someone is in the shed 16 hours a day. A human is in there with them, picking up eggs or any injured birds, checking feed and water, ventilation and lighting.

"There's always something to do."

He said the industry perception was that free-range farming was harder than cage farming.

"They do go outside, you've got to get them all back. There are hawks and wild cats or whatever outside.

"To get them back inside and up on to the bird aviaries, what I do is create their daily routine in where they lay eggs, where they eat, where they sleep.

"Where they sleep every night is where they'll stay for the rest of their life cycle. If I go into the shed at 9.30 tonight, the lights go out and I might be lucky to find 10 chickens on the floor.

"They all do it themselves now."

Chicken whisperers - and chicken chasers - are some of the unusual roles that Kathleen Webber, founder of salary benchmarking platform LiveRem, has noticed among the salary data.

Others include a thinner - who picks fruit off trees so the rest grow bigger - a poultry boner, hatchery driver, cheese quality controller, water spider - who keeps a factoryline stocked - and bingo co-ordinator.

"When someone says they're a water spider or a chicken chaser, you naturally want to know more," she said.

Nathan Williams runs the largest free-range farm in the country. He plans to triple in size. EG. FREE RANGE EGGS

"The names are memorable, but behind each one is a practical job that an employer needs done. Most of us experience these jobs through the end result - food on the supermarket shelf, electricity at home or a production line running smoothly.

"We rarely think about all the different people and roles that make that possible.

"One of the fascinating things about working with pay data is seeing the sheer variety of work people do. Even within a familiar industry, there are specialist roles many of us have never heard of.

"There's a useful careers lesson here - don't judge a job by its title. Look at what the person actually does, the skills involved and where that experience could take you.

"You might never have considered becoming a cheese quality controller or a drone pilot asset inspector. Sometimes, discovering that a job exists is the first step towards finding work that interests you."

Williams said finding staff was hard, with a lack of training available, which made it a hard industry to break into.

"It is very labour intensive, and not many people like being dirty and sweaty, and scratched by chickens all day. A lot of people have a fear of chickens as well, especially when you see 30,000 in the shed.

"It's not for everybody. Chickens originate from dinosaurs, they're like T-rexes.

"They are very temperamental, and they'll get a read on your body language or your heartrate. If you're panicking, they all start panicking.

"If I'm calm and relaxed, then they all are. You can't cause them any stress, because they're birds, and they'll start flying and smashing into everything."

Williams said he could not imagine doing anything else.

"I have 120,000 chickens, the largest free-range farm in the country, and I plan to be three times the size in the next 3-4 years. It is a seven-day-a-week operation from 5.30 in the morning until 11 o'clock at night.

"You get a hundred thousand eggs the next day, no matter what, it doesn't stop. There's no getting out of it.

"It's a lifestyle I chose for myself, unfortunately... but I love it. Challenging though.

"Every day, I'm like, 'Why am I doing this to myself?', but then I get back up the next day and go again."

World.title: Why is my gas so expensive? Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, 'Money with Susan Edmunds'.

For several years now, I have been battling the principle behind Genesis Energy requiring every residential LPG customer to rent two 45kg cylinders, however little gas they use. Genesis makes no exceptions. For careful, low-use households, that means paying more per kilogram to rent the cylinders than to buy the gas, at around $179 a bottle. I know of no other household service that makes customers pay for more than they know they need: for example no one is made to rent a second fibre line.

The policy treats low-use customers' properties as a storage facility for unwanted empty cylinders, while charging them monthly rent for the privilege. It leaves frontline complaints teams reciting the rulebook, with no apparent mandate to question whether the policy is fair.

As a semi-retired person living alone, one cylinder lasts me about 18 months. I have an open fire and electricity for other heating and cooking. I use LPG mainly for a gas hob; it is also connected to a gas fireplace in a separate room that I use once or twice a year. I pay $138 a year to rent the two cylinders and use about 30kg of gas a year, so the rental alone costs me about $4.60 for every kilogram of gas I use. A household using 10 bottles a year (450kg) pays exactly the same $138, which works out at about 31 cents a kilogram. My second cylinder has been empty since late 2022. Genesis refused to collect it in 2023, and this month confirmed in writing that rental applies "regardless of whether both cylinders are actively being used". When I challenged it, I was told I was free to go elsewhere.

I thought it sounded very odd that you're in this situation so I approached Genesis.

A spokesperson told me that the company is sorry that this has taken so long to resolve.

"We too often explained our standard product and the reasons for it without properly considering whether it was suitable for [the customer's] needs."

It said its standard LPG service used two 45kg cylinders to offer continuity of supply, so a customer could use one cylinder while arranging a replacement for the other.

"This reduces the risk of a customer running out of gas when they need it most. Changing an existing installation to use one cylinder isn't as simple as disconnecting the second; it needs to be assessed to ensure it remains safe and suitable.

"We don't have a final solution for [the customer] today, but we're continuing to work through her situation. [She] has kindly agreed to share her perspective with our product team, which will directly inform our review of how we support low-use customers and how clearly we explain who our standard service suits. We're also looking at how we can improve the way we listen to customers' individual circumstances and use their feedback to identify opportunities to improve our products and services."

I know that your concern is primarily with the principle of the issue but I think in this instance it could be that the most useful solution is to take up the suggestion to go elsewhere for your gas.

Paul Fuge, who is general manager of Powerswitch, says most people who are using gas only for cooking can switch to a barbecue-style gas bottle that they can then manage themselves. He said the alternative would be to try to get off gas completely, although that is not practical in some cases.

I've just bought Allbirds in their Black Friday sale. I've had several pairs before, same style, and bought the same size. These ones are slightly different and are too big! But their website says all Black Friday sales are final sale and can't be refunded or exchanged. Is that fair?

Consumer NZ says, under the Consumer Guarantees Act, a retailer isn't obliged to provide a refund or exchange if a consumer changes their mind after they've purchased a product. However, a retailer still has to provide a remedy when a product is not of acceptable quality or isn't fit for purpose, including products that are on sale.

"This is a particularly interesting one because if the size and style has been purchased previously then the person who's bought them could reasonably expect a new pair in the same size and style will fit. We recommend they reach out to Allbirds and explain the situation - see if they'll offer an exchange of size."

My question relates to New Zealand Post and stamps. I had assumed stamps were legal tender. Having bought a birthday card a little late, I wanted to get it couriered. I knew this would cost more, so I placed two stamps ($3.60 each) on the card, then went to the NZ Post Outlet where I live, and asked to pay the difference to have the card couriered. The courier was to be $9.20 they told me. The difference would then be $2. However, they refused. Can NZ Post legally refuse to accept stamps as payment?

NZ Post says whether stamps can be used as a payment for its services depends on the type of service being purchased and whether the NZ Post outlet has the technology required to issue a tracking barcode.

"In this specific case, we would need more information about the service the customer was trying to purchase and the location they visited to understand why they were unable to use stamps as payment."

World.title: Amount of wastewater overflow not known after issue at Wellington treatment plant
World.content:
This story has been updated after Tiaki Wai provided more accurate information

Wellington's water authority says a recent wastewater overflow was caused by a problem with the water treatment plant's UV disinfection system.

The failure occurred at the Wellington Wastewater Treatment Plant at about 3am Saturday morning and led to a discharge of treated wastewater that emerged near the mouth of Karori Stream.

The authority, Tiaki Wai, said the plant was now operating as normal and it was working to establish the cause.

There was also a failure at the Western UV Weir Gate on Friday afternoon led to partially treated water being discharged in the Karori Stream between 12:40pm and 4:37pm.

Tiaki Wai said it did not yet know the volume of wastewater discharged in either event.

People are being advised to stay out of the water in the immediate vicinity of the Karori Stream outfall pipe into Cook Strait - four kilometres northwest of Red Rocks, over the weekend.
