World.title: Confidence and supply most sensible course for Opportunity, says former United Future leader Peter Dunne
World.content:
Former United Future leader Peter Dunne believes a confidence and supply arrangement is the most sensible course of action for the Opportunity Party.

Friday's official results showed the coalition needs Opportunity's support to form a government, or risk a hung Parliament and the possibility of another election.

While the leaders have not been meeting on Saturday, RNZ understands staff-to-staff meetings have taken place, including between New Zealand First and National's chiefs of staff.

Opportunity remains open to a coalition, confidence and supply deal, or sitting on the cross benches.

Dunne, who negotiated five confidence and supply agreements with both Labour-led and National-led governments, did not think the outcome would be a four-way formal coalition.

"I suspect we're going to get a form of confidence and supply arrangement, which means that Opportunity would give the government support on confidence and supply in some of its key policies, but be free to go whichever way it felt on other policies, which would give it some flexibility not to support initiatives from either ACT or New Zealand First or even National that it didn't didn't agree with."

Peter Dunne. RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

Dunne said confidence and supply would give Opportunity the advantage of being part of the government, and therefore able to be involved in key decisions, but without it being so tied that it was simply seen as another arm.

"That still doesn't free them entirely. They still have to carve out their own niche and agenda. And I know in United Future's case, for instance, we frequently voted against both the Labour-led government and the National-led government on matters that weren't covered by our confidence and supply agreement, and which we disagreed with them on, and yet there was never any threat to the stability of government."

The challenge for a confidence and supply partner was differentiating itself so that its voters saw it was providing stable government while also achieving significant policy wins, Dunne said.

"It may mean you swallow a couple of dead rats along the way to get those things, but you've got to promote your achievements, being stability and policy gains, alongside the things that you might not find that palatable."

Sitting on the cross benches and requiring the government to require its support on a bill-by-bill basis was also an option.

"It would mean probably either abstaining or supporting on confidence and supply only, and everything else being negotiable. That's one option, but it does reduce their leverage a little bit, because if they've given support for confidence and supply, then the government may well feel it can go ahead anyway and take its chances on other stuff," Dunne said.

"So maybe that's an option for them, but I think probably a confidence and supply agreement with a few wins along the way might be a better choice."

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong did not rule out the possibility of sending the country back to the polls if a deal could not be reached.

But Dunne did not think there was much public appetite or tolerance for another election, and voters would not want instability.

World.title: Election result raises questions about fairness of electoral process, political scientist says
World.content:
A Victoria University political scientist says the election result has raised multiple questions about the fairness of the country's electoral processes.

The final count has deadlocked Parliament, leaving Christopher Luxon reliant on Opportunity to avoid a return to the polls.

Dr Lara Greaves said electoral rule changes, the problem of parliamentary overhang, disparate party donations and even the timing of the election could all be seen as compromising how well the next government actually reflected the country's political will.

"I guess that's the task going forward, to figure that out. It then becomes a bit of a vibe test as to whether the public believes that is a legitimate result that we can go off," Greaves said.

Greaves said electoral rule changes which prevented voter enrolment less than 13 days out from the election effectively suppressed votes that could have altered the outcome.

She said the fact that there were nearly 200,000 less special votes could be interpreted as a consequence of the barriers to voting put in place by the change.

"We have had a similar number of voters as last election. There's population increase, there's more people ageing into voting, there are more people migrating to New Zealand [and] more people eligible to vote. So what happened to those 200,000 people that are not accounted for in the results?" Greaves said.

ActionStation Aotearoa director Kassie Hartendorp. Supplied

ActionStation Aotearoa director Kassie Hartendorp said the electoral rule changes locked out voters that would have typically supported left wing parties.

Hartendorp said young voters, Māori and Pacific communities were overrepresented in those likely to have been caught out by the changes.

"Over the last decade we have been moving closer and closer to making it easier for people to vote and the question we have to ask is 'why did the current government change the rules to make it harder for people to vote?'," Hartendorp said.

Hartendorp said the changes had further disenfranchised voters at a time when trust in the democratic process was already diminished.

"A lot of people simply pay attention to elections when it gets close to the day and, as a result, about 200,000 people did not cast a vote and we've got a marginal election [where] only thousands of votes could've made a difference to the outcome," Hartendorp said.

World.title: High-heel skipping and handbag throwing: Perth's queer sports history uncovered
World.content:
Competitive handbag throwing and high-heel skipping were once acts of political defiance in Perth.

Both disciplines featured in what was originally known as the city's 'Gay Olympics', which ran annually from 1979 to 1999 to raise money for gay and lesbian charities.

They event also pushed for law reform at a time when consensual homosexual sex between men was still illegal in Western Australia; the decriminalisation of which only began in 1990.

The games were a colourful way of bringing the LGBTQIA+ community together. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

Volunteers at the West Pride Archives have been sifting the event's history ahead of Perth hosting the 2030 International Gay Games.

Jo Darbyshire, co-convenor of West Pride Archives said Perth's original games had a strong political edge.

"Being visible out in the community and not being shamed was a huge element to (them)," she said.

Australia's longest-running gay nightclub, Connections, had a team base at the games. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

"We were still fighting for gay law reform, for gay men in particular to be able to have sex with other men without being harassed by the police or charged or considered dirty and deviant."

Marches and colourful floats were part of the parade. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

The games galvanised the community, but fundraising was also a key part with money going towards things including the telephone bill for the Gay Lesbian Counselling Service.

The games were held in Perth from 1979 until 1999. (Supplied: Tim Grant/ State Library of WA)

"That sort of power over helping our own communities enabled us to have the courage to really push for gay law reform and equality in the law," she said.

" We refused to just roll over and die. "

'Winners with Muscles' receiving an award from Holly Wood at the McGillivray Oval in1983. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

Tim Grant photographed the event in the 1980s, and said it was a unique chance to document his community, as it was forbidden to take photos inside bars and clubs at the time.

"It was safe and one the few large-scale spectaculars that my local community could ever have at the time," he said.

Costumes and fashion played a big role in the games and the community. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

"I felt I had no restraints on what I could photograph on the day, as I was a known face and just a part of the scenery."

The Girls of Head Office Women’s Team #2 at the Opening Parade in 1982. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

International Gay Games

Ray Currell, 78, said the local event was "very important" for the community.

"It was great, we had high-heel skip, the handbag throw and then there were some serious events," he said,

" [The games] meant freedom. I've always been gay, I've never hidden the fact. "

West Pride Archives volunteer Sophie Herbert and Ray Currell hold his badges from international Gay Games. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Currell also helped organise the first Perth team of around 30 members to participate in the New York Gay Games in 1994, which coincided with the 25th anniversary of the Stonewall Riots.

Team Perth went to New York for the Gay Games in the 1990s. (Supplied: West Pride Archives)

The Gay Games do not require any qualifications for participants.

"As long as you could afford to get there and compete, they let you," Currell said.

Held every four years, Currell competed in five Gay Games and said he would still compete if his body allowed him.

Team Perth participated at the Sydney Gay Games in 2002. (Supplied: Adrian Lily and Ray Currell)

Perth to hold 2030 Gay Games

Perth will host the international Gay Games for the first time in 2030, which is expected to attract thousands of people.

At the 2026 Valencia Gay Games, more than 50 Western Australia participants formed the Australian contingent.

It is expected to be far larger when it's Perth's turn to host.

Ray Currell participated in five international Gay Games for bowling. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Sophie Herbert, volunteer at West Pride Archives, said it was "heartwarming and inspiring" to discover the light side of Perth's LGBTQIA+ history.

"They were very brave in the way that it was just people existing and going out and having fun — but just by doing that was an act of protest in itself," she said.

"Although there was so much awful stuff happening at that time, people were resisting in their own way and that's really inspiring."

She said she hopes the Gay Games sparks the local event to be resurrected and encouraged people to donate their photos and medals to the West Pride Archives ahead of the 2030 Games.

World.title: Nathan Lyon axed as Australia names Test squad
World.content:
Corey Rocchiccioli has ended Nathan Lyon's 13-year reign as Australia's first-choice spinner, with the veteran tweaker one of three players axed for the Test series against New Zealand.

Selectors on Saturday unveiled a 13-man squad for the home summer, with spinner Rocchiccioli and Queensland batter Jack Clayton named in their first Test squads.

Lyon, Cooper Connolly and Marnus Labuschagne are all gone from the team that lost a series decider to South Africa in Cape Town just four weeks ago.

Steve Smith is fit again and will return.

Australia Test squad vs New Zealand Pat Cummins (captain), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Jack Clayton, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Michael Neser, Matthew Renshaw, Corey Rocchiccioli, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc

Beau Webster's future also appears clouded, missing out on the squad entirely after being dropped for the Cape Town loss after playing Australia's previous five Tests.

The omission of Connolly and Webster means Clayton is every chance of debuting in a reconfigured top seven, after averaging 74.83 in the Sheffield Shield this season.

Selectors have left the door open for another player to come into the group, with Cricket Australia confirming a 14th man will be added after next weekend's Sheffield Shield round.

There is also nothing stopping selectors changing their squad between Tests, given it is a home summer.

But still the most seismic decision of all comes with Rocchiccioli's selection ahead of Lyon, the nation's second leading wicket-taker of all time.

Lyon has been Australia's first-choice spinner since being recalled to the Test side midway through the 2013 Ashes, after briefly being dropped for Ashton Agar.

He has also formed part of every Australian Test squad since his debut tour of Sri Lanka midway through 2011.

At age 39, there are now serious questions over his future in the Test side.

Jack Clayton drawing on AFL experience Jack Clayton says missing out on the AFL draft has taught him how to deal with the pressure of chasing a Test cricket debut for Australia.

Lyon has made clear he wants to play in next year's tours of India and England, and as it stands he remains determined to fight back into the side.

He took six wickets at an average of 43.67 in Australia's most recent series loss to South Africa, where he was left out for the second Test in Gqeberha.

The 145-Test veteran has since returned to the Sheffield Shield and taken seven wickets 43.28 for NSW across two matches.

"Nathan has not quite had the impact we would like with the ball in recent matches," chief selector George Bailey said.

"We also know he has an extraordinary record and his experience, knowledge and skill can still be valuable to the program we have moving forward."

Lyon's axing also calls into question whether Test cricket's most successful bowling quartet in history will take to the field together again, alongside Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc.

Rocchiccioli, meanwhile, has been on the fringe of Australia's squads in recent years.

The 29-year-old has taken 18 wickets at 33.88 for Western Australia this summer, and showed his all-round ability with a century against Tasmania last week.

Whether he debuts in Perth remains to be seen, with Australia every chance of playing Scott Boland as one of four quicks.

"Corey has been a strong performer in domestic cricket for the past few seasons and has traits that are well suited to Australian conditions," Bailey said.

AAP

World.title: MotoGP world champion Marquez announces shock retirement
World.content:
Marc Marquez will take his final bow in Valencia after the eight-time MotoGP champion announced on Friday that he would retire following the 2026 season finale, ending one of motorcycle racing's greatest careers.

The Spaniard made the announcement days after wrapping up a record-equalling eighth premier-class title in Portugal, drawing him level with Giacomo Agostini.

"Thank you to everyone who's been part of the journey. I hope you've enjoyed it as much as I have. This will be my last race in MotoGP. We made history," Marquez said in a video recorded in the Valencia garage.

Loading Instagram content

The announcement came as a surprise after Marquez, who won six MotoGP titles with Honda before joining Ducati, signed a contract extension with the Italian team earlier this year that was due to run until 2028.

The 33-year-old said he decided to retire at last month's Japanese Grand Prix after the physical and mental toll of repeated injuries and operations began to weigh heavily on him.

"Sometimes you need to understand the situation, but it's true that the situation this year was on the limit," Marquez said.

"When I signed the contract in March, as always, I was super optimistic and I didn't know that I would have another surgery on my right shoulder (in May)."

Marquez said he had begun to "feel the fear" despite remaining determined to compete and had also been troubled by brief recurrences of double vision after the Indonesian and French grands prix.

He recovered within days on both occasions but said the episodes made him more cautious.

"It was one of the main reasons why I controlled the risk and why I crashed less this second part of the season," he added.

Marquez had been expected to lead MotoGP into its new 850cc era, with compatriot Pedro Acosta's arrival at the factory Ducati team viewed as a symbolic passing of the torch.

There were tears in the Ducati garage and among the crowd when fans at the Circuit Ricardo Tormo were told the Spaniard would be competing in his final race this weekend.

Jorge Martin, his main rival for the 2026 title, appeared stunned, while Marquez's brother Alex, who had been told of the decision during the Japanese Grand Prix, watched with a sombre expression.

From rookie champion to all-time great

Marquez swept into MotoGP in 2013 and won the title at his first attempt, becoming the youngest premier-class world champion at the age of 20.

By 2019, he had amassed six championships with Honda and appeared virtually unbeatable, a blur of orange and red tearing through the field.

Everything changed at the opening race of the 2020 season in Jerez, where he crashed and broke his arm.

The injury began the darkest period of his career. Marquez underwent four operations, abandoned several comeback attempts and suffered blurred vision, all while trying to push an underperforming Honda bike far beyond its limits.

He later spoke of wondering whether continuing was worth the pain as speculation about his retirement intensified.

Instead, Marquez took the decision to leave Honda and make the switch to Gresini Racing, which was using year-old Ducati machinery.

He slowly rediscovered his belief, ending a 1,043-day wait for victory in Aragon before securing the factory Ducati seat that would change everything.

"I had my second life (after leaving Honda), and I enjoyed my second life in MotoGP," Marquez said.

In 2025, Marquez claimed his seventh MotoGP crown in Japan, a feat Acosta likened to basketball great Michael Jordan's return from baseball to lead the Chicago Bulls to another NBA title.

Erasing a 102-point deficit

What followed in 2026 was perhaps even more extraordinary as Marquez overturned a 102-point deficit to retain the championship.

After failing to win early in the season and then crashing in France, he underwent surgery on his shoulder and a fractured foot, missing his home grand prix while his rivals collected victories and points.

He sat eighth in the standings but won six of the next nine rounds, as Aprilia rivals Martin and Marco Bezzecchi faltered, before sealing the title in Portugal with a round to spare.

If his seventh championship was his most emotional, the eighth cemented his place among the sport's greats and was marked by a celebration rich in symbolism.

Marquez climbed a staircase as the silhouette of a goat, shorthand for "greatest of all time", appeared on a screen behind him before Agostini presented him with a commemorative golden helmet.

Reuters

World.title: Wallabies end 2026 with massive loss to Ireland in London
World.content:
Wallabies coach Les Kiss admits his side has "work to do" after finishing their 2026 campaign with a 38-14 defeat to Ireland in the Nations Championship at Twickenham.

With the Rugby World Cup in Australia less than 12 months away, the result in London saw the Wallabies end the Test season with a 6-7-1 (win-loss-draw) record.

They finished sixth in the Nations Championship, one spot behind Ireland.

Trailing 17-7 at half-time, the Wallabies were made to pay for several wasted attacking opportunities when camped in Ireland's territory.

They earned repeated entries inside the Irish 22, but a Kalani Thomas try was all they could show for their efforts in the second half.

Ireland, on the other hand, crossed for three second-half tries, a tally which included a double to reserve forward James McNabney.

The Wallabies, ranked seventh in the world, lost five of their last six Tests for the year.

A win over world champions South Africa in September was a rare highlight for Kiss's troops.

"Every team above us [on the world rankings], bar one, we haven't been able to beat," Kiss told Stan Sport.

"We've got work to do."

Irish reserve James McNabney scored a late double in the win over the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Seb Daly)

The Wallabies opened the scoring against Ireland in the 21st minute following Jeremy Williams's converted try.

World number two Ireland, who was coming off a 20-17 win over the Springboks in Dublin, replied on the scoreboard with tries to Robbie Henshaw and Nick Timoney.

Sam Prendergast converted both and added a penalty goal on the stroke of half-time to establish Ireland's 10-point lead at the break.

Robert Baloucoune scored Ireland's third straight try early in the second half and following Prendergast's conversion, the Wallabies were trailing 24-7.

Thomas's try, and Carter Gordon's conversion, closed the gap, but McNabney's brace inside the final 10 minutes of the match helped ice Ireland's winning margin.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Roos are 'finally able to say' the words they have refused all season
World.content:
All season the North Melbourne AFLW side was not allowed to use the word "three-peat".

The team came into the year as back-to-back premiers and outright favourites for the flag. They started the finals series as minor premiers, having lost just one game (to Hawthorn), their first defeat in three years.

Roos create AFLW history with three-peat North Melbourne defeats Melbourne by 26 points in the grand final to claim a historic third consecutive AFLW premiership.

For the duration of the year, the AFLW world was talking about the Kangaroos' incoming third consecutive flag. But not the Roos themselves.

As Jasmine Garner said post-game, it's a cliche as old as football, but one that's tried and tested: treat the season as one game at a time.

Then the siren sounded. They had defeated Melbourne by 26 points under lights at Princes Park after beating Brisbane the two years prior.

And they let the emotions overrun them.

North Melbourne is the first side in AFLW history to claim three consecutive premierships. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

All Australian Erika O'Shea said it was one of "the best moments of my life, 100 per cent".

"Oh my god, it's the most surreal feeling,"O'Shea told ABC Sport.

"Nothing will ever feel like this. I started crying instantly when I heard that siren.

"I think a sigh of relief, but also just all the hard work that we've done during the year, and yeah … three-peat. I can't believe it.

"To finally be able to say it with a smile is the best thing ever."

Head coach Darren Crocker said it was up to the AFLW community and media to decide whether the side was a dynasty or not, but he was pretty sure the consecutive flags made for one.

He said the 2024 flag — the first AFLW cup for North Melbourne — meant a lot. The second broke new ground when the first side became the first to go back-to-back in AFLW history.

And the three-peat felt pretty good.

Even opposition captain Kate Hore said "we'll talking about this team forever".

Jasmine Garner won her second best-on-ground medal on Friday night. (Getty: Daniel Pockett/AFL Photos)

Garner said this year was more difficult than last.

"I always had the belief that we were good enough to do it, but you know, this year, it hasn't been perfect," she said.

"We've lost one game in 42, but we've been challenged. We've had injuries. We've had different hurdles pop up along the way.

"But we felt this year we were kind of building slowly and we kept our best footy to the finals. I think that's what got us over, our experience and our calmness.

"I reckon this final series has been the best it's ever been, but it's just so good for women's footy. Just really proud of the group."

The players were finally able to let the emotions flow after a challenging but near flawless season. (Getty: Daniel Pockett/AFL Photos)

Kangaroos forward Kate Shierlaw said this win made her the most emotional of the three.

"I'm very overwhelmed with emotions. Relief, excited," Shierlaw said.

"It's just like a lot of hard work over four or five years … just Kearns [Emma Kearney, North Melbourne stalwart defender and Shierlaw's partner] and I having a great time out here, living our dreams. Three in a row."

Shierlaw and Kearney hinted at possible retirement. Shierlaw said she would "talk to the club" and Kearney told the broadcast she may have played her last game.

World.title: Australia 'have to be better,' humbled by England at rain-soaked Gabba
World.content:
England has taken a 2-1 series lead in its T20I series against Australia with another dominant victory on a rainy Friday evening at the Gabba.

Australia was bowled out for just 108 in 16.5 overs, its lowest ever T20I score on home soil when batting first.

The 23,536 Gabba fans may have feared whether, after three superb Sheffield Shield games went down to the wire this week, they would see a second lopsided white-ball contest in as many matches following England's dominant victory at Carrara on Tuesday.

And although Riley Meredith (3-30) and Billy Stanlake (0-46) provided some jeopardy with their own vicious pace, the result was never in doubt.

"A very disappointing night. We have to own that," Mitch Marsh said.

"Some of our [shot] selection was not to up to it tonight, but I said to to this young group at the start of the series I don't want them to fear making mistakes.

"Probably tonight we needed to be more calculated and understand the conditions we were playing in.

"That was a belting wicket - as good as the Gabba can get - so no excuses. We have to be better."

England comfortably chased down a revised target of 93 with 43 balls to spare, sealing a seven-wicket victory.

Jamie Overton was irresistible, bowling with pace and ferocity that Australian bowlers have terrorised Englishmen with for decades at this ground, taking a career-best 5-12.

Jordan Cox scored an unbeaten 33. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

England has traditionally been carved up by Australian quicks at the Gabba, but this time the shoe was on the other foot.

England won the toss and bowled first, with former Australia coach Darren Lehmann saying on ABC Radio that "Australia will be looking for 220, maybe more," and were on track early despite Mitch Marsh being caught at mid-on for 11 off Dawson's bowling.

Jake Fraser-McGurk and Sam Harper both hit out, smashing five sixes between them before both fell in consecutive overs; Harper for 26 off 14 balls and Fraser-McGurk becoming Overton's first victim after an 11-ball 22.

Nikhil Chaudhary, scorer of 66 and 45 in his last two innings for Australia, forwent the power displayed by his colleagues to deliver a range of delightful dabs with a delicacy and deftness at odds with the slogging shown elsewhere.

Overton wasn't having a bar of it, though.

The 32-year-old Devonian aimed a sharp bouncer that cracked into Chaudhary's helmet in one over, and thumped Tim David on the forearm with a 142km/h the next.

The next ball, David (6) was out, hooking a 145km/h snorter straight to Henry Crocombe at fine leg, with Overton claiming the wicket of Joel Davies (3) soon after.

Chaudhary literally hit back for Australia, smashing a fearsome drive straight back at Overton, who was smashed on the thumb in his follow-through.

Jamie Overton delivered some blows, and took one himself. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

After a short delay for treatment, Overton had Chaudhary (19) caught after he spooned a lofted drive straight down long-on's throat.

Overton still was not done. Ben Dwarshuis was beaten for pace and edged behind for a four-ball duck, a double-wicket maiden to finish, giving Overton the second-best figures by an England player in T20 international cricket.

Adam Zampa's dismissal was the first wicket Overton did not play a part in, when he edged Dawson behind for 3.

But Australia's malaise deepened when Mitchell Owen, Australia's last real batting hope, was catastrophically run out for 16 by Phil Salt trying to take a mad second run to cover.

Curran, who went for 16 in his first disastrous over, ended Australia's innings in his second, bowling Billy Stanlake for a duck as Australia were all out for 108.

England started well but lost Phil Salt (5), caught at cover off a rising Riley Meredith delivery, and Aneurin Donald, carrying on with his big-hitting ways by belting six boundaries in a 13-ball 32.

The first brief rain delay 3.5 overs into England's reply gave Australia time to regroup, with Stanlake underlining the hosts' renewed vigour by knocking Harry Brook off his feet with a spectacular bouncer first ball back.

Billy Stanlake felled Harry Brook with a brute of a bouncer after the first rain break. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Meredith then took two wickets in the next over as England stumbled from 1-45 to 3-49 in six deliveries.

After a further delay that wiped three overs from England's chase, a revised target of 98 set by DLS method, Meredith should have had another, Chaudhary dropping Jordan Cox when the wicketkeeper was on 1.

Dwarshuis then shelled a tough caught-and-bowled chance on Banton with the Englishman on 9.

Another rain delay, with England just seven runs short at that point, further reduced the target to 93 in 16 overs, with the tourists comfortably making it with 43 balls to spare as Jordan Cox (33) and Tom Banton (10) steered them home.

England is now two wins from two in T20 cricket at the Gabba, having beaten New Zealand by 20 runs en route to the 2022 T20 World Cup title.

Australia was beaten for just the second time in nine completed matches, its first T20I defeat since losing to the West Indies in 2013.

England can seal the five-match series on Sunday at the SCG, with the final game in Canberra on Wednesday.

World.title: Roos create AFLW history with three-peat after downing Dees in epic
World.content:
North Melbourne has become the first club to claim three straight AFLW premierships after downing Melbourne in a thrilling grand final.

The Kangaroos were pushed to the limit in wet conditions at Princes Park, but kicked the last three goals of the match inside the final five minutes to run out 6.8 (44) to 2.6 (18) winners.

Kangaroos skipper Jasmine Garner was named Best on Ground after finishing with 26 disposals and five clearances to go along with a goal.

North came out of the gates kicking the first three goals of the game, but were pegged back when the Dees kicked the next two to cut the margin to six points at half-time.

Tayla Harris was inspirational for Melbourne in the second quarter, kicking her team's first goal of the match after taking a towering contested mark inside 50.

With rain increasing after the main break, the second half turned into a dour slugfest as both teams held each other goalless in the third quarter.

The Kangaroos were forced to defend grimly for much of the final quarter as the Demons drew to within one goal with five minutes remaining, but proved to be too strong in the end, with Bella Eddey's final quarter goal proving to be the eventual backbreaker.

North forward Blaithin Bogue was the only multiple goalscorer of the match, kicking both of her goals in the final few minutes to seal the premiership win.

Follow the live blog below for a blow-by-blow recap of the AFLW grand final.

World.title: Matildas legend enters arena of greatness in milestone match
World.content:
It was almost imperceptible.

The slightest shake of her head as Steph Catley listened to Matildas coach Joe Montemurro describe her as one of the world's best footballers.

It was as if she disagreed with the label. But there is no disputing the veteran defender's standing in the game.

She is among the world's elite and one of Australia's greatest ever, as a player, leader, and humble champion.

Against Colombia in Canberra tomorrow night, she will become just the seventh Matilda to reach 150 caps; three other members of that club are in this squad.

"This team feels like my family. We've grown up together, and I'm honoured every single time I touch the pitch with these girls, and I wear that jersey," Catley said.

"So 150 times is massive, and I'm very, very proud of that."

Steph Catley says it's special to reach the milestone at home. (ABC News)

Catley has been at the heart of this generation that has driven women's football in Australia at full throttle, from the shadows into the spotlight.

"I think the work that the previous Matildas have put into this team and women's football has been incredible," she said.

"But this group has done so much for the game, for this team, for women's sport in general.

"There's still a long way to go, but what we've achieved so far has been incredible."

Catley is a fierce presence on the pitch, whether playing for the Matildas or Arsenal, and, at 32, is still very much in her prime.

Steph Catley has been a mainstay of the Matildas' defence for over a decade. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

But when she took the time to reflect on her career, the tears welled up in her eyes.

She said the emotion made it hard to talk about, but she regained her composure and did it anyway.

"I'll never take it for granted that I'm able to represent this team and play for my country," she said.

"And even representing Arsenal, it's everything that I dreamed of as a kid. It's everything I've worked my entire life for, and 150 caps is massive.

"And you do get to a point where every day gets a little bit harder on your body and mentally. But I think being around the girls and the fact that we are like a family … I want to be the best version of myself for them.

"That's what drives me, I think, and my family as well. They're all the way over here in Australia, and I've played overseas pretty much my entire adult life.

"So those sacrifices are big, and I think you want to make it worth it in the long run."

Steph Catley says her teammates and family drive her to keep going. (ABC News)

Montemurro has been a constant in the Catley journey, from coaching her in the A-League Women, to Arsenal, to the national side.

His affection for her as a player and person is clear.

"I've had the honour and the pleasure of working with what I think is one of the world's best footballers, but more importantly, as a person," he said.

"We should be proud as a country to have someone of the calibre of Steph Catley in our midst and growing up and hopefully still with us for a while.

"But what she's given on the field and off the field, I think, has been absolutely special and very unique in the world of football."

Steph Catley has captained the side for extended periods during Sam Kerr's various absences. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Catley, like so many members of this Matildas' golden generation, has achieved so much but is still missing a major international trophy.

Her tearful interview after losing the Women's Asian Cup final in March was filled with the feeling of a missed opportunity.

Time has helped reignite the fire to try again.

"We really could have won that tournament, so I think that was tough for us to take," she said.

"It just builds that hunger for the next chance that we get, another step to build towards what we want to achieve."

Tech.title: The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price
Tech.content:
If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June, you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199.

The M5-equipped MacBook Air is a good middle ground if you need more power than the MacBook Neo — which, thanks to a $100 discount, is $599 — but don’t want to splurge on a MacBook Pro. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls.

Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model, the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display, or one of the M6-powered machines. A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable.

Electric minivans could be the ultimate in utility, with room for passengers, gear, and huge batteries. While VW’s ID Buzz only gave us 200 miles of real-world driving on a charge in 2023, China’s BYD has just announced a flagship purple peoplemover that can go an estimated 559 miles (900 km) on electricity.

It’s called the BYD Whale, and some back-of-the-napkin math suggests it lives up to the name. The van would be bigger than a Honda Odyssey, bigger than a Chrysler Pacifica, and bigger than a Toyota Sienna, at 17.3 feet (5,270mm) long, 6.5 feet (1,996mm) wide, 6 feet (1,815mm) tall, and with a 123-inch (3,130mm) wheelbase.

Image: BYD via Autohome Image: BYD via Autohome

According to an auto-translated press release, the vehicle should have room for seven passengers and seven suitcases at a time, not that the company has shown off its interior yet. You can see a prominent sensor cluster on its forehead, though, and it’ll come equipped with LiDAR for advanced hands-free driving.

Photo: 车若初见 (Weibo) Photo: 车若初见 (Weibo)

CarNewsChina points out it’s actually not the first with 900 km of CLTC battery range on board — Geely’s all electric Zeekr 009 minivan also claims to offer up to 900 km of range in one configuration. But BYD’s also claiming the can charge its battery from 10 percent to 97 percent in just nine minutes, and it get you from 10 percent to 70 percent in five minutes, according to Electrek.

The Whale will also come in a 248-mile (400 km) plug-in hybrid version as well, and the company’s planning to ship it in China in Q1 of 2027 for around 300,000 yuan. That’s roughly $45,000. As we’ve reported, Chinese cars are becoming quite competitive. Will they make it to the US?

In Brief

The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

Tech.title: Is Alice Huang a spy or not?
Tech.content:
The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week.

What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S. intelligence has reportedly tracked Alice Huang’s contact with an officer of China’s spy agency, but officials haven’t offered public evidence that she was commissioned to target Nvidia’s chief. In the past week, after President Trump successfully pushed to bring Jensen Huang back, the administration has played down the allegations it once circulated internally. Whether that reflects new intelligence or political pressure is the big question.

Undisputed reporting shows the claim emerged from the White House itself. It first appeared in a highly classified memo written in March under the oversight of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated to White House officials ahead of Trump’s trip to China in May. The memo formed the partial basis for the New York Times’ initial reporting on the scandal, published Oct. 29 and its existence was first reported on Nov. 8.

The memo did not definitively say, according to the Wall Street Journal, that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. CNN, by contrast, has reported that the memo concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

What’s better established is that Alice Huang was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) is Beijing’s civilian spy agency, responsible for both foreign intelligence and domestic counterintelligence. Last weekend, the Times, citing people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports, reported that Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from the spring of 2025 until this fall, a period that overlaps her relationship with Jensen Huang. (The Chinese government has called the spy claims a “smear,” and Megaspeed says Huang left the company in August 2025 and that its business is legitimate.)

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was Trump’s personal defense lawyer before taking over the Justice Department, told journalists on Tuesday: “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.” On the same day, Trump said a pardon was an option for Jensen Huang but that he did not think one would be needed. Senior intelligence officials reportedly told Congress that the government apparently has no actual evidence that the MSS directed Alice Huang to pursue an affair with Jensen Huang.

None of those statements necessarily exonerates Alice Huang as an intelligence agent. Instead, they support the alternate theory that the Chinese government didn’t tell her to begin the affair and that Jensen Huang broke no law by having it.

From a certain angle, the circumstantial evidence surrounding Alice Huang looks quite suspicious. She was a top executive at a company investigated for illicitly channeling Nvidia chips to China, and her husband, Kang Wei, is said to have even closer ties to the MSS, with some sources saying he worked for the agency.

The timing of the government’s reversal is at the heart of the matter. Trump has said he lobbied the board “directly and indirectly” to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, so it wouldn’t be surprising if officials who serve at his pleasure were recasting the case in terms that satisfy his agenda. That wouldn’t necessarily make their assessments wrong. But unless new intelligence has actually resolved the question, and none has been publicly identified as yet, that backdrop is critical to keep in mind. CBS has also reported that Rubio has privately voiced concerns about aspects of Jensen Huang’s return.

Earlier this month, CNN reported that the intelligence community was still working to understand Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang and that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove she was acting as a spy for Beijing. After a briefing by top intelligence officials earlier this month, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said he was unsure whether she was a spy or a “useful idiot.” And this week, the Wall Street Journal pointed out that under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, top corporate executives routinely maintain ties to the country’s intelligence service without being formally deputized as assets.

The crush of conflicting claims, most from anonymous government sources, obviously leaves large questions unanswered as to what actually transpired. Some of those questions that naturally spring to mind:

Alice Huang is said to have been under U.S. surveillance for over a year. If the government suspected her of espionage, why wasn’t Jensen Huang warned earlier (and privately, so as not to cause the stock-market-destabilizing maelstrom that followed the more recent disclosure)? One explanation that has been given is that alerting the Nvidia chief might have tipped off Huang that her cover had been blown.

If Alice Huang was a spy, what information did she pass to the Chinese government, and what influence did she actually have?

Most critically, how did the allegation reach the public at all? The likeliest answer is a leak. A source told CNN that Rubio briefed Trump on the intelligence in May, yet Trump has since said he only recently learned of the concerns, and in October he presented Jensen Huang with the National Medal of Science. Officials who felt they could not get through to the president may have turned to reporters instead, which would explain how the contents of a memo whose existence has never been disputed found their way into print. What remains unclear is who leaked it, and whether they anticipated the fallout.

There are answers to all of these questions, of course, but when the public will get them is anybody’s guess. Jensen Huang is due to appear before the Senate Banking Committee next week, and by the look from the statements of some of its members, he’s likely in for a rough ride. Unfortunately, congressional hearings, particularly public ones, rarely unearth secrets that haven’t already been disclosed.

Tech.title: X finally gets parental controls after 20 years
Tech.content:
After 20 years of existence, X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see and interact with on the platform. But unlike most platforms’ implementation of such controls, X is putting its own spin on the system by giving teens a say in the matter.

The company said accounts belonging to 13-to-17-year-olds will be set to “protected mode” by default, meaning they won’t be able to see sensitive content, and won’t be served targeted ads. However, X is allowing teenagers to retain a measure of control over their accounts, letting them see what restrictions were made to their accounts. Parents and guardians will also not be able to read their teens’ private messages, see search or viewing history, or post as their teen.

The controls let parents see how much time their teen spends on X per week, set daily limits, require their approval for new followers, limit feed recommendations and videos to already followed accounts, filter specific words, turn off sensitive media, specify who can send their teen DMs, and see who they are messaging.

The controls arrive months after X came under fire for a lack of controls preventing the platform’s AI chatbot from being used to generate sexualized images of children and women. The social network has also long been rife with child sexual abuse material, misinformation, AI bots, and openly lets users post porn.

X has generally not been a platform aimed at teenagers, but that doesn’t mean they don’t use the platform. A 2024 study found that nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids have an X account. The platform itself requires users to be at least 13 years old, though that’s not a high bar given the kind of content on the platform.

“Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, head of safety at X, wrote in a blog post.

Tech.title: A month with the iPhone Duo has changed how I use my phone
Tech.content:
For years, the definition of a premium smartphone depended on its cameras, processors, and how light it felt when you stowed it in your pocket. The iPhone Duo challenges that concept by asking consumers to pay more for a fundamentally different smartphone experience, even if it means sacrificing what they’ve long thought of as high-end features.

In a little under a month of using the Duo, I’ve found that the trade-offs I was initially concerned about matter far less to me than I had expected. What’s been more interesting is how the Duo’s foldable form factor has changed my everyday habits, including how I interact with apps, which apps I use, and how I organize and personalize the phone itself.

I also easily forgot a number of my initial concerns about switching to the Duo. The apps, for the most part, are now optimized for the Duo; I’ve reacquainted myself with Touch ID; and I don’t miss the Pro Max camera on most days.

That’s not to say the Duo doesn’t have its shortcomings. I still miss that telephoto lens sometimes, and I’m still longing for Face ID — though not as much since Apple shipped a face unlock feature in the latest update. But after a month of using the Duo, I’ve found these compromises have had less of an impact on my day-to-day experience compared with the benefits that the new form factor brings.

Multitasking feels more natural

I was surprised by how much I’ve grown to appreciate the Duo’s multitasking capabilities. Initially, I didn’t think I’d regularly use it to view two apps side by side, given the still fairly limited screen space even while the phone is unfolded, especially compared with an iPad. But I’ve found myself snapping apps to both halves of the screen more often than I had imagined.

For starters, Apple has made this side-by-side mode incredibly intuitive and easy to use — you simply drag the app over to the left or right side of the screen and drop it into the target box that appears.

I have regularly taken advantage of this feature to do all sorts of things.

Image Credits:Apple

I really enjoy keeping X open as I read through the news, which allows me to switch back and forth between the article I’m reading and real-time reactions to it. Sometimes I’ll keep email or Slack open on the side while I’m working on something else so I don’t miss an important message or notification.

And much like the overstimulated members of Gen Z (which I am not), I sometimes like scrolling social media while engaging with some other media off to the side.

Case in point: I passively watched Netflix’s “Love is Blind” reunion while reading the gossipy tweets and Reddit posts about the main characters on the other side of the screen. This sort of TV watching behavior used to be called second-screen viewing, but now it’s morphing into something new. Everything is happening on one screen, so should we call it “Duo screen viewing,” perhaps? It makes me long for even more interactive TV experiences where commentary and content are combined.

It really is like having two phones

I’ve noticed another shift in my behavior since adopting the Duo as my main device. When I’m out and about, the Duo feels more like an (arguably heavier) iPhone mini. For those who still miss smaller iPhones, the Duo is the next best thing. Despite its weight, the phone feels small. You can cover it with one hand; you can type with a thumb; you can reach the top and bottom easily; and you can even fit it into your front and back pockets. The Pro Max now feels unbelievably strange in my hand — how was I ever comfortable wrangling this giant rectangle?

The Duo’s small screen works well when you’re on the go, especially for short interactions like responding to a quick text or pulling up directions to a destination. It’s not as great for mindless scrolling, which I appreciate, as it forces me to engage with the real world instead of killing every moment of boredom or unease by opening up apps.

An illustration of the Apple iPhone Duo is displayed at a store in Krakow, Poland, on October 27, 2026. (Photo by Karolina Janik/JPix/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Image Credits: / Getty Images NurPhoto / Contributor (opens in a new window) / Getty Images

But when you’re home or somewhere with time to kill, you can unfold the screen and enjoy your apps super-sized. It’s the best of both worlds.

I find that I instinctively unfold the phone when I’m preparing to watch videos, because the larger screen is best for that. It’s also unfolded if I’m shopping, as it’s more convenient for looking at products, zooming in to examine the details, or complete checkout forms.

Generally, I also unfold the Duo when I’m actively using apps. This setup has also allowed me to rethink my Home Screen layout: With the Duo closed, I prefer to see just widgets on the small screen with key information like weather, time, battery life, and so on. Meanwhile, the only app icons on the Home Screen are those in the dock.

The Duo apps are ready now

In the weeks since its launch, most of the apps that weren’t yet optimized for the Duo have been upgraded to support its foldable form factor. In mid-November, Apple said there were over 200,000 Duo-ready apps, and in my experience, that certainly feels true. A majority of my so-called “daily drivers” — with the glaring exception of key Google apps like Gmail and Drive — have dropped the black band on the side of the screen that was frustrating early testers of the phone.

Most apps now take advantage of the available space, whether that’s on the Duo’s small front screen or the wider, unfolded one.

I’ve also found it interesting to see the different interpretations developers have had for how to best optimize their app for Duo.

Some have used the form factor as a way to bring in some sort of novelty: there’s a note-taking app that opens and closes like a notebook, with pages you can write on with the Apple Pencil; a retro Walkman-like music player; a tiny typewriter; a gaming handheld; a game where you close the phone to make grilled cheese.

Image Credits:Tiny Computers

As much as I love the whimsy of this group of apps, I appreciate how my everyday apps feel better to use on the unfolded screen. Spotify, at last, feels less cluttered when it has more screen real estate. A number of note-taking, list-making, and calendar apps also feel somehow more usable when spread out.

The Netflix app is actually fantastic with its support for multiple viewing modes, which include playing video on the closed outer display, the “laptop” orientation with its big player controls, and the “tent” mode.

Image Credits:Apple

Other developers have similarly reimagined how their app would work if it had originally been designed for the Duo’s small and larger screens.

One good example of this is Sofa, a handy utility for organizing the books, movies, TV shows, podcasts, albums, and games you want to check out. When the Duo is closed, its navigation is tucked off to the right side in a vertical bar, while the main screen focuses on the items you’ve saved. But when the Duo is unfolded, the number of items displayed on the screen also expands into a two-column layout, with more of your items featured on the screen and your lists on the left side. It doesn’t feel like two different apps, but like you’ve opened up the app itself and given it more space to spread out.

In terms of your daily social media scroll, apps like TikTok and Instagram have been updated to be perfectly usable on the Duo, whether the phone is open or closed. When closed, TikTok now stretches the video to cover the screen, instead of showing the ugly black bar. Scrolling short-form videos on the Duo, while unfolded like a slightly smaller iPad mini, has become my preferred way to watch.

Image Credits:TikTok screenshot from folded Duo

I’m reading more books

Here’s another surprise: I’ve spent less time with my Kindle, and am instead reading books on my Duo. Unfolded, the Duo is a decent enough replacement for an e-book reader, albeit it can be a bit more stimulating as it’s not an e-ink device. However, the matte inner screen isn’t quite as bright and distracting as your typical glossy OLED display. There’s less glare and softer reflections, but there’s also something about the display that just feels calmer than a smartphone, allowing you to more fully engage with a book’s text.

Unfolded and held vertically, reading on the Duo feels a lot like reading on the standard Kindle, at least in terms of hand-feel. And putting your phone into the “Do Not Disturb” focus mode can help you not be distracted by incoming notifications and messages while you read.

You can also unfold the device while keeping it in landscape orientation, with the screens bent slightly inward like a real book. For even more fun, you can turn on Kindle’s page-turn animation, which makes it seem as if you’re turning the page in a physical book. And I love how you can “performatively read” using an app like Book2Life or Actually Read — they display the book’s cover on the Duo’s outer screen as you read the text on the inner screen.

E-book readers will likely find they can carry one less device when they’re out and about, because the Duo can stand in for whatever Kindle or other reader you typically keep in your purse or bag. You can save the Kindle for other times, whether that’s at home, on long travel days, or when you don’t want to worry about sand getting into your $2,000 phone.

I don’t need a PopSocket

On the big-screened iPhone 17 Pro Max I used to carry, I tended to keep a PopSocket of some sort on the back because the phone was both heavy and large, which made it hard to hold for longer periods of time. The Duo is similarly heavy, but its shape makes it far easier to hold in one hand without the extra help.

Folded, you can do the usual one-handed hold where the bottom edge of the phone rests on your pinky, your other three fingers cradle the back, and your thumb is free to navigate the screen.

Unfolded, the Duo’s like using a small Kindle or iPad mini, where two hands are required. You also don’t need a PopSocket for balancing the phone on the side, because it can be propped up like a tent or opened like a tiny laptop. Or, if you prefer, Apple and others offer Duo cases with a built-in stand. (Apple’s case comes in navy and taupe, though, so if you’re not boring, you’ll probably want to shop from third-party vendors).

If you think you still might need a PopSocket at times, or you just aren’t ready to give it up, the brand now makes a slimmer version: its Low-Pro Grip. There are other competitors, like the OhSnap grips, which aren’t a bad alternative either.

It’s inspiring personalization

There’s something about the Duo that seems to have kicked off a new iPhone personalization trend, at least judging by what I’ve been seeing on social media.

Unlike a regular iPhone, where every phone case is simply a shell that offers a degree of protection based on the materials used, the Duo case lineup provides far more variety.

You can buy cases with and without built-in screen protectors, and some use adhesive to better stick to the outer screen, while others don’t. Some cases let you customize the band around the outer screen with a different color than the case that protects the rest of the phone.

Then you have cases that cover the hinge, while others leave it exposed. There are cases that offer holes where you can attach straps, wristlets, and charms. Some of those have attachment points at the bottom and others on the side.

Essentially, there are a lot of options for customizing how you want to carry the Duo and how you want to express your own style.

I’m also now starting to see whimsical cases that come with attached pens. (Thank goodness — most of the pen cases so far have been kind of plain!)

I also believe there’s something about the Duo that particularly appeals to women. Maybe because it’s small, or maybe it’s because you can attach a strap to its side and carry it like a little purse. Or maybe because, like a purse, you can deck it out with chains and charms — a choice that’s grown increasingly popular as young people have embraced whimsical, retro tech as a way to express their individuality and sense of fashion.

The Duo easily lends itself to this trend, perhaps even more than a regular iPhone. It becomes an accessory you want on display, not one buried in a bag.

Before switching to the Duo, I spent a lot of time thinking about what I’d be giving up by moving away from the Pro Max.

I’m surprised to find that, a month later, I only think about what I’d have to give up if I switched back to a traditional iPhone. It’s not just the extra space of the unfolded screen I’d miss — it’s all the little habits I’ve developed around having different screen sizes for different purposes.

The Duo makes me pause and think about how I want to use an app. That small moment of deliberation, before I even open the phone, has helped me break some of my more mindless smartphone habits, particularly around social media.

That’s not a benefit I could have anticipated if I’d judged the device by its specifications alone.

Tech.title: Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
Tech.content:
It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.

GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).

The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.

Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda, who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.”

Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids.

“We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder, managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.

That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI.

“We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.”

As millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public. At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s $81.3 billion IPO. At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time.

But when the Anthropic team rang the bell on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large.

The AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star. The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas. Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out.

This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with mind-numbing slop on YouTube, lawyers cite nonexistent cases in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “Year of Efficiency.” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade.

The final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be hard to distinguish gameplay footage from real life. These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating new landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities.

The video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI. Google’s Project Genie, which launched earlier this year, allows users to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM. The stock prices of several video game companies faltered around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers.

“The notion that somehow new tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.”

Zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though. On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.”

Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI.

“You won’t even have to ask,” Musk wrote on X. “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.”

This is the paradox of “Grandthropic” week. GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice). GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate.

“Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder said. “Creative output requires deletion, right? Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion. And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.”

GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms.

The game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor. People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest missions involve driving around doing errands and putting up drywall to make your girlfriend happy. Don’t worry — there are still car chases and shootouts — but in a moment when AI feels suffocating, GTA VI is such an artistic achievement that it is reaching audiences that don’t even like violent video games.

The ultimate fantasy of GTA VI is no longer to role-play as a criminal — the fantasy is just taking your time to relish the mundane and explore an expansive world that developers were given the time and space to perfect.

Tech.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
Tech.content:
In Brief

S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.

Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.

The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.

A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

Tech.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
Tech.content:
SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.”

The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

Musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”

This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

Tech.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
Tech.content:
OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.

The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.

That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.

Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.

While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.

Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.

The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

Tech.title: Apple Stays Winning as Smartphone Sales Continue to Slump
Tech.content:
RAM prices are continuing to put the squeeze on smartphone sales, and even people who typically buy less expensive phones appear to be holding off on upgrading.

According to a new report from Counterpoint Research, smartphone sales in the third quarter of 2026 fell by 9% compared to the same period in 2025. The report attributed the drop to rising memory costs, which are hurting sales at the low end of the Android phone market.

In terms of market share, Samsung held steady at around 25%, while Motorola, Google and other companies saw their slice of the pie decline. Where did those sales go, you might be wondering? Unsurprisingly, Apple’s broad range of iPhone models — from the 17E to its newest foldable flagship, the $1,999 iPhone Duo — bumped the company’s share of the smartphone market from 50% to 57% since last year.

More from CNET

Smartphone-makers with cheaper phone lineups suffered due to component costs, particularly memory, eating into their margins. “There, OEMs have little room to absorb a higher bill of materials without raising prices or cutting volume,” said Counterpoint Senior Analyst Emily Herbert.

The slowdown in phone sales has been happening all year. In the last quarter, the market slumped by 20%, more than was expected at the time. The build-out of data centers to support the ever-expanding AI industry has led to shortages of memory components. In turn, the prices of those components have spiked, raising prices of not just smartphones, but game consoles, PCs and other electronics.



Will the holidays save smartphone-makers?

Black Friday, Cyber Monday and the Christmas gift-giving season typically mean strong phone sales for companies like Apple and Samsung. But the memory component crisis isn’t going to go away that quickly, and prices of phones are still higher overall.

Counterpoint predicts that smartphone sales will remain weak in the next quarter and that US carriers may be more selective about the promotions they offer this year. AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon are also seeing declining sales and customers are getting choosier about committing to phones that often cost more than $1,000. People are also looking to second-hand and refurbished phones instead of buying new.

“Consumers are timing their purchases around the best deals more than ever, if they buy at all,” said Counterpoint Senior Analyst Maurice Klaehne. “This year’s holiday sales cycle will look quite different from usual.”

Setup is definitely a little more involved, with a clean water tank that you need to mix cleaning solution into and the need to have an AC outlet somewhere in the area. The trade-off is a significantly deeper, more powerful cleaning than what you get with a handheld battery-powered spot cleaner like the Shark StainForce.



Using the Little Green on the toughest and oldest dried stains left by my pukey old man cat left me impressed with just how deeply it cleaned my carpets. The pristine result makes this corded cleaner well worth the extra setup, and even at full price ($130), you won’t find fault with its power or portability. Bottom Line At $85, its lowest price in a year on Amazon, the Bissell Little Green Mini is an easy buy if you have pets and carpet.
